_childDocuments_.review: Outlast Trials had a solid structure during EA. You had base programs that prepare you for the endgame content: Program X and Rebirth. The whole point of this was to make it difficult and give players an incentive to play the hardest mode. Now with 1.0, not only did they make Program X infinitely easier, but the whole reborn system is just horrible. Genesis is pretty much the base programs and you can get the same amount of tokens there as you would with the harder difficulties. I'm not against the idea of giving everyone a chance to rebirth freely, but it should be earned like it was before. Genesis tokens should be a one time thing and you should have to play Program X or Ultra to get the tokens. Like I said earlier you can play the easiest trials with 0 enemies and get the same rewards as you would on the higher difficulties. If they don't plan to revert this change they can make it better by doubling or tripling the amount of tokens you get from X/Ultra. The fact that you can complete all of Program X and still not have enough tokens to rebirth is insane. There's no reason for most people to play X/Ultra if the rewards are the same anyways, and this will actually kill the player count too. I've already seen people spamming sabotage the lockdown 20 times to rebirth and complain the game is boring and repetitive. If more people hop on this train, give it a month or two and the player count will be lower than it was in EA except for the new content releases.At this time I've been reborn 361 times and I don't plan on continuing the grind towards 1000. Don't get me wrong, the game is still great but it feels miserable for people grinding reborns.

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like every couple of years, Red Barrels breaks down my door in their best Santa costume, steals roughly 30 or so dollars from my wallet, tells me I've been a good girl, and leaves a new Outlast game on my nightstand when they leave in the morning.No, but seriously, as a long-term fan, I knew I was gonna enjoy myself from the very beginning. And yeah, I did. And while it may not be the best Outlast game, it has the potential to be.My biggest beef with this game is the overall lack of content, which I'm hopeful will be solved with future updates. As it stands right now though, there's 3 main areas, with 9 overall missions, and 2 main enemies. The rest of your time spent in this game will be you repeating these same missions on higher difficulties. The only reason it remains entertaining is due to the interactions you'll have with your friends or random people.The second thing I hate is how lobbies work. You can't control if you're joining someone else's lobby or if they're joining your's, you can't see their level before you're in the same lobby, can't see what mission they're doing, etc. It makes it extremely difficult to get a lobby sometimes, and you'll often have people randomly leave as soon as you start a match, which f's you over.Finally, I won't spoil it, but I hope they expand on the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outlast Trials is a case study in how cooperative horror games should be designed. The synergy of every structure in place from a gameplay standpoint is phenomenally fun and terrifying. It continues to give players reasons to play via an incredible progression system that ensures players will always have something to work towards as they continually torture themselves in the name of psychoscience. On top of this, trials feel distinct and personalized to each "prime asset"--charismatic serial killers that stalk the players alongside normal enemies in every trial environment, offering a certain level of charm and distinctness I haven't felt in a co-op horror game in some time. The game also offers incredible acting performances, coupled with some fascinatingly well-written and disturbing dialogue and narrative. You very well may find yourself getting lost in this game's lore, just as equally as you will find yourself disturbed at the well-represented forms of psychological abuse and manipulation your character will undergo in-game. This however won't ever be on your mind for long, as you'll be having too much fun with friends to be focusing on the atrocities committed before your eyes. On harder difficulties, you and your teammates will likely be too focused on completing your tasks safely to even realize how evil what you're doing is--creating a synergistic relationship between player and protagonist in a way that only a game can. Both you and your reagent will be completely desensitized to violence in the name of completing trials efficiently and safely, which intentional or not, is brilliant.This title is not without its flaws however. Some trials and MK-Challenges find themselves being considerably more tedious and poorly designed than others. One has you attempting to slowly carry dangerous buckets of acid through maze-like level design with constantly changing paths that shift on a timer, and another has players attempting to power generators in a dark building filled with awkward paths, unconventional routes, and confusing objective placements. These undoubtedly will be grating to many players, coupled with a bizarre usage of incredibly obvious AI artwork that only serves to make the games presentation come off as trashy and childish at times compared to its usually incredible appreciation for creativity and originality.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite featuring similar gameplay to its forebears, The Outlast Trials is a tedious and repetitive run-away simulator. The raw fundamentals of the series have been tortured until it is no longer about surviving under trauma and instead about exploiting AI and enduring overused mechanics. Deranged foes camp objectives and players must run circles through maze-like levels in search of randomly placed items. Solo players might find a few spooks early, but horror is quickly replaced by boredom. For those that like doing the same mundane tasks with others: the floor is yours, to cover with enough viscera to drive anybody loopy.

Rinse your hand in cold water to prevent rice from sticking to your hand2) add oil (about 3-5 tbsp) to a large pan or wok and wait till it's hot (medium high heat)3) slice or chop your mushrooms into your desired sizes4) cut your chicken breast into bite sizes pieces. Add salt to taste and let it dry brine5) add your mushrooms and sauté until tender. Add a few pinches of fresh ground black pepper and garlic salt during the process.6) once your mushrooms are done, set aside and remove any excess liquid in your pan and change your oil if necessary7) add your chicken and cook until crisp or tender (up to you). Add salt and pepper to taste8) set chicken aside and sautee your onions and garlic. If you decide to add bell peppers, sauté them with the garlic and onions9) once the garlic and onions (and bell peppers) are tender, add your rice and mushrooms and mix10) mix your oyster and soy sauce. 11) add your sauce into rice and mix12) add your msg and mix. Add garlic salt and fresh ground pepper to taste.13) add your frozen veggies, mix then cover your rice with a lid and let steam (5-8 minutes)14) serve with scallions (optional) and enjoy(Adding freshly scrambled eggs is also a good idea but is optional)

_childDocuments_.review: Red Barrels invites you to experience mind-numbing terror, this time with friends. Whether you go through the trials alone or in teams, if you survive long enough and complete the therapy, Murkoff will happily let you leave… but will you be the same?SYNOPSISSet in the era of the Cold War, human guinea pigs are involuntarily recruited by the good folks at the Murkoff Corporation to test advanced methods of brainwashing and mind control. In a world of distrust, fear, and violence, your morals will be challenged, your endurance tested, and your sanity crushed. All in the name of progress, science, and profit.SURVIVE: SOLO OR COOPYou’re all prisoners of Murkoff trapped inside their facility. You can choose to complete the trials by yourself or you can tackle them in a team of 2, 3, or 4 players.Coop is never forced when it comes to mandatory objectives but working together can be highly beneficial.Whatever the number of players in your party, it’s about surviving and getting out.Ultimately, your goal is to complete Murkoff's therapy and earn the right to be released back into society. In order to do so, you must complete the Trials and the MK-Challenges.Trials are immersive story driven therapies that take a certain time to complete. Mk-Challenges are shorter therapies occurring in modified or redesigned section of an existing map.HIDE OR FLIGHTIn pure Outlast fashion, the core gameplay involves avoiding enemies, hiding from them, and trying to run away. Murkoff will provide tools you can use to increase your stealth capabilities, create opportunities to flee, slow down enemies, and more. However, you will have to earn those tools and work hard to improve them.The tools will allow you toStun enemiesBlind themSee through wallsHeal yourself and people around you.Murkoff will ask you to perform disturbing tasks in each trials or mk-challenges. Only after completing those, will you be allowed to exit the Trials or the MK-Challenges.CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATIONCustomize and create your own trial patient.Your cell is your home while you complete the therapy, you can decorate it however you wish.Choose your tools, upgrades, and perks to fit your playstyle.Meet the Denizens of Murkoff’s Sinyala Facility in The Outlast Trials. Each one of them will try and help you get through the Trials in one piece! Think you’ll make it?INVESTIGATEYou’ve been abducted by the Murkoff Corporation to undergo unethical experiments that will modify your psyche and behavior throughout the Trials.Collect documents and items that will help prove Murkoff’s malpractice against its patients.The Process:Break the Self: Murkoff aims to break down the test subject’s fundamental beliefs. Aspects of self-identity are systematically attacked. Like boot camp or indoctrination, the goal is to force a person to purge themselves of anything held sacred or taboo, the things that limit their behavior. The constant assault on identity, guilt and self-betrayal eventually leads to them breaking down.Build the Self: It’s a bad cop, good cop principle. The rejection of the old ideology leaves a vacuum into which the new ideology can be introduced. As the antithesis of the old ideology, it forms a perfect attraction point as the person flees the old in search of a contrasting replacement. This progress is accelerated as the new ideology is portrayed as harmonious and ideally suited to the person's needs. Collegiality and calm replaces pain and punishment. Just at the point when the person is fearing annihilation of the self, they are offered a small kindness, a brief respite from the assault on their identity.Salvation: Faced with the stark contrast of the pain of the past with the rosy glow of the future that the new ideology presents, the person sheds any the final allegiance to the old ideology, confessing any remaining deep secrets, and takes on the full mantle of the new ideology. This often feels, and has been described by many, as a form of rebirth. It may be accompanied by rites of passage as the person is accepted and cemented into the new order. The rituals will typically include strong statements made by the person about accepting the new ideology fully and completely, swearing allegiance to its leaders. Saluting flags, kissing other artefacts and other symbolic acts, all solemnly performed, all anchor them firmly in the new ground.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great, at least the first 20 hours in (or so).After the first "rehabilitation program" completion, you pretty much have all the necessary upgrades and stuff to steamroll through most of the advanced-difficulty missions (which is actually still pretty fun), since by then, you have figured out how the AI works, and if you do f*ck up, you usually know what you have done wrong, or at least what you could've done differently.While there is a lot done right about the higher difficulty, the later missions' difficulty (around 20+ hours) is just pure idiocy. Because you get pretty OP, the devs probably thought that the usual difficulty amplification (you know, the usual "more enemies, more traps, more dmg recieved, more alerted enemies etc) isn't enough, and decided to artificially increase the difficulty, simply by enabling the enemies to cheat.No, I'm not talking about the elevators, I'm talking about the enemies not behaving according to the established mechanics.It doesn't care it doesn't have you in it's FOV, it still sees you. It doesn't care you just sneaked completely through dark without ever making a sound, it's still gonna appear right in front of you as you open the only door leading to your objective, even though you've just juked and stunned them on the other side of the map. It doesn't care it's not in attack range, it's still gonna levitate towards you in the middle of a "reaching" attack and hit you for most your HP, because f*ck you, thats why.Don't get me wrong, there is a lot done right about the game overall, just the replayability past the Advanced Program is horrendous and you cannot get anything done unless RNGesus blesses your run.Possible fix and QoL improvement would be a high-level Amp enabling you to use a brick to escape prime-enemies grasps.That being said, it's a solid 7.2/10. Too much water.Still waiting for some real new content, those two "new" missions (Sabotage the Factory, Tilt The Scales of Justice) are a joke. It's the same missions you've been playing over and over, just wrapped in a different coat.TLDR; Good game, but later high difficulty program is really not worth it, because enemies are just plain cheating.

_childDocuments_.review: First off some postives:The graphics is great, the perfomance is okay and the tutorial at the beginning is fantastic because it felt close to the previous Outlast gamesAnd that's about it.This game is no Outlast to me. It feels way more like Dead by Daylight but with NPCs. I played solo so far and while the first trial could be won (I didnt at first because at the end the enemy just kept camping the switches) you can obviously tell they only had multiplayer for this game in mind, which I absolutely dislike. At first I loved the idea of being able to play with others, because I thought the game would be on the same story level as the previous games, but it surely isn't. It just gets so annoying so quickly when you want to play it alone but can barely get any progress because the game was mostly meant for multiple people in one trial.I also dont't understand why there is even the option to find a group when you just get thrown into an already existing group, only to then get kicked out or not even accepted because they're friends. Either I was just unlucky, or the system doesn't search for lone people to put them together into a group, I don't know, but it sure annoyed the hell out of me. Sure, it's an early access so I'll cut some slack with the AI issues and such, but I dont see the point of multiplayer, when you're mostly forced to play alone anyways when there is currently no friend available. All in all, in it's current state, I wouldn't buy it if there are no friends to play with. Unless you like getting through the first trial, only to then get messed up to the point of quitting in the continuing trials.I honestly wish I could get my money back, but the first trial alone took 2 hours to finish. Very disappointed, I had hoped for an Outlast continuation that is on the same level of horror as the first two games and DLC. But Outlast Trials is no horror, just stressing and annoying. Currently hoping future updates will make the situation better.

All players can pick from different "rigs" that facilitate different play-styles and bring out different players strengths; as well as picking from "mods" and other add-ons to "sneak in" to your trials. Honestly, if you enjoy taking your time with the survival side of the horror genre, this is an excellent game; since stamina is limited and you need to think strategically to hide from enemies and collect objectives, both in multiplayer and single-player, this isn't your game if you prefer a fast paced FPS game.

_childDocuments_.review: *The Outlast Trials* attempts to bring the intensity of survival horror into a multiplayer setting, but unfortunately, the experiment falls short of capturing what made the original *Outlast* games so terrifying. The shift from a single-player horror experience to an online co-op format weakens much of the suspense and isolation that were central to the series’ success. Instead of the tense, solitary atmosphere that *Outlast* fans expect, *The Outlast Trials* often feels more chaotic than creepy.The gameplay, while retaining some elements of classic *Outlast* mechanics, lacks the polish and depth to make it feel truly satisfying. Objectives and tasks are repetitive, and much of the tension dissipates with multiple players sharing the horror. This setup could work if balanced carefully, but here, it undermines the fear factor, making it hard to fully immerse in the horror when you’re constantly coordinating with other players. What was once a game of careful stealth and spine-chilling scares feels more like a generic team-based horror that struggles to keep its footing.Graphically, the game maintains the dark, gritty aesthetic of the series, but the visuals can’t compensate for the lack of atmosphere. Moments that would otherwise be terrifying lose impact with the multiplayer format, and the overall quality of gameplay feels underwhelming, especially for longtime fans expecting the same quality of horror.In short, *The Outlast Trials* is a disappointing attempt to bring *Outlast* into the online realm. While the concept had potential, the execution leaves much to be desired, and the game struggles to deliver the quality and intensity that made the original games stand out. As a survival horror, it simply doesn’t live up to expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the single best cooperative horror game I've ever gotten my hands on. Repeatable, atmospheric trials that with the right company can make for a genuinely fun and scary experience. My only gripe is the scares get old fairly quickly in this kind of system. I hope to see more intense scares or a more thrilling atmosphere in the future. The Root Canal is an incredibly unnerving and terrifying location regardless of the amount of players in the trial. The addition of some skills was a fun goal to work towards, and they don't feel *too* out of place for the feel of the game. Thankfully none of the skills feel like they change the game fundamentally, and regardless of if I have more stamina or not, chases feel intense. Constantly looking over my shoulder in case of an ambush, or accidentally stepping too close to a psycho in the trial, even realising I have an unexpected third player in my trial was always a thrill. Giving the player a voice that actually can talk feels really neat, and I'd like to have slightly more talking in the final product for that extra bit of flavour to the game. Nothing crazy, just little things like groaning out an "Oh god..." when searching for the keys in their...containers, or other one or two word lines for various other actions. Peeking from hiding places, getting jumped by psychos, being downed, things like that could benefit from the occasional comment from the player character.TL;DR the game's a 10 out of 10 for me as it is right now, and it remains the single most incredible early access game I've played. Aside from personal wishes for greater scares and locations, or some added atmosphere to your player, I can see nothing that could make this game better than it already is. Obviously more maps and scares are coming, so grab it now while the early access price is still cheap!!

_childDocuments_.review: **SPOILER WARNING**TO PREFACE: I did not attempt to play this game solo, as I played the entire game as a trio. This was the general consensus of the three of us after simultaneously completing.TL;DR-Game extremely well made, worth picking up, but definitely leaves some to be desired. 7/10-Very fun cooperative experiences, especially towards the beginning. It was an absolute blast to play the first trials and learn the flow of the game.-Division of labor between multiple people seems fair, never did I feel overwhelmed with tasks when playing as a group. -Environment, enemy and general art is fantastic, reminiscent of the previous Outlast (for obvious reasons), but I would even say they stepped up the grotesqueness of this game compared to the previous (somehow). -The mini-trials using the same "realm" as the main trials adds a level of connectivity, which I appreciate. We would begin trials with an epiphany of sorts, recognizing the area and how to loop enemies. -The FIRST time you view the cinematics, they were amazing. The approach of no "screen-locking" cut scenes was a great decision, as watching live cinematic while being able to walk around is a fantastic touch. The initial start of the trial was also interesting, although a vote-skip button should be added when replaying levels.-The voice acting and audio design in general was very polished and well done. I could almost always detect enemies using audio. The voice acting really helped to bring these characters to life, which is reminiscent of the original Outlast .-Great progression system, leveling up feels satisfying.-Cosmetics and room decor was fun to play with.-Arm wrestling.-The leader-board in the main area I enjoyed, nice touches like this are appreciated.-The tutorial was absolutely fantastic, as I was quite literally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants playing through it.-Spare for occasional frame drops, the game runs amazing. -Character customization could be improved, ex: rig customization feels lacking, along with not being able to switch a helmet and hair.-Game play loop CAN feel extremely mundane and repetitive, as only three trials are the backbone of the  entire game at this moment. You find yourself doing the same trial with the same objective upwards of three times. Note: I understand that more content is likely coming, I am merely speaking on the CURRENT state of the game.-Enemies can occasionally feel unfair and too abundant, especially on the harder difficulties. It began to feel quite frustrating as we got to levels with the "high density of enemies" label. Especially when some enemies will blatantly camp the final objective, like at the end of kill the snitch for example. My group found themselves being mercilessly camped and bum rushed by enemies whose entire pattern was to circle the final objective. In my opinion that is not good game design, just frustrating and artificially boosted the "difficulty" and time of the trial.-Towards the end, the lack of tension building began to backfire on the game-play loop. As again, frustration crept up as enemies will mercilessly surround the objective or any general area the player is in.-The final trial was the real summation of almost all of the gripes listed above, as simply four objectives took upwards of an hour to complete, enemies felt unfair and simple tasks felt arduous. -In my opinion, solo play is almost an afterthought, as the solo-experience is obviously under-cooked to say the least. Relegating the objectives to solo play undermines the cooperative aspect of distributing the work.Final Consensus:The cooperative experience is this games' bread and butter, if you are looking for a game to play with your friends, this is a fantastic choice even at this current "under cooked" stage. If you are looking for a comprehensive, narrative driven game, or enjoy a solo horror experience, then this game simply isn't for you. This is a enjoyable game at its core however, and the frameworks are well-defined and simply fun. The sour aftertaste of some lackluster levels shouldn't deter you from trying this out.

_childDocuments_.review: So far, this game has exceeded my expectations. I was initially put off by this being a multiplayer game; Outlast 1 is probably one of the best horror games ever made, so I was worried this was going to be another Dead By Daylight clone. I was wrong.The game is completely PVE, there are no microtransactions, and it is extremely well made for an early access game. I played the first two levels with one friend, and I don't think we encountered any bugs.While initially the game is very scary, I can see how it could get repetitive and predictable. There are only 3 levels out right now, but they are large and very detailed. The intro and the first two levels were terrifying, but we failed the second mission the first time and had to replay it. The second time it was much less scary, and we kinda figured out how the game works, so we were able to speedrun it pretty easily.My only worry is that since you will be playing on the same maps, but different objectives depending on your mission, it will start to feel repetitive and not scary at all. The previous Outlast games were less scary with each playthrough, but that's the case for all horror games. Being in an unfamiliar place with monsters hunting you is the scariest thing, but that goes away once you learn the maps. My only concern with this not being another single player entry is that instead of being a long journey where I am constantly in new territory, I am just going to learn the maps and figure out the quickest ways to traverse the area and run/hide from enemies.Despite that, the game is extremely well made, feels good to play, and the graphics are amazing. I can run the game on the highest settings without any issue, and I haven't even upgraded my PC in a few years. I'm excited to see what's in the full release. Even with my concerns about the game, I have no regrets spending $30 on this.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outlast Trials is a horror movie in reverse, in ways both good and bad. Instead of screaming in terror when something jumps out at you or stabs your character in the face, you usually just laugh as your friends make fun of you from their hiding spots. Instead of a clueless group of protagonists who get picked off one by one, the enemies hunting you and your teammates are the ones with the hilariously poor decision-making skills. While the early access version of this cooperative horror game proves the concept and has a couple of very memorable maps, it’s not one of those games that’s sprung into being almost fully formed. Expected bugs and general lack of polish aside, there’s just not much content yet. Even so, I had an overall good time with this silly, gory, and uneven slaughter fest even in these early stages.The Outlast Trials throws you and up to four of your friends into insane and improbable Saw-like “death games” in which you must work together to overcome the gory terrors that await. What little story there is so far doesn’t amount to much: you’re abducted by an evil corporation and kept in a prison under the guise of rehabilitation, but instead are subjected to a seemingly random series of murder playgrounds. You can glean some mildly interesting bits of lore by collecting compromising evidence that immoral company men apparently left lying around its death courses, but it’s not exactly mesmerising stuff. And that’s okay! You’re playing The Outlast Trials because you want to see a crazy lady use a sock puppet to drill a guy’s face off, and there’s certainly an abundance of that.

_childDocuments_.review: Outlast trials is good.Well designed levels with multiple approaches to multiple situations. Everything feels dynamic because it is. There are enough trials to play for about 40 hours id say as a casual player, that + trying to get good grades for every stage which might add a couple hundred more. ( not very casual at that point ). I do hope they add more enemy types and programs ( programs are basically locations ) Currently there are a few enemy types with some differences, some they could add include a ranged enemy and a crawling enemy that grabs players from holes or something like that.On the horror side of things its Outlast, not much to it than that. If you were scared of Outlast 1 or 2 you will be scared of this one, maybe even more scared. Enemies are ruthless and will hear you from quite far away, luckily there is a sound for detection so you aren't completely clueless.The game does a lot to overwhelm the player, there are constant threats with little to no downtime. You will not get a good grade from your first few trials, but it does feel rewarding once you do.In terms of difficulty, as i just stated the game is hard. Way harder than the previous titles. You might think playing in COOP makes it easier but its actually well balanced. While you have more shortcuts and ways to approach situations in COOP, you will also have more objectives and longer animations. Solo you cant do risky plays, but you have faster animations and less objectives which lets you do things slower without sacrificing time.Customization is OK, you unlock more options the more you play which is a good thing since it rewards clean runs and more runs. Acting is some of the best, i love Leland Coyle ( dont know the actor ). All the side characters the grunts and stuff are extremely well acted aswell.The game is great, get it if you like horror games / coop games / challenging games.

Although the cooperative gameplay is thrilling, it's not particularly scary. In my opinion, the co-op aspect diminishes the scariness of the game, compared to a solo experience.I'm also happy with the customization options for your character and the little room you stay in. It's all acquired through currency you earn by playing the game and doesn't involve any microtransactions (and I hope they never add any).Right now, my only pet peeve would be the lack of replay value. _childDocuments_.review: A Terrifyingly Thrilling Cooperative ExperienceRating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)Review:"The Outlast Trials" is a spine-chilling addition to the Outlast series that brings a fresh cooperative twist to the survival-horror genre. The game plunges you into a nightmarish world where you and your friends must work together to survive the gruesome trials set by the sinister Murkoff Corporation.Gameplay: The cooperative gameplay is the standout feature of "The Outlast Trials." The thrill of navigating through horrifying environments with friends adds a new layer of tension and excitement. Each trial is meticulously designed to keep you on the edge of your seat, with unique challenges that require teamwork and strategy to overcome.Graphics and Design: The game's visuals are stunningly grotesque, perfectly capturing the eerie atmosphere of the Outlast universe. The attention to detail in the environments and character designs enhances the immersive horror experience, making every moment feel like a descent into madness.Story and Characters: While the overarching story may not be the most memorable aspect, the characters and enemies you encounter are unforgettable. The grotesque and absurd villains add a unique charm to the game, making each encounter a terrifying delight.Replayability: "The Outlast Trials" offers high replay value, thanks to its well-crafted trials and the unpredictable nature of cooperative gameplay. Each escape feels like a hard-earned victory, and the desire to improve your performance and explore different strategies keeps you coming back for more.Overall Impression: "The Outlast Trials" successfully blends cooperative gameplay with the outrageous horror elements that fans of the series love. It's a unique and memorable experience that will leave you and your friends both terrified and exhilarated. If you're a fan of survival-horror games and enjoy cooperative challenges, this game is a must-play.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Outlast Trials" was an electrifying experience from start to finish. Red Barrels has once again delivered a spine-chilling adventure that surpasses its predecessors in both terror and innovation.The standout feature of "The Outlast Trials" is its cooperative gameplay, setting it apart from earlier titles. Collaborating with friends or fellow gamers to navigate the eerie Cold War-era mental asylum adds an extra layer of tension and strategy. Coordinating movements, sharing resources, and relying on each other in terrifying moments of chaos create an immersive and nerve-wracking experience unlike any other in the survival horror genre.The game's atmospheric design is simply exceptional. From the flickering lights casting eerie shadows to the hauntingly realistic audio, every detail contributes to a sense of impending dread. The asylum's diverse environments keep you constantly on edge, never allowing a moment of complacency as you uncover the disturbing secrets lurking within its walls.The developers' attention to storytelling shines brightly in "The Outlast Trials." The narrative intricately weaves through the challenges, keeping players engaged and eager to discover the truth behind the sinister experiments taking place. The characters' depth and the unfolding plot twists add an emotional weight that drives the gameplay forward.Gameplay mechanics are polished and intuitive. The incorporation of stealth, problem-solving, and timed actions keeps the gameplay dynamic and engaging. The sense of vulnerability against the relentless adversaries and the limited resources available heighten the adrenaline rush, ensuring that every encounter is heart-pounding and memorable.Additionally, the replayability factor is commendable. Multiple paths, choices, and endings encourage revisiting the asylum, offering a fresh experience with each playthrough.In summary, "The Outlast Trials" is a masterclass in cooperative horror gaming. Red Barrels has once again proven their prowess in delivering a nerve-wracking, immersive, and deeply haunting experience. Brace yourself for a chilling adventure that will linger in your mind long after the lights are back on.

_childDocuments_.review: Upon hearing of Red Barrels and their attempts at making an online Outlast, post Outlast 2, I'd been a little timid to the idea for what Outlast 2 had laid out with the new mechanics it'd introduced in how one interacts with the environments in Outlast 2. I felt like in a way Outlast 2 had innovated enough but fell short in the narrative department due to the focus being pushed too much elsewhere. Despite this, Outlast 2 had felt familiar, over feeling like more of the same, but its story was just... trying very hard to be a bit cryptic? And all over the place.Upon actually PLAYING Trials though, I can confidently say my expectations were and even still are rather subverted, in the best way possible. They cut the fat, some unnecessary manners of traversal, and doubled down on the gameplay-focus by introducing the ability to actually 'fight back', buying yourself a window to react to approaching enemies by throwing bottles, bricks, even utilizing certain special tools in the form of 'Rigs' which you can build in a way that's to your style of gameplay. Let that be being more stealthy, more quick, more defensive. The variety of perks and what you can utilize with Rigs is rather contained yet robust.The overall level designs of the escape rooms in this game are very labyrinth-y yet pretty congested, with a wide diversity of environments to get lost in while you tediously task-work your way out of the games variety of trials, which they continue to add with each passing update. The 'named' enemies inhabiting the levels are also rather interesting characters, which the game allows you to learn more about thru its various lore documents you can find on occasion. The worldbuilding is interesting, the premise of what Murkoff is doing to those that wander into its grasp keeps you questioning ethics and what exactly Murkoff has to gain. Funny enough, this game is very anti-authority and isn't shy about showing that, despite you being a lab rat.My largest complaint with this game, which I hope Red Barrels can shed the need of, is the AI disclaimer. I abhor the usage of AI art in any content medium, and I'm doing all I can to not let that cloud my judgment of this game, but it's very hard to not be critical of it. In their disclaimer and I quote; "...Throughout the development of our game, we may leverage AI-based tools to assist our team in content creation..." which to me says either -- A) They're using datasets in order to create reference art to then create their own work off of -- B) They're gathering their own images and such to feed an AI machine to train a dataset that'll help them curate work to litter around levels -- or the unfortunate latter -- C) They're simply posting AI imagery around and simply polishing turds.It's a bit too ambiguous for me, for which I quote again in the latter of their statement; "...Please rest assured that what you see in the game reflects the creativity and hard work of our team. Examples may include pictures and/or posters used in some of our environments..."I hope it does, Red Barrels. I'm honestly being optimistic for your sake. You know if you ever want to abandon AI and find references for your work you can always look to the community that truly loves your games, being the found-footage/snuff/horror analyst community that has a TROVE of YouTube content for you to inspire yourselves with. It's hard to want to give any form of AI that isn't helping an NPC pathfind or something even an inch, knowing that much of it began off of stealing from others. Despite my rather glaring, personal gripe with a tool they may use, they are at least transparent about it and I feel could be further transparent, and it luckily doesn't bear an impact on any of the games other assets, for the game does have a visual identity luckily, and has a lot of care going into its variety of decals and signage, really selling you on the timeframe the game inhabits. Outlast Trials is great with friends, or even by yourself. It will test your patience at times, but the reward is worth the tussle, and the game is pretty generous in how it levels you up, unlocking more and more tools for you to toy with amidst its trials and tribulations. Honestly, I'm keeping my review at a solid thumbs up since Steam lacks a mixed button of sorts, but the AI disclaimer truly worries me. I will continue to timidly enjoy this game until I see something I deem too blatant and lazy on Red Barrels behalf to warrant supporting this game further. Continue to be as transparent as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outlast Trials : By Triple F"The Outlast Trials," developed by Red Barrels, is the latest entry in the Outlast series, reimagining the franchise’s core horror experience by introducing a multiplayer twist. Set in the Cold War era, "The Outlast Trials" diverges from its predecessors by placing players in a sinister government facility run by the Murkoff Corporation, where human test subjects, or "volunteers," undergo horrifying psychological and physical experiments. While the previous Outlast titles focused on single-player survival horror, "The Outlast Trials" allows up to four players to work together in escaping Murkoff’s experiments, creating a unique cooperative horror experience that expands on the franchise’s themes of helplessness and fear.The story of "The Outlast Trials" is a dark commentary on mind control, human experimentation, and manipulation, grounded in a retro, Cold War-inspired atmosphere. Players assume the role of captives who have been coerced into Murkoff’s "trials" against their will. The narrative is delivered through disturbing environmental storytelling, grim notes, and ominous broadcasts that unveil Murkoff’s twisted motives. Although light on direct storytelling, the game provides enough clues to construct a chilling narrative that questions the limits of human endurance and ethics. The episodic structure of each trial allows players to uncover new elements of the story gradually, building a coherent but unsettling image of Murkoff’s cruelty.A unique feature of "The Outlast Trials" is its cooperative multiplayer design, which stands in stark contrast to the solitary horror of the first two games. Players can team up in groups of up to four, tackling trials together. This adds a layer of social horror, where players are forced to make difficult choices: Do you save a teammate from a monstrous enemy, or use the distraction to make your own escape? This dynamic increases the tension and forces players to strategize collectively, blending teamwork with individual survival instincts. However, the game does not rely solely on cooperative play; it is also fully playable solo, though the experience becomes more challenging as players have fewer options to distract or outwit enemies.The gameplay in "The Outlast Trials" retains the franchise's familiar elements like stealth, hiding, and evasion, while introducing new mechanics that encourage teamwork. Players must complete specific tasks to progress through each trial, such as collecting items, solving simple puzzles, or activating mechanisms. These objectives, however, are laced with danger; terrifying foes roam the facility, each with distinct behaviors that require different strategies to avoid. The trial structure adds a sense of urgency, as players are frequently under threat, and teamwork often becomes essential in escaping these nightmarish scenarios. The game balances these elements effectively, making each encounter feel tense without relying too heavily on predictable jumpscares.The addition of a limited customization and progression system further differentiates "The Outlast Trials" from its predecessors. Players can earn and unlock various skills and items that improve their chances of survival, such as temporary speed boosts or healing supplies. However, these enhancements are balanced to prevent players from becoming overpowered. Instead, they serve to personalize each player’s experience, adding slight advantages without sacrificing the core elements of helplessness and vulnerability. This progression system gives a sense of reward without reducing the difficulty, a careful balance that keeps the game challenging and tense throughout.Visually and atmospherically, "The Outlast Trials" excels at creating a setting that feels oppressive and gruesome. The environment is filled with disturbing details like graffiti on walls, flickering lights, blood-stained floors that contribute to a consistently tense ambiance. The sound design plays a significant role in building this atmosphere, from distant screams to the unsettling hum of machinery. Each environment within the trials is designed to be as immersive as it is horrifying, pulling players into Murkoff’s vision of an experimental hell. The retro Cold War aesthetic, combined with elements of psychological horror, makes for a distinct and memorable backdrop that feels refreshingly different yet still true to the Outlast universe.One potential downside to "The Outlast Trials" lies in its repetitive nature. The trial-based structure, while effective for multiplayer horror, can feel predictable over time, as objectives often follow similar patterns. Additionally, for players who prefer a tightly woven single-player story, the lack of a traditional narrative arc may feel underwhelming. However, the game’s focus on multiplayer horror is executed well enough to engage players seeking a cooperative experience, and the constant fear of imminent danger keeps the game’s tension high, even as objectives repeat. Red Barrels has crafted a balance between horror and multiplayer mechanics, though its appeal may vary based on player preferences.In closing, "The Outlast Trials" successfully reinvents the Outlast formula for a multiplayer setting, merging the series’ trademark horror elements with cooperative survival in a uniquely grim setting. Its combination of teamwork, resourcefulness, and tense gameplay makes it a compelling experience for those who enjoy horror with a social twist. While the game’s repetitive objectives and minimal narrative structure may not satisfy every type of horror fan, "The Outlast Trials" offers an engaging and innovative take on survival horror. For fans of the franchise and newcomers alike, it’s a terrifyingly immersive experience that explores new depths of fear and desperation, proving once again that in the Outlast universe, no one is safe, not even with friends by your side.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not the biggest Outlast fan, mainly played the first game and the Whistleblower DLC, enjoyed it, never really cared about the second game because the setting just didn't grab me.That said, I wasn't expecting much from Outlast Trials, especially when I found out it would mainly be a multiplayer game. However before the game released to Early Access, they offered players a Beta access to try for free, so I checked it out just out of pure curiosity and... I loved it?The game is in 1.0 now and a lot has changed, mainly for the better I would say.First off - yes, it is a multiplayer game HOWEVER you can absolutely play it solo, and the game also accounts for that, scaling the difficulty appropriately. So if you're more of a single player kinda guy/girl then you've nothing to worry about, and vice-versa, you will enjoy the game if you like playing with your friends too!With the general plot of the game revolving around you being a test subject for Murkoff's sick experiments, set in the past before the main games take place - I feel like it's a very smart way for the developers to get away with doing whatever they like and tie it around the original games as they please in a way where the shoe is going to fit. That said - certain characters and events from the 1st game are referenced here where it makes sense. On top of it, thanks to mentioned setting of the game - the developers are able to cleverly give us whatever maps they want, which is a very good thing because it can potentially offer us a lot of different environments and it will always make sense.Graphically, I have to say the game looks great! Even upon getting like unreasonably close to things, the LOD and the resolution of items seems to always look stunning.I will have to complain about one specific graphical setting in particular though, that being RayTracing. Before I say anything - yes, my machine is more than capable of running RT, however this game just STRUGGLES to run it, constantly stuttering to the point where the game becomes unplayable. I'm not sure whether or not that issue has been fixed because I just haven't bothered checking it out again, having been let down every time I tried. On top of it, the times when I did play with RT on in this game - it offered absolute minimal difference. The lighting stayed literally the same I feel like, the only real difference was the fact that you could see your character reflecting in the TV screen (which is very situational) and that you could see a (very poorly looking) reflection of yourself in the mirror without having to interact with it (talking about the lobby mirror in your room where you change your character). Most pointless setting in this game I feel like, absolutely tanking the performance for no reason too, unless something has changed.Outlast Trials offers a lot of different enemies to look out for and they're all well designed and voiced EXTREMELY well, from all the different sounds and grunts, up to the screams and, oh god... Some of the voice lines... I have no idea what sick mind came up with some of these lines, but please adopt me xDGameplay-wise, it works like you would expect an Outlast game to work, with some little puzzles here and there, looking for keys, fueling gens and all that.At the start you will mostly hide and run away before dying miserably, but eventually you get used to the game, and you will start to unlock special rigs and other perks which will make your game a lot easier. For me personally, a lot of the rigs turn the game into something way too combative for my tastes, and the rigs are very, very powerful. I always appreciated the lack of combat in Outlast games, where you always had to resort to running and hiding, whereas here it will very often turn into indirect combat. Thankfully, the new Barricade rig hit that sweet spot of giving me enough tools to survive to feel like I stand a chance, without being combative, though - it's still slightly too good for me with how insanely quick it recharges.Additionally, when playing in COOP, the game will offer you certain COOP actions, like boosting each other over obstacles to open up a shortcut, something entirely absent from when you play alone, I think that's a fun way to encourage working together. Oh, and also, playing in multiplayer will introduce a new enemy, and I have to say, without spoiling anything - sometimes the "combination" can be very vile, like really hilarious at times :DThe new update also introduced a new Rogue-like mode, it plays very nice in my opinion - offering a challenge for people who got way too comfortable with the game and I'm looking forward to playing it more!

_childDocuments_.review: "The Outlast Trials" is a disappointing and lackluster installment in the acclaimed horror franchise, failing to capture the essence of what made its predecessors great. Despite its promising premise and cooperative gameplay, this game falls short in several key areas, leaving players feeling underwhelmed and frustrated.One of the biggest issues with The Outlast Trials is its departure from the atmospheric horror and psychological tension that defined previous Outlast titles. While the game retains the same basic formula of hiding and running from terrifying enemies, it lacks the same sense of dread and suspense that made the original games so memorable. The scares feel predictable and formulaic, with jump scares replacing genuine moments of terror.Adding to the frustration is the game's lackluster level design and uninspired gameplay mechanics. The environments feel bland and repetitive, lacking the same attention to detail and atmosphere that fans have come to expect from the series. Similarly, the gameplay feels shallow and uninteresting, with little in the way of meaningful progression or challenge.Furthermore, The Outlast Trials suffers from a lack of meaningful cooperative gameplay. While the game allows for up to four players to team up and tackle its challenges together, the cooperative elements feel tacked on and poorly implemented. Players are forced to rely on one another for basic tasks like opening doors and activating switches, but there's little in the way of true teamwork or coordination.Additionally, The Outlast Trials' technical performance leaves much to be desired. The game suffers from frequent bugs, glitches, and optimization issues that detract from the overall experience. From stuttering frame rates to game-breaking crashes, these technical shortcomings make it difficult to fully immerse oneself in the game world, further diminishing its appeal.In conclusion, The Outlast Trials is a disappointing and lackluster entry in the Outlast franchise that fails to deliver on its promises. With its predictable scares, uninspired gameplay, and technical issues aplenty, it's hard to recommend this game to anyone other than the most die-hard fans of the series. Save your time and money for a more fulfilling horror experience elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: "Furry Sex" transports players to an imaginative world where anthropomorphic characters and adult themes combine to create a unique, interactive experience. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoys the Outlast series, and was disappointed to learn we weren't getting an "Outlast 3" years ago, but instead getting a multi-player Outlast experience, I will say that this game, even in it's current early access state as of May 24, 2023, has exceeded my expectations.  Not only does the game look and run/perform extremely well, from both my experience and from what my friends have told me, but even for a strictly PvE experience, the challenge feels "good" and the gameplay and gameplay loop itself is fun and keeps me wanting to come back for more.  At this time I have mostly played with friends in groups of four (quads), but I did go in solo the other night and what an experience that was as well!Compared to other PvE, up to 4 player co-op games, that I've played and enjoyed as of late, including Phasmophobia, Ghost Watchers, Demonolgist, Inside the Backrooms, and Escape the Backrooms, The Outlast Trials definitely shines bright and the price tag, again in my opinion, is easily justified.  The sense of progression in The Outlast Trials feels very good.  You earn cash that is used to customize your character and room and vouchers that are used to unlock abilities and upgrades.  Some things I would like to see added for the full release include, Steam achievements.  The game does have badges you can unlock which also seem like they tie in perfectly to achievements.  In addition to the progression system and things you can purchase/unlock it seems like achievements can be plentiful if the devs choose to do them.I do enjoy the in-game statistics board that shows the statistics of yourself and of those in the same pre-trials area, however, I think it would be nice to see these any time you want in a menu.  I know some of these statistics are available in the existing in-game menus, but I don't think everything is currently present.If it is monitored for cheaters/hackers/exploiters, I would also like to see public leaderboards for the Outlast Trials.  Perhaps something along the lines of showing what map/trial was actually performed, how many people were in your party, how long it took you to complete the trial, your grade(s), etc.In a similar regard, from the in-game menus, I would like to see separate grades.  In other words, if I escape a trial solo versus with a crew, it just saves the best grade on the screen.  I'd like it to have separate grades for solo play versus group play.  Or if they wanted to get more granular, grades for solo, duos, trios, and quads for each and every trial.  I feel that too could help some players with replayability and a reason to go back to the trials, even if you earned an A+ already.I know you can disable/unequip any rigs you want, but I don't see any option to disable any prescription/pharmaceutical enhancements.  This isn't something I personally wouldn't normally do, but I feel there are players out there who sometimes may want to go back to the "basics" and have no upgrades or equipment of any kind equipped.  Despite these minor criticisms, I cannot recommend The Outlast Trials enough to those who love an intense, fun, and sometimes hilarious, PvE experience.  While you can still play this game solo and definitely have fun, I feel like it really shines when playing with others.Note: This review was initially written on May 24, 2023 with 20.5 hours on record.  I also played the closed beta/demo/playtest for The Outlast Trials in October 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: Manage to release a Reagent (prestige) at the 38 hour mark.This new Outlast, which is a prequel of the first games, is a nice change of scenario, however there is some lack of terror with clumsy “jumpscares” and usually not very frightening events. One should think, as a game before the events of the first games in the series, the change to heavy survival horror and cooperative was needed to build it. It still remains within the Outlast lore where violence and crazed up enemies are present, only from another era.In every trial you must complete a set of objectives with different gameplay factors, some better suited for up to four players. Singleplayer is still an option but when it comes to primary trials, doing those with teammates is a must. As a guinea pig you must tread with caution, observe the enemies around, and do the best to outmaneuver their movements. Of course, there is special bosses who move and attack faster and harder than your regular foe. Stealth remains as a loyal companion but eventually you have to run and hide.What it surprised me is that you actually can defend yourself (finally!) by throwing bottles and bricks, and using special equipment that stun your enemy population. No longer one has to depend on heavy stealth and shutting doors to stop anyone. Although if you don’t have nothing on you, or the boss is on your tail (as they’re only stagger by projectiles, but still vulnerable to Riggs), they become a decent option. Vaulting remains here and you can also slide while running. Jumping through windows and breaking doors while running remain available, but you have to watch for the noise you make, or someone nearby may listen.Featuring coop moves such as rolling gates, barricaded ones, and also reviving are some of the features in the Trials. There are more items to use than Outlast 2 and you can share them. Everyone will have to take care of themselves as it remains the core of the whole game: don’t get hit, don’t die. It will seem selfish, but because even when reviving and healing, Murkoff will know someone died and it will have an impact on the group score after the trial. Triggering loud traps, getting hit, knocked out and executed, will lower your personal score. And that’s all there’s to it. You can buy cosmetics and better gear, but at this point there isn’t much to do, other than playing timed chess at the lobby. For a title still on early access, there is some fun and can be quite teaching to help new players, but it will get quite repetitive and for that I won’t be playing it soon until new stuff is released. It’s still quite addictive if you want to do what I did.So goodbye for now, and don’t let the doctor teach you about dental hygiene.Edit: Nominated for Steam Awards 2023 - Better with Friends!

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend outlast trials to those who enjoy playing horror games with friends. The only reason I do not is because of the most recent update. My friends and I noticed a nosedive in terms of performance, we all have relatively updated PCs w/ great graphics cards (we got the 4070Ti), so performance shouldn't be an issue. Lately, the trials have been a glitchy mess, we just finished up a trial for me to fall through the map and be stuck in the trial until the timer inevitably runs out, we both didnt want it to add to our trial failed count so we stuck together until the end. This has been a trend since Bambino's trial came out. Also the amount of tickets we need to get is an insane amount. I'm a college student so I usually can only play like 3-4 trials a week, if not every two weeks due to work and school. I want to get some of the cosmetic items from the deluxe catalog but that seems too far out of my reach. It is also bad for newer players because they may fail trials and have a harder time adapting to all the new mechanics and wont even claim the items in the catalogs or from the task section. The four different currencies also confused my friends who started the game literally last week, and I had to explain what the different ones were, how to claim items, and the purpose of ascension or freeing your agent, which I couldnt really give them a compelling reason why other than to say you did so. Also, its getting harder and harder to convince my friends to play because they already played through the base trials and then they don't know the game well enough to play the harder trials/game modes. The MK trials being separate from a specific game mode is something I enjoyed because it allowed my friends and I to experience the prime reagents while completing "new" objectives like feeding the children or dealing with witnesses. TLDR; The game is okay, it has the following issues:- Performance issues which causes people to lag/glitch in trials regardless of their settings- Hard to reach goals (stamp collecting + catalog grinding) for new and old players. - Not enough information for newer players (what currencies buy what items and more)- Not an appealing end game (Reagent Release)- Repetitive gameplay especially with the MK trials being taken away and placed under a special gamemode

_childDocuments_.review: Edit (June 2024):Outlast Trials has been in full release for several months now and is still a phenomenal product. They've added new programs, cosmetics, voicelines, endings, modifiers and more. As of now I only have two negatives to say regarding Outlast Trials. One, Red Barrels has clarified that they do make use of AI-generated art for filler art found in the environments of the trials, including posters and pictures that are unlockable for the player to equip in their cell. While they have stated that this is done so that their creative teams can focus on more important assets that require more work, I still stand against the use of AI-generated art in general, even if it is just filler environmental details. I would rather Red Barrels remove and/or refrain from continuing to use AI in their creative arts process, as their environments are already highly-detailed and making use of this technology just contributes to the ethical issue of plagiarizing actual artists to generate new content. Secondly, I am concerned about the game's longevity, as while it is still a good game I can't help but feel a disinterest in opening the game now that I've unlocked 99% of cosmetics and completed the vast majority of the game's challenges. Obviously I have a lot of hours in the game, but at this point the game has lost its scare factor and I feel that when I play it's just to grind for tokens to unlock FOMO cosmetics. While the devs are aware of this, I don't really know what they could do in the future to change this. If they added new programs, I feel like I would be interested in playing through them once or twice and then probably closing the game again.Original Early Access Review:In none of my wildest dreams did I expect a co-op Outlast game to be this damn good.Welcome to the Outlast Trials! Your participation is voluntary but the exit is locked at all times. You're stuck in this hellhole until you can prove yourself worthy enough to get out. Can you survive? Can you prove yourself? Can you be reborn?Co-op Outlast is pretty much exactly what it sounds like. You and up to three other players are loaded onto a shuttle train and into a simulated environment of horror. You're given simple objectives, such as transporting a payload, finding keys, opening valves, but the entire time you're being hunted by psychotic individuals, hell-bent on killing you in a gore-tastic way. Just like the Outlast games, you're equipped with night vision to see in the dark, which you'll learn soon enough is the safest place you can be. Manage resources such as batteries and health to make it all the way to the end of the trial, receiving a grade based on your performance. Complete enough trials and you'll be tested on a final exam, where the modifiers are deadly and the stakes are high. Complete enough exams and trials and you'll receive one shot to earn your freedom and get out of here.For what it is, Outlast Trials has an incredibly surprising amount of replayability. Playing more unlocks unique cosmetics to make your Reagent look completely your own. Decorate your cell back at the facility with decor ranging from beautiful to twisted. Unlock loadouts and perks that drastically affect your in-trial gameplay, such as stun mines and healing gas and speed boosts and more. Re-doing a trial means you're more familiar with what will happen, allowing you to change your strategy and push for a perfect grade. Outlast Trials is also flat-out scary. I am an avid horror game fan, but my first session of this game (going in completely blind) was some of the most intense horror experience I have ever had, so much so that I had to take a break purely to prevent myself from hyperventilating. Playing with my friends, we were all screaming at all of the intense ♥♥♥♥ that happened. Even now, when I've been reborn once and am speed-running late-game trials, my nerves still get put on edge by this game. It's got an incredible atmosphere to it that is so fear-inducing.To top it off, Outlast Trials is an *EARLY ACCESS* game and is already a phenomenal product. It is rare to see such a polished, fun-to-play early access build, and it's so exciting knowing that there is even more to come with this game. I highly recommend you pick up Outlast Trials, and if you can, convince a couple friends to pick it up too, it'll be a wild ride.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outlast Trials" is a formidable addition to the Outlast franchise and a gripping survival experience in the world of video game horror. This game throws you into the midst of a malevolent experiment from the Cold War era, putting your survival skills to the test in an innovative way.Pros:Intense Horror Atmosphere: The game keeps you constantly on edge, making you feel like anything could happen at any moment. The sound and visual design contribute remarkably to this terrifying atmosphere.Well-Designed Gameplay Mechanics: The Outlast Trials brings some interesting innovations in terms of gameplay mechanics. The ability to cooperate with other players to survive adds a new dynamic and raises the question of who can be trusted in such a situation.Intriguing Story: The game features an intriguing story that reveals more about the Outlast universe, providing answers to questions fans have had for a long time.Cons:Some Bugs and Technical Issues: I experienced a few minor bugs that, while not significantly affecting the gameplay, could be improved through future updates.Co-op Learning Curve: The game requires good coordination between cooperating players. Initially, this aspect might seem challenging for some players.Overall, "The Outlast Trials" is a captivating horror experience worth exploring. Fans of the Outlast series will find many familiar elements and a story that ingeniously ties into previous events. Despite a few minor technical issues, the game offers a truly unique cooperative horror experience on the market.This is definitely a title that horror genre enthusiasts and Outlast franchise fans shouldn't miss. Together with friends or other players online, get ready to step into a terrifying experiment and uncover the horrifying secrets of "The Outlast Trials." Enjoy the well-orchestrated fear and the grim atmosphere of this captivating game!

_childDocuments_.review: Good execution for what is exactly Outlast but co-op.I haven't played Outlast 1 or 2, but as someone who enjoys co-op this is a fun time with friends, even more so if they are easily scared. Haven't seen any performance issues and the objectives are tied into the context of the map's theme and layout.The lobby system is neat, while character customization is limited, it's pretty cool that you can decorate your room and have friends visit. The room options don't leave much freedom either but how it ties into the lobbies is well-designed.If I had to complain, it would be the lack of map/enemy variety in conjunction with it's somewhat hefty price tag, but the underlying systems (great connectivity in multiplayer and the fact that I can't remember any bugs I encountered) are very solid which is extremely rare for an Early Access launch.With the price tag in mind, if you're on the fence I'd say maybe wait half a year and see how much content they added by then, otherwise I recommend this co-op/horror blend wholeheartedly.

_childDocuments_.review: Terraria Review - IGNThis indie sandbox adventure is much more than a 2D Minecraft clone.BY NATHAN MEUNIERUPDATED: MAY 6, 2012 11:59 PMPOSTED: MAY 25, 2011 8:29 PMImagine what Minecraft might be like if it had been made with pixel art sprites and released in the SNES era. That sums up the overall vibe of Terraria pretty well. It also explains why I just can't seem to tear myself away from the darned thing. This devious little indie sandbox title borrows so many ideas from Notch's game that it essentially is Minecraft in 2D, but it also beefs up the familiar gameplay in exciting ways. There's a lot more creepy crawly stuff to kill, and the staggering number of doodads you can MacGyver together into deadly weapons to slay them with is mouth-watering. Say what you will; there's some gnarly fun to be had in these uncharted depths.After you're done customizing your sprite character, Terraria dumps you on the colorful surface of a randomly generated pixel world with nothing more than a handful of tools and the vague sense that you're meant to build stuff, explore the terrain, and battle monsters. Figuring out exactly how that's done is a little puzzling at first. There's a lone guide wandering around the surface, though his advice is random. The lack of a tutorial meant I had to consult the game's Wiki page to get a better sense of how things work and what can be built. Even so, it didn't take long to get the gist. Though there aren't any real story elements or epic quests to conquer, the strong fantasy trappings instill a desire to adventure nonetheless. There's magic, monsters, and mayhem waiting both on the surface and in the dark caverns below. Uncovering unexpected new prizes and perils is a big part of the game's charm.The entire game world is destructible, and breaking block lets you collect core resources like stone, wood, and iron that can be used to make cool gear or build structures. Rarer resources are dropped when you slay skeletons, floating fanged critters, and other monsters or when you dig deeper into the subterranean underworld. Since such a large portion of Terraria's gameplay revolves around foraging for different components and seeing what you can build with them, the drive to explore every nook and cranny of the landscape kicks in right away. But it's important to temper your desire to set out exploring in hopes of amassing huge quantities of loot with the pressing need to build shelter and expand your spawn point's home base.Life on the surface follows a day/night cycle. Exploring topside during the daytime is safer – you can pick flowers, roam around, chop trees, and kill weak slimes that roam too close. It's also a perfect time to build houses that serve as shelter and attract helpful NPC characters to your settlement. Things get dicey when night falls; zombie hordes and floating eyeball beasts come out in droves, forcing you to fight or flee. That's less of an issue once you get a sturdy settlement started.The village development aspect of the game is a clever addition – once you discover it exists. You can throw together bare-bones shacks or craft elaborate fortresses that tower upward into the heavens. Either way, you want to deck them out with enough accoutrements to lure NPCs to your village. These support characters can heal you, sell you items, and offer other helpful services. You have to complete a specific task to attract them, and even then they only appear if you've created a room (complete with walls, furniture, lighting, etc.) for them to stay. This offers some tangible incentives to spend time building, beyond the desire to lord over a large stronghold.DIG, BUILD AND PREPARE FOR BATTLE.Having an elaborate and ever-expanding home base to return to on the surface is satisfying. However, the dark, foreboding underworld is where the real action is. Everything you need to make the most basic items like torches, furniture, and healing potions can be found near the surface, but you have to adventure deep below to uncover the rarest materials. This is where Terraria's gameplay feels more like an old-school action platformer and where it really sunk its hooks into me. Digging for ore eventually uncovers sprawling caverns that are home to many varieties of creepy creatures. Giant slimes, skeletons, burrowing worms, and tougher beasties roam the dark, and they often come charging at you while you're excavating. Exploring is a lot fun on its own, yet it's the strong emphasis on combat that's really appealing. For one thing, stopping to battle monsters breaks up the monotony of digging. Creatures also drop coins that can be used to buy shop items. There's an added risk versus reward element to combat too. Getting killed causes you to re-spawn on the surface with your gear intact, but you'll leave a chunk of your precious coin stash behind.The real impetus behind adventuring is driven by the insanely deep gear crafting system. Almost everything you pick up in the game is a component used in forging some crucial piece of kit. There are well over a hundred different weapons and items to build. Though some equipment is more functional – like protective armor, grappling hooks that lets you navigate with greater ease, and treasure chests for storing loot – most of the stuff designed for cleaving monsters into itty bits is just sheer badass. Magical boomerangs, laser pistols, spell books that shoot fireballs, light sabers, and ninja stars are just a handful of the crazier weapons you can build. Hunting down the rare items you need to build the best weapons is obsession forming.SET UP HOUSING AND VENDORS WILL MOVE IN.A few other cool nuances enhance the absorbing tasks of exploring, building, and battling away. Journey to the farther reaches of the surface world, and you'll inevitably run into The Corruption – a teeming mass of demonic turf filled with extra danger and extra rewards. You'll also uncover demonic altars for forging special items that can be used to summon one of the game's three spectacular bosses to fight (sporting awesome names like "Skeletron" and "Eater of Worlds"). Terraria's multiplayer mode is a blast too. Co-operatively exploring and building with friends or strangers is even more enjoyable than going solo, depending on the folks you play with. Finding an open public server to play on is a real drag, since most fill up within minutes of being posted on the game's forum. The good news is you can create your own server and share it with your pals (or post it online for others to join).VerdictThough on the surface it looks like just another "me too" indie game seeking to ride the coattails of Minecraft's success, Terraria expands on the familiar sandbox gameplay with a greater emphasis on combat and adventure that proves very satisfying. Fresh elements – like an absurdly expansive weapon crafting system, a broader scope of monsters to battle, and a slick retro 2D presentation – make it a stand out among the pack. Hell, it took all the resolve I could muster just to shut the game down long enough to write this review. That's rare indeed.In This Article

_childDocuments_.review: Fine to play both co-op and solo. Different types of trials in different maps with different objectives to do, at the end you get a grade for how well you did. While the idea and game play are fine the limited options do however make it quite repetitive once you get some hours in. There's some events every now that provide you with limited cosmetic items but that's about it. Recently added catalogs give some grinding you can do but that's about it. Can't say anything about public matches as I haven't played them (only co-op with friends and solo). Some maps/trials are always available but some are on rotation which in my opinion limits the already repetitive game play even more. Overall I would say the game is fine, nothing mind blowing, nothing game breaking. It's the type of game I play when I don't feel like playing anything that requires more than two brain cells and for that purpose it is fine.

_childDocuments_.review: This is how to do a co-op horror game. Suspenseful gameplay, incredible polish, and ZERO microtransactions. I was a little skeptical when this was announced, but Red Barrels absolutely knocked this one out of the park.Oh, and if you don't have friends to play with, it lets you do everything in singleplayer as well. So if you're a horror fan, you have no excuses not to buy this.
_childDocuments_.name: The Outlast Trials

_childDocuments_.review: Been looking for a game like this for a looong time. There are few horror games that pull off progression and above all replayability. Can probably count them with one hand. Some have gone too far from horror, so maybe even less. As it stands, this is an absolute banger of a game.That being said, my only concern for the future of Outlast Trials is it being always online. Its an Early Access, but its such a solid experience, both solo and coop. It may seem like such a small thing to worry about now, but as much as I hope for a bright future ahead of it, there's a chance something might go wrong, and this gem goes offline forever.Just to end it as a little letter to any dev that might stumble upon this review, thank you. There's so much love and effort put into this game, and it shows. I could nerd out on everything I love about it, but it all sums up to this, the care a small dedicated team, willing to go through their own trials to bring out such a solid game. No editions, no microtransactions, no passes, an actual game.A+
