_childDocuments_.review: If you're like me, you were impressed by how stylistic this game is, and that holds true! This game is absolutely beautiful to look at. Every single moment of this game is like looking at an art piece.Playing is a different story. You'll find quickly that there are very few ways to play that get you far. The easiest being to stick with normal swords that strike fast, have decent damage and range. Then, you poke enemies through floors until they die. The game becomes a lot of that as you get your sword really strong, rinse and repeat.The reason I bring this up is that the combat is the roughest part of this game and it's the main focal point as well. It's intentionally sluggish to create difficulty, which is fine. But it's so intentionally sluggish that you find there's not many diverse options for you that allow you to actually kill any enemies. Slow swinging strong weapons are so slow you have to cancel your attacks to dodge most of the time. Plus, swords work just fine. You can kill with like 2-3 hits with a sword before the enemy gets an attack out anyway.Progression is rough too. You are going to have to die quite a bit to then build up residual funds to stand a chance. That's not uncommon in games. But the clear jump between that feeling of "I need to die more" and "I'm prepared" is jarring. I think it'd be preferable to slowly feel like you're getting stronger.After you fully beat the game once, there really isn't much in terms of replayability unless you are a completionist. You can make weapons stronger, you can unlock some new ones, but not too much more than that.Overall I had fun with trying to learn the game but after 10 hours, I'm not dying at all to go back to it. I also would not recommend picking it up at full price. If this game is on sale for 50% off, watch a YouTube video of the combat and see if you like it
_childDocuments_.name: GetsuFumaDen: Undying Moon

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, Konami and the development team take a good amunt of risk with this game. A sequel to an old japanese only famicom game that few remember outside that country? Sounds like a mad move! But.. they indeed make a cool revival... but something must change to better fit with the original Getsu Fuma Den... or at least take a good aim at his target audience.I will explain what I mean...Getsu Fuma Den: Undying Moon is, basically, a side scroller platform action with A LOT of elements from rouge-like games (and i notice some Darks Souls vibe too... I HATE TO SAID IT, but I can't put aside my fear that this game would be another DS clone.. only 2D). The game itself is really fun to play, feel a little rigid for the platforming aspect but I know it can be fixed with patch and whatnot. The thing that I don't like, though, are said rouge-like elements. It make the game less enjoyable to me. Its should be more focus on arcade side scrolling like the original or at least make possible to come back to the Getsu Clan hideout more easly so you dont loose all your stuff when dieing... and in this game you die A LOT!Personally, I'm okey with the full vision Konami and the team at GuruGuru embrace for this game and make the experience both deep and fresh, but this direction is not for everyone and will confuse and discurage fan of the original for sure. So to me, the gameplay need a lot of feedback to better understand the target this game is aiming for.Thats it, thats all i have to sai about the gameplay (the major concern point for me). Let's talk about everything eals... ITS AWSOME!! Music, graphic, art style. Everything really shine and give the game a unique feel... it really seems like a moving painting! (at least for me). I'm digging the art style and it should never change with subsequent update. It's perfect! :DThe option said "voice" but in game, there are any... i guess because its early access so its kind of normal.I raccomand it? Why yes. I mean, if you like the genre than the game its really cool and you will have fun no doubt, but for me... I will wait until Early Access is over... hoping that my suggestion will reach the developers. For now, give this game (and Konami) some love, it deserved it.

_childDocuments_.review: They rushed to 1.0 after a relatively short early access phase. Very few things were added during the time and a lot of promises were broken. The gameplay loop is also just lacking overall: enemies are more annoying than challenging, the grind for meta-currency is insanely long and incentivizes farming the early zones without making real progress. To try to make progress quickly in runs, you're forced to upgrade only 1 weapon at a time and discourages experimentation. The second character they added feels too similar and doesn't add any replayability really. I felt like I got baited into the game with the amazing music, art and first boss showcase (the subsequent bosses are much more lackluster in comparison). Game is all style, no substance. Seems like they gave up when sales weren't high enough during early access so they just released something mediocre.

_childDocuments_.review: I prefer the combat of this game to Dead Cells. One of my problems with Dead Cells is how quick the game is. I like the slower pace that GetsuFuma has with less enemies but slightly longer fights. There are also a lot of interesting mechanics taken from games like the soul series, specifically bloodborne visceral attacks. All enemies have a break point where when you break them, you can do a Slay Attack (visceral attack from bloodborne). Unfortunately, the combat and the visuals/art of the game are the only good things about it. EDIT: I am updating my review. As of 28 hours total in the game, I have all blueprints unlocked for weapons, sub-weapons, and talents. I also completed the game on the hardest difficulty. I have to still give the game a negative review. If steam allowed neutral reviews I would give this a neutral instead. Here is an updated list of problems and an explanation of new problems or problems that have been fixed/were an oversight by me. Thanks to steam review word limitations, I am unable to list pros, but if you're interested in what I liked about the game, feel free to comment in my review and I can provide a list. I will not be updating this review anymore until more significant changes are done or until the game is released.Another thing to note, the developers have addressed some issues that many players were having on updates. Potions are now received always from lore-texts (one per-stage), Hitboxes on demon enemies are adjusted, and the visual effects from blood are reduced to make it easier to see the playable character. This was done 5 days (May 18th, patch on May 21st) after the games release. This is promising to see active changes so quickly.Cons:These are my main problems with the game. I'm writing this review because I took a look at the GetsuFuma roadmap, and the next big update is releasing a new playable character. I feel the developers need to focus on the core systems they have in place of the game before delving on optional things like "more playable characters". There is a good game here, but unfortunately it's missing the mark on a lot of things. To put it to perspective, Dead Cells was released in early access at $17 and even at that point in time, the game had more polish on weapon variety, NPCs, and progression. I'm still interested in the game and what Konami has to bring to the table here. The game looks amazing, and I think the bosses are very well done on their difficulty, visual representation, and elements in the fight. I'll be keeping my eye on updates and would love to someday change this negative review into a positive one.

_childDocuments_.review: presents an ambitious attempt to revive a classic game, but it falls short in several key aspects. While it boasts stunning visuals and a captivating art style that pays homage to its predecessor, the game struggles to maintain the same level of excitement and engagement throughout.One of the major drawbacks is the lack of responsiveness in controls. Certain actions and movements can feel clunky or unresponsive, resulting in frustrating moments during combat or platforming sections. This detracts from the overall fluidity and enjoyment of the gameplay.Furthermore, despite the beautiful aesthetics, the game suffers from limited variety. The levels, enemies, and items can feel repetitive after multiple playthroughs, diminishing the sense of excitement and exploration. The sparse narrative also fails to create a compelling story to drive the player's motivation, leaving a void in terms of emotional investment.The other issue is the same graphics, because when the animations of the enemies are mixed up, it's hard to know what's going on. And this can become the road to the starting location.While Getsufumaden: Undying Moon attempted to incorporate roguelite elements with procedural generation, the execution falls somewhat flat. The replay value starts to wane after a few playthroughs, as the procedural generation fails to provide sufficient variety and freshness to keep players engaged in the long run.In the end, I leave a positive review, because the game is able to give many tens of hours of good mood, with a challenge and a test of your skill. P. S. If you want to unlock Kunoichi, you must defeat her between mission 2 or 3 by playing on Commoner or higher.

_childDocuments_.review: What a niche game. It hits such a sweet spot for me! Dead Cells is one of my favorite games of all time. I have 80+ hours into it on Switch, and repurchased it for Steam Deck. I’m also an huge Ukiyo-e (Japanese woodblock artwork) enthusiast. So when I saw GetsuFumaDen, I felt like someone must have created this game just for me. :) However, I was concerned about the tepid reviews. I’m so glad I gave it a shot. The look of the game is absolutely stunning, if you’re even the slightest bit into Ukiyo-e. The gameplay is reminiscent of Dead Cells, so if you like that and want more, GetsuFumaDen is a worthy take on the genre. While combat may not be quite as smooth (just a hair less responsive, maybe?), I can easily overlook this, given the unique mechanics and what appears to be a deep network of synergies. (I’m only an hour and a half in, and admittedly don’t understand all of the mechanics quite yet, though that speaks to some complexity, which excites me. That said, my only critique so far is that the game could perhaps do a better job of explaining things. Despite tutorial pages that do pop-up, it’s maybe a tad confusing all at once. Though, there are some decent guides on Reddit.) The combat and exploration is quite satisfying though, and feels well-polished. The lore is a lot of fun to peruse as you collect it within the Hall of Treasures. I’m incredibly impressed with GetsuFumaDen, as someone who came into it with unreasonably high expectations. The quality of the art direction—rooted in Japanese mythology—is really the highlight for me, and the Dead Cells style gameplay is well-executed. Side notes: I’m playing on Steam Deck and it’s almost flawless. I’ve had a couple of momentary screen-freezes, however I’m playing on the highest quality graphics settings. Also, I saw a lot of people saying that the game doesn’t boot up due to some glitch with accepting the Terms of Service. This wasn’t a problem for me. The Terms took a little while to load in (I ultimately hit a white screen after a minute or so?), but I simply backed out of that screen, was then given the option to accept the terms, and proceeded into the game without any issue.

_childDocuments_.review: OG Getsu is a great game, never thought we'd get a sequel let alone one THIS good. Difficulty is great, rewarding both enemy/boss memorization and upgrading. Only minor complaint is upgrading items takes ages but the newest update seems to have fixed that.Enjoyed the original Getsu? Get this. Enjoy Rogelites? Get this. Enjoy Metroidvanias? Get this. Enjoy great games? GET. THIS.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don't know how to start with this review. I go through my backlog to finally play what I have there, start a random game and get absolutely stunned by the presentation, go through the artbook and marvel at what's there... just to have my initial impressions shattered after playing for a few hours and cursing Konami louder than I have ever done in my life for what they have done to what could have possibly been one of the best rogue-lites of recent years.Before I begin, I have to mention that GetsuFumaDen: Undying Moon is a single player rogue-lite game, but still requires an internet connection in order to run. Please be mindful of this before purchasing the game.If there's one thing that the game does extremely well and puts it in front of everyone to see, it's the visual style. In a time when nearly anyone who makes a rogue-lite goes for common pixel art designs or normal 3D models, the madmen at GuruGuru took the capabilities of Unreal Engine 4 and created a 3D game with an incredible art direction. The developers have nailed the artstyle for GetsuFumaDen's revival, making the whole game look like an old Japanese painting that has come to life, with all of the enemy designs and depictions being directly based on them. One look into the game's artbook reveals how much care was put into designing the visual aesthetics of this game and I honestly cannot praise the devs enough in this regard.But unfortunately, I cannot say the exact same thing about the music. While the music tracks are done really well, some of them make you think maybe there wasn't any clear direction as to what should be done with them. Sometimes you hear traditional-inspired music, sometimes you just hear glorified ambience, sometimes you hear the composer going wild with electric guitars, and sometimes you hear abominable mixes of multiple genres. For example, the first boss' theme (Unfettered Chaos) goes too hard for a first boss, and the rival boss fight (Onwards! GetsuFuma) has this jarring transition from traditional to dubstep, then retro and then going back. And this lack of consistency feels jarring.I'm gonna say it: This game needed more time in the oven. It has everything it needs to be a great rogue-lite, but needed more development time to iron them out.If I wanted to explain the gameplay of Undying Moon in brief, I would say it's basically Dead Cells mixed with a little bit of Dark Souls. If you have played Dead Cells before, you already know the basics of Undying Moon's gameplay. The only difference is that Undying Moon asks you to engage with enemies in a safe manner by observing their attacks, baiting them and punishing accordingly instead of being fast and efficient. It also gives you bonuses that increase your damage output upon doing certain actions like clashing attacks with the enemy or surprising them to encourage this playstyle. This should already be a recipe for greatness, but the game fumbles this potential because of its gameplay loop.The game works like this: You go through a level and upon getting to the end of it, you are teleported to the boss arena. If you manage to kill the boss, you will be given the choice of going back to the main hub (Getsu Estate) or continuing to the next level. If you go back, you will keep all of the resources you have collected. But if you choose to continue and die before killing the next boss, you will lose everything; unless you have unlocked some skills beforehand that let you keep a percentage of the resources after death.This can make the game absolutely repetitive to go through, because the numerous resources you need for upgrades drop randomly, and their amounts are extremely low in early levels. The grind is absolutely real in this game and if you never find out how to get past the first two bosses, you will be stuck in this repetitive loop of beating first level, beating first boss, going back to the estate and repeating everything from the beginning. And even if you look past the repetitive gameplay loop and try to power through, there's not much in the game. Aside from one unlockable character, there's nothing else to find and whole game consists of you doing everything over and over again, with nothing to break the flow or add some actual value to your incomplete runs.And there are a bunch more issues that can suck the fun out of the game and make it appear very dull. These include additional levels being locked behind random key drops, frequent leaps of faith in some of the levels and the camera system being unable to show if you land safely or not, level layouts becoming repetitive after the first two hours, enemies being placed in locations where it's incredibly hard to fight them, or some enemies detecting you from far offscreen and attacking you through the environment. Even the unlockable character which could have added some variety to the gameplay ends up being lackluster as each character in the game has a separate skill tree, further increasing the need to grind.Whatever I mentioned so far are all issues that could have been ironed out with a little bit of dev time and feedback. Because it is apparent that the devs clearly had passion while developing this game and couldn't possibly have done this on purpose. So why no such thing has happened?You know what's worse than the game's potential not being realized? A publisher that kills the game prematurely. There were a lot of stuff planned for the game. The devs could have improved the game significantly and made a rogue-lite classic. But unfortunately, the publisher of this game was Konami.Two additional playable characters, a whole bunch of enemies, multiple bosses, a number of weapons and a few maps are already in the game in an incomplete state. The devs even had a roadmap to add these stuff properly. But what happened? Version 1.0's release was rushed and all of future updates were cancelled, resulting in a game that was panned by the critics for feeling incomplete. And since Konami has already done a Limited Run Games release, this means the game is considered finished by them.So, to sum everything up, Konami digs up a Japan-exclusive franchise that was dormant for 35 years, allows a developer to create a new game in the said franchise and release it in early access to fine-tune it over time, the developer goes all-out in the visual presentation department and creates an incredible looking game with vast gameplay potential, Konami does ♥♥♥♥-all when it comes to marketing the game and makes a shocked Pikachu face when it doesn't sell like hot cakes, and then the development process is finished pre-emptively because the game is not a financial success. Literally everyone who has played this game knows that it has immense amounts of potential. You have a game that has an incredible, and dare I say one of a kind visual presentation, and THIS is how you treat it? You have the perfect ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ recipe to make "Dead Cells but in Japan" and you do THIS to it? Only an utterly incompetent company such as Konami can do that. Great job guys. Keep on screwing up. Go make Metal Gear Survive 2: Electric Boogaloo while you're at it.Another victim of Konami's utter incompetence. It is visually stunning, looking like a Japanese painting that has come alive, but the rest of it clearly feels unfinished, unpolished and rushed.

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly visually stimulating game with wonderful character design and excellent style that really comes together for a presumably lower budget game. Being based on an obscure but excellent game that deserves more love is a bit of a boon, too.However, the gameplay is completely half-baked. So many things in the game are highly inconsistent and it takes away from what is almost a fairly tight, decent run-based experience. The progression is incredibly poor, mostly giving you number increases to make it a little easier next time with very, very little variance in runs outside of choosing a different level path.Could potentially be fixed with some tweaks and patches to make the game's behavior feel more consistent and to make progression more rewarding, but in its current state at time of writing, I really can't recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: So, my first thought about this game was: "Hold up, Konami's making games again?!"Second thought was: "....and it's a niche title and NOT a more recognised name."Third thought was: ".... and sh!t, it's quite good! Even for early access! You guys OK down there at Konami HQ? Just that you're acting like...... well NOT Konami."  all seriousness though, taking the rogue-like approach to a metroidvania title is an interesting spin, and fundamentally, it works well. Gameplay leans heavily towards being more tactical and methodical than it does being stylish and fast. And since you have limited ways of healing, you're forced to consider how best to dispatch your enemies while taking as few hits as possible. It's not quite dark souls, just enough to keep you thinking. The most 'style', goes into the visual direction of the game. They've gone all in on the shinto folklore theme. And with the cell shading, the game literally looks like a Yakuza tattoo come to life. And I think that's awesome!Considering this is still 'early' access, one should consider my critiques to be suggestions here.....It doesn't feel like there's much of a story going on here. A pit to hell has opened up, Fuma, or Renge has to go and seal it, and also Fuma's brother is missing. Since there's no spoken dialogue, characters have the same charisma as cardboard. This doesn't need to be the case: Hades has proven that you can have an engaging story with your roguelike. Give us a reason to care about these people. The difficulty spike is...... weird. Bosses are actually the easiest things to beat in the game. They telegraph their attacks hard, and it becomes embarrassingly easy to stomp them without taking hits. At least until you encounter the 5th boss. Then, you MIGHT win..... if all your gear is platinum rank 6 at a minimum, and even then you're not walking out of there with any healing scrolls. There's really no difference between Fuma and Renge. Fuma is slower, but has higher health. Renge is faster, but has less health. There might be a difference in attack power, but the moment your gear is silver or above at a certain rank, you're one shotting most enemies, so you won't even notice the difference. So you pick Renge, because if you're anything like me, you're a man of culture. While it's great that we have a wide choice of melee and ranged weapons, I would have preferred certain weapons to be exclusive to either Fuma or Renge, while perhaps having a few more techniques with said weapons. As it is now, they're just character skins. That being said, it's a very tidy package overall, with plenty of replayability, so it gets a recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review while playing the v0.4.10 update (Nov. 4th 2021), and the game is in Early Access so take the review with a grain of salt upon further updates. I like this game and can't wait to see how it evolves but at this stage I do not recommend anyone buying it right now, wait until it is fleshed out and hopefully perfected.PROS:+ Beautiful artstyle, boss intros are honestly to die for and sometimes have me rewatching em cause they are so pretty.+ Good music that is nice but doesn't get stuck n your head in a grating way.+ Interesting in-run level-up system via Soul Devour which allows you to level up Main weapon damage, Sub-weapon damage, Health, or create a potion. You save up souls then devour when you hit a certain amount of souls at 1, 2, 3, and 4 to level up each stat respectively. Letting it overflow resets the counter back to 1 and awards you 3 Soul Memory for weapon refinement.+ The balance between doing an Attack+, Sub+, or Health+ run is really quite nice and even refreshing. No one playstyle seems overly stronger than the other (Sub+ arguably the strongest once you unlock final variation of bows, bombs, kunai, and rifles but those all require cooldown management).+ Simplistic but unique weapons with 5 variations of each type, with the Umbrellas being the most fun and unique ones imo. Swords are for basic slashes and timed counters, Dual Blades for fast slashes and quick Demonization build-up, Clubs for slow meaty hits, Gauntlets for fast up-close punching, Spears for long range poking along with some decent Demonization build-up, Umbrellas for high break damage and perfect blocks (which deal heavy break damage), and Whips for very far-range precise hits for crits.+ Interesting stagger system in the way of "Break". Certain variations of weapons deal higher break than others which allow you to stagger an enemy or boss into critable state where you use "Slay" which basiclaly one-shots normal enemies and deals about 1/3 HP to bosses. Umbrellas being the king of breaking enemies fast.+ Demonization being a decent "don't get hit" reward where if you attack enemies without getting hit you build up Demonization which teirs up giving you more movement speed and attack power. If you get hit you lose it. (To not have to put separate thing in cons... there is a non-intended con to Demonization in that the effect that plays while maxed makes readability of nearby enemies horrid sometimes)CONS:- Base gameplay isn't engaging enough to encourage replaying after unlocking everything in this current patch. After grinding materials for so long you don't really wanna play the game much anymore, you've already experienced it all fighting the same enemies and learning to kill each boss stage in under 30 seconds.- Levels are long and repetitive, you will see the same tile-set over three times in some instances. If you want to clear and get every last soul and soul memory to level up with which ofc you'll want to do it just feels way too long.- Your options for third stage are both annoying level-hazards in the Misty Peaks of "Have most enemies be cicadas that throw bombs from off-screen that explode into smaller bombs while your screen gets cluttered with a foreground fog effect" or Snowy Graveyard of "Extreme gusts of wind that you have to walk out of to have them stop + SPIKES... spikes everywhere on the bottom of the map". Hard to pick which is more annoying, but I do DESPISE the fact the wind in the latter stage takes about 20 or so seconds to disipate if you don't walk out of it meaning you can be waiting to do a precise jump over spikes for 20 seconds all because the stage said "wind storm now"... fun and engaging stage hazard amirite...- Some enemies have poor readability when it comes to exactly when they will attack, some even will just stand there looking at you for a few seconds if you don't attack them or in the instance of the water spirit just repeat their diving animation and not attack for long periods of time while remaining invincible- Enemies can and will lock onto you from off-screen, leaving you in situations where an enemy will qeue a rush attack from off-screen, one starts flinging a large projectile off-screen before you jump up to a platform leaving you with you jumping up into a projectile you had no way of knowing was there, and one starts throwing a projectile down through the floor from off-screen which all three leave you with not enough time to react and taking damage.- The grind for maxing out the ABILITY to max out gear is insane. You use materials you get during a run to "refine" weapons permanently to unlock the ability to use Soul Memory in a run to non-permanently level up a weapon (+20 attack, +5% attack, +5% break, etc.). The system isn't inherintely bad its just a nauseating hour-bloat grind for ability to get the benefits, it took me 60h to max out all of the current weapons/sub-weapons and their respective 5 / 9 variants.- The drop-rate of the most used materials feels the same as the drop-rate of the "rarer" materials used for refining leaving you with 600 left-over Demon Lord's Fang while running out and grinding just for the (seemingly should-be) more common Great Demon's Fang (easily the most-needed material for refinement). And with no way to transmute materials those 600 Demon Lord's Fangs are just going to waste and mocking you.- The other character you are able unlock, Getsu Renge, only appears in-between stages randomly through an event system called "interruptions". After 60h and getting every other achieveable achievement I still hadn't unlocked her I asked "whats up with that" in the Discussions. Turns out there is an option in the title menu to "Disable interruptions" which is quite vague and I had checked yes on when i first booted up the game; no one when first booting up the game would know what checking that on means and there is no warning to specify (iirc).- Collision detection on ledges is sometimes horrible. Normally your character just zooms to grapple to it ala Dead Cells platforming, but others your feet will be firmly touching the top corner of a platform and your character will stay in the falling animation then glide off as if he forgot his own game's mechanics. Sometimes a similar thing happens while jumping over enemies, you'll just get kinda stuck.- There is lack of balance in status effect applying sub-weapons. Bows, Caltrops, and especially Kunai are just king when it comes to applying status effects while Bombs and Bracelets feel like a joke when you wanna apply Bleed/Fire/Poison which take multiple hits to proc the full effect (Ice/Parasite/Slow only require one hit no matter sub-weapon type so these are fine on any). Bows/Caltrops/Kunai all are able to hit enemies multiple times quickly to fully proc effects, while Bombs/Bracelets only hit things once or twice then have to slowly recharge meaning you only get a small part of the effects. Which means when unlocking Sub-weapons sometimes you are just unlocking worse items that have no real specific use, might as well just unlock the damage-focused variants of Bombs and Bracelets; adding insult to injury to the insane grind time.

_childDocuments_.review: Looks like Konami have decided to start making games again, and they've chosen a remake of the 1987 Super Famicom classic to kick off with.  sees you control the 27th head of the Getsu Clan as you quest to kill the demon lord that has broken loose and unleashed hell upon the Earth. You'll have an array of weapons ranging from katanas and spears to warhammers and battle umbrellas with which to slice through the demons in your way. The game utilises a classical Japanese art style and the gameplay borrows heavily from other rogue-lites such as  and . The first thing that will strike you about Undying Moon is the artwork. It's an utterly stunning looking game. The Japanese Ukiyo-e art style is beautiful, and there's a huge amount of detail crammed into every nook and cranny. All the sprites are insanely detailed and the animations are superb but special mention must go to the bosses, who are all unbelievable to watch and easily the highpoint of this game's strongest asset. Even the backgrounds are a joy to watch with the Hell stage a particular delight, as it shows souls being tormented in various ways. The main drawback of the graphics is that they're too crowded at times. Often, there's so much going on that you'll miss the enemies' attacks and get hit. The gouts of blood that shoot from the them are large enough to obscure your entire character. This isn't an issue for the weaker demons that go down with two or three hits but it means that, with the stronger enemies you're either fighting blind or using hit-and-run tactics. Sadly, the sound and music aren't as good as the artwork. The audio design isn't anything special and seems quite poorly mixed in places, although it is quite good on the few occasions it pokes through. There are times when the music drops out completely and other times when it's a major distraction. There's no voice acting for any of the characters, which is quite jarring when there's a dialogue-heavy scene, as the whole thing plays out in near total silence with the characters just standing there. It's like watching a Harold Pinter play. In terms of storyline, there's not a lot. You get one brief scene at the beginning showing the protagonist staring at the hell-hole and being told that, now that your brother has disappeared, it's up to you to save everyone. From then on what little story there is is told via a series of glowing stones that act as journal entries from your brother and the text during the loading screens. The levels aren't really explained either. There's no lore behind the different settings, and they feel like stock level designs right off a checklist: Lava level? Check. Snow Level? Check. Mountain level? Check. With all the lore contained in Japanese mythology, a really compelling narrative could've been written. It feels like a wasted opportunity. The gameplay is a combination of the combat from , the look and feel of , the death and rebirth mechanics and level design from . You've got a small choice of weapons, each of which have different variants. While I won't go into the specifics of each weapon, you can reduce it down to a choice between three types: Fast with low damage, slow with high damage or the katana. The sub-weapons are all ranged weapons and divided into two sections: short-range grenades, caltrops and magic bracelets and long-range kunai, bows and guns. The levels are randomly generated to keep things fresh throughout the many playthroughs but, after a few runs, you'll quickly notice how certain layouts repeat themselves over and over. They're just too bland to survive repeated viewing, which makes the search for the level's exit tedious. It feels absurd to criticise the artwork on a game that looks this good but more variety in the level design is badly needed to prevent getting through them a chore. In fact, if I could use one word to properly describe , it would be this one: grind. The crafting, weapons and skill progression system are laborious tasks that need far too many items to get through and the item spawn rates are far too low. The grind should come as a natural by-product of playing the game, not be the point of it. That's also assuming you don't die too often, which you probably will. The penalties for dying on runs are ridiculous and you'll lose nearly all the items and skill points you were carrying at the time. When combined with the sheer amount needed to upgrade, coupled with the fact you can't store your skill points, it's too much. I mean, even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥  offered you the ability to go back for all your stuff. The enemies are your usual choice of demons, beasts and ghosts. They all only have one attack and move in really simple patterns so it won't take too much to figure each one out. Due to the lack of variety in the enemies, this has the game getting really boring after only a few playthroughs. In addition to adding some new foes, a few of them could do with a redesign, in particular the ranged ones. Most of them can shoot you through walls from two screens away and they're infuriating. Having a knife spin through the ceiling from an enemy you've not even activated yet, when you're busy fighting something else will have people rage-quitting this in droves. It's really poor design. The combat, for the most part, is quite good. It's not as fast as Dead Cells and it feels weighty and natural and it's a lot of fun. There are issues with hitboxes and the windows for the parry and dodge are quite janky. The tutorial is terrible at explaining the mechanics. I went through it twice, thinking I'd done something wrong and cancelled it early, it was so brief and uninformative. It does nothing to explain the parry/slay and flash mechanics and does a piss-poor job of explaining the soul harvesting concept. This is one of the few areas of this game that needs a complete re-tooling. While  is a very solid game with a huge amount of potential, but, unless it's balanced properly, we'll never get to experience that potential. It looks unbelievable and has a superb feel but it's completely undone by a crippling difficulty curve, sluggish progression and some truly awful enemy design. The level artwork needs some more variety and the combat needs to be tightened up. Also, the weapon and stat boosts need to be re-worked so they actually have an appreciable effect. I'm sticking with my recommended rating because all these issues are easy to sort out. It'll take some work to add more content and revamp the tutorial and enemy designs but, when it's done and, if they do the updates right, when this game comes out of early access next year, we might just have a dark horse contender for best game of 2022.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I have completed one difficulty on this now. I can say it's not everythign I had hoped for, but I do enjoy it - and the devs can polish it up nicely. My main issues are grinding for materials, souls, elementals shards.. there's too much junk, and you need a metric ton of it to get any sort of meta-progression. you can piece-meal it by repeating level 1 ad-nauseum. not fun .  There's quite a few levels and bosses. It kinda operates on that dead-cells hook where you choose the path of levels you want via teleporters. You get different choices based on where you went prior. I dig that. What i DO NOT DIG, its the misty level design, and the Water area level design./ Misty level is GIGNATIC. and you have to hunt out these giant eyes to kill to release the seal on the door to the boss. the level si SO HUGE, and it takes SO LONG. My issue with the water level is it's poorly designed - it's all leap -of - faith jumps, bc you can't see below you, and the map shows you a void. it requires a trial and error approach to progression. I absolutely hate it. Everything else is sublime. the art, the animations, the bosses - the settings. it  all clicks in a satisfying way. You have a decent arsenal at your disposal ( with two attack functions per wep, like regualr attack and a parry, for instance ) and you have the soul-devour system.Think Gradius power-up system, and you're half way there. earngin a soul allows you to either consume it right away ( whcihy will increase your main wep atk power for all main weps ) or store it, and collect another. if you store it, now you can uconsume it to gain sub wep power + store 3, you can raise your max Hp, and store 4 - you get a health potion. the more you pump into a particular stat, the less the effect is. first hp up increases it by almost double, but the 3rd time around, you get about 300 hp. You can also build your meta stats, build up wep stats, starting weps, and quality of them between runs ( and levels ) you won't get far if you die, however. so it's recommene4ed to stop back at the getsu cal hub every time you complete area 1 until you have stovked enough materials for some decent upgrades. otherwise, every run is gonna be " your first run " I still highly recommend this - it's early access bc they wanna polish it up. PC stuff   - Vsync in options-  Various settings for garphics liek AA, Bloom, textures, etc- UNLIMINTED - framerates (  supports UW and maybe 4K,.  ) Runs nicely for me, smooth and not-too-bad loading times. _childDocuments_.review: 8/10 GetsuFumaDen offers a unique take on the “dead cells” roguelike formula with splashes of dark souls influence. The graphics/art and music are of very high quality and most of the gameplay is also. Some of the combat systems, upgrade mechanics and other features take a while to understand the nuances of (perhaps they could have been explained better in-game). Weapon and character unlock currency accumulates slowly, drip by drip. After completing the first difficulty and attempting the next higher the game transforms with a significant spike in challenge. Defensive first focused parry and retaliate strategies become a lot more powerful and useful. I think this is a nice touch but I could see some people being put off by it as you basically need to relearn how to play the game. There are some components of the game that do not feel finished or fully worked out. The upgrade trees on a lot of equipment are way too situational. Sometimes its hard to differentiate interact-able foreground items from the background. Additionally, the final boss seems to be lacking in its attack pattern. Overall, this is a great game and worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Obviously (and possibly "rightfully"), this'll be compared to Dead Cells.  I'll try to judge the game based on its own merits, but Dead Cells comparisons will of course seep through.  Bear in mind, I have only cleared 3 stages, so this will be a general overview.  And to be fair, I only have 30ish hrs on Dead Cells and have only cleared it on 0BC.Pros- Amazing art style and music.- The combat gameplay.  It's essentially a copy/paste of Dead Cells - 2 main weapons, 2 sub weapons, a healing potion, and a roll/dodge.  However, the main weapons are all melee (unlike Dead Cells) and have to be swapped in/out of active use (also unlike Dead Cells).  I actually prefer this setup more, having my ranged weapons as sub-weapons.  Sub weapons are basically all ranged attacks, except for some caltrops.  There's no real turret-type sub weapons like in Dead Cells, which were my favorite in Dead Cells, but don't seem necessary in GFD.  - Also like Dead Cells, the maps require exploration and have teleport nodes.  Sometimes the exploration is enjoyable.  Some maps, it's ehh...  Some enemies can be annoying and the only real incentive to explore beyond the mandatory parts is the vendor who sells mats.- Weapons have variants and have their own skill trees you need to unlock.  It's a cool idea in concept.  The execution?  I'll discuss below.- The Devour Soul mechanic is a neat take on mid-run upgrades.  Each soul you pick up (about 1-3 per stage, then 4 after a boss) cycles through 4 upgrades of main weap dmg, sub weap dmg, HP, and dropping a potion.  Afaik this and random glyph stones in stages are the only way to re-supply your healing potion.  Anyway, when a soul is highlighting one of the 4 upgrades, you press a button and it gives you that upgrade for your run.  Then it resets back to having no soul to use for an upgrade.  A bit hard to explain, but it is compared to some system in Gradius.- A really good records/archives/encyclopedia feature.- A nice tutorial section in the settings menu.- Getsu Renge (the unlockable waifu).Cons- The banking system for mats.  So, this is related to upgrade/skill tree system mentioned above.  You basically have to farm for mats.  Each stage drops mats that are used to upgrade weapon skill trees, unlock weapon plans, upgrade your character stats permanently, etc.  However, if you die mid-run, most(/all depending on the mat) of these mats are lost.  This CAN be mitigated by other permanent upgrades.  This sounds fine, actually like Dead Cells.  However, you CANNOT bank those mats towards upgrades mid-run.  You must have the required amount for that upgrade mid-run.  To compare to Dead Cells, just got a new plan for a weapon that costs 50 cells?  Well you need all 50 cells at once to unlock it, rather than bank 20 or 30 cells towards the unlock between each stage.  However, you have the option to end your run after a boss and you'll keep those 20 or 30 cells permanently.  So, you are basically incentivized to intentionally end your run in order to bank your mats just to unlock weapons, upgrade your stats, etc.  It's not a BAD system, per se, but it's not a very fun one either.  It almost seems to defeat the purpose of a roguelite/like, feeling forced to intentionally end runs just to hoard mats for upgrades.  Of course, maybe I am just used to Dead Cells' system of mid-run banking.  And the system doesn't feel TOO burdensome, since early stages are not too big/long.- No potion refills between stages, except for the Devour Soul mechanic.  This I really dislike.  Although, again, maybe just b/c I'm used to Dead Cells' (and other games') system.  So, as stated above, 4 souls drop after a boss to "devour".  If you have 0 potions after a boss, the only way to refill just 1 use of a potion is to cycle the 4 souls (or cycle X amount) to get to the potion slot to use the soul on.  You cannot devour the soul to upgrade anything else (unless already slotted closer to the potion), and you only get 1 potion use anyway, instead of your max.  Maybe not a BAD system, again, just not what I think I like.  It does force some interesting decision-making.- Same button to pickup items and swap weapons and interact can be cumbersome in some situations.- Despite variants w/ skill trees, not a ton of weapon variety.Overall, it's a good game and is different enough from Dead Cells to give it a try.  It does incentivize some farming, rather than simply just enjoying a run.  But maybe that's a good thing?  The combat is essentially the same, but tweaked enough to where I prefer it over Dead Cells.  But the meta-progression and mid-run maintenance is definitely a downgrade from Dead Cells, imo, although it does have some neat ideas like passive skill trees for weapons.If I had to choose between Dead Cells and GFD:UM, it would honestly be a tough choice.  I think Dead Cells has better rogue-design sensibilities, but GFD:UM is just more fun to pick up and kill stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: The game was just as fun as I hoped when my friend recommended it to me. I played quite a bit and got decently far, and was hoping to finish the game in a few weeks or so. But sometime around the start of July, the game stopped working. I was confused, and took a bit of time to try and fix connection issues on my end, but shortly after looking it up, it seemed EVERYONE had this same issue. It was something on Konami's end. Why this is even an online game to begin with is baffling, as it has NO online features, yet requires a connection to play. Until the game is fixed, (which at this point is doubtful) my review will remain a negative.Edit: They released something that tries to tell you how to fix the game, but I can't figure it out, and didn't find a clear guide to tell me how to fix something like this. Tried deleting my folder in Local and in SteamApps and then verifying through Steam to re-download everything, but it still didn't work. Gotta wait for an ACTUAL fix to the game I guess.Edit 2: The hotfix notes sure didn't help me, but a steam guide from another person with this issue sure did! This steam guide helped me to fix the (404) network issue.~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~Final Review:The game is good, yes, but is unfinished and abandoned. The devs left in entrances to stages that never came out, and the difficulty only goes to four flames rather than the expected six flames, (because the flames are in the hands of a statue with six arms.)After a few runs, it quickly becomes apparent that enemy variety is severely lacking, as you see almost all the enemies in the game after running through the base difficulty, and only see an additional miniboss after a new difficulty, and three after getting to the final difficulty, in addition to repurposed traps in all stages.The meta progression is alright, but certainly needs a second look to allow for more ability to diversify, not to mention you need materials to upgrade your weapons, but only really need 5 specific materials that are used in almost every upgrade for any weapon, (ex: ghoul bones, greater demon fang, holy dragon bones, and some other ones). By the time I beat as close of an end as this game had, I had about 500 materials of all types except those 5 or so, which were the useful ones.For the spirit materials meta currency, they need a buff in drop amount I believe, because I had to run through the game so many times to get enough to max out the basics of health and damage for the final difficulty. It felt almost required to do so since my damage before those upgrades felt like I hit a brick wall, and any damage I would take would leave me at 1 health.Overall, the game is fine at the lower difficulties, but quickly becomes repetitive at the later difficulties. This definitely isn't worth the base price, so try and get it on sale for around $10 or go through a different site to get a cheap key, (I got the game through ♥♥♥ for about $4, just make sure you get a GLOBAL steam key, very important.)

_childDocuments_.review: Bought it to give Konami a chance (rather, a slap to wake them up from their pachinko, mobile and slot machine madness) and what do you say, I'm not disappointed at all!I am actually new to the rogue like / lite genre (not Castlevania/metroidvania though, which I grew up playing) and I haven't played Dead Cells, which everyone says this game borrows a lot from. _childDocuments_.review: Having to post this review breaks my heart. While I don't hate this game I am changing my review to a negative because of all of the wasted potential. On April last year this game was announced on a Nintendo Direct and got an Early Access release later that Spring. I was really hyped for it since I am a big fan of the original Getsu Fuma Den and almost immediately bought it once the Early Access begun. While it was really crude back then I had high hopes for it since I was expecting it to improve massively once it reached version 1.0.The game still feels unfinished and in fact didn't change much at all from version 0.4.10 which released last November. I wouldn't be surprised if this game didn't receive the attention Konami had hoped and cut funding to the team forcing them to release what they had instead of taking their time polishing and perfecting it.So how's the gameplay? Well this game is compared by everybody to Dead Cells and for good reason. However it doesn't manage to get even close the same amount of quality as it since it falls victim to many mistakes that other roguelikes overcame years ago. The combat is slow and methodical, which isn't a bad thing but you'll soon realise how cheap the enemies are. In just the first level there's these statues that throw rocks through walls and these giants with hammers that can drain half your health bar in two hits and even combo you. I think the devs knew this since if you play on Apprentice mode, the easy mode of this game, this enemy doesn't spawn. This however feels like a rushed solution to the problem instead of actually balancing them. This wouldn't have been that bad but there's a lot of them sometimes there's two next to each other or they're standing on a very tiny platform, making them harder to hit that they have to, which brings us to the next point: The randomised level design isn't that great because the level usually boils down to being full of tiny corridors and cavings that lead nowhere. Upgrading takes a long time due to there being way to many materials which forces you to mindlessly grind. This was probably done to pad the game. This also nullifies the other playable characters, especially if you grind Apprentice mode since they don't spawn at that difficulty and by the time you unlock them Fuma is already too powerful to drop. Also, they don't offer much variety since they're not too different from him. Renge is just a faster and weaker Fuma.Included in the Deluxe edition is a soundtrack, artbook and a copy of the original game but it's a waste because it isn't translated to English. However there's a guide on Steam telling you how to pach the game yourself but unfortunately playing it like this disables achievements.It baffles me that the devs put so much effort to the graphics and soundtrack of this game but the gameplay is so amateurish and dated. I can only hope that there will be future patches which fix and add to the game, or even better the devs use the assets for a Getsu Fuma Den remake or Metriodvania sequel, but I am not expecting too much from Konami.Before I begin can I just say what a great idea this game is? Never in my wildest dreams was I expecting Getsu Fuma Den to get revived. However, unlike the original game, which was a 2d metroidvania, this game is a roguelike with metroidvania elements, much like Dead Cells.Pros:The artstyle, I love itThe gameplay is really enjoyable and I can see myself sinking a lot of hours into this, even though I don't play roguelikesThe game is still very early on but what is here lays the groundwork of a very deep and expansive gameBy buying the early access version you get the original game for free (though it's only in Japanese), a soundtrack and an artbook that you can find in the steam download folder of the original game (go to Steam/common/Getsu Fuma Den not Getsu Fuma Den FC). These bonuses will be available in future as part of the deluxe version for a higher priceCons:The translation is very rough in some places as of yetThe menus are very cluttered and kinda unintuitive. Especially the upgrade menuThe balancing of some of the enemies is a bit off.

_childDocuments_.review: Action plateformer roguelite. Very similar to dead cell if you have played that.You traverse procedurally generated maps with their own gimmicks and cast of enemies while aquiring new main and sub weapons to increase the power of your character over the course of your run. You can also increase your stats or aquire more health potions with a progressive upgrade system. In total, a run will span over a total of 6 stages (5 since one is only really a boss fight). For the second and third stage, there is currently one alternate path to take, featuring their own gimmicks, enemies and boss fight.Pros:-The game looks and sounds fantastic. It's honestly jaw dropping-Upgrade system during a run is interesting, and i'd argue that in concept i like it more than the scroll system in dead cells. The balance feels a bit off though and i think you'll always want to focus on hp and then maybe a few points here and there if you are not in needs of potions.-Combat overall feels good, i like most of the weapon types, running and jumping around is satisfying. I don't mind that some moves leaves you grounded and unable to dodge as it adds an element of risk. It's a bit janky sometimes but ill exlain it more in detail in the con section.-Combat is pretty in depth once you figure out all the different mechanics. You can interrupt and do massive damage by attacking when the enemies would strike (called a flash in game), you can dodge roll, you can use break specialized weapons to put enemies on their knees for a one shot kill (or like a huge chunk of the hp bar on bosses) which also rewards you with weapons. It's cool.-A decent amount of content overall, nothing bad or great. For an EA release it's pretty good.-Overall a very solid foundation which should only get better during the course of it's EA.Cons:-Feels too grindy overall and is really punishing due to loss of all resources on death. It does get better on the third difficulty and you don't really need much at first but yeah. The grind is rarely not in the back of your mind when playing this game in it's current state. It's by far the worst aspect in this game.-This is subjective but this game meta progression being mostly based around passive stat upgrade or benefits for future run isn't that interesting. It just leads to enemies being stupidly tanky as you climb up difficulties until you get some points in the right upgrades so in the end... it doesn't really add anything but mindless grind for something that doesn't feel particularly exciting when unlocked. You simply catch up with the new difficulty. -Bosses are cool... but are overall pushovers. Especially the ones with breakable parts because they break far too fast and paralyze the bosses. Stuff like centiped (2nd boss) or even the spider (4th boss) usually last longer because they do not have breakable parts. I'd like to see the boss get stronger/faster as you climb difficulties or some changes to be made. Currently once you have finished the regular stage on higher difficulties you might as well consider you are done with the level.-Some mob hitboxes are really weird. They linger too much, it doesn't feel like they hit you at all or it just feels they are not made of progressive hitboxes (the mace onis for example) but rather instantly cover all the way.-I feel dodge rolls and weapon special parries could help with more active frames as well. Once i understood how flash worked i didn't even bother with regular counters much, outside of the umbrella one which seems to result in a massive break damage output. For the katana weapon it felt rather pointless.-For keyboard + mouse users i feel that looking up and down with the camera needs to be added when you keep rpessing up or down on top of having their own binding. It could be a opt in or out option.-Gestion of ledges can be a bit annoying and is really one of the main aspect in the control i don't really enjoy. Too often some enemies are on some very tiny ledge and you want to dodge roll behind them when they attack... but you end up falling, or climbing up in a bad spot. Even just dropping of ledges sometimes is annoying because you want to fall and move in the same direction of the ledge, but it's so permissive you end up climbing back up. I dunno, maybe it's just a nitpick and bad enemy positioning but it was really frustrating sometimes. Kinda the same with enemies on small area with a crawl space. Often you will just dodge roll behind them only to find yourself rolling under the crawl space when all you wanted was to get behind the enemy.-Procedural generation could help with more tiles as you can see the repetition pretty fast even in the same levels, and it often leads to dead ends with no enemy or chests.-Parasite condition is too strong, it pretty much destroy the game difficulty by providing an infinite healing source.-The first area and 2nd fire area seems to pretty much share the same layout, but one is about going downard while the other is going upward. All the other maps area have their own gimmicks and layouts so it sticks out like a sore thumb. Basically the second map feels like it has no real gimmick going for it on top of giving a really cheap feel to what is not very representative of the game, i'd like to see some sort of trap or gimmick added to the stage and more distinct layouts to differenciate it.-No qwerty supportm i; french qnd i; tired of hqving to chqnge ;y keyboqrd region zhenever i plqy q gq;e due to q lqck of the bqsic option thqt is chqnging directionql inputs. Thqnks for understqnding. Qnd yesm i; hoping this nonesense gets the point qcross.All in all it's a pretty promising game, but with some minor and major faults i'd like to see fixed during the ea period. I thoroughly enjoyed my time with it and will come back to it whenever it gets some major content update to see how it evolves.

_childDocuments_.review: GetsuFumaDen : Undying Moon is an incredible game full of charm. You actually CAN'T be wrong with this artstyle. Everything is colourful and reminescent of Ukiyo-e art and it feels like you're actually playing in a living painting.The gameplay is pretty addictive and it could remind some things from Dead Cells, but I pretty much hate this comparison. Does a roguelite platforming action game always have to look inspired by Dead Cells? I guess not.For a simple approach, let's make this true for a moment. GetsuFumaDen is a japanese Dead Cells, slower paced, but still incredibly violent in the combat approach. It feels methodical, orgasmic, just to see burst of blood coming from your foes and the sound effects add a lot to your enjoyment.You get to play with numerous main weapons (Katana, spear, huge club, dual blade...) and secondary one (Bow, canon, kunais, bombs...) and you have to make your way through different levels in order to get better equipment and SOULS. Souls are pretty much mandatory to your success, as you'll need to devour them to power up different stats for your character (which are Main attack, sub attack, health, and potion).This is pretty much a classic roguelite but the complexity is that it's not really a beginner friendly roguelite to recommend to anyone. Dying in this game results in the player losing almost everything he earned in the past run. To counter that, you'll get the choice of going forward to the next level OR leaving the realm and going back to the Getsu camp, the latest will stop your run and you'll have to go through the first levels again but at least you'll keep everything you earned.There's a lot to say about this game and I can't cover all of it, but as a huge roguelite fan, and a newcomer to the GetsuFumaDen series (never had the chance to play the first one on Nes before that), I'd say the game can be extremely fun if you can endure (too much?) all the farming, because the progression is actually REALLY slow and upgrading weapons will take you hours.Also I have to point out that the platforming section is pretty rigid, sometimes you can't position yourself correctly next to an enemy because the platforming you're on is really small, the jumping ability is way too oldschool to be classified as enjoyable. But after a few runs, it will feel natural to play the game.That doesn't mean it shouldn't be addressed for potential buyers though.I'd totally recommend the game if you really want to play a game with good aesthetics and simple but fun combat, but that's not a 100% YES as the game has some issues with progression and platforming sections. This is Early Access though, I hope the game will improve a lot, because that could be a really good title to have in your game library. :)

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve successfully completed a full run of the game now at the base difficulty so I feel okay giving a verdict on it now. This is probably my favourite roguelite since I dumped 100 hours into Dead Cells on the Switch. And that makes sense. Structurally this game is very, very Dead Cells, right down to the controls, map structure and how the different biomes are linked together, etc. Combat feels (and looks) great and there’s a wide variety of weapons to experiment with. Naturally for a game like this there are plenty of different weapon combos and synergies to discover and aim for that can change the course of a run. Where the game distinguishes itself from Dead Cells (besides the phenomenal art and theme) is how it handles weapon unlocks and upgrades. First you gather enough materials to unlock the weapons as possible drops throughout a run, and then in your actual run you will get the chance to upgrade the weapons for the duration of that run. I found it engaging enough to keep me pushing to explore more of the map rather than just search for the exit and leave for the next biome. During a run you will also collect the souls of certain elite enemies (or as drops from larger chests). Consuming these souls grants you a passive boost to either your main weapon, sub weapon, health pool, or grants you a health potion. You don’t get to pick, however. Holding one soul then consuming it boosts your first stat (main weapon damage). Holding two then consuming them boosts your second stat (sub weapon) and so on so forth. It’s an interesting risk vs reward system that has you constantly considering whether to use the soul now or hold out for more to get some more health or generate a health potion for yourself. It’s also a super fun system to game and make yourself super powerful with. Eventually you’ll find patterns that work best for your play style and find that your able to upgrade in certain ways to take down bosses that uses to be challenging in mere seconds. It was a super fun and satisfying progression curve. I think a lot of people on the surface will look at this game and write it off as a Dead Cells clone and move on. That would be a mistake in my opinion. There’s enough engaging content here to make it worth giving a go, especially if you nab it on sale. The one slightly negative I would have to say is that the platforming is not quite as tight as I would like it to be (here Dead Cells far outshines this game), but it never detracted from the experience for me personally. And finally, give whatever artists worked on this game a damn raise. This is far and away one of the best looking games I’ve ever seen. It looks like a Japanese painting in motion, and it’s genuinely breathtaking at times. This game will definitely be towards the top of my top 10 at the end of the year and I will be sticking with it through the further difficulty levels going forward. PS: It plays absolutely flawlessly on Steam Deck if that’s a consideration for you.

_childDocuments_.review: 👺 It's obvious that Konami revived the old IP to use it in a currently popular genre. The budget was clearly modest, but the devs were able to squeeze the most out of it. The game is beautiful, but hellishly small. With an approach like this, this would be better off being a metroidvania (like the original). The mechanics take some getting used to, but then it becomes quite fun. The weapons are really different in use, with significant variability depending on personal preferences. The design of everything is awesome, especially the bosses (literally old paintings come to life). However, the locations quickly become dull; this lacks variability in the structure. This definitely needs content updates, which won't happen. There are complaints about the effects overload on the screen, but didn't notice this. The difficulty is quite casual, if you don’t take the higher ones, with “sponge” enemies. Don’t expect much and you’ll get 10h of nice experience, counting a few grind trips, but even a couple of hours more and you’ll unlock almost everything available.

_childDocuments_.review: Getsu Fūma Den: Undying Moon is a reimagining of Getsu Fūma Den, released on the Famicom on July 7th, 1987. Players assume the role of Getsu Fūma, the 27th leader of the Getsu Clan, who goes on a quest to fight various demons and other baddies in order to find his brother.Much like the original Famicom title, Getsu Fūma Den: Undying Moon is an action side-scroller featuring various arrays of Yōkai (Japanese spirits) for you to hack-and-slash through. However, unlike the original game, Konami has decided to jump on the Roguelike bandwagon with this one.Now, is the game any good? . . .Well... yes and no.When I say "Yes", I mean there is a lot of great ideas here (some of them lifted directly from 'Dead Cells'). I love the Japanese aesthetic; backgrounds/graphics look pretty good and using different types of weapons to cut through yōkai is fun. There's definitely a solid game here, but it is not without its issues.For one (well... not one); the controls feel kind of stiff, dodging can be hit or miss, some of the monsters hit boxes (and your own) feel off, some of the latter maps (I'm looking at you Misty Peak) are waaaaaaaay too large and tedious to navigate, and grinding for materials is an absolute bore. Once all of those issues have been addressed by the developer, then I would definitely recommend checking it out. Because, like I said, it has a solid enough groundwork laid out; hopefully the developer will take our feedback into account and implement some changes.

Really this game crossed the line where it was no longer profitable and Konami dropped it harder than they dropped Kojima and Metal Gear. _childDocuments_.review: Considering Konami's infamous exploits these latest years, I didn't imagine it would be possible for them to release a game with this kind of quality. The art is simply gorgeous, the animations are fluid, it plays and controls well, the music is a delight, the sound effects are cool and, despite a few negative quirks (e.g. it does feel grindy in the beginning and weapon rarity only influences drops during a run, being thus pretty much worthless and an afterthought) I had a thoroughly enjoyable time with GetsuFumaDen.The game does require a bit of patience and adaptation in the beginning, like all games of the genre, but once the player understands its systems, I found that everything flowed very well and that the difficulty was very fair in both Commoner and Veteran. Devotee, the last difficulty, is quite the challenge but in a good way. If you stuck with the game until then you should be able to understand and deal with whatever it throws at you. Some situations can be very tricky but they never felt unfair to me, with the few deaths I faced feeling due to my own carelessness and not any kind of weird shenanigans.The game is playable from beginning to end and what is there is pretty good but there are places where you can see there's still content to be added (a few torii at the end of the stages are closed, with no current way of opening them, which should mean that new stages are planned. There's also indication that the developers plan to add more playable characters, weapons and sub-weapons), so I hope the game continues receiving post release support. But, let's be honest, it's Konami we're talking about, so, I'm not holding my breath and am happy with what I already played.

_childDocuments_.review: i'd recommend this game to anyone who enjoys sidescrollers such as castlevania however this game is MUCH harder and about as long as a classic castlevania game. The more you explore the more you can scavenge for weapons, temporary power ups and material for permanent power ups or perks. You can choose to go back home to bank your materials but you'll have to start from the first stage but if you choose to go on and you die.. you'll only come back with a fraction of the material you've collected so choose carefully. _childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I have not yet beat the game on Commoner Difficulty (although have reached the final boss area multiple times)This first sentence will carry most of the weight of what this review says: The game is beautiful, but doesn't feel like that much of a roguelike, at least not right now.That said, it is very fun, and feels rewarding when you manage to scrape by and beat the Nth boss to save your mats for progression. While at first the 'lose materials upon death' progression system was frustrating, I find that it adds an extra element of thought to the game that can be pretty cool sometimes: "do you have the confidence in your acquired items and strength now to push one more boss, or will you take the guaranteed materials you've collected so far now?" Even taking that into account, however, keeping your materials on death aside, things take a relatively LONG time to unlock. This game seems designed for you to fairly easily get at least two bosses deep per run early on (as in within your first five runs), and so worthwhile progression I've found only really comes from runs that go three or more bosses deep after you get the first few "Level 1" upgrades to your character (since each area is progressively larger, it has more enemies that drop mats, etc.). If you don't, however, like grinding materials to upgrade weapons that you like (since there's a chance you won't see them during any given run anyways), the good news is that the Nameless Katana you start with each run can EASILY be used to carry you through the first three zones when upgraded (provided you use the Soul Remnants or whatnot at the end of the first boss). Be sure that what you want to upgrade is what you use resources on, however, since at least right now one third-level upgrade takes around one and a half hours or so to get, unless you're pretty quick at the game already by that point in time, which most people very well might be. This moves on to game clarity. Some people I've seen take a bit of issue with the screen clutter that can happen sometimes, generally with soul-holding enemies or in certain environments, but the only time I have occasional issues with it is when enemies overlap or while fighting the boss in Ancient Battleground (not spoiling anything else), a fight that has particularly bad visual clarity and can feel very bull-sh*t-y because of that if you let it go on too long. Overall, the game is very fun, and feels very rewarding, I can imagine even more-so on difficulties higher than Commoner, and while its visual style is a HUGE success, I think it falls a bit short on the mechanical/random event, etc. side to really call it a roguelike. While yes, it has permanent progression and yes, it has RNG in weapon/sub-weapon drops, as mentioned earlier, the latter part is largely able to be ignored if you enjoy using the Nameless Katana, it's just so consistent that unless you hit some insane high-roll main weapon, you might as well ignore the rest until you get many zones into a run. I would appreciate the grindiness of the progression being toned down a bit numerically, but losing (most) mats on death I think is fine and sometimes interesting, creating cycles of frustration/satisfaction to accompany the risk/reward of pushing further into a run. If you like AMAZING art styles, a few questionable translations, not-very-intuitive upgrade mechanic descriptions, and running through hell with a sword and a dream, I'd say it's a definite cop.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very underrated. It's a roguelike game which means if you die you start over. BUT, don't let that scare you. It took me about 40 minutes to clear the game from start to finish after my character's health and skills were upgraded. Weapons you unlock are kept, as are health upgrades, skills, etc., and each run sees you upgrading your preferred weapon for that run-through. Bosses are not terribly difficult and all in all, this game is very fun and keeps you coming back for more. The weapons are diverse, gorgeous, and very varied in playstyle. Some bits of advice:- Upgrade health and potions FIRST -- max these out- very helpful to train the skill that lets you start a stage with 5k/10k coins -- critical for upgrading your chosen weapon quickly- This game is all about amping and juicing your weapon via the upgrade dolls (you will know what they are when you play) from stage 1 down to the boss - master that and you will rip through the game.Go ahead and get it on sale, it's smooth, violent, and an absolute blast to play.

_childDocuments_.review: Getsu Fuma is quite an old game since the 80's era when the old Nintendo (Nes) was clashing against its rival: the Sega Master System. It was during the start up of the video games. And yes, the game came from that far.GetsuFumanDen: Undying Moon is, more or less, the sequel of the old Nes game. The first boss in Undying Moon is also the final boss from the old NES game. So you know that will not be the final boss, once again. So you will dig deeper in Hell to get to the source itself of all Evil to stop it. Once and for all.Thought, the game itself is quite a long journey in Hell. It took me about an average of 1h30m for finishing a winning run. So be ready for your time. Since on your first runs, you need to be careful. As you die, you will lose everythings on you. But,  fortunately, you can stop a run after each boss, in exchange that you litterally stop it and restarting anew. At least you will safely store the materials you do have gathered to upgrade yourself with permanent buffs.You kinda need it because it is not the enemies that it will be your difficulty in this game: It will be the clunky control and gameplay that you will need to fight against. I am quite serious, the clunkyness in this game can make you some mistakes which it could turn a hit from an enemy into to an almost lethal blow. As their attacks are caligraphed, it is easy to dodge them. But with that kind of gameplay, this is where the challenge reside. And whenever you finish a victory on your runs, you will unlock the new difficulty level, getting harder and harder. So far, I reached the Veteran difficulty (after 2 victory runs) and I can say that I can get myself a wipe under 2-3 hits, while the enemies are litterally tougher compared to the precedent difficulty I have done.Aside of that, the music and the art style are pretty well used. The graphic looking with the art might be cheap with the animation of our characters and enemies, but with the 2D effects, it is quite a good looking that we do forget these awkward details. In the end, GetsuFumaDen: Undying is a good game. Not perfect, but it gives a bit of a roguelike root from the old time with a touch of a modern roguelike. I do enjoy it as time to time, not passing hours on it.I say 1 full victory run can satiate your dose of the day or the half of it if you wish to do another shot.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite not playing Dead Cells (but being very familiar with the Roguevania concept and that game), I have to say I thoroughly enjoyed (and will continue to play) GetsuFumaDen: Undying Moon, and prefer it vastly over Dead Cells (but not Abyss Odyssey, which I consider as the first true Roguevania game alongside Rogue Legacy) due to two VERY crucial reasons: the art and the Japanese mythological setting. The game looks stunning with its clever use of Ukiyo-e artstyle, although the readability of the second level (Hellfire Cliff) is a bit unclear due to busy animated background. The impressive roster of level-specific enemies and bosses never gets stale, especially since you unlock harder difficulties as you beat the game on available ones (and which, in turn, add new enemies or new attacks to the existing ones, even different end levels). There are quite a few different weapon classes as well, each with its own unique moves, strengths and weaknesses, as well as sub-weapons which are mostly ranged (aside from CQC gauntlets, caltrops and passive-effect talismans). Both weapons and sub-weapons also come with unlockable passive boosts which (once unlocked) can then be activated during your run for added weapon effects/buffs.The music, while not particularly memorable, fits well with its use of traditional Japanese instruments.Finally, I wholeheartedly recommend GetsuFumaDen: Undying Moon to every Roguevania aficionado, and especially to fans of Japanese mythology.

_childDocuments_.review: Graphically beautiful and I LOVE the art style. The game play itself is perfectly fine too! But it has one tiny detail that makes this game super infuriating to play: when you die in a run, you keep almost nothing. I kept getting stuck on the boss of level 2 and I just couldn't beat him. I take far too fewer hits to die and the game is far too punishing. Even with two heals, I have gone through them both by the end of level 2. And it wants me to attain 40 of these yellow and 30 green yin/yang signs to do the first upgrade and you only get to keep 1 per run! I read online that after level 2, it all unlocks being able to save and you get to keep everything but I wouldn't know what that's like. Before I started this review, I did the perfect run: I was not hit once until the boss of level 2. And then I was defeated by the boss of level 2. It's just been 7 hours of that: getting to the level 2 boss and dying. And no real way to upgrade my stats to fix the situation unless I want to grind the first two levels 30-40 times or get good enough to defeat the level - whichever one comes first. Neither of which I have the patience for.
