_childDocuments_.review: Stranded: Alien Dawn is a game that caught my eye from the moment I heard about it. Developed by a talented team and published by an ambitious studio, the game aims to take players on a thrilling journey of survival and exploration on an alien planet. I'm happy to report that Stranded: Alien Dawn has delivered a captivating and enjoyable experience that's worth checking out.Graphics & Visuals: 9/10The graphics in Stranded: Alien Dawn are nothing short of impressive. The alien world is beautifully realized, with a diverse range of biomes, flora, and fauna that make exploration a visual treat. The character models are well-designed and the animations are smooth, adding to the game's overall polish. Dynamic weather and lighting effects further enhance the immersive quality of the game's visuals.Gameplay: 9/10Stranded: Alien Dawn offers a unique blend of survival, exploration, and crafting gameplay elements. Players must gather resources, build shelter, and craft equipment to survive the harsh environment and uncover the secrets of the alien planet. The game also introduces a variety of alien creatures, some of which are hostile, adding an extra layer of challenge and excitement. The gameplay mechanics are intuitive and well-balanced, ensuring that players never feel overwhelmed or bored.Story & Narrative: 8.5/10The story of Stranded: Alien Dawn is engaging and filled with intrigue. Players find themselves stranded on an uncharted alien world after a mysterious event, with their primary goal being to discover the truth behind their predicament and find a way back home. The narrative unfolds through exploration and interaction with the environment, keeping players invested in the game's unfolding mystery.Sound & Music: 9/10The audio design of Stranded: Alien Dawn is top-notch. The soundtrack is atmospheric and fitting, perfectly capturing the sense of wonder and danger that accompanies exploring an alien world. Sound effects are expertly crafted, from the ambient noise of the environment to the eerie calls of alien creatures. These elements come together to create a truly immersive audio experience.Replayability: 9/10With its procedurally generated world, diverse biomes, and dynamic events, Stranded: Alien Dawn offers a high degree of replayability. Players can experiment with different playstyles, tackle challenges in new ways, and discover new secrets with each playthrough. Additionally, the game's developers have promised ongoing updates and content expansions, ensuring that players will have plenty of reasons to return to the alien world.Overall: 9/10Stranded: Alien Dawn is an exceptional game that delivers a unique and enjoyable experience. Its stunning graphics, engaging gameplay, intriguing story, and immersive audio make it a must-play for fans of survival and exploration games. With its captivating alien world and high replayability, Stranded: Alien Dawn is an adventure that you won't want to miss.
_childDocuments_.name: Stranded: Alien Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: The worst thing about this game is that an early access survey pops up in game every twenty odd minutes.That being said, I really enjoy Stranded Alien Dawn.  It's your basic colony/town sim with a few novel twists.  Citizens are pregenerated rather than being RNG citizens.  The research/resource discovery progression system allows you to develop without being totally overwhelmed at first.I do wish there was an option to turn of the "wave" attacks that occur periodically.  And I wish there was an easier way to deal with colonist clothing.  That being said would definitely purchase this game again.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for fans of survival and base building games looking for something fun and polished but that may not have some of the depth/replayability of some of the genre giants. However, there is enough content to be more than worth the full asking price and well worth it on sale. Personally I enjoyed it more than RimWorld, even though there is no contest in RimWorld's greater depth.+Visuals+UI+Options, customization, mods+Variety of game modes and goals+Wide range of research+Variety of clothing/weapons/armor/tools+Variety of crops+Intuitive building and infrastructure+Variety of buildings+Animal taming+Exploration, scavenging, observation+Choices for some events/adventures+Overall balance, ability to respond/overcome obstacles-Far too few creature types-Very slow pacing-Resource gathering for buildings can be slow/grindy-Progression of recruiting survivors can be slow/uneven-Very slow research-Survivor interactions limited/uninteresting-Lacking story, character development-Custom characters only through mods, cumbersome-Heat and clothing management can be awkward

_childDocuments_.review: I've stayed up several nights well into the AM because I completely lost track of time playing SAD, I absolutely love the sims, base building, and survival games, this game blends all 3 relatively well, more than once I've described it to friends as "the sims in space(or on an alien planet) with combat and crafting"My only real gripes are that there aren't enough furniture and decorative items, there's a few you can get on the workshop but as far as I can tell none of them actually do anything and they're completely cosmetic,occasionally there's a few bugs but its nothing a quick save/reload hasn't been able to solve,I'm incredibly excited to see what future expansions/dlcs add to SAD, I'm hopeful to see new scenarios added such as or at least similar to:The Opposite of Guardians whereby you take command of the Consortium and must recapture Hope,perhaps even a multiplayer component to go along with that for all scenarios or scenarios specific to multiplayer, where each player can choose to either control the survivors protecting Hope or the Consortium, would probably need a map/seed double or more in size to the current ones to give enough space for both sides to build up a base and potentially allow for turtle-ling strategies, Also Consortium specific Characters to choose from as your human military personnel and commanders, also starting off with several defense/attack bots, but not nearly enough to take on the survivors early on.An expansion upon the existing Military and Trading outpost scenarios where you're tasked with building up larger much more elaborate versions of each, say a small town or settlement or even a city for trading, where you'd need to dedicate large sections of the map for power, farms, housing, retail/office space etc and then based on how many amenities and things are available you get a larger civilian population making its home in what you've built up,and for the military scenario,Building up a large scale installation to take on sentient hostile aliens or make peace and fight off other hostile aliens depending on respective species or faction, The Consortium or something akin to the Xenomorphs from the Alien franchise whereby hordes of highly aggressive aliens are endlessly rushing you from all directions.Aside from new or expanded Scenarios, I'd love to see: -the ability to build diagonally or even in rounded shapes-Raising up or flattening ground such as the impact sites of spaceship debris, if need be add in terraforming research as a way to learn that and then expand it to include advanced research optiions to allow for creation of other more massive projects such as rivers mountains or other such things -larger story buildings as per my ideas for new and expanded scenarios, Tunnels and bridges across gaps and expanses in rock formations and mountains, and being able to use certain sized rocks or mountains as the foundation for allowing you to build into the mountain side or on top of a mountain, Edit/additon: Glass ceilings in order to be able to construct Greenhouses as a more energy efficient way of growing plants in regions that have winter as a season or even in the other regions as a way to stop or dramatically reduce the likelihood of plant blights and diseases, automatic watering and fertilization systems, with the addition of harvest service bots and delivery drones so much of the day to day running of a base is automated why not plants too?I had several other Ideas and things I'd  like to see, will update review as they come back to me, Overall I love SAD, its been my go-to game for well over 2 or 3 weeks and likely will be for quite a while.

_childDocuments_.review: Alien Dawn has much to recommend it: a wonderfully presented world, engaging tech progression, and a wide diversity of different resources to manage. They've made good use of the 3D perspective allowing for multi-floor buildings of whatever shape the player chooses. I didn't experience any bugs, except when it came to demolishing multi-level structures.Unfortunately, Alien Dawn is also in many ways an imperfect imitation of Rimworld, right on down to the key bindings in some cases. Storage is a mess with few options and a lot of fussing and fidgeting. The ticket system for production made its way over from Rimworld, but they botched automatic priorities and the game will forget manual priorities the moment the player switches them off.Build options are sparse, suggesting to me an aspiration for Workshop creators to pick up the slack. The social system between colonists can be safely ignored and its obscure enough to be simply irrelevant. Combat is a bland retake of that found in Rimworld with challenge so mild as to make me wonder why it's in the game.I think less reliance on Rimworld as an inspiration would have benefited Alien Dawn, but ultimately this game is defined by features which feel started, but not finished; good ideas wedged into the limitations of another game's concepts. I had to check twice that I wasn't reviewing an Early Access game. Maybe this beer needed more time in the barrel.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Rimworld, get this game asap. I'm absolutely hooked. It's HEAVILY inspired by Rimworld with about 70% of the game being near identical. It also runs very smoothly. One thing I really like about this game compared to Rimworld is the fact that you have to "observe" fauna and flora before you can do anything with it or really see its info. You can't plant anything until you've found that plant in the map and observed it. You can't see an animals hunger levels, health, etc, until you've observed it. There's also a lot of QOL features that one would usually need mods for in Rimworld.
_childDocuments_.name: Stranded: Alien Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down the worst task scheduling I've ever seen in a game. You give the order to mine some stones or ore somewhere. One of your guys will walk there, which takes him a thrdr of a day to get there, then mine ONE rock and then walk that huge distance back to base to - and I kid you not - refill some wall torch. And do you know what makes this even better? He doesn't even carry the stone he just mined back to base. You have 5 furnaces right next to each other to produce bricks for a house that you're building. All 5 furnaces are done burning a load of bricks and need to be emptied. One of your guys goes to a furnace picks up ONE load of bricks out of that furnace and carries it to the construction site. Let me get this straight: They can carry 20 times that amount of bricks. If he would go to the storage and pick up bricks there, he could pick up 20 times the amount he's carrying from that one furnace. Why doesn't he pick up the bricks from the other furnaces RIGHT beside him? Why doesn't he refill and start them before carrying the bricks off?The NPCs are so SUPER frustratingly bad programmed it will make you pull your hair out. They have absolutely no ability to plan ahead, e.g. "Will I be hungry when I arrive at the location where I have to work so that I will immediately turn around when I get there to go back to base and eat something? Should I maybe eat something now?". They are in complete ignorance of their surroundings when working on a task, e.g. the example above with emptying just one furnace although several others are next to it that could be emptied too.The option to give direct orders to one of your NPCs doesn't help much either. From what I have observed, after doing a couple or even just a single task of the things that you've given a direct order about (e.g. pick berries of 10 bushes), the NPC has a chance to just ignore your order and keep on doing what he wants to. To use the example of the 10 berry bushes, an NPC may pick the berries off of 3 bushes or so and then leave. Bizzarly that "check to see if the NPC wants to do something else" only happens after finishing a progress bar, but not while that NPC is working on a progress bar. So an NPC that has simply chosen on own to research a certain project, which takes a long time to finish the progress bar, may stay at the research table until he's "ravenously hungry" or sleepy to the point of almost fainting, which can easily be 12 ingame hours, but when you give him a direct order to, let's say build that last 10 walls of your vitally important defensive structure, he may just wander off (literally to take a walk or play an instrument for recreation), after finishing 3 walls in maybe 20 ingame minutes. THE DESIRE TO PLAY THE DIDGERIDOO IS NOT AN ACCEPTABLE EXCUSE TO DISOBEY ORDERS!This game is SO super grindy, but not because you have to do a lot of action A to be able to afford object B, but because there's just SO MUCH useless overhead due to the sheer incompetence of your NPCs task scheduling.  Other things that are badly implemented are the moral system and the research tree. The issue of the research tree is pretty simple: You'll be done with all research after about 1/4 of the time you need for a playthrough. Very rarely you'll stumble on a special research project when doing exploration, but that is really rare. In 18 hours of playtime that happened 3 times to me and it took about 15 minutes in total to research these new research projects. The moral system is another thing that looks good on paper but is badly implemented. In short: Your people will sometimes just lose it and have a mental breakdown during which they are uncontrolable no matter what you do. Your NPCs can have a nice bed in an air conditioned room, they can have a variety of tasty food, several opportunities (and items) to have leisure time (dart games, music instruments, sports equipment)...but then you read something like "Had a an argument with Nancy" in the details of their moral status page which impacts their moral by a value of -18 (on a scale of 0 to 100). Several of such trivialities can add up and when it pushes their moral score to a value below 20, they have a breakdown. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ TRACY, JUST BECAUSE NANCY WAS MEAN TO YOU AND THE FACT THAT YOU HAD SOUP FOR DINNER INSTEAD OF RATATOUILLE DOESN'T GIVE YOU THE RIGHT TO GO BERSERK AND SMASH OUR ONLY DIESEL GENERATOR!To summarize my review: This game isn't hard, it's just frustrating. The sheer incompetence of your NPC in executing their tasks produces so much overhead that the game progresses painfully slow. It's not relaxing either because every few minutes you'll be attacked by animals that just spawn at certain times and you'll have to manually order your NPC to go to combat stations. _childDocuments_.review: I wanted to express how much I enjoy playing "Stranded: Alien Dawn." _childDocuments_.review: I have nearly 100 hours on this game, so I can say fully with confidence: This game rocks. First off, shout out to the devs, who had been making impactful updates ones a month for 6 months straight. We got a new planet, new scenarios, new characters and abilities - and now that it's out of Early Access, it really has a ton to provide.I really value the replayability of this game. Though I fully understand the mechanics and functions of the game, each new seed offers a different layout and its own challenges therein, before even having to change the difficulty level. I love that you can randomize characters for an even bigger challenge (or advantage!), and I've pretty much started a new game with every update during early access and now just to see the full effects of it all. The visuals and design are so much fun and for the most part the survivors are smart enough to get tasks done on their own. The hierarchy system for activities is fantastic, and especially for the scenarios with larger numbers of survivors, being able to designate certain types of tasks for them makes everything really efficient. Having the survivors want to have celebrations, music nights, etc. is really nice, and I wish it happened even more than it already does. It's fun that they can also fall in love and get married - there's nothing like romance when stranded on an alien planet! The game is not without its flaws, but I would say that only rarely did any of these things annoy me enough to really be a bother. Nit-picks would be as follows:- When butchering animals with meat and hides, the survivors always take the hides back to the camp first, and not the meat, which goes bad a lot quicker/birds will eat at. It should probably be the other way around.- Speaking of, the hauling system I would say could be smarter. Expanding the hauling area when a survivor is going to pick something up would mean they have less trips to make. They can usually handle the quantity of items that are around, but they'll only go for items within a small range of their original haul unless you direct them further.- The randomized aspects can be too much sometimes: I spent nearly a year scavenging and salvaging on one map before I got any electronics, which meant I couldn't get electric items nearly as quickly. Yes, I could take a balloon, but even just a few of all the electronics bits should exist in the spawns nearish to the starting point. - More music. The one track is nice, but having some variations of it would even make a better impact. - Prioritizing activities: right now, when you prioritize multiple activities for survivors, they do them left to right, and you can't switch the order (which is frustrating). I wish there was a way to prioritize the items/actions on the map (i.e. constructing something, tailoring something, salvaging, etc.) so that survivors who have it marked as a priority will just get it done first, and then default to their hierarchy. Overall, a fantastic game you can play over and over again, and knowing even more updates are coming, one that will always have something new and exciting for you to explore and experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Stranded: Alien Dawn is that rare gem of fluid base building, colony management, and a bit of tower defense. My four survivors crash landed on an alien world. Three of the four were happy to be alive and got right to work - but Krista broke down crying and was worthless until she got herself sorted. As a father of two daughters, I can tell you this wasn't unexpected behavior. But eventually we built camp shelters, gathered the resources from our ship, and set out to explore the unknown. One of the great features of this game is how you must observe and study the alien flora and fauna before putting it to any use. This makes the early game interesting - especially on the first playthroughs when you, the player, are new to everything.Once studied, each plant and animal is well described, allowing you to make intelligent decisions regarding their use as resources. This, along with the time honored Research Desk, allows you to advance your knowledge and capabilities as your settlers expand their base, building housing and defenses. And the way this game handles building vertically is, for the most part, intuitive and simple to implement. In fact, I found the user interface as a whole very intuitive and easy to work with. You might benefit from a few YouTube tips and tricks videos here and there, but for the most part you won't need them. Regarding performance and appearance: this game is streamlined and ran perfectly for me - something many other games can't boast. And the landscapes are highly attractive - both colorful and varied enough to be appreciated. While no game is perfect, this one offers a complete and enjoyable package for the base building enthusiasts who have enjoyed Rim World, Going Medieval, and the like. My only complaint - and it's a minor one - is that sometimes the end-game pacing can seem too drawn out. My colonists have built everything they need, have all the food and resources they could want, but now I have to wait in-game days or weeks for the end conditions to trigger. In this regard, each playthrough overstays its welcome - but only marginally. And I found this to be the case for each scenario, including Crash Landing, Trade, and Military. Having said that, though, this game offers three very satisfying scenarios; and each scenario feels like it has a beginning, middle, and end. I much prefer this to open-ended forever games, or games where the end takes soooo long to achieve, it's just not worth it. There are too many games, and too few hours in life. But, for the most part, Stranded: Alien Dawn respects your time and effort.In the end, my base was built, my colonists survived (though some were slightly scuffed along the way), and there is a great little recap at the end of each scenario which highlights key moments of your journey. I am very thankful I found this game, and hope others find it as enjoyable as I did. 9 / 10 for me - well done![Next, I have to see if my colonists can survive the desert. Maybe under a different moon. And for goodness sake, will someone please cheer up Krista!]

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, first things first! I really like the concept of this game! I've enjoyed Rimworld and thought "Hey, what an experience it would be to have something similar, but with a more 3D world"? And here we are. Tl;dr: + Good game-play, + Good base building  - Character development/interaction - Enemy varietyOverall, Recommend, but recommend more with sale. Looking forward to future with game.I like the fact that there is character backstory and personality, and that this affects game play. I recall I had Jayla turn into Layla and thought it was a bug, turns out she just has DID and that is a game play mechanic. Quality work there. I enjoy base building too. It works, I have no issues, and it is fairly customization in terms of sizing. In one game I built a sprawling fortress of wood, and had trouble defending it, in the other I built nano-carbon bunkers and was safe from everything from giant bugs to nukes - not that there are nukes but you know. Some improvements I would like to see would be echoing other commenters. FOR THE LOVE OF ... why have a wedding arch in the game when everyone constantly hates each other? There is no point... like is there a potential for double beds and children in the future - sort of a biotech moment? Would love it if so! But if not, there needs to be a revamp for the social system. In addition, MORE ENEMY VARIETY. In my first game I saw and fought every  enemy in the game. I enjoy them, they can be challenging, especially in large numbers, but if there is going to be random waves of enemies, it would be nice to have more of a mix of animals, OR perhaps attacks from other "colonists" or tribals on the planet perhaps? Just something to spice up battles. Those are my two main gripes, but overall I do have over 40 hrs on this game for a reason. I recommend it, and even more so with a discount. Would love to see mod support or just additions to the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Its a decent game that falls short of good. If you have played Dwarf Fortress or Rimworld this is similar. For example happiness, a survivor wakes up after a full rest, eats a meal, relaxes a bit, heads off to work in a great mood. At the end of the day though they are approaching a mental breakdown. The morning buffs have worn off, and they have grown a bit hungry, tired, and now its dark out.As you progress it feels like you should be able to accomplish more with less direct work, but with a few exceptions it just gets worse. _childDocuments_.review: The similarities to Rimworld are fairly obvious, but I think the game managed to miss the points of Rimworld that make it great.In stranded dawn, you are in control of a handful of not randomized survivors, that dont really have any real personality besides being fussy eaters, and constantly choosing to wear summer clothes when its cold outside. Them breaking down has little to no impact on the game, and is largely forgettable. They will also occasionally catch an illness, that will also lead to nothing dramatic. Nothing seems to be an urgent matter at all in the game, so much so that Im not sure its possible to lose.This is what they did wrong when making a 3D Analog of Rimworld, Rimworld gets all its flavor from its pawns. Randomized, often snapping for insane reasons, having personality, getting addicted to drugs, being filled with bloodlust to where when they snap they will kill their fellow pawns. They will have conversations about things in game and have differences leading to potentially violent escalations. They can catch a cold and have a real risk of dying from that cold, even after spending the whole time in a hospital bed. In battle they can savagely beat the limbs off another character in hand to hand combat in a trance state. All Flavor adders that Stranded: Alien Dawn lacks.It really feels more like a more simple resource management and colony simulator style game, no real risk, pretty relaxing, with fairly trivial waves of bugs to fight and uninspiring building mechanics filled with limitations.Its still a game I enjoy playing and probably will still play in the future considering Mods could probably greatly enhance the title, but its a far stretch from the amount of detail, suspense, and joy Rimworld has.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has so much potential but is ruined by mind-boggling terrible decisions. The way the power/tech and clothing/temp systems are handled are great and interesting. But it doesn't matter because the beginning of the game (or at least the survival scenario, the one every game of this genre focuses on) is so horribly balanced that it becomes seriously unfun. The primary issues are the way things are paced, the terrible AI, and the uneven balance between you and enemy NPCs.The biggest issue is how slow you move. So many items, buildings, etc require a ton of resources and upwards of 6 to 18 hours to build. That's fine... except it takes that much in additional time just to walk. It should not take 1 or more hours to travel small distances. A small settlement of 30 tiles should not take 2 hours to walk from edge to edge. This becomes further compounded with the atrocious AI which will be working on one thing but not continue doing the same thing right next to them but instead walk across the entire camp to work on another (similar) thing.. before walking back. There's no internal logic of priority or time with the AI. And if you slow yourself down by minimizing spread of planning, like structures, you waste tons of game-time that could have been spent more productively.The AI is so terrible, you can select a SINGLE animal to hunt, the NPC will go attack it.. get attacked by.. get a literal papercut ("superficial bite"), and try to run to a bed to rest... while the NPC is still alive and attacking. On the other hand,  your base can be under attacked and a non-drafted (not directly controlled) npc will randomly decide to fight the BIG insects.. bare-handed. Without being attacked, while behind walls. Any form of healing is more baffling because the game will try to heal non-life threatening people while someone with their guts spilling out is told "good luck". Which, going back to the horrible walking speed of the game, a bleedout time of 5 hours is a death sentence.Fighting enemies is so terribly uneven it's just unfun. You can build walls and towers, but people on towers can't shoot at 90% of the enemies at the wall because they "can't see" them. Sometimes random plants will block YOUR LoS of enemies but THEY can see/attack you just fine. There is no stunning or instant-killing of enemies, you have to deal 100% of HP to kill them. But they CAN stun/knock-out you or INSTANT KILL you by pure random rolls. Hey, that'd be a cool feature.. if the game was centered around a PRESET roster of characters. Which means there's a very limited amount of people you can recruit, let alone actually find and get into your camp. And losing 1 person out of 6 or 7 people by literal random chance is absurd and effectively ends the game. Especially when finding new people is a random chance that isn't even uncommon, it's straight rare. There's one setting that ups the chance to get your first 2 additional people and that feels like a necessity with how absurdly low the chance is. This is even worse because the "armor" barely offers any protection despite the length of time it takes to make any of it, enemies usually attack at night (lol good luck ever hitting them before you unlock high tech light sources), but THEY have insane armor that makes non-guns practically useless... especially when bows and crossbows have insanely low range that the ranged enemies outrange. Because of course.TBH 7 people in your base is already pushing it. Because, again, the walk speed is so damn low that building shelters/houses for more than that would make your town/base unfeasibly large time-wise. Which only lightly touches upon how long it takes to build structures (very, very long).I'm sure the game becomes painfully easy when you can access the high-tech stuff like a base of automated turrets and mechs. But GETTING there is unfun.

_childDocuments_.review: What if you combined The Sims with a survival game in an alien setting? You get this, basically.The thing I always disliked about survival games is that they're massive time sinks/wasters, because YOU have to do everything yourself. Here, you only do the planning, and other people do the job for you, which is great, if they actually do what you want them to do, which is where the Sims aspect comes into play.These people are morons, absolute, and utter morons. They'd rather starve to death than actually eat an emergency ration or fix themselves a quick meal if they think that ANYTHING you've told them to do is higher on the agenda, like smelting metal or sewing shirts. No, you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you don't need to work until you die, and just because I told you NOT to eat the emergency rations, when there's plenty of food available, in an EMERGENCY you can, of course, eat them!What I'm saying is: the game can be intensely micro-management-heavy. I had 6 survivers by the end, and everything was working, but I still needed to micro-manage quite a few tasks, like ... closing and opening a window, you know, things you'd think somewhat intelligent beings would do "on the fly". The whole window situation is crap anyway. These people can eventually research a nano printer ... and make windows out of carbon, instead of putting some damn glass in their windows, so they can have a look outside and feel happy WITHOUT freezing to death. (The nano printer is encased by glass, by the way).But in all honest, the game is good fun for at least 10 to 20 hours. My only problem is that I do not feel the desire to continue now. I've researched everything, I have a giant battle mech that can single-handedly deal with any threats, I'm more than self-sufficient, the only real danger now is stupidity and age, since apparently the only thing left to do is wait for a space ship to rescue me. So far I had one come by that offered to take ONE of my guys away, which I naturally declined, because if one leaves, everything will go to ♥♥♥♥, and I don't want to end up with less and less survivors. It's all or nothing!The other 2 available scenarios have you construct a trade hub or a military outpost, but apart from a few scenario-specific things, there's not much different from the survivor scenario. At least, not at first glance, so nah ... there's also another DLC scenario, but the reviews are mixed, and it's quite expensive!So, my suggestion is to just take it all in in 1 game, then let the game rest for a while, and if you feel like it, you can return to it later, test out a different scenario, other survivors, other maps and challenges, higher difficulty, etc.

_childDocuments_.review: If you think Stranded: Alien Dawn looks like "Rimworld, but 3D graphics," you are not far off. That is more or less what it is. If you have played Rimworld (itself a kind of "Dwarf Fortress, but 2D graphics"), you'll feel right at home with the interface and how to get stuff done, some of the gameplay challenges, and overall vibe.However, Stranded: Alien Dawn lacks the scale, depth, and polish of Rimworld. S:AD has simpler systems, smaller game areas (there's no real planet map, just your local crash area), and a much smaller array of everything, from the tech trees to survivors to resources, critters, and things to do. You will end the game with a much smaller number of survivors. The systems feel less precisely balanced. S:AD is flat-out easier, too (though not "easy", particularly as you are learning the specifics of the game) since there's less to manage and balance as a player.The biggest disappointment is the standard endgame, which is absurd: your survivors are rescued, one at a time, slowly (over many days). This removes the survivors from your base and world (with all their gear) while you face wave after wave of critters. The first time you experience this, you will almost certainly lose. But once you know it is coming, you just have a lot of tedious tooling up and building to do so you can "wait it out". Personally, I just quit once that part starts.Ultimately, I'd describe Stranded:Alien Dawn as a more casual gaming Rimworld-ish experience. That's not bad, and arguably worth it: Rimworld itself can be kind of insanely long and deep. Stranded: Alien Dawn, as a lighter experience with 3D graphics that you can complete in a few nights seems like a win to me. And unlike other promising contenders, S:AD is finished, complete, and playable. Recommended with some reservations.

"As the army of scarabs are on the warpath, they come across somethingthat caught their attention. A small wooden house made of wood, which appears to be an easy pray for some fresh meat. As they approached, they suddenly sawtwo of the windows open up, immediately follows byan volley of arrows and lasers. As they pushed forward, closing in on the house, two more windows slammed open. _childDocuments_.review: I strongly recommend this game.If you are like me a person that is used to survival city builder (Banished, Planetbase) and someone that appreciate interaction between its characters (This war of mine) you should play this game. I'll tell some points that marked me, you'll choose if they are relevant to you or not1) Base buildingIn this game, you need to craft your base, litteraly. Its not "i build a kitchen" and all the module are inside, no. You have to take into account the size of the kitchen, the technology used inside (warmed with wood? Electricity?) the localization of the kitchen, because the warmth it produce will be useful to other room... Or a pain to other room. And of course you need to store the food you produce, in a cool place, but also a place that isnt too far away so your character dont waste too much ferry timeTo be improved : As on any production device, its too complicated for me to know what will the kitchen produce, there is something like 20 meals (i love it!) with 20 recipe (i love it!!) but you have to make a list of priority of the things to produce, and something need ingredients that needs themselves to be crafted... And your character wont do this crafting so kinda all of advanced meal will be often undoable2) Characters buildingSome are interested in some domain and will increase their skill very fast, it is simple but efficient and allow you a bit of RP. Plus, if they do the stuff they like (lets say combat) they get a positive modifier (+18), if they do this a lot, they get the state "euphoria" that make them even more efficient. To be improved : I would add more negative and positive trait (yet manageable) to force the player to think the best way to have the most efficient crew. Today you can quasi ignore the things your characters like3) DisastersThats the bad point to me. Not that the disasters arent a good idea but you have no visibility on the time they'll last (which isnt illogical in beginning of game, but less after a few years) and there is no good command toggle, like on planetbase, to tell your characters to go out of the base or in (for example). During "toxic ashes" your character will suffocate if they go outside, but their chores are outside, so you need to manually gather them and force them in your house. During exceptionnal heatwave, if you are a moron like me and have no air conditionner, you want them to spend time outside (it would be interesting to be able to have a modifier for places in the shadow outside)4)  Characters interactionLets not lie; its a work in progressFor now your character like or dislike each other, but i dont really feel any differences in their treatment of othersTo be improved : Give more tastes to human relation. GRRMartin said "the only think writing about is worth is the human feeling". That would make the difference between a good and a extra good game to me5) Tech treeAs often, the tech tree is too fast (you can basically have carbon laser sniper in two years, starting from scrap) but its not really a problem to me, it might be to hardcore fans. Maybe it would be interesting as in XCOM or Ark to add more "tiers" in technologies (Craftman (wood => stone)weapon) / advanced craft  (iron => steel) weapon and tools  and so on. This way youd progress all the time but wouldnt go from zero to big laser warrior hero in a pair of year6) ObservationThe big deception, i think you should be able for the animals as for the plant to know what they produce, and how to exploit them (yes im capitalist)..To be improved :  Domestication of animals and breeding is a must go6) My opinion as for nowThe game is expensive, absolutely unfinished. There is not a lot of bugs. And as you can see my opinion is very positive, why?Because the roots of the game are very good, the ideas behind it too. The team is active and we already had an update (a new map). I think the best idea would be to wait 3/4 months and see if other update have be done, that would maybe make my comment wrong.TL: DR, go and buy it !

_childDocuments_.review: This is a classic survival game that is original in its genre for a variety of reasons: first, because of the strong characterization of the characters, which involves a good level of micromanagement with the goal of meeting the various needs of our crew. Second, because there are not many survival games where you have to manage a colony starting from scratch, on a generally hostile planet. The scenario, therefore, is quite good.However, there are some aspects that could be improved, of course. First of all, this game suffers from the same flaw aswell as many other survival games: at the beginning the difficulty curve is very steep, where resources are low, it is extremely laborious to procure them, and the available technologies are few. As the game progresses, as we discover new technologies, as our crew gets a few survivors, things get easier. The increased agressiveness of the local fauna is not enough to get us in trouble if we develop the right technologies (such as combat mechs).Maybe  a little more variety in approaching the endgame would be nice, perhaps introducing hostile human NPC opponents, introducing new natural disasters, in short creating new challenges when our colony is well structured and stable.In addition, more locations (planets) to colonize, perhaps introducing environments with unbreathable air that force the crew to wear, outdoors, suits and respirators, would introduce further variety, as well as more opportunity to explore the planet with small teams.Overall, however, an excellent, enjoyable game that perhaps in its current state suffers from poor replayability when all the environments have been explored.

_childDocuments_.review: Quite captivating, but nonetheless annoying and has a lot of room for improvement in term of optimization.  This is not like Banished where you can just set-it-and-forget-it.  The characters require constant micromanagement because the AI seems extremely inept at order of operations or self-preservation.  For examples:1. There is a salvage site faraway.  A character assigned to that salvage site attempts to leave camp and head to the site when they are at 50% hunger (or rest, or relaxation), so they spend half a day to walk there, then when they get there, they immediately turn around and run back to camp to eat (or rest, or relax).  AI should be optimized to know that, the character should fill up on those bars BEFORE heading out if those bars are low.2. There was a battle to wipe out a bug nest, and there are lots of carcasses laying about.  A character assigned to butcher and harvest the meat, would only butcher, but once they're done, they don't pick up any of the meat and just heads back to camp while leaving it all on the ground.  AI should be optimized to know that, if the character is going back to camp, they should simply gather all the nearby loot while they're at it.3. A character can only carry 1 type of item at a time, so if there are lots of types of items, each a very small amount, then the number of trips the character needs to take to gather all of the loot, becomes astronomically large.  Surely it cannot be that hard to code it, so that the character's Physical stat determines how much "weight" they can carry regardless of type of item.4. The in-game text is full of "engrish" and grammatical errors.  The tutorial is excellent, but flavor text in other places could use some proof-reading...5. Player-controllable units cannot shoot through ceilings and walls, as expected.  So why then is it that Hostile ranged units (Shriekers, Hummingflies) can shoot through ceilings and walls?  Something is grossly wrong with the coding here.  6. Characters with dietary restrictions, should not just starve themselves to death if their choice of food is not available given the circumstances. The vegetarians, for example, should simply suffer a Happiness penalty or something if forced to consume meat when plant food sources are scarce.
_childDocuments_.name: Stranded: Alien Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DRIf its your first survival-sim game I would recommend this heavily starting out since other games expand upon the mechanics greatly however, offer very little hand holding compared to Stranded: Alien Dawn. If you're looking for a different or unique take on the genre you might want to find something else or play Stranded: Alien Dawn i with mods.Stranded: Alien Dawn is undeniably a visually pleasing game. The alien landscapes are brimming with vibrant colors and intriguing details, drawing players into this uncharted world. While the soundscape successfully conveys the alien atmosphere, the survivors' repetitive vocalizations became a little grating over time.Unfortunately, getting used to the controls/mechanics can be a minor hurdle in the early hours. Actions often felt less precise than I'd hoped for. Stranded: Alien Dawn takes clear inspiration from genre heavyweights like Rimworld, but initially, some core systems like combat and medicine felt a bit too simplistic.The early game may feel a bit tame for seasoned survival sim fans, but the challenges ramp up as you explore and draw more attention from the alien wildlife. Be prepared to make some tough choices to keep your colony alive.Stranded: Alien Dawn boasts a captivating setting and the potential for engaging survival gameplay, but it initially feels oversimplified, and clunky controls take some getting used to. It has a burgeoning modding community, offering potential ways to customize the experience. If you're intrigued by the idea of a space survival adventure and are willing to invest time to unlock its strategic depth, Stranded: Alien Dawn may still be a worthwhile journey. However, those looking for an immediately complex and polished experience might want to wait and see how the game develops with updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Stranded: Alien Dawn

_childDocuments_.review: It's a good (but not great) game. The positive aspects are the crafting (very well balanced), the music, and the interfaces. I like that there are a lot of mods in the steam workshop to tweak the game.What I'm disappointed with is that the resource management aspect is quite easy, especially once you get through the early stages of a mission. Most things are quite plentiful and easy to grow yourself once you have observed them.The main difficulty modifiers seem to be the weather (makes it a little tougher, but pretty easily managed) and the frequency and intensity of attacks from the local wildlife. For me, the battling the animals is by far the most boring and repetitive part of this game. I wished they had focused less on the combat stuff and more on making it a challenge to find and produce the items you need to survive, particularly in the trade scenario. It feels like they went all in on the combat aspects and added the other stuff for a bit of variety but not really to challenge players in any significant way.

_childDocuments_.review: Not just 'Rimworld but 3d' but far more basic in features and stiff in how scenarios play out as well. Huge, gorgeous maps but you'll never even visit more than 15% of one due to slow movement speed and no vehicles. Lots of research and cool features, but a static RNG will lock you out of a good number of them. Static colonists with backstories, but they don't interact with each other in meaningful ways. A tiny variety of weapons and armor, structures are boring as well. There's some interesting alien species, but enemies are just waves of mostly earth bugs-but-bigger. Maybe there will be more updates later, but as far as Rimworld clones go this one is thoroughly disappointing for now.

_childDocuments_.review: A really good isometric Survival/colony management game. The technological tree could be expanded too, to add more flavour.Some stuff that requires a fix ASAP:-once you create crops you will spend a considerable amount of time repelling wild beasts, trying to eat your food. Building a fence just adds more wasted time, since the fence needs to be repaired very often. Wild lfe searching for crops should be intended as a random event imho.-your survivors will be haunted by every sort of sickness of the body and mind. Basically at least one of your survivors will be ALWAYS sick in a way or another, in a sort of rotation of pain and desperation. Recreation utilities don't seem to help that much (they don't even work at all imho...). Rimworld has a similar mechanic too, but remedies are more effective and frequency is more balanced.-strange to say but this is the first time in a game like this that crops give an enormous amount of yeld, which basically requires a LOT of space to be stored and before refrigeration basically you loose 90% of your yeld before winter comes... Some more balancing in yeld amount and time to spoil could be took in consideration.-Not sure but i think it's not possible to level the terrain. _childDocuments_.review: A game I really want to love, but just don't.It's beautiful, it has great mechanics (for the most part), the controls are pretty good (that there's no way to turn off edge scrolling is my biggest complaint!) The core of a solid and highly polished game appears to be here......but it's just... boring.There's a deep research tree, but progressing through it manages to feel both trivial and a chore at the same time, and unlocking stuff never feels like a reward, because it just means "more stuff to do" when you're already constrained by how much stuff you can actually get done with your characters.This ends up being a running theme: every bit of new gameplay you unlock ends up being a "so what?" because you're already capped on how much stuff you can fit into the schedule, and the new things are largely just the same things as the basics, so what's the point? You've already got that covered. You don't ever feel that you're progressing.Then you get escalating alien attacks that appear to have little to do with your progress and exist "just because". I've encountered no themic explanation of why a bunch of random critters spawn outside my base and attack me every 15 minutes. It just feels super gamey and immersion breaking, and rather than building tension it's just an annoyance, one you either deal with easily or utterly wrecks you.There doesn't seem to be any actual gameplay mechanism to ride this difficulty curve without tech rushing combat stuff and doing nothing else, and hoping RNG doesn't slap you with a bunch of permanent negative modifiers on your colonists that will degrade your save for the rest of eternity.None of this feels like a challenge, it just feels arbitrary and leads you to hoping you notice your already-slow colonist has randomly been slapped with a -10% speed modifier for the rest of the game before you progress too much further so that you can save-scum to just avoid having even more fun sapped out of the tedium.Oh right, tedium. Game is hella tedious. Even on max speed, everything takes FOREEEEEVER to do. Not helped by the fact that colonists will take so much time walking even the length of your base to chop a single tree of wood before immediately turning around to go get a meal, then walk back, chop another tree, then walk back again to play darts, then walk back to chop a tree, then get tired. I get it, building an efficient base is a thing, but colonists move so slowly that you need to build a full set of entertainment buildings and food stores and everything every 20 squares to stop this, and I'm already bored just writing that, let alone hating the idea of idiotic base designs to deal with gameified mechanics.And ultimately, what's the point? The game never feels like it has a point. It doesn't feel like you're telling a story like Rimworld or other self-directed experiences, nothing that interesting ever happens. I've sunk thousands of hours into games like Dwarf Fortress, Rimworld, Banished, and Factorio, and every single new save I created in those felt like it had a story, even the ones I set out with no theme or idea behind. I remember those experiences even years later.This game, I load my save from yesterday and I'm like "so, what was I doing? I dunno and I don't really care", at no point have I felt like I have even a self-imposed objective I'm working towards. Nothing at all ever feels like progress or a success. It just feels like a grind to nowhere, and then the game will tell me I've won. Or that I've died.Either outcome fills me with the same indifference.

_childDocuments_.review: The opinion that this game is Rimworld3D isn't quite wrong.  It COULD BECOME Rimworld3D, with time,attention and dedication of the dev team. It is said it crashes. But this one also takes inspiration from Space Haven, which is particularly noticeable in the menu system.  I like seeing reuseable ideas.  They do it in Metroidvanias; you pick one up randomly and you know virtually all the controls going in.  Likewise this, if you know Rimworld (I have 3600+ hrs).There are balance issues of course, and an awful lot of things that need to be done before this can be considered Rimworld3D.  But the foundation is here.  I'm in early in hopes it will help the game grow.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend this title. It's very rare that I request a refund for a game on Steam, but in this case I did.First and foremost, the game has no soul. There is no immersion whatsoever; the art and music and everything are just kind of... blah. It lacks any kind of style or character.The 'choose from these pre-built characters' aspect is a huge mistake/weakness. As others have stated, most of the characters are terrible, so it's really more like 'choose from these ~6 or so characters that are not so horribly unbalanced as to be unplayable.'The game is very very simplified and dumbed down compared to say RimWorld, DF, Songs of Syx, etc... it's a lot of prebuilts and templates. The combat is a joke, it's just swarms of alien insects occasionally attacking you, which you attempt to corral into a path where you have built some turrets to deal with them - kind of lame tower defense style. There don't seem to be intelligent races or other settlements opposing you.For bonus points, the devs have already raised a lot of red flags... If you read closely in the EA text, they say that EA will last at least 6 months." HUGE red flag - EA generally goes on for a couple of years at minimum. Then in the discussion forums when players asked about a roadmap, the devs cryptically responded that "we don't have a roadmap to share at the moment, but we can say that there will be updates coming to the game in the future." Uhhhhh yeah obviously. Holy crap do they not understand what EA is all about? Seems like they don't. If you are expecting a lot of additional content, I wouldn't hold you breath - nor do I get the impression that updates are a priority to the devs. It strongly feels like they think they basically have a complete game here, and they are just using EA to beta test for a few months and then will call it a day. (Maybe their plan is to then roll out a bunch of DLC with stuff that really should have been included in the base game?) The laissez faire attitude toward updates is especially concerning when one looks at the forums and sees the steadily increasing number of bugs and issues being reported - no way to remove spoiled food, insulation issues with doors and doorways, and issues with placing structures and objects on structures, to name a few.Oh and they are shutting down and deleting comments in the forums when they don't like what players have to say. So again I say... maybe they don't really understand what EA is all about.

_childDocuments_.review: I´m really sorry but at this moment I cannot in good conscience recommend this game. Here is why: While the overall design looks beautiful and allows an in-dept management of the various aspects of a survivor camp, herein lies the massive problem this game has - micromanagement. The camp and character management of Stranded: Alien Dawn is ridiculously complex to the point that the game is unplayable. You cannot just order your characters to do anything directly. You mark what is to do, which leads to a storage shelf marked to be emptied and deconstructed to keep standing where it stand for days (literally!), resulting in the stuff in the shelf being exposed to the elements and rot away. You enter orders to make new clothes and nothing happens for days. It says "waiting for resources", but nobody picks up the resources and makes the bloody clothes. So, somewhere in the complex chain of getting stuff from the storage, bringing it to the tailoring table and making some clothes is something missing. The problem here is that you have no idea where to start looking, which is - how do I say this nicely - ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ frustrating. The game needs a major overhaul of character behaviour and mechanics (oh yes, they behave like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ morons - run out in the cold for no apparent reason and then complain about hypothermia) as well as complete redo of tasking and commands. Also an overhaul of psychology/happiness aspect is urgently needed. For space travellers they not only ♥♥♥♥♥ about everything, but also don´t do anything about it, no matter how many toys and distractions you build for them. Happiness goes down fast and is sometimes just impossible to restore - or it stays low, leading to one temper tantrum after the next, which is just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying and frustrating. Until this is done, I cannot recommend this game and give it a 4/10 - do not buy. Sadly, given the layout, look and feel, possebilities etc. I would have given this game an 8/10, but character behaviour, controls, happiness etc. are so bad and frustrating that I have to take off 4 points. Edit: I managed to make the moron survivors to somewhat do what they were supposed to do by clearing the schedule and leaving the activity in place they are supposed to do - but that didn´t really work as they do everything else before what they are supposed to - unless you stop any and all production lines too. However, that leads to other things not being done etc. So no, no actual improvement here but a kind of workaround that comes kinda close to a solution. Again, it cannot be that making a couple of shirts takes all summer.Too bad close enough only counts at throwing horseshoes, handgrenades or thermo-nuclear weapons. 4/10 it is.Edit 2023: Since the game left early access, I though I had another go at it. Sadly they didn´t solve any of the problems I mentioned. They smoothed a bit around the edges, added some features, but the problems I mentioned remain. Well, so does my verdict - 4 out of 10, do not buy.

_childDocuments_.review: (updated 2024/10/22: Just finished my first scenario. Only thing I wanna add is that the contacting spaceship with radio bit is needlessly dragged out. one person at a time and only 1 out of every 5 or so spaceship carry passenger. I'll try the second scenario to see if the same problem persist. but even then every other problems persist. building/deconstructing is still a nightmare. the restriction, NPC action que, and AI pathing is a mess. I personally think all the restriction should be lifted, just let the players build and do whatever. it's better to play a silly game than a lousy game which is what I'm looking at.)(updated 2024/10/16: about 25 hours in I'm close to finishing my first run. and I can definitely say that the building system is a mess. this game doesn't do topography; the landscape is immutable, you can't cut or fill anything and if the land is uneven your only option is to tilt you base, which end up costing a astronomical amount of resource if you're building any sizable room if your terrain is even a little bit inclined. also, as I'll mentioned it again at the end, when connecting two room via a stairs, the stairs has a fixed incline rate so it takes a lot of fidgeting to find the right height and distance to connect two different room with a stairs. again, if you terrain isn't completely flat. and as many people have pointed out, this game have zero vehicle, not even a push cart, so your builder walk everywhere and carry everything by hand. and if that last ingredients you need is half a map away, then you have to send a worker to slowly walk over there and slowly walk back which takes half a day. I honestly don't know why there aren't any vehicle in this game, none whatsoever, it's almost like the developers came from some magical froopyland where the concept of vehicle doesn't even exist. so even though the alien theme is kind of nice, there is still a lot of glaring gap when comparing to other more developed base building simulator.)I'm only 13 hours in but by god this game frustrate me. In short, Stranded Alien Dawn feels like a weird combination of the base building genre and the sims. On one hand you have to gather resources, research technology. While on the other hand, you literally need to hold your shipmates' hand; you need to tell them what to eat, schedule their breaks, make sure they sleep well just like in the sims so that they can remain productive. And quite frankly, I'm not sure the two genre is a good mix.Lastly, one more thing to rant about before I tie this off for the time being. The base building aspect could use some work too. _childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderfully immersive gaming experience that scratches my fantasy base-building itch. Like many others, I'd liken the character-control to Rimworld and the base building to Dawn of Man, yet, the graphics and art style brings this science-fiction based alien theme to brilliantly rendered life with a good serving of The Sims realism in there too. PROS:1) Seamless and stable game play...if there are any bugs, I've not encountered any during 124 hours of exploration so far. 2) Breathtaking landscape graphics, and truly beautiful alien animal/insect designs and skins. I enjoyed the 'Observation' tasks to discover and correlate all the species in the current game world. I also love that every biome type will have a couple of different types of fauna and flora, as well as altered recipes to keep things more mixed as you play through Sobrius (Temperate Meadow), Desertum (Hot Dry Desert) and Saltu (Humid Jungle).3) Micro-management heaven: put item counts on or off and designate what can be stored on a shelf or in a stockpile, and what should not. Have fun building your base its own large storage warehouse because you'll need plenty of space to keep the vast amount of items and ingredients you will encounter.4) Research, Build & Craft everything you're going to need to first survive, and then, to thrive. There is always plenty to do here, sometimes, more than you can handle with too few colonists.5) Identify fauna and flora, then farm, cook and produce saleable products in order to conduct trade with passing spaceships, and also, to buy in anything you desperately need with the currency of Galacticoins.   6) Take care of your survivors, pets and animals with God-Like control: you can draft and move all your characters, and give them orders according to what you want them to do immediately, later or when they find the time for it in a task queue system.  7) A WINNER for me: You can turn off the attack threats as you make the choices for your initial game set-up, and play either the chilled out or fighting-tooth-and-nail-for-everything type of game that you most enjoy.   CONS:1) Character pathing is sometimes needlessly indirect, but it's not the greatest frustration if you just leave them to get on by themselves. They eventually get to where they are going, even if its not via the most direct route.2) Some of the micro-management needs a little tweaking, for eg. the animal feeding troughs. If you feed a carnivore, expect that your entire stock of 300 dried meat will end up in the trough because you can't designate half your stock to colonist consumption, and the other half to farm animal consumption. But again, only a minor frustration and there are ways to work around that. 3) The Electrical Grids and accompanying producers/users system of 'control switches' is quite complicated, and requires a vast amount of resources to build once you get to the point of trying to establish radio communication with the inter-planetary world, and beyond. Perhaps I just don't understand how to get it to cross-function or I'm doing something wrong, but it never works out correctly for me. I just bypass the automation mishugas and simply make my colonists switch stuff on and off as I need it. It's not brilliant, but it works.I confidently recommend this game to fans of base-building, micro-management, and jeopardy/combat in colonising fantasy-realism worlds. You're going to enjoy unpacking just about every aspect of this one. The developers have put a lot of love into it and it shows. It is well-worth its current asking price so I am pleased to support the on-going development of this richly created game by taking it on as one I will be buying more expansions for, as and when they are released. I'm looking forward to the onward journey.   You've done a magnificent job so far, Haemimont Games.  Regards, GQ

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for September 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before October 1st, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.Why won’t you do the job? Stranded Alien Dawn is made by the same company that makes Tropico and Surviving Mars. For Stranded, you have a squad of four characters who survive a spaceship crash and the player will decide actions that your group needs to carry out. Players might have their team observe plants, and animals, and gather resources to build shelter. It’s a typical survival game, including alien monsters that will become very hostile. However, as I played Stranded Alien Dawn, I just got more frustrated. I wanted my characters to observe a plant. Only one or two characters could do that. Scavenging was limited to a couple of characters. For most of my playtime, two of my characters sat around being idle, and the game didn’t give me clear guidance on why they did nothing. Perhaps it’s about the actual skills the characters had, but they should have had enough. There’s a huge lack of information and it became far more frustrating than anything, and before I knew it I was bum rushed by 16 beetles, who killed my team because I hadn’t researched Weapons yet and couldn’t defend myself. Admittedly, some of this will probably come from tutorials and more. But it also just doesn’t feel intuitive at all to understand what characters are thinking or wanting to do. There’s a level of micromanagement here that seems unrealistic for what the game is offering. Pick this up if you’re willing to invest a long time into the game. However, the frustrations I felt with Stranded are similar to the Frustrations I had with Tropico and Surviving Mars. It’s probably just what this developer wants to make at this point in their career. There’s a solid fanbase for this type of game, but it’s like pulling teeth just to understand what’s going on. If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: To summarize what this game is: it's basically Rimworld 3D. Everything in the game is more or less shamelessly stolen from Rimworld. I mean almost literally everything. To the point where I suspect that a lawsuit from Rimworld would have a pretty good chance of winning in court. Now, if there ever was a game you'd want to make a 3D version of, then Rimworld would be a pretty dang good choice and so this is a pretty dang good game. And Rimworld stole a lot from Dwarf Fortress in turn, so anyway...Standed: Alien Dawn is not quite as complex as Rimworld though. Those who might find Rimworld a bit too intimidatingly complex might like this one better - it is very similar but without the extreme micromanagement possibilities of Rimworld. Unlike Rimworld you cannot (as of yet anyway) create your own custom characters. Instead you have to pick from a pool of pre-generated but well-made ones. You'll ideally want at least one NPC who can fight, one who can build, one who can farm etc from start, or you might find yourself overwhelmed by aliens or starving to death. You start with 4 but can find up to 8 in total (or 10 with a recently added option). Each of course with their own skills and quirks, all got some strength/weaknesses. Like for example one guy is a real killing machine in combat, but others find him intimidating and he knows he is dying (and will eventually do so after a few in-game years). One girl is a  research genius but real clumsy with most practical matters and doesn't help out that much initially save for coming up with new inventions. One guy is a great jack of all trades but got a real bad mood and easily gets depressed. And so on. Characters can train most skills though if you let them grind enough, so this is mostly a matter for early on in the game. They also seem to be more or less compatible with other characters. Some are family. Like in Rimworld, they build up positive/negative relations with other characters. Romance is supposedly possible, though so far I've yet to see it myself.The game is nicely bug-free for an early access game. The devs should be given credit for being focused and making sure everything is running smoothly before coming up with new features. Far too many games suffer from "new creative features are fun to make, while bugs are unfun to track down and hard to fix". This game could easily have a tonne of graphics glitches for example, but there's just a few very minor ones.Graphics aren't really top priority for this genre of base building survival game, but the graphics are very nice by genre standards and I was able to crank them up quite a bit while still running smoothly on a pretty old gamer PC. There are a few minor glitches but nothing major, overall it looks real pretty, with day/night cycle, weather and season changes making the map change its look quite a bit over time.I particularly like the visual item storage system. Every single thing you farm and stockpile can be placed in piles and shelves that literally grow by one item at a time - stuff isn't just tossed in piles with numbers or some container with an inventory window. So you can literally see how much food you've stockpiled for the winter or when it is dwindling (yes there are numbers too of course). Building materials and the like is best stored outdoors underneath a roof in a shed, while more precious items like crafting ingredients and medicine is best to store on shelves inside the building.Like Rimworld, food eventually grows stale unless refridgerated or frozen. Early on you can store food in cold rooms and similar to make it last longer, before you invent electricity and fridges.You can research picking and similar preservation technologies which are handy early on.And like Rimworld, you pretty much need one of your characters to be a 'kitchen slave', cooking all day long. Well, you don't -have- to - many forms of food can be eaten raw without health consequences, but you really want the mood bonuses from food as the most efficient way by far to keep morale up. The better the cook, the fancier the food you can unlock and the better the mood bonuses.I think some of the crafting and cooking timers are a bit unbalanced. Like, a crafter could spend all day making simple smoke pipes out of dried tobacco and then the whole gang smoke that up in 5 minutes in the evening... not time well spent. For complex things like making firearms and electronics, the craft timers are better balanced.The combat system is quite crude and there's not many options. Basically rifle > pistols > bows > melee. Supposedly you should build your own automated defenses and mainly rely on those when a hostile creature attack wave spawns. But once you got your hands on a couple of sniper rifles, you can have a few of your characters solo the whole attacking horde. Initially these don't attack instantly but stands around waiting for a while before doing so (like in Rimworld...). While they do that you can have your snipers pick of a few, pull a smaller band of creatures away from the horde, kill 'em off and then repeat. This feels a bit poorly balanced and the hostile AI is dumb as can be. Well they are mindless zerg:ish aliens I guess, but still. But on the other hand you might not have the luxuary of having several combat-oriented characters and then automated defenses is the way to go.Healing skill doesn't play as big a role as it could. Unless you get completely mauled and nearly whiped out in an attack, characters can quite easily heal themselves even with poor skill. Characters with trained healing only get to shine when someone is really close to death, which doesn't happen often at all once you got the hang of defenses.Also the very detailed wound/body part system of Rimworld/Dwarf Fortress wasn't used, for better and worse. No craftable cybernetics or organ transplantations as of yet, though it smells as if this is something planned for the future.One of the very few original features of this game (as in not also present in Rimworld) is that you initially don't know anything about the alien plants and creatures. Someone with high research skill has to study them first. Is this edible, is this dangerous, what can we do with this etc. And once a plant is studied, you can grow it using farming instead of chasing it down in the wild. This is a nice system but the lack of RNG is a huge missed opportunity. Imagine if some plants had random characteristics every playthrough. Imagine if some plants were very similar and if you didn't study them you risked picking a poisonous one instead of the real. Imagine if there was a herbalist skill so that if you send Connor the mercenary sniper to gather herbs instead of Laara born a farmer, you'll end up with poison ivy for dinner. That would have added another dimension to the game but alas procedural generation of this wasn't implemented.Overall, a very good base builder/survival game. Nice new content is getting added, previously a whole new desert biome was released, as well as a taming/pet system.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent competitor to Rimworld. Good as it is now, but man if this thing had gotten more content this could have been an easy recommendation over Rimworld. As it stands, I think most people will agree Rimworld is the better game, but I can't imagine many fans of Rimworld wouldn't also like this game.Basically this is a colony sim that took inspiration from Rimworld and in many ways tried to improve or at least change the formula. There are no randomly generated survivors, instead all of them are unique characters with their own traits who when they die, die for good. This actually allows for some interesting situations such as trying to play around a character who refuses to do certain tasks, or having a limited amount of time to finish the game before a character's terminal health condition kills them. Each character also has a unique character model with every item of clothing. Compared to Rimworld, this makes it so each character has more actual "character", but it also means there can only be a limited amount of characters in the game. Every character will always be a known quantity rather than the randomness of Rimworld.In terms of general gameplay, this game has one serious advantage over Rimworld, and that's the introduction of a Z layer due to it being 3d. Height matters for construction and for shooting. Combined with the freedom you have in room construction, you can create very elaborate bases, with platforms for elevated turrets and areas where the walls will block ranged enemies from shooting in. Even the tutorial actually does a good job of showing how this can drastically impact optimal base defense strategies. Speaking of, the tutorial is overall pretty good, which is unusual for this genre of game.Other than that, there's typical colony builder gameplay mixed in with some unique mechanics. You farm crops, tame and hunt animals, build structures, do research, craft gear, cook food, and treat wounds. Where things get a little interesting is in requiring "observation" of local flora and fauna before you can figure out what to do with most of it. It's an alien world with things none of the survivors have seen (and dogs for some reason), so they have to spend some time learning about it in order to figure out uses for plants, or how to tame animals. There's also an expedition mechanic where you send survivors on hot air balloon trips to look for resources or check out sites off map, occasionally resulting in you obtaining various unique rewards such as other survivors or gear you can't craft yet.The main issue holding me back from recommending this over Rimworld to most people is simply the low amount of content. There's plenty there, but not plenty compared to Rimworld, which is still clearly being worked on. It's not clear if this game will ever get another update, but it really does not need much more in order to really stand out as a top tier colony sim. The main issue right now is the low enemy variety. There's multiple scenarios, but outside of the DLC one, each one just has you fighting a few varieties of bugs, which eventually makes having automated turrets and mechsuits feel like a bit overkill. The DLC scenario adds robots to replace the bugs, but again, it's still not a lot of variety.
