_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is already spectacular and blows away some finished retro shooters this early in early access (only Episode 1 is out as of writing - 7/16/2022). My full meandering review follows:The closest thing to this is definitely Doom Eternal, down to the double-jumping and boost-dashing, though it does not have the health/armor/ammo loop. Overall, it's very fast-paced and more vertical than actual 90s shooters - but as of writing you  use the console to lower the game speed if desired (code is "slomo 1.0" where "1.0" is default 100% gamespeed. I set mine to 85% most of the time). (and "story")Think Painkiller or Serious Sam rather than Quake or older Doom games; rarely does Turbo Overkill have enemies waiting and muttering in small rooms before you enter them. Instead, rooms where you fight are usually enormous and arena-like, with enemies warping in either all at once or in waves as you kill them. Levels are usually very big, taking me on average just over an hour to complete, but if I wasn't obsessively looking for secrets in all of them - another super important feature of 90s shooters - they'd probably take a third of that or less. The levels are just super-cool. Most of them are outdoors, in an exaggerated cyberpunk megatropolis, down to the pink and blue neon everywhere and absolutely constant (acid?) rain. One level has several rooms that appear to be outdoors, until stray bullets hit the screens that make up every wall and you can see the skybox is just a facade for hollow metal infrastructure, which you can get behind for tactical and equipment-finding purposes. Another is set on a hovering train moving through robotically-fast flying car traffic, and at certain points you're forced to ditch the train to jump from car to car. My favorite level is literally the entire Peach Trees apartment mega-block from the movie Dredd, down to the squished remains of the hobo caught in the threshold of the main blast door. Generally the levels will let you backtrack as much as you want, with only a few exceptions where there are points of no return near the end. I wish these points were a little more clearly-defined, but it didn't generally stop me from finding every levels' six collectibles (three each used to unlock one mutator mode and challenge level). Also, the levels don't do a whole lot to restrict you from speedrunning them, in terms of invisible walls or intangible ledges to keep you from climbing. It means you can easily skip rooms or go out-of-bounds to places that you're not supposed to see if you try, but I much prefer it to the alternative.Also, I was surprised to hear some dialog throughout the game, which currently consists of the player character's flying car AI, the megacorp exec who hired your character, and the main villain, the rampant AI named SYN. It's not frequent (which is better than , ), but the voice acting is the same quality you'd expect from any high-budget game.The guns each have two firing modes; some use right-click to quickly transform the gun from one mode to another, but most use right click to fire a different projectile that takes a long time to recharge, temporarily locking both modes of the gun off, though you can switch weapons to keep shooting during this. Most guns feel distinct and useful, though I never felt that the shotguns were quite right in terms of their balance of damage/firerate/penetration/spread. Not that they're bad, but they're just kind of weird. The biggest case of redundancy, I think, is the smgs' and minigun's primary fire modes, but for space reasons I won't go into detail here.Melee is restricted to sliding into enemies which automatically uses the chainsaw-leg, which does more damage the faster you are moving prior to activation and slows you down slightly with every enemy killed. Much as its hyped up, I didn't really care for it. Thankfully it's never necessary to use.Turbo-Overkill uses a system somewhat similar to Bioshock for upgrading your character - you collect money as coins called Zhen that explode out of random fallen enemies (often unreachably dropping into bottomless pits), and can spend this on augments to your bionics or unlocking your guns' secondary fire modes, both at vending machines spread around each level. A third vending machine allows you to equip up to two augments into each one of your limbs; augments say which limb can receive them. At the time of writing, only the legs and left arm are used, where your right leg (the chainsaw) mostly receives melee bonuses (with one exception) like heal-on-chainsaw-kill or chainsaw-slide-faster, your left leg gets things related to non-offensive movement (faster-dash-recharge, wall-jumping) and your left arm mostly gets augments to your lock-on rockets superweapon.However, some of the augments are just too important for me to ever consider replacing. Faster-dash-recharge is the best augment, hands-down, for combat or just getting around levels to explore. Wall-jumping might have some combat utility, but its main feature is allowing you to jump two more times than normal (provided any vertical surface), which is indispensable for exploration. For whatever reason, your rocket-arm gets "Zhen magnet," which makes coins just go straight to your account rather than needing to be gathered (or lost in a bottomless pit), which is basically a must-have that locks off a rocket upgrade until you buy everything else you want. Also, since I didn't like the chainsaw-leg much, once I got "Steady Footing," the only non-offense augment for the right leg which makes your normally-slippery-feeling movement perfectly stable, I didn't look back.The graphics are a lot like another amazing retro-shooter, Prodeus - low-res textures and low-poly models, but with modern lighting, reflections, and other effects. They're lovely. Plus, this game has (skippable, if needed) cutscenes that actually look phenomenal given the simplicity of the models.Speaking of Prodeus, Turbo Overkill's enemies are much better in terms of visual design than Prodeus's current offering of "vague orange gremlin" and "vague blue gremlin". They tend to go down in hordes, but they all look quite distinct and also just pretty awesome as far as bionic body-horror. Sort of like more lively and cyberpunky Quake II Strogg; though less grim, asymmetrical, and industrial. Not better or worse.The soundtrack is phenomenal. At first I thought it was another Andrew Hulshult score - which would not be an insult by any means; he just seems to do the music for  retro shooter - but it's a lot more "electro" and varied than Hulshult's sort of industrial-electronic-metal stuff. From what I can find, it's all done by "Gribblesnap," one of the game's devs (though I'm not exactly sure how many people are on the dev team). As you move throughout the levels, the bgm subtly alters to keep things fresh, and basically any time I was taking a second to think about how to get to a potential secret, I'd catch myself thinking how damn good the music was.I can't say I really "noticed" the game's sound effects much, which could ironically be due to the volume of the music - though I left the sound settings at default.There are a few places where I can tell it's not totally polished - mostly just being able to get (stuck in) places you weren't meant to, and some things related to the vehicle segment - but it's not Skyrim-buggy or anything. It doesn't crash, and the game autosaves frequently enough that I never lost more than a minute or so of progress. No big deal.Again, this is (very) early access, and everything is already well within the margin of error for "finished" AAA titles these days.it's good. it's a good game. get it. yes.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't be fooled. This is called a boomer shooter or a retro shooter, but it's closer to Doom Eternal than anything else. Doom Eternal meets Blade Runner. Minus Doom Eternal's ammo management and the weapon-to-enemy pairing. Instead, this game is a greatest hits of all the best FPS mechanics. Dash, double jump, wall run, grapple hook, ground pound, slide, slowmo, weapon upgrade, body augmentations, jump pads, it's all here and it all feels useful and worth engaging with.The combat arenas just keep coming. They are always good, always getting crazier. By the third episode, I wasn't sure how the game could get more intense and frantic, but it does. You know those games that allow you to enter a kind of flow state? Turbo Overkill does that. Turn the FOV way up, turn the volume way up, and let the subconscious parts of your mind take over. Every night this week I've felt like I was in a trance.What are AAA devs even doing? Seriously, who else is out here providing FPS campaigns this good? Id? Anyone else? The retro shooter scene can no longer be considered a gimmick, it's no longer just a fun little romp in the nostalgic hay. It can no longer be ignored or downplayed: this is where the real talent is currently located.On top of excellent combat arenas, solid guns, smart upgrades, and incredible music, it also offers a pretty neat story. It's not exactly Baldur's Gate, but it's also not as simple as something like Duke Nukem 3D...even though Jon St. John is in it.No gun reloading, no puzzles, no annoying recourse management, no downtime, no data entries to read, no cover system, no stamina system, no useless weapons. It's the perfect pepperoni pizza of a game that hits the spot in a way few games can. If you're a fan of fast paced FPS titles, then this is an must play. Oh, and it never does that thing where you arbitrarily lose all your weapons and have to get them back. The game ought to be nominated for an award just for that decision alone.

_childDocuments_.review: It honestly pains me to review this as early as I am but seeing how the game's core combat is going I don't imagine adding a couple of new weapons and some gimmick missions are gonna do anything to save this.For the record the game isn't too hard or anything, I actually found it quite easy even on the second-to-hardest difficulty, which is what I usually start with on these games. That being said, after playing the game for about 40 minutes, I already feel like I've experienced half of all the game has to offer me.At its best, Turbo Overkill is a game that can be best described as the lovechild of old DOOM & Ultrakill; extremely fast gameplay where your character feels like he's perpetually moving at Mach 10 with some additional movement gimmicks that are fun to play with at times, but aside from that this game has a lot of things missing out on it that I can't say I truly enjoy.None of the enemies are memorable. Enemies generally blend in with the environment and are extremely small and hard to notice, making it usually very annoying to shoot them with more accurate weapons, despite how generous the game can be with those at times. Regardless, the impact of shooting and killing enemies just.. isn't there. There's no satisfaction beyond the ridiculous aspect of what you're actually doing; i.e., moving at inhuman speeds with a chainsaw for a leg dual wielding uzis and a sawed-off SSG wannabe. Enemies usually blow up in very well made gore and viscera but the gore itself is so tame and just blends in with the rest of the environment, not to mention the sound design for most of the weapons feels weak as hell and makes some guns just outright not fun to shoot.Turbo Overkill is an objectively fun game at its core, but it's missing a lot of extremely important keys that I think just hold it from being as good as DOOM Eternal and Ultrakill were, even though both games have their fair share of issues as well.Why am I still recommending it?Like I said, it's a fun game at its core and if that's all you care about then by all means buy it, it's very amusing for the first few minutes and if you care for the story and deeper mechanics I'd recommend you check out the rest. However, to me personally, this game is limited behind a couple of technical issues that are mostly personal and I'd understand if not everybody had aligned thoughts; the game is far from perfect, but it is worth what it's worth. Try it out on sale if you want, full price is ok too.

_childDocuments_.review: This game puts most full release games to shame, and there's only about a third of the game out right now. The full game is expected to release in 2023 and I seriously cannot wait for the additional episodes to be added as we reach that final release date.While the campaign is obviously not completed as of me writing this review, what's currently there is extremely satisfying. The plot is simple enough, but the maps are varied, each level feels distinct from the last, and the gameplay works so well. You move fast--not too fast--with a range of movement options at your disposal including a double jump, a quick chainsaw-leg slide, wall running, sticking to walls, and wall jumping. Alongside that you have a good set of weapons with alternate firing modes which makes most weapons feel entirely new. Each weapon packs its own distinct punch, and there's a chaotically satisfying amount of destruction going on with bodies exploding and environmental set pieces ready to detonate. I felt myself smiling with a near-psychotic glee as I gave buildings a chainsaw leg makeover with blood, guts, glass, bullet holes and burn marks. This game's visual style is on point as well; it's classic cyberpunk flare to the max, which pairs really well alongside a simple plot (though that simplicity has room to be expanded upon in future episodes) and a finely tuned gameplay loop. The game also respects player intelligence and skill level, allowing you to problem solve in particularly difficult parts of a level or find your way around huge maps with only minor help to set you in the right path. There are also collectibles which are keenly hidden, I haven't collected them all yet but I plan to once I finish writing this review.There are some minor flaws so far. I haven't encountered any glitches or crashes, but there are some moments in the game where the difficulty fluctuates between easy, just the right amount of challenge, and difficult. I never became infuriated (I played on Street Sweeper, the game's "Hard"/middle difficulty) but I'd like to see the difficulty curve ironed out in future episodes. There are also some augmentations in this game that are way, way better than others. I tried out an augmentation that causes an explosion when you land from a significant height and found that it wasn't as good as what I used throughout the entire campaign which was a combination of health and armor drops given with each chainsaw kill. You also only find augments for your left and right legs as well as your right arm which means you'll quickly run out of slots for your collection of augments, hopefully there's an upgrade allowing you to equip more augments in the future, but I assume we'll get more augments in the full release so this doesn't bug me too much. As I said, these are all minor flaws, but I wanted to point them out as I couldn't help but notice them in my playthrough.This game's a Doom-like that--if the full release nails the landing that this game sets up--I might like more than Doom. For one, I'm a sucker for the Cyberpunk look: I love a neon future. And for two, I'm a fan of games that take off the training wheels early and tell you to figure it out yourself. Lastly, I love a game that knows how to balance plot, gameplay, and aesthetics to create a brilliant package that's a delight to play over and over again. Congrats Turbo Overkill team, you've earned yourselves a fan for life.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a game. With the resurgence of hyper retro-FPS games since the release of DOOM 2016, Turbo Overkill stands at the pinnacle of the genre due to its intensity, diversity in playstyle, and sheer badassery.The game stays fresh, consistently introducing new abilities, mechanics, rides, and ways to obliterate enemies late into the game, and with the number of augments for your body, you can always try something new if you're feeling too OP or bored.This game is the ultimate perfection of all the best qualities from all the other retro-FPS titles you've heard of. If you like hyper-intense and difficult FPS games, GET TURBO OVERKILL, you will not regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall stellar game. Everything from the soundtrack, the guns, abilities, graphics, etc. are great. Despite the early access title, this game is quite polished. My only real complaints are a few of the checkpoints could be better placed, the motorbike in episode 2 handled like an unbalanced tank, and that enemies sometimes had some weird pathing behavior. Other than that, I loved it! I can't wait for the final episode's release!

_childDocuments_.review: As of right now unfortunately i cannot recommend this game. World is really beautiful, killing enemies and overall gameplay feels satisfying but there are 2 glaring issues that made the game a pain to go through. First and the most important one is the game has no invincibility frames when you get hit. This wouldn't have been a major problem if there wasn't this many projectiles at all times coming at you. You can literally be at full hp and in just a blink of an eye, you are dead. Worst thing about it is, most of the time you can't tell that you are getting hit until its too late. I got annoyed by this a lot especially because i chose the average difficulty. The game isn't hard to be honest, it is just unfair. Second issue is, you will get lost quite a lot. There are mostly no indicators pointing where you should go. Again this wouldn't be a problem if the maps weren't quite big and confusing. I have spent a quarter of my time playing this game searching where to go.There are also some minor issues such as some bugs, some weapons and upgrades being useless or too gimmicky.The game is still in early access which means that the issues i have stated can be fixed/improved. I will keep an eye on Turbo Overkill and play the upcoming updates and see what comes out of it. I really want it to turn out good because underneath the issues, it has a massive potential to be a great game. Sadly at the time of my review, it's not worth your time.

Bobby Kotick cried when he saw the average Steam score here. Do you really want to keep making Bobby cry??? You heartless monster.Also, holy crap the soundtrack is the best of the year, and that is NOT an exaggeration. It starts out with the usual darksynth vibes but episode 3 knocks it out of the park with orchestral arrangements, a JAZZ METAL track, and more gravitas than Hans Zimmer flushing a toilet after taking a giant BWOOOM into it. This one is 2 Fast, 2 furious, and simply 2 good for most gamers. We deserve so much less than this. Jokes aside, Turbo Overkill is an absolute artistic achievement. _childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is a cyberpunk/fantasy first-person shooter game that takes place in a world inspired by classic cyberpunk novels and movies, as well as fantasy classics. Turbo Overkill makes other FPS games look like a joke.The game starts out easy enough as you learn to navigate the world and gun down basic enemies. But Turbo Overkill is not for casual players. Even on the easiest difficulty, it will make you cry for your mommy. Once the game gets going, you’ll be up against multiple enemies at once, sometimes with rockets or lasers. And to make matters worse, there are often even more enemies off-screen firing at you.It’s impossible to fight this kind of onslaught with a regular gun, so you have to get creative in order to survive. Luckily, Turbo Overkill has some seriously cool special weapons that help turn the tide of battle.Among new Indie FPS releases, Turbo Overkill is a welcome blast from the past. Though it may not reinvent the genre, it has enough elements that make it fun and worthwhile. Do you want to ask your grandma what the name “Apogee” means? Then Turbo Overkill might be for you!Overall Rating - 8/10FULL GAMEPLAY WALKTHROUGH PART 1 -

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun and polished for a fast paced shooter.On the technical side, the game ran well and I encountered very few bugs: in a few cases I got stuck in the level geometry, but then a failsafe teleported me back to a safe spot after a few seconds, and in another case I got softlocked by a broken level trigger but reloading the last checkpoint fixed it.All the weapons are fairly useful and interesting, and they can be combined in creative ways instead of the extremely boring "use A on B" seen in Doom Eternal.Enemy variety is pretty good, even the lowest tiers are different enough to require a bit of attention.The levels also aren't bad, but you have so much mobility that it's easy to sequence break by accident and in some cases skip past large chunks of them.Secrets aren't terrible, no wall humping required in this game, but given the sheer size of most levels they can be pretty tedious to find even when no attempt is made to hide them: in some cases, the opposite is true and you'll just walk into a "secret" by looking to your side as you follow the intended path.Difficulty is odd: I was playing on Street Cleaner (the middle of the 5 difficulty levels), and around the halfway point the game went from "very easy" to "very hard", with plenty of attacks dealing 300+ damage when the most you can stack is 200 health and 200 armor.At least, the augments you collect in-game and the mutators you unlock by finding secrets offer plenty of ways to fine-tune the difficulty level: for example, you can enable infinite ammo and instagib to breeze through even the hardest difficulty, or disable all weapons but your chainsaw leg and triple enemy spawns to turn even the easiest difficulty into a bit of a challenge.Finally, there's a level editor and that's always nice.Worth playing, even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, easily, the best FPS of 2023: an absolute masterpiece for the ages.The level and character design, the art, the relentless pacing, the music, the movement of the character, the weapons, and finally the special abilities, are simply sublime.It offers the best aspects of the old shooters, in a modern package.What's most incredible is that it's been mostly developed by a single developer, some superhuman named Sam Pebble, with only some assistance from Apogee - from what I understand mostly in term of ideas and direction.It's also very long as a playthrough will probably take you between 15 and 20 hours.No doubt I will be replaying this regularly as a true classic of  the genre, up there in the pantheon, with Doom and Dusk.Cherry on the cake, I have heard an interview where the developer said Apogee was a fantastic publisher to work with, such a pleasure to see the legendary name return with an enormous, bombastic, outrageously fun and over the top bang.If you like this kind of game, it hardly gets better than this.

I'm a sucker for any kind of cyberpunk-themed game, but I've been playing others of late and "boomer shooters" more generally (, , , , etc.) and not having nearly as much fun as with  (TO). _childDocuments_.review: Turbo. Chainsaw. Leg.Turbo Overkill is an excellent modern first person shooter. A member of the twitchy shooter club, it is a fast paced game that encourages constant movement and weapon switching, while providing excellent environments where to do so, with an outstanding weapon rooster, and good enemy design (with some caveats here and there).The music is overall excellent! The composition and progression throughout the game is just great, perfectly in tune with the game themes, and pumps you up just right. The music sounds production (that is, the mixing and post production) is also outstanding, making the whole thing very cohesive. The same goes for the sound design; weapons sound are very nicely done, and so are the enemy, environmental, and voices for the most part. I will note that there is some recurring "sound stacking" bugs with coins and some specific sounds (remember BUILD Engine sound stacking bugs? Exactly like that) that do need to be addressed, because they can occasionally hurt :(.The game graphics are also beautiful; the levels themselves are colourful and very detailed, and the backdrops, set pieces and in game cinematics also show a great level of care into making sure that everything is detailed and pretty, but still allowing the player to (mostly) understand what to do and where to go at all times. Fittingly, the level design is amazingly well done; they are giant environments, and even with the usual trope of keys and backtracking, still make for immersive set pieces that flow really well. Your movement options are very versatile and overall quick; sliding (with a side of chainsaw), dashing, multiple jumping, and grapple hook, all of which encourage constant and rapid movement, both of which are 100% required to survive basically all the time. Everything you could want out of a modern FPS is there, and done very well (except for the starting delay of the grapple hook which I just hate ¬¬). It reminded me of ULTRAKILL at some points, but here, the flying around shooting things and looking awesome is done both out of necessity, and just pleasure :P.The weapon rooster is just great; every single type of weapon that was ever done in an FPS is included in it (except for a BFG I guess). You get 10 slots overall, plus extra modes for each which almost gets you 20, and despite the quantity, all are implement solidly. Mostly every type of play is accommodated within it, and while enemies have "weaknesses" that encourage using specific weapons, you can still do your own thing if you want. On that note, the implant upgrade system is nice; it allows to bolster specific skills and movement options, but with limited slots, forcing you to choose specific ones depending on what you favour the most. The enemy design is pretty nice too; graphic wise, all look amazing, and fit a function within battles and overall in the game. Johnny is very much a glass cannon; the game makes it clear that movement is required at all times, but it will occasionally thread over the line of cheapness, rather than challenge, and this is probably my main and only complaint about the game: The cheap instakills. A single enemy can just wreck you with some of their attacks, and the game will repeatedly throw hand fulls of them at you at some points, along with buckets of common enemies. On Streetcleaner difficulty, I counted 3XX damage from a SINGLE attack that left me alive with 4 health from full health and armor (and some seem to do even more than that!), and even lower enemies can just take 1XX health/armor in a single swipe. In all cases, there seems to be some "random" variation of damage; after some out of nowhere deaths that pissed me off, I stopped to probe damage from single enemies, and found that sometimes they would do 20 damage, and sometimes 150, with no clear indication of why. The solution was basically to get good and not get hit at all, but as noted, it felt pretty cheap at some points. I do not want to think how bad this would be on the higher difficulties :(.That said, I do not think this overshadows all the good things the game is and does at all; Turbo Overkill is an outstanding example of a modern day FPS that implements basically everything we have learned about these kinds of games throughout the years, and does so well.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't normally do reviews, but Turbo Overkill has been on my radar for a while, so I'm happy to give a short review after 90 minutes of play (so far, anyway, I expect to get plenty of replay value).So, Turbo Overkill. You can pretty much gather the visual style from the trailer, and the gameplay - a retro inspired completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ mental shooter. If you liked the Doom games (either the early versions, or the 2016 Doom/Ethernal new versions, you'll love this. Quake? Ditto. Unreal Tournament? Also ditto (although there's no multiplayer). Combat is fast, furious, and filled with gibs.It does remind me of Strafe, another similar shooter that came out a few years back. And I will heartily reccomend both.My only (teeny tiny) criticism is that it would be nice to be able to view the settings and options before being kicked into the game. The music, the visuals, it's obvious a ton of effort has been put into this. You'll see snippets of inspiration from other games, plenty of collectables, plenty of replay value and lots of secrets to discover. And hey, there's a Demo, which you don't see often these days. Give it a shot, what have you got to lose?

_childDocuments_.review: Not usually into boomer shooters—they're fun but not particularly gripping—and I usually end up putting them down a few hours in. This one though, has enough meat on its bones to keep me going.The boomer shooting is solid, propped up by it's killer gimmick: the chainsaw leg, letting you mulch your way around an arena. It just clicks in the way DOOM's dismemberment system does, keeping the flow of combat fast and continuous.I thought I'd get tired of the hammed up genre-drenched dialog, but the performances actually pull it off. Combined with a sprinkling of set pieces, the game feels complete, not just a collection of arenas strung together by a theme.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're looking for a blazingly fast retro-style shooter, you will like this game.Leveldesign is generally really creative and cool, with tons of variety. However, there's also some stinkers, both in episode 1 and 2. Episode 2 especially suffers from some horribly unbalanced encounter design. You can pretty much breeze through the game up until a couple of levels into episode 2, where you will hit a massive difficulty wall. The game just throws you into tiny arenas with a ton of enemies. It's not just hard, it's frustrating. While I didn't mind the vehilce levels like many other people, the game would be better if they were replaced with something else. The vehicle section in episode 2 was definitely better than the section in episode 1, but still.The game suffers from some massive feature bloat. There's tons of stuff in the game that is only used once or very rarely, like certain pickups. The game is cleary... inspired by Doom Eternal. Half of the small features, like the body upgrade system, could probably be scrapped and the game would be better for it. Looking through your augmentations for minor upgrades just kills the pacing.The guns have creative visual design, but there's mostly nothing too special. Expect standard oldskool shooter archetypes with some quirks. This is not bad at all, but probably good to know.Story is... there. I like it as a backdrop, and each level has a cool introduction animation. Nothing to complain here.Visuals are great and the game runs like butter. However, the bright neon colors everywhere are an issue if you're playing on higher difficulties. It's really hard to make out projectiles and silhouttes sometimes, which makes it hard to dodge stuff. Some of these effects can be disabled though, which helps a ton if you need it.Sounddesign is great, though nothing special. It does it's job. Some weapons could use a little more punch (looking at you double barrel shotgun).Soundtrack is fantastic. Fits the game and action very well.All in all, Turbo Overkill is a great game, plagued by some minor, fixable issues. Nevertheless, I loved almost every second of it.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been an avid fan of FPS games ever since we got our first family computer in 1995. Between then and now I've played damn near every shooter worth playing. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely underrated, great game. I went in expecting just another average boomer shooter but it really develops past expectations as the game progresses in pretty much every element.Starting off with the most core mechanic of boomer shooters: the shooting. It stays true to the tried and true method of no aiming down sites, no reloads, satisfying gibbing animations, and extremely fast weapon swapping. The arsenal in this game starts off basic (pistol, shotgun, assault rifle) and then evolves to include incredibly novel weapons (orbital laser, a rifle that telefrags enemies) that standout even in a genre saturated with great gun ideas. Additionally, upgrades are well thought out and all the aforementioned basic weapon archetypes become something WAY more. They never become stale to use. Secondly, movement in this game is very fluid and familiar. Accelerate or stop on a dime as you skate past enemies delivering your preferred brand of death. It doesn't try to reinvent the wheel in movement tech but I much prefer it that way. Sliding, dashing, double jump are industry standards and it does a good job of adding a gimmick to also make them lethal. Then we have story. Most stories are pretty minimalistic or basic in this category. But while basic, T.O.'s story is so over the top that it stands above most others. The cutscenes were way more enjoyable than they had any right or need to be, and the characters actually intriguing with a personality that places them beyond being just another voice or target.Coupled with a great story, we have incredible, lengthy level designs. There are some absolutely gorgeous sets that hit the requisite cyberpunk theme, but also some truly awesome set designs. One in particular for me was fighting in flowing traffic on top of flying vehicles backlit by the glow of a neon city, and then boarding a moving train to fight on, in and under it, to finally disembarking and continuing at a station.  Lastly we have the gimmicks. It's not enough for games nowadays to just have guns and sprawling levels. T.O. decided to take the route of making movement in this game deadly and at higher levels, a necessary weapon. But it only adds to the fluidity of the game if properly used. There are also numerous body upgrades you can swap out that, while not drastically changing your playstyle, will add to it in satisfying and noticeable ways. The final important gimmick to mention is a favorite of mine: bullet time. I'll just add that I'm happy they included it so you can see your destruction in glorious slow-mo while also providing a brief respite amidst combat chaos.As a final note, I have to say that the demo truly does not do this game justice. I tried the demo and was on the fence of purchasing this until it went on sale as it felt like another average boomer shooter. The demo only superficially demonstrates the core game mechanics loop and fails to elaborate on all the wondrous points above since it's a demo. If you're looking for a game that's not so supremely complex like Ultrakill but hits that quake-like / doom feel of fluid combat, this won't disappoint. Hope this game somehow hits it big and the devs add more onto it, but right now it seems very underrated as a sleeper hit.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, after two previous reviews that were "I want to recommend, but can't yet", I'm happy to say I can finally give Turbo Overkill a big fat . The chainsaw leg works the way it should again. Problems with checkpointing seem to be fixed. Navigating the levels isn't a pain anymore. And fights are properly fun again instead of just a grind.The gunplay is great, the music is fantastic (special mention to Sunset Synthetica which somehow mixes Djent, Electronica, and  of all things) and the story is the good kind of wallpaper that simply gives you motivation to flying-chainsaw-kick cybermonsters in the face. Levels have a lot of cool gameplay setpieces and interesting visuals. Augments let you lean into gameplay styles, and of course I mostly went with chainsaw buffs. Many points in the game also go extremely hard into bodyhorror and existential/cosmic horror, which I'm a fan of and here it's done pretty well, I'd say even better than INCISION did.My only negatives are personal taste:Gianni Matragrano is now on the same tier as Steve Blum or Tara Strong where I'm tired of him being in  lately, and without spoiling, you will hear him talk A LOT in the second half of Turbo Overkill.Also, the audio logs don't really contribute much to the story. I don't even know who some of the characters are because they never appear in the gameplay or cutscenes, and I know at least one non-character is just some youtuber I've never heard of. That being said, you  just skip them.Those two very subjective complaints aside, I'm glad to consider Turbo Overkill to now be one of those "must buy" boomer shooters.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is a very special game, and I highly recommend it. I give it a 10/10, I would give it a 9/10 for no co-op campaign, but I respect it too much to lower it's score. The music is an incredible 10/10, and the SFX is 9/10 because it's just barely not chunky enough for me. The graphics are cohesive, and the gameplay is immaculate. Story is quite fitting, no notes. Rating up here because I can't expect anyone to read what I've gushed below lol.I've been playing shooters a long time, and I was very good at them, I hesitate to say I could have gone pro but when your scores are comparable to people who cheat, you tend to wonder. Anyways, I love hyper mobility shooters. They're not as common as they used to be, and the big names, like destiny 2, come with their own problems.So for the last 10 years or so, I've not really been touching the genre. Everything felt the same, as imo, most FPS combat has been largely stagnant. It feels as if most lead designers seem to think that merely adding newer, zanier guns is the equivalent of adding new mechanics. Sure, guide-able bullets is rad with snipers, dashing is a nice addition, and combat slides are fun, but at the end of the day, none of this is a great departure. In the FPS genre, there are three extremely common types; cover, looter, or one of the boomer shooter revival games. They make up about 75% of shooters and if you've played one of a type, you've basically played all of that type. Not to throw shade at each, but at this point it's rare you find anything with a  twist on gameplay. Just varying levels of execution.Turbo Overkill is different. It gives you a chainsaw leg that can be used in tandem with all movement tech. You can chainsaw slide jump/dash/circle strafe. All weapons have different firing modes making each gun effectively 2 guns, each alt fire being just as effective as the primary, albeit for different situations. Augmentations for your character exist as well, which make additional changes to movement tech. You can basically tool Johnny to be good at whatever you like best, and for me, that's the chainsaw. Unless I am playing endless mode, I often forget I have guns because the movement tech is so strong. Use that as you will.There is a lot I am not covering, but I'll put it this way; no weapon is a dud, no mechanic is just a gimmick, and sewing it all together while you play basically turns you into a chainsaw tornado that ♥♥♥♥♥ out bullets, fire, missiles, and the blood of your enemies.But to close off this meandering review, I will conclude with a story. I played through episodes 1 and 99% of 2 on the 3rd hardest difficulty. Having not really played FPSs much over the last 10 years, I had become pretty rusty. I was still better than most but just that, firmly above average. I had a pretty easy time for most of the game, just chainsawing through everything for regen, then brute forcing anything that I couldn't just instantly decapitate with a chainsaw dive. Pretty much only died when I did stupid ♥♥♥♥ like chainsawing into explosives.Then... something strange happened.I hit the boss for the end of Episode 2 and I was just getting annihilated. I was timing my dodges, trying to strafe as well as I could, but it was an uphill slog during the first 2 or 3 phases of the fight. I was being forced to "get gud". The more I started to weave the movement techs together; the double jump, chainsaw slide, dash, and grapple hook. The more I started to succeed. But on the 4th phases I just hit the wall. Up to that point, I was timing things, as you would for a boss fight. I was doing what the last 10 years of shooters had trained me to do, and I was losing.Then I had an epiphany: why am I timing things? How fast can I actually move?Everything changed. I started weaving grapples onto the boss for speed and ending with the saw to carry the momentum, only ending the slide to merely change direction, boosting my speed back up with the dash. If you're running during combat you're playing the game wrong =p. It felt like I changed from a dude with a chainsaw leg to a chainsaw leg with a dude passenger. If you don't feel like a racecar with chainsaw wheels, you're doing something wrong. I became ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ untouchable. The tables completely flipped, and I trounced the boss no problem, like they were an ant to my chainsaw'd shoe. Continuing through the game I realized I was playing significantly better, not just movement tech but everything in general. It was like I'd Ascended.That bossfight forced me to understand the mechanics, gave me a challenge I actually wanted to overcome, and in return, my rust is gone. For the first time in years I was thrilled to play an FPS. I love it, I feel revitalized. I feel a sense of joy in the genre that I've not felt in a decade. Actually new mechanics. Actually new game tech. Not just new executions of old features, actually NEW THINGS. There will be more than the current 3 episodes, and I for one cannot wait for more. As a single player experience, this game stands tall above it's contemporaries. Well worth your money, sale or not. A truly refreshing experience I won't forget, and will continue to play for years to come.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, do NOT make the same mistake I did - Going in with my "experience" in DOOM Eternal, Ultrakill and DUSK, and choosing the highest difficulty immediately! I had fun for a few levels, but then rooms started to take longer and longer to clear, and all of a sudden I wasn't having fun anymore. I put my ego aside and lowered the difficulty, and found out that it's way more fun to just wipe out hordes of enemies as stylishly as possible than to spend tens of minutes grinding out a single room just for the "satisfaction" of it all.Here's what makes Turbo Overkill stand out. You're given options - LOTS of options. Enough weapons to fill an entire numpad, each with unique abilities of their own, and plenty of augments to offer unique build choices that you can constantly swap in and out. Meanwhile, the enemy pool to use your stuff on is quite limited in variety, with every enemy introduced in the game always sticking around up till the end. It's the specific rooms, environments, and situations that the game puts these enemies in that makes combat more interesting. You're encouraged to mix up your playstyles & play with what you enjoy the most, and you're consistently fed new toys to play with as you shred through levels too. A large part of Turbo Overkill's gameplay is finding your own fun with what you enjoy to play with, because many of the actual enemies you fight won't be changing as you go. It borders on the line of repetitiveness pretty closely, and it COULD be your biggest problem with the game if you aren't interested in diversifying your playstyle. If you're into that, then it becomes a boomer shooter playground.When I was nearing the final areas of the game, I started to wonder how big this games' budget was. It consistently impressed me with how damn good the environments looked for the entire game - I was partially expecting the game to fall off at some point, to stop introducing new gear, for the environments to stop looking as clean as before, but that never happened. The bar for quality was kept up the entire time. My only gripes with this production is that the UI feels unfinished in a few areas - Missing subtitles, dialogue never pausing when the game was paused, and a lot of unnecessary "markers" that show up on interactable objects in the game. The game also has a poor checkpoint system, where the game will register a checkpoint when you pick up collectibles or pass through invisible checkpoints on the map, even if it's in the center of a bunch of enemies about to kill you, or if the collectible can only be reached by using Turbo-Time, and respawning there means getting softlocked...All in all, it's a solid time.

_childDocuments_.review: Cyberpunk perfection. A lot of this game is so well done that its hard to believe all of it comes together. The music, gameplay, and the striking visuals in each map is an excellent thing to witness. I have some minor issues with the game, but nothing crazy. However, the big issue I have with this game is the difficulty. Playing through the first two episodes when the game was 1.0 was a pretty smooth ride, maybe a bit too easy on UV difficulty. Waited a bit for any issues to be ironed out before playing through episode 3. I fired up episode 3, and was met with an entirely different game completely. If you seen videos of this game before these patches, I assure you they were not playing the same game I was.Look, Turbo Overkill is a pretty generous game with checkpoints and allowing you to quick save most of the time, but the game turned into one shot simulator really quick. The last couple of levels were really awesome but tipping the scale into ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ kaizo status. Almost every high tier enemy has the ability to one shot you, hell a random projectile from a mid tier enemy could instantly kill you, full to dead. Some of the combat scenarios had some of these enemies in hard to reach spots that dying was pretty much a common occurrence. Now this game has a lot of tools to kind of mitigate and get around the difficulty, but man, the game doesn't have great audio direction for some of these abilities. You will die and asking your self many times "what the hell killed me." I also got hit with a spear from a enemy you can't even see with the fog on. If this is the intended experience, I respect the hell out of it, but I don't see a whole lot of people pushing through what I did on UV or above. I love challenging games, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I was praying that I wasn't walking around a corner into a one shot ability after a long multi phase boss so I don't have to go through that again. It felt like I had to play perfect or I was not beating some sections of the game.Damn, what a game.

_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: Its Doom eternal on roller skates. Its a fun blast that just throws everything at you and keeps escalating straight off a cliff. The game copies a lot from other media but if you stop to think for a while the styles it borrows can feel a little stitched together. Because of the copying of game mechanics too, some of them transfer the same flaws as the original games or they just feel redundant here. The primary and secondary fire modes don't always complement each other and some weapons and secondary fire modes fill up the same purposes, just like in doom eternal. The dash is there but the chainsaw slide makes it feel redundant and it could have been a fine thing to base the movement on its own. Wall running is there just like in titan fall but it doesn't come in to play during the combat unlike in titan fall. The grapple hook doesn't feel that intuitive with the speed of this game.During the heat of the combat I started forgetting some of the abilities like slow-mo and chainsaw arms because there is just so much to use but not enough reason for it always. Because the game has less of a focus on resource management I could find my self in a longer battle than I expected and run out of ammo with little to no ways of making it back.The game is most fun at the medium difficulties as a focus requiring breeze because on the higher difficulties the enemies, even the smaller mooks instakill you. This creates frustrating repetitions and the loose game mechanics don't facilitate "dancing on the razors blade" like playing.The story is chaotic and starts to veer VEEERY heavily in to Doom eternal DLC territory with techno babble, Ai gods -and sidekicks. The best parts of the story are the more tragic moments of seeing Johnny becoming something that he doesn't recognize and how his past is fading away from him. The question if that is even a bad thing is very interesting to me. Sam carries all of the exposition and I see no reason why johnny couldn't have a voice or toughs of his own akin to Blazkowicz from Wolfenstein. Johnny isn't an empty icon like Mickey mouse nor is he an established hero like Doom guy. The music goes above and beyond. (I liked the game, I just have critiques of it.)
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: The game in its current state is ok, but I can't recommend it as it is now. It starts off strong with good mechanics, great level design, and has a wonderful aesthetic. These things are what originally drew me to the game, but now having played a fair amount of it.... The game just doesn't maintain the same quality from start to finish. Enemies from the start already suffered from blending in with their environment, but this becomes far more of an issue as the game goes on. It doesn't help that the game has many of it's later fights in super large arenas with break neck action. Another issue is the enemies themselves. Far too many bullet sponges. This is a very serious issue that makes fights feel like a slog to run through. This also creates an issue for ammo. I need to dump hundreds of rounds into enemies at times only to realize the game is barely giving me enough ammo for the next enemy encounter filled with sponges. It forces you to play less aggressive and choose your battles (which is not the intended idea behind the game). When your action shooter is encouraging me to avoid enemies, you've made a poor choice in design. This isn't a bad game, but games like Ultrakill are already doing what this game is trying to do and better. Buy that instead
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe later game gets better, but:The only thing i think about when playing this game is why other games are cool, but this one isn't.Enemies feel like gray blobs, none of them are memorable, and none of them have weaknesses or a special way to deal with them(except drones, but i don't feel like they belong to this game considering that you can't kill them relying only on your movement), all you do is just dodge random projectiles and shoot them with whatever you have ammo for, or just ignore them. After playing Quake, Half-life, Doom 93 and most importantly Ultrakill, this is just not itI have only 6 out of 15 weapons at this point, but even now i don't understand why you need 2 shotguns and 2 full auto guns(smg and lmg) if they're not that much different. You could just remove smg(3) and the bigger shotgun(2) from the game, and you wouldn't lose anything.Locations suck most of the time. _childDocuments_.review: Very mediocre so far.I understand there may be bias due to me being a massive fan of Ultrakill and also enjoying DOOM Eternal quite a bit, or maybe even I set my expectations to high and the disappointment only exacerbated my already negative feelings, but my god is this game boring.This game feels like it should have been perfect for me because it's a culmination of a bunch of ♥♥♥♥ I love, some of which it even delivers; the music and overall aesthetic/world design is amazing. It just feels so bad to play. To clarify, it's not really even that difficult (I play on second hardest diff), but the game doesn't require any creative thinking and there's so little cool/satisfying ♥♥♥♥ to pull off, which is only worsened by how boring the enemies are. No cool interactions or anything, they don't at all compliment each other or the player, it's just "hold m1/ctrl over enemy/group of fodder till they die" and dodge a couple projectiles here and there. None of the guns feel particularly nice to use, audio design is meh, enemy designs are cool ig but nothing striking, couldn't give two ♥♥♥♥♥ about any of the characters or story (not that any of that is super important for me in games like these), movement is cool aside from the pathetic jump, but yeah none of it works for me. This wouldn't be fixed by upping the damage to 7X the regular and getting one shot by everything. It's a fundamental issue with the design of the game.Edit: After finishing the game, my general criticisms remain, especially the issue of the difficulty being between "you won't ever die" and "you will be randomly one-shot from a particle of dust", but the gameplay does get way more dynamic and fun, still not to the standard I'd like but it is undeniably a good time. Other than that all my praises only have rung more and more true; the environments and music is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ incredible, just wish I could give a single ♥♥♥♥ about any of the characters, and that the game didn't take so long to engage me. 7/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only about to finish Episode 1, but daaaaaaayum is the game nice!The shooting is pretty much flawless, the chainsaw leg is just pure genius, the movement is unrestrictive and very fast (I can never ever not praise a fast-paced game, seriously!) and the art style shows a lot of love put into it. The music is awesome, just a banger after banger 🤘The collectibles on each level leave me scratching my head. I'm usually a very thorough player, but I still come up 1 casette or chip short in some levels. Not that I particularly mind for this type of game, but if you're into collectible hunting - you have your work cut out for you (unless you use guides, which is a lame way to play).Lots of options to tweak various aspects of graphics and controls, including one of the best TAA implementations I've seen in a game (separate sliders for various aspects of TAA - frame blending, motion, sharpening, etc to make it look just right for you!)The game runs at 4K maxed and is just permanently pinned at 165fps on a 165Hz screen for me (though I do use an RTX 4090 - my CPU is pretty old). The mouse input always feels extremely responsive, which is exactly what you'd want in a game like this 👍The cyberpunk-y visuals REALLY pop on my Quantum Dot display, with beautiful and vibrant colors all-round! A display with a deep color gamut genuinely does this game justice.A lot of people compare this with DOOM 2016 and such, but I like this one better, because it's so much faster and more fluid (and DOOM was already very fluid in terms of movement and combat!).So far - I have...nothing negative to say! I'll update the review once I've played more and/or finished the game.--------------------EDIT 1: Episode 2 finished. Still loads of fun and the amount of enemies and combat speed overall both get a healthy jump vs Episode 1. Some arenas really keep you busy and focused!Still can't say I have any complaints. Maybe the visibility during powerup pickups could be better, but that's about it.--------------------EDIT 2: Finished the game. The last boss took a few reloads to figure out what to do with it (it wasn't really immediately obvious from the S.A.M.M's dialogue), but once I figured out what to do - no problem at all. So I guess I see what some people meant about the last boss being a bit odd, but really no biggie in the end.Other than that - LOVE the game - it does a lot of stuff better than DOOM 2016/Eternal, so in my book - this game's gold 🤘The music just never got tiring or repetitive either - there was just always something new to listen to, which is awesome!TURBO OVERKILL absolutely deserves all the glowing reviews it got! 👍

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is one of the most frantic fast-paced FPS games I've ever played. Almost all of the guns are perfect; the pistols are still useful till the end of the game (unlike a certain game that rhymes with boom) and all the weapons have a use in combat. The only gun that make my balls crunch is the sniper; it doesn't feel useful during combat and feels jank, whenever I'm forced to use it (especially in the last level) minor amounts of blood surges through my balls in the worst way humanly possible. The enemies are mostly good; most serve a purpose in constructing a fight and all are instantly recognisable. The only enemies I don't like are the flying sentient poop holes, they never actually harm me they just annoy me and the buff ass TV head guys, they are essentially the same is the skinny ♥♥♥♥♥ that run at you but bigger and goofier. The only times I got lost in a level were more related to my soft pressed in skull rather than the game so I guess the level design is good. The game is a little bit too long; it feels 2-3 hours longer than it really needs to be. The bosses are kinda mid unfortunately, they all feel either extremely easy (i.e syn and that artifact ♥♥♥♥) or feel mildly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ (i.e Maw and Ripper (Ripper only because I had to use the sniper and Maw because phase 1-2 are hard then 3-4 are piss easy)). Overall I give this game 8.94/10.01.

_childDocuments_.review: There is something really special about this game, the quality and attention to details/weapons/animations/level design/gameplay and music is something I haven't seen since the original Perfect Dark came out, well that's what my initial thoughts were.Runs on the Unity engine, and while the developers have managed to get the best from a difficult engine than most there are some fps issues on the level infestation, it might just be limited to my setup or this level but then MSI AfterBurner showed no bottlenecks, with only 4 cores really doing most of the work below 50% and the others around 20%, GPU 59% usage, maybe it's a thread optimization issue.But I have to mention some downsides of the game, it is hugely dragged out at the end (unfortunately they didn't know when to stop), add to that the difficultly ramps right up despite changing the it's level, also they take away the quick save system leaving you to repeat sections over and over till you want to pull your hair out, they do add it back later for a bit but then you are on a timer to kill waves of enemies (they also take the quick save away again) while trying to navigate which way to go, the end boss fight feels like it never ends along with what comes after it.Anyhow at the start  when it's doing things good it's Just that magical (also earlier levels are shorter which is good, they feel better than the massive longer ones) feeling you get from very few games, but with endless bugs after release and the way they chose to do the last two awful tedious levels/boss fights really is sour to the point I got to the last terminal and just gave up (as If the MAW battles weren't enough) after what seemed like endless retries of trying to do it on time and falling with the grapple hook or missing with the sniper shots while the timer runs out, then having to do it all over again, this is not fun and IMO not what fun gaming is about but more about frustrating the player to the point of hating/forgetting what was good about the game to begin with.Despite the bugs I recommend the first two episodes as there is still some fun to be had but I do not recommend episode 3, as a full game I do not recommend so maybe get in a sale and skip the last episode to save yourself endless frustration and annoyance.
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: It is quite hard to put into words how good I think this thing is, but if you'll allow me a few, I want to add some context to maybe help make a point: In all honesty, at the moment I've become a bit fatigued with all the "Boomer Shooters", that's not to say i don't enjoy them or anything, but we have been fed well over the last few years and I think I'm pretty full, so yesterday with the release of 1.0 of this game I decided to boot it up as I bought it in early access initially and enjoyed it but didn't think too much of it at the time, I remembered it as a cool shooter with fast movement and a funny chainsaw-leg gimmick that still kinda blended a bit into everything else but I figured now that it was out I'd give it another go....I binged this thing over the last day because I couldn't get enough of it; it was fun and fast but what started getting to me was the sense of scale and ambition, an early level had me going through a tribute/parody of the Megacity "Peachtrees" from the Dredd movie, I thought that was kind of fun and novel until I looked down about 20 minutes in and realised how many floors of this building I'd fought through... this level wasn't using the aesthetics of the megacity as a fun reference, it was using it to create an immense sense of a journey because I didn't fight through a bit of a megacity, I fought through all of it, floor after floor going up and up, sometimes outside and looping around to higher floors, hitting the roof and still going...The scale of it was overwhelming and yet the game made it feel effortless, the frame-rate stayed high, the level's pacing felt well tuned, and the combat and platforming all flowed into each other with variety and great pacing and I was just floored by it...And then the game refused to stop being constantly interesting and ambitious and fun; the sights and sounds were varied with little vehicle segments that didn't feel just gimmicky but actually felt like they gave certain levels their own individual sense of pace and flow. I don't want to spoil it but some of the levels just feel like such an adventure and yet beyond that the combat remained fantastic to match; this is a game that up at no point did I find any gun redundant, even the starting pistol became a gun that I was using consistently in the last levels of the game; every gun has its moments to shine and yet it was never in a way that I felt arbitrarily forced to need to use a certain gun, I used every gun because every gun was useful right up to the end. Beyond that though is just the absolute speed you can get up to in this. A lot of air control, chainsaw legs, double jumps, and boosts can all be chained together for absolutely insane jumps and platforming that the game does expect you to do and yet it's never overwhelming; it's always smooth and responsive and I never lacked confidence in making some of the absolutely absurd jumps the game demanded. Obviously different people have different tolerances for first person platforming but for me I adored it and never had any frustrations with it.Look I can go on all day, the game ran really well for me, the game looked great, sounded great, the soundtrack was varied and fun and there were some absolutely phenomenal tracks, especially in the last episode, Add to that the fact that custom levels are a thing and then I look at the price of this game and honestly....I think that's a steal, i would easily recommend this at twice its asking price, I genuinely would.I really do think this was something special and my only worry in saying that is that I'm overselling it, I don't want to ruin your experience in doing so but at the same time I want to be honest about my experience, and it was a phenomenal one.If you find yourself enjoying this even half as much as I ended up doing, then you will have had a really good time :)

_childDocuments_.review: Play as Johnny Turbo and saw, grind, blast your enemies to hell as you battle the evil AI bent on dominating this cyberpunk dystopia. Turbo Overkill has creative level design, creative gunplay, and creative visuals that all mesh together to make a great game. You have CHAINSAWS on your LEGS!The level design is awesome, the game keeps introducing new features, combinations, or layouts to keep things fresh. On some levels you get level-unique vehicles such as hover cars or motorbikes. The boss fights are great, they are engaging but never unfair. I love the use of leitmotif in the game. The music is great, fits the theme and augments the brutal gameplay.The progression is also great, with new weapons and tools being introduced to you throughout the game, as well as upgrades for existing weapons. The weapons are creative too, your starting pistols lock on to and splatter groups of enemies, your first shotgun can launch an electric stun blast, a gun can call in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ orbital strike laser, and you get a sniper rifle that telefrags enemies.There is a plethora of creative upgrades that you can customise to fit your playstyle. Some can even change your playstyle alltogether. I was very happy late in the game when I got an upgrade that allowed near-instant weapon quickswapping for some nasty combos (however it may be a liiiiittle overpowered in that it allowed me to ♥♥♥♥ out rockets at a faster rate than a chaingun, but who cares it's a blast)The story is pretty simple. I didn't expect to like it, but I actually enjoyed it quite a lot. Each level starts with a cutscene that characterises the crazy badass that is Johnny Turbo. I grew attached to these scenes, your AI companion, and the big story changes at the end of each chapter.Overall a fantastic zoomer shooter... I heard people are calling these zoomer shooters nowadays? Overall Turbo Overkill sits slightly above Doom Eternal and slightly below Ultrakill in fun factor for me at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a fun game made by an amateur developer, and it shows.The game itself is fun, with understandable mechanics and fun enemies. if you like other movement shooters such as ultrakill or doom you will like this. just buy it its worth it. but here are some cons that ive found.Difficulty settingsthe difficulty settings in this game rely on the same awful method of every other game in the genre of making you a glass cannon. its very obvious they didnt test the different difficulties, because on the higher difficulties the game becomes impossible without cheesing the game. higher difficulties increase enemy dmage output, projectile speed, and walk speed. later difficulties prevents you from buying ammo (not a big deal), and prevents health packs from spawning outside of killing enemies. the final difficulty level, murder machine, is something i can oly describe as ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. 6x damage, 2x projectile speed, increased enemy run speed, and no health packs outside of enemies. they did not test this difficulty level, while playing on thsi difficulty it is simply luck whether you survive or not, and its impossible without using two specific augments. it is very common to enter a boss with no hp, and be unable to beat it because you cant heal, forcing you to restart.speaking about the bosses, they suck. theyre just boring, simple, and one dimensional. revolving around a specific gimmick that youve seen a in every game known to man, or just being boring. it doesnt help that the cutscene plays everytime you start again. because they didnt think putting a checkpoint after the cutscene was a good idea.oh yeah, the checkpoints, they suck. checkpoints happen before big fights (not after so if you die after a big fight you just spent an hour on you gotta do it again), when you interact with a shop, or when you pick up a collectable. there is a non zero chance of soft locking yourself by interacting with a shop just as your about to die. the reason its this way is because the game is designed around quicksaving for some reason, which you cant do on the later difficulty levels.overall the game is fine, dont play it on the final difficulty level and you should be fine. its a good game made an amateur developer, and it shows.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill hits three demographics really damn hard: Quake III fans, 80s action film buffs and cyberpunk fiends. It’s a fast, explosive, loud first person shooter that doesn’t pull any punches and showcases the best retro shooters have to offer while adding a healthy layer of modern game design elements.As Johnny Turbo, you will be wallrunning, double jumping, dashing, gunning, swapping weapons to deal with some ridiculously long recover animations and skating on your chainsaw legs through an ocean of lamp-headed zombies (weirdest sentence you’ve read today, I bet) on your way to defeat your traditional Big Bad of cyberpunk: a rogue A.I. named Syn.Nothing particularly complicated about the overarching narrative: a cyborg kills both street and corporate scum while going after crapshoot toaster in a hi-tech/low people sprawl. The structure of every level is in itself an homage to the Doom structure we all know and love: most levels, you have to collect two different color keys and progress to the next unopened door while occasionally dealing with gauntlets of enemies. The color palette is vivid and neon-drenched, a cold, artificial maze to serve as a backdrop for the rain of gore that fills up the screen during most encounters.Even the overarching structure follows the 90s shareware-type formula: 8-mission episodes that get increasingly more difficult and really test your grasp on the movement and shooting fundamentals you’re gradually introduced to as you gain more tools and power-ups. You can spend the cash you collect from your fallen enemies at talking vending machines (à la Bioshock) and then augment yourself with different modules. You’ll also come across upgrade chests that you have to find the key for. On top of that, every level has three tech chips and cassettes you can collect, the former unlocking gameplay mods you can activate, to varying degrees of utility (and some punishing effects).The guns you find are also more or less what you’d expect from a classic shooter — nine firearms, each with their own special alternate attack. Knowing what to use against which enemy will be critical to surviving the more difficult levels in the second and third episode, where tight-spaced gauntlet events don’t give you a lot of room for error — one-punch enemies destroyed me more than i’d like to admit towards the end of the game’s second act. Still, the controls are so responsive, the gameplay so fluid that I can’t in good conscience blame the game for my own shortcomings - rather, I felt rewarded once I finally figured out how to overcome every fight. Classic arena concepts like map control — knowing where to get armor, health, temporary buffs and ammo especially during the third episode when things can get hairy in a split second will make the difference between progress or a loading screen. Jump pads, suspended platforms and the need to always be in motion to avoid death make for a really intense, engaging gameplay experience that really evokes that classic feeling of getting your blood pumping. The mechanic you will probably use to kill most enemies won’t be tied to any firearms, however. Johnny Turbo’s ability to skate on his chainsaw leg can be further enhanced with cybernetic augmentations and has the considerable advantage of instagibbing most basic enemies without expending any ammo. It is useful both for escaping impending death as well as dashing through enemies, and with the right build it can be a reliable source of health and armor (there are multiple Collector-type chips that reward you with a bit of health and armor every time you kill someone while skating into them).It cannot be overstated how eclectic Turbo Overkill’s sources of inspiration are, a philosophy that oozes into the level design itself. The radio chatter references classic lines from Aliens, there’s a clear similarity to Judge Dredd’s “Peach Trees” sector in the “Appletree” section, most of the achievements are named after one-liners, tropes and classic action film titles. There are easter eggs galore, little gems that reward those who are exploration-inclined with nuggets of memberberries. Going through the game and getting all these hyperlinks to other works really enhanced my experience and made the whole thing feel like an homage to what kids today would probably call “boomer media”, but really enables the narrative to take a lot of detours through atypical levels and over-the-top, explosive changes of scenery.You’ll drive a flying car that looks straight out of Blade Runner as you traverse immense gaps between skyscrapers and escape Syn’s Laser Beam Eye on a motorcycle that reminded me of Akira. At one point, you’ll even pilot a mech, and none of these sections feel shoehorned in: there’s always a degree of integration that ties the experience together really well. Killing mercenary bosses gradually unlocks a few really useful upgrades: micro-missiles you can send at multiple targets, an 8 to 12 second bullet time and a grappling hook.Platforming sections, though not many, are pretty fun as they will have you using all of your navigational boosters: you can double jump, double dash, hook onto things, wallrun (a Titanfall 2 flashback ensues) and telefrag enemies with your sniper rifle. Put all of these things together and I anticipate a really fun time for speedrunners and explorers.Special mention to the sound design and especially soundtrack: the track selection is on point, really knows how to create tension and imbue your mass murder ballet with a sense of rhythm. It becomes orchestral during boss fights, swivels into trance during traversal sections and cyberpunk-themed fights, takes industrial undertones when you’re navigating the rust-dominated sewers and frankly is just stellar all around. Once you’re done with the campaign, you can take a shot at the game’s Endless Mode (a survival arena that changes layout every few levels and has a separate upgrade/arsenal progression tree from the main story). I guess if you’re looking for a downside, you have to remember that Turbo Overkill is an indie game and the graphics aren’t exactly current-gen in terms of lighting, model poly count or effects. But the design works so well I frankly didn’t care - there are more creative ideas and decisions in this game than in the vast majority of AAA titles for about half the price. You can tell that Turbo Overkill is the result of labor done with love, the kind of shine that can’t be bought with piles of money and focus group checklists.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is without a doubt one of the best first-person shooter games ever made, I'd say even close to the level of Doom Eternal. The game play certainty lives up to the name of the game and the movement is unparalleled compared to any other game I've played. I can be dealing with like a hundred enemies at once while simultaneously playing The Floor Is Lava all the while moving at like 400 miles per hour and somehow my brain is comprehending what I am doing. AND THE CHAINSAW LEG. In this game you have a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chainsaw attached to your leg with a jetpack on it. You can go zooming across the entire arena or even propel yourself mid-air while immediately tearing through a line of like 50 enemies. I haven't obtained it yet, but I noticed there is a grappling hook somewhere in this game, and I cant even imagine how much more movement this game can get. No other game makes me feel quite like a crack addled rocket propelled spider monkey than this.100% worth your money.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is an absolute masterpiece of a game! From the moment I fired it up, I was greeted with jaw-dropping visuals that pushed the boundaries of what I thought was possible in gaming. The neon-soaked cyberpunk world is a sight to behold, and every corner is filled with intricate details that make it feel alive and vibrant.But it's not just about the visuals; Turbo Overkill delivers on gameplay in spades. The fast-paced, adrenaline-pumping action is a rollercoaster ride of fun. The controls are buttery smooth, allowing for precise movement and jaw-dropping acrobatics as you mow down hordes of enemies with an impressive arsenal of weapons.The level design is top-notch, offering a perfect balance of exploration and intense combat encounters. Each level feels unique and presents new challenges, keeping you on your toes and eager to see what's next. And speaking of challenges, the game's difficulty curve is just right – tough enough to keep you engaged but never frustrating.The character development and story are surprisingly engaging for an action-packed game like this. Turbo Overkill weaves a compelling narrative that adds depth to the world and keeps you invested in the protagonist's journey.The soundtrack is an absolute banger, with a pulse-pounding electronic score that perfectly complements the game's fast-paced action. It's the kind of music that will have you tapping your foot and feeling like a cybernetic killing machine.In summary, Turbo Overkill is a tour de force in the world of gaming. It's a visual spectacle, a gameplay delight, and a must-play for any fan of the cyberpunk genre or action games in general. This game sets a new standard for what we can expect from indie developers, and I can't wait to see what they come up with next. Bravo!
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: This is probably the most polished fps/boomer shooter that I've played!The Story is well told and has a lot of entertaining moments that never make it dull. The Characters are really well voice acted and are always fun to watch. The Settings are so well developed. The cyberpunk setting is pretty cool and the level designs for this game are just a joy to play through. Visually, it's amazing. Performance was solid throughout my playtime and i didn't come across any bugs or glitches. The Art Direction is perfect with it having a modern retro style about it that fits nicely with the boomer shooter genre. Sound and Audio were brilliant with the soundtrack just being filled with banger after banger and the audio is so satisfying especially with the guns.In terms of gameplay, I think that this might be the best boomer shooter you can get on steam. Movement feels smooth and fast pace. Weapons are all well varied and it never felt like any weapon was useless. The secondary fire for these guns also adds a lot for players to experiment with. The augment upgrades are pretty well developed and gives variety as to how a player can approach the game. The enemies are a great challenge and differ from one another in the best ways possible. Finally, the boss fights in this game are just awesome with the 2nd last boss being a treat to destroy.Overall, Turbo Overkill is definitely one of the best boomer shooters that I've ever played and feels the most polished out of all of them.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the campaign and overall this game is pretty solid. If you're a fan of the "boomer shooter" type of FPS like Dusk, Amid Evil, Ion Maiden, Prodeus, etc then this is a pretty solid bet. Guns feel nice to shoot, you move at lightning speed, music is serviceable. Story is cheesy as expected, I mean if you watch the trailer you basically get what this game is. The name is Turbo Overkill for god's sake. My only complaint is the levels get to be a bit long and the game kinda wears out its welcome by the end. I put 15 hours into this and pretty much ran through levels as fast as I could the entire time, and by the 10 hour mark I was pretty done. Feels a bit weird to complain about TOO MUCH content, but a game like this needs a bit better pacing. I'd give it an 8/10 overall. Worth a buy, especially on sale.
