_childDocuments_.review: I can wholly recommend this game to anyone who likes Doom or Ultrakill. Its incredibly fast paced and offers plenty of opportunities to go crazy with your weapons. It remains balanced throughout and the only time i found myself struggling was when i wasn't using my arsenal to its full capacity. There is a wide variety of enemies that all function differently, while never feeling like too much of a bullet sponge. I started off by playing the demo and i bought the full game almost immediately after finishing it. You get excellent air control and plenty of opportunities for dodging. Theres no unique gimmick or advanced tech that this game runs on, and mostly keeps things interesting through its fantastic set-pieces, super fun weapons and high-speed movement.The campaign is extremely long, providing me with roughly 20 hours of content (i was taking my sweet time experimenting, exploring and getting lost though, so expect something closer to 15 hours). The gameplay changes up frequently so i never felt like it was getting boring. Fair warning, the story takes some time to get started and only really speeds up around the halfway point. Despite this, the story was actually really fun to follow along with, the characters were interesting, and the cutscenes were funny. The ending scene has me hyped for a sequel. The visuals are fantastic and really bring that "boomer-shooter" vibe into the 2020s. The enemies, weapons and levels have great readability most of the time even if sometimes its a bit vague on where you need to go.One major help in improving my proficiency was discovering how much the game depends on the chainsaw-leg. You should be using this thing every 5 seconds with the armour and heal gene addons to keep your health up. My only minor criticism is that in terms of performance, Turbo Overkill is fill-rate limited. This wont be a problem for most as this game can easily run at 60fps 1080p with no issues even on mid-range or even low-end hardware. Considering it has a native TAA implementation, (and a very good one at that) it would be a massive help if there was some sort of upscaling tech, such as FSR 2.2 or FSR 3 to maintain high framerates at high resolutions. The game frequently dropped below my target 165fps at 1440p and i ended up having to cap it at 120fps. I know, these may be minor problems considering most people don't play like this, but the performance was similar to Doom Eternal at max settings, and i expected it to be much better considering the art style of the game.All in all, just buy the game, its some great fun. Good Hunting.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is a really fun game. A long game, but a fun one none the less.As far as I know, this game is made up of three episodes and each one has eight sectors to play through. Sectors are huge and can take a while to finish, especially if you're a completionist. Fortunately for us, we play as Johnny Turbo, a heavily augmented "street sweeper" who can get from point a to point b faster than you can in other games can with noclip turned on. Johnny's mobility is nuts. He can triple jump, double dash, rocket/shotgun jump, grappling hook, and chainsaw-slide his way through a sector, killing anything with a pulse while discovering secrets. Just remember there are at least 24 sectors to get through. And if you've gone through all that and finally beaten the game but find yourself still wanting more things to eviscerate with your chainsaw augmented limbs, you're in for a treat. In addition to its lengthy campaign, Turbo Overkill comes with secret levels to unlock and community made custom levels to try out. There's even a free demo available, which is itself longer than other games are in their entirety. So yeah, you'll definitely get your money's worth.While I might think the game can run a bit overlong, resulting in repetitive gameplay (which is easily remedied by playing in small doses), I'm still giving Turbo Overkill a solid recommendation. Why? Because far be it from me to ♥♥♥♥ on a dev for putting too much content in their game at a single price, no DLC needed.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill 3/4Turbo Overkill is probably the most ambitious oldschool/boomer shooter I've played, certainly my favorite since Dusk. Turbo nails that frenetic pace of combat I love from the most recent of these FPS titles like DOOM: Eternal or the aforementioned Dusk. Turbo is more conventional in that it's generous with its ammo and it doesn't subtract from your arsenal as the campaign goes on. This had the effect of the game starting to feel repetitious the longer it went as I had solidifed my preferred tactics and the game didn't really encourage me/ask me to deviate from them. That said, the campaign stays fresh with new locales, set pieces, and a few new mechanics introduced with each of the game's episodes. The movement controls like butter and the shooting feels great. The only thing I think that's lacking comes with the audio. I wish the enemies had more barks to give them personality. Aside from that, this feels like a AAA game: the campaign is surprisingly long, each level feels like it has its own song, there are secret collectibles to seek out to gain access to secret levels, and that's not even to mention the mod support.

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is a game that channels the spirit of Doom Eternal with its frenetic pace and inventive mechanics, including a chainsaw leg. The game's official 1.0 Patch coincides with the release of Episode 3 Part 1, which fixes bugs that have affected the game since its initial beta release. The player assumes the role of Johnny Turbo, a unique character with a blend of human and machine features, navigating a dystopian city controlled by an evil AI named Syn. Armed with arm rockets and a chainsaw leg, players battle enemies and rival bounty hunters.The game is visually reminiscent of 16-bit classics like Doom and Blade Runner, infused with a modern touch through Unreal Engine 5. Turbo Overkill offers a wide array of weaponry, explosive action, and nostalgic nods to classic FPS titles. However, some features like the grappling hook and slow-motion function are introduced later in the game, slightly dampening initial excitement. Despite its wild ride of fast-paced combat, platforming, and humour, the story mainly serves as a backdrop for the intense action.The level editor is a standout feature, allowing players to create and explore user-generated content. The game's pacing, while exhilarating, can lead to repetition and wear thin over time. Nonetheless, Turbo Overkill offers around 15 hours of mutant-demolishing entertainment, with dynamic FPS tunes enhancing the experience. The game manages to successfully capture the adrenaline rush reminiscent of Doom Eternal and delivers a distinct blend of humour, action, and gameplay innovation. While it excels in various aspects, it also presents challenges in terms of level design, controls, and difficulty spikes.

_childDocuments_.review: (The review is more like a 'somewhat' rather than a 'no')This game is almost incredible with some major flaws I cannot ignore.the first critical flaw is motion sickness issues, I'm not one to feel like throwing up when playing games, and I've never been diagnosed by a doctor for motion sickness, the incredible speed of the game started to get to me a tiny bit when I first picked it up, but its negligible, but, and spoilers ahead, however, if you want to know my general review, at least one level has terrible flashing lights, the hardest difficulty is unfair (skill issue on my part prolly) and some other small things. if you ever get this game, and wanna start on a hard difficulty, go to the second hardest.the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ car level, is impossible to play, not the first level where you're driving the car, but the one after that, the flashing lights, and the level designed around jumping on cars made the already difficult game, into something I can't beat, which was a bummer since I was enjoying the game up to that point. I don't know if its the first few rooms, or if its the entire level, but its awful.now, no good criticism comes without a solution, and the way I would solve it is by getting rid of the constant flashing lights on the textures, I checked for a bit in the settings for a way to turn off the texture flashing, but I failed to find anything, I'd also reduce some other motion in the levels (make cars flying by a little rarer) if that, and thats it.I have other issues as well, but its mostly for the hardest difficulty, which I played on for my experience of the game, you will get insta killed at 100 heath by almost anything, even some of the junk enemies, but health is also stupid rare, and it makes a gameplay style of just don't get hit, this promotes playing like a ♥♥♥♥♥, until the chainsaw power ups later, which barely help execpt for staying up with your health, rather than surviving most harder fights.solutions I would make to make the harder difficulties more fun will beA: make micro missiles refuel your armor with every enemy hit/killed (doesn't stack so you can't hit and kill and get shields twice), this makes using your missiles more wisely exciting, as its directly tied to not only blasting enemies, but your survivalB: make the chainsaw leg heal on hit rather than kill, and buff its healing. (wanna note, if this is what it already does, then mb, I only really noticed the healing when killing enemies, I couldn't get back in to check, and theres no wiki to check ether) I think heal on damage, or at least heal on interaction (with a cool down on each enemy) would make it more fun to get active in fights, making it heal on hit then cool down would stop any chance of it being spammed.C: nerf junk enemy pls :pleading: the reason why I even say this is because of the shot gunners early game and the grenaders later on (episode 1) and this is because, if your at 400 health, the max as far as I know, you will still instantly die, now, throughout the game, I didn't really need to run and hide, but the grenaders surely made me do it, and it was more boring than anything to have to fight them. Hardest difficulty not fun (play it second if you do play the game) buy it if you can stand both tons of motion, and flashing lights, at the same time.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after finishing DUSK and Quake 1. It holds up, one of the best retro shooters I've played and one of my new favorite games. If you like cyberpunk and retro shooters, this is is champ.Verdict -The atmosphere is peak cyberpunk, a colorful but gritty dystopia accompanied by a bombastic sythwave soundtrack that keeps you banging through the levels. The graphics are a slick modern-retro. The combat keeps you on your toes like it should, the story is pretty cool, the main character is cool, the chainsaw leg is super cool. The game is just cool, man. Did I mention how cool the soundtrack is?CONCLUSION - If you like retro style shooters and/or enjoy cybperunk settings and 80's movies, you need to get this game.If you only buy games on sale, this game is wholly worth the full $25.Gameplay - The gampelay is what i wanted from a retro fps. Zipping around the map and mag dumping fools. You get a sweet chainsaw leg ability to mess around with, you get alt-fire upgrades for your weapons and body augments to upgrade and customize your play style. Enemies are abundant and can swarm you and bigger enemies get pretty tanky all of which encourages on the fly thinking and constantly switching up your strategy mid combat or die trying. I played on Street Cleaner difficulty and had a good time tho it's not uncommon for encounters to get a little sweat at times.Level Design -I like how the level design encourages flinging yourself around the arena, it pairs exceedingly well with the spray and pray attitude of your weapon loadout. The only downside being the movement mechanics can feel inconveniently floaty at the wrong friggin time. None of the levels took me more than an hour but I spent a lot of time looking for secrets which aren't easy to find.I think the game peaks as a whole in Episode 2 and the second half of Episode 1. The setting and stakes are tactfully introduced and the payoff feels good. The level and encounter designs are on really on point here. Vehicle's were the low point for me in my opinion but some of the levels are cool and there aren't a lot of vehicle sections and they don't overstay their welcome. Episode 3 is where it hits the fan. Levels are a fustercluck of enemy swarms and a generous helping of tanky enemies. You cannot relax for a second especially in the final boss rush. This jams up the flow of combat which does a little disservice to the mechanics but the game very much ends on a bang and i can respect thatStory -I didn't buy Turbo Overkill for the story but I was pleasantly surprised. On top of playing like a cool 80's action flick, I got pretty invested in Johnny's struggle of having everything taken from him while being thrust into the role of galactic savior. It fits perfect for the setting and puts and extra gear into the gameplay. The bounty hunters are a bit whacky without going over the top and have real motivations, even if it it's just getting paid. I love how the main villain is played as an unapologetic edgelord D-BagMy only two gripes are 1. conquering the universe is an overblown threat, galaxy sounds a lot more believable and more threatening. 2. no Ripper gf  :c

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is a well-crafted old-school FPS game with ridiculously complex mechanics that are easy to learn but hard to master. The gameplay mechanics include double-jumping, air-dashing, wall-running, grappling hooks, and of course, the iconic chainsaw slide, whereby you slide across the floor while shredding anyone in your path with the chainsaw built into your prosthetic cyborg leg. And the weapons bring their own unique mechanics too! For example, there's a sniper rifle that kills its target by teleporting you to their exact location, thereby "tele-fragging" them, i.e. blowing them to pieces as you take their place. There are also heat-seeking missiles, a flamethrower, plasma rifle, double-barrelled shotgun, and more, with alternative fire modes too.All of these mechanics would be pointless if you could easily beat the game just by running and gunning. But even the second-hardest difficulty is brutal compared to the average FPS, so the game really forces you to get good, which I appreciated.Overall, I highly recommend this game to fans of "boomer shooters" and fast-paced FPS games with a high difficulty ceiling.

If you love boomer / movement shooters at all then you absolutely need this game now.

_childDocuments_.review: You're an amalgamation of gadgets, flesh, and an assortment of weapons that shreds everything and everyone at 50 MPH in vertigo inducing levels.This is basically Sonic Adventure meets Doom Eternal and it's being completely ignored for some reason. It's legit some of the most fun I had in a while in a SP FPS and I even forgive all the jank attached to it. Because you're basically grapple hooking, chainsaw legging, animation canceling, slowing down time, and shooting missiles out your anus while giving the finger to your enemies with combat that never seems to come to a grinding halt like so many shooters.Play it now. This shooter is filled to the brim with excess; yet somehow doesn't feel bloated in the slightest. That's quite a feat in this landscape.

The game really pushes you to use the entire arsenal that is given to you. If you get stuck on a level, you can purchase plenty of crazy (and cool) augments to use at your disposal. _childDocuments_.review: Light 6 /10This is unfortunately one of those games that start very strong, and with each passing episode gets worse and worse.Latest and (thankfully) final Episode 3 feels almost like a completely different game, without any thought put into the level design, compared to Episode 1.Speaking of level design: the intricacies and creative encounters are replaced with never ending arenas full of random enemies, weapon balance gets more and more unhinged by the chainsaw leg being so much superior to everything else, you'll end up just sliding around, doing nothing else.Enemy variety also got hit, with episode 3 struggling to come up with basically anything new or exciting.The difficulty also vanished at some point, leaving me bored out of my mind killing the same enemies for hours to end, without any challenge at all.I advise the developer to kick the early access next time, or take more time with each episode, cause this really feels like a rushed product just for the sake of releasing it ASAP.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute gem. Wonderfully goofy and fun. A non-stop Adrenalin ride from stat to Finish. Lets start with the boring stuff. While the story is fine, it's pretty generic. A super A.I wants to take over the world and you have to destroy it. A few twists and turn along the way but that's pretty much it. it's not really the point of these games to have a interesting story it's just a backdrop so we can do cool sh*t anyway. I will mention the good characters and voice acting, all of the characters are petty eccentric and i think the voice actors did well to accurately portray them. Also S.A.M.M is definitely best boy. Now let's move on to the important stuff, and Turbo Overkill certainly doesn't disappoint. I loved all of the weapons and all the upgrades. The weapons feel distinct and the upgrades are unique and interesting as well. Not to forget your chainsaw leg which carried me through the whole game. Whats most surprising is that the vehicle combat is also absolutely amazing as well. All of this combined and you get one of the most fun and best designed boomer shooters ever. There's a lot going on both in combat and mechanics. Despite this it plays very smoothly and precise. If gameplay is all that matter to you then look no further. It's also worth touching on the sound design. For the most part it's good: the music has bangers from start to finish, with the boss battle's being standout hits. The weapon sounds however seemed a bit lame compared to the loud and bombastic rest of the game. Overall it's well worth it. The gameplay in my opinion is the best from the boomer shooter genre and it never gets old introducing new things all the way to the end and breaking up the run n gun parts are some great vehicle set pieces for some verity. My few little issues should not put you off this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: I've been on a boomer shooter kick as of late and this has to be the best of the bunch. Fun story, great setting, perfect voice acting for this type of game, buttery smooth gun play, intense shootouts, the weapons all pack a nice punch, the chainsaw leg slide was a nice touch, and the turbo mode (bullet time) saved my rear end more times than I can count. I highly recommend this game to any FPS fan.
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: One of the better boomy shootys. Only parts that were terrible were the story, dialogue, and voice acting. There are 25ish levels and it never got boring. You slowly gain your arsenal of weapons, new movement abilities, and perks. You might be driving a car in one level, then flying a hoverbike or a helicopter in another. The level design has a great mix of narrow hallways and arenas. The final levels of each chapter up the arena count considerably, while the earlier levels of the chapter tend to have more linear sections. Weapons are great. Classics and some new ones. Each has an alt fire. The movement of the game is its shining attribute. You have a dash, and a slide, and other unlocks. You can slide in mid air to get more distance. Once you get the hang of it, its hard not to slide and dash everywhere you go in addition to double jumping. You are just one step below flying pretty much and its awesome. The game would have gotten stale without the chainsaw leg, it, and the acrobatic movement are the heart and soul of this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: Retro cyberpunk Doom Eternal, with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ chainsaw leg. Interesting artstyle, great gameplay, and a killer soundtrack with a surprisingly engaging story for a boomer shooter. The difficulty can feel a bit inconsistent at times, and usually goes from "too easy" to "I'm dead" faster than you can react, but it doesn't stop Turbo Overkill from being an absolute blast. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Turbo Overkill

_childDocuments_.review: Turbo Overkill is rad.Featuring a diverse selection of monstrosities eager to tear you apart and an equally diverse range of weaponry to put them down with Turbo Overkill is not only a great arena shooter, it's one of the best games in it's category.Every level throws in something new, whether it's a fresh face to blast apart, a new toy to assist with the blasting, some new traversal puzzle, the occasional vehicle level to keep the ante as high as it'll go capping each section off with a climactic boss battle that will put your skills to the test.Three episodes split up into a myriad of levels from water logged docks and winding canyons of scrap metal to the insides of a super sized flesh beast and the besieged capital ship of a mercenary outfit.No good cyberpunk dystopia would be complete without cybernetic augmentations and Turbo Overkill has a plethora of options, most augment your abilities; reduced cool-downs, extra damage and tweaks to the functionality of related abilities, all customisable to your preference.If you're into movement shooters, arena shooters, boomer shooters or any variation on that style of game, heck even if you're just getting into first person shooters in general I can't recommend Turbo Overkill enough.10/10

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic game, a blend of familiar faces that manages to feel fresh and fun the whole way through. Part Ultrakill, part Doom 2016, I even felt traces of Serious Sam in there at times. Although there are multiple inspirations, the biggest influence is definitely Ultrakill, and that's a great thing. There were even times that I thought to myself, "I should be swapping weapons more if I want to get a good rank on this level." And even though it won't get you an S-Rank, this game is well designed enough that you do end up getting a good reason to swap weapons often, in the form of a swapping = damage augment.I think that's the theme of this game, really; well designed. There were only one or two times that I had to look around for where to go, meaning the level design was really great and it flowed naturally. All the weapons were satisfying and fun to use, toting interesting secondary functions that give each weapon depth. It should go without saying that the movement is fantastic and fun while also being easy to pick up and go fast right away. Love some big boss fights and, while the story wasn't anything profound really, it's a good backdrop to get you to said boss fights. My only complaint really would be that a couple of the levels in Episode 3 dragged on a bit, but that's no big deal really.Overall, this game was absolutely delightful and the pictures on the steam page don't even do it justice. It's actually way more fun than it looks. If you're even slightly interested, I'd definitely recommend it. Without hesitation.

_childDocuments_.review: Some high-quality entertainment, it's impressive how ambitious the whole project is. Gets very good towards the end especially. The guns feel satisfying, have interesting designs and a great overall feel, there's a lot of them, they're all at least a little interesting. Very high-intensity combat, there are absurd amounts of enemies you face at once. When your arsenal is filled with insanely overpowered gear, facing a gigantic horde is pretty great.The dialogue feels amatourishly written at times. I'm not a huge fan of some of the character/enemy designs (The protagonist looks so absurdly ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I cannot stand it, he looks like he had 17 beers and passed out in the mall parking lot. Pizza-stains-on-the-wifebeater-core aesthetic. Seriously I cannot stress this enough - my dad looks more badass.), and most of the OST is forgettable techno-jibberish. I wish the weapon wheel would deploy quicker, I wish it were clearer when you're taking damage - it's easy to not even notice when you die.Other than that - the game is just good, I had a blast.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a boomer shooter with an emphasis on fast paced movements. The chainsaw attached to your leg helps with that because you can pick a direction and start shredding for an instant speed boost when you're on the ground. Good fun.I only have one gripe: I find the amount of augments available versus the space for them to be kind of...weird? Like all of them are something I want but some are just better than others so once you get a particularly useful mod it's gonna stay slotted forever. For example: there is an augment that boosts your chainsaw damage but there is a wide gap in health between enemies that can be instantly killed with the chainsaw and those that can't. The augment just makes it so that now chainsawing the big guys in multiple passes is now an option instead of suicide. However, there is also a pair of augments that give you health and armor just for damaging things with the chainsaw. This turns any mob of minor enemies into a health pack that rewards you for just jamming into the whole crowd guns blazing. Cool. Except most of the game is facing a ton of little guys and a couple big dudes, so this set of augments is kind of the best in slot for general play. That being said, with some of the movement and agility augments I cannot wait for this game's speedruns. I already found a couple skips with just the wall jump augment.

A quality idea, and a quality execution of that idea.Highly polished mechanics and gameplay.Johnny Turbo is a god amongst men.I need to buy a chainsaw now.

_childDocuments_.review: As a millenial, I highly recommend gen z to play this boomer shooter!In all seriousness, this has to be the best retro shooter that I have played for a very long time -- maybe even the best one in this millenium. It has everything that was considered fun in the 90s: a great soundtrack, interesting "vertical" level design, a neat selection of weapons, tons of blood and gore, rocket jumping, air dash, wall runs, a totally bonkers story and -- last but not least -- a chainsaw leg slide! I also really like that the game allows you to play at your own pace -- you are not constantly forced into close-quarters arena combat, but you can choose whether you want to  engage head-on with you chainsaw leg or whether you want to solve problems in a remote manner using the plasma rifle or gatling gun.If there is one thing that I have to critize then it's the fact that the chainsaw leg somewhat destroys the game's balance: Engaging pretty much all less-than-boss enemies with your chainsaw leg is by far the most effective way of dealing with them -- especially when you upgrade the chainsaw leg to restore your health and armor after each kill, you become pretty much unstoppable...

name: Lost in Play
detailed_description: Buzz 'Ultimately, Lost In Play is like curling up with a good book, and four hours later you'll suddenly wonder where the time's gone.' - Rock Paper Shotgun Next from Joystick Ventures About the Game Help a brother and sister on an uplifting epic adventure to find their way home. Solving puzzles, escaping a horned beast and meeting quirky goblins are just part of the journey! Lost in Play is a journey through childhood imagination with thoughtfully crafted puzzles and colorful characters. Play as a brother and sister duo on an adventure to find their way back home. Between reality and fantasy, the siblings explore the enchanted forest of a horned beast, start a rebellion in a goblin village, and help a team of frogs free a sword from a stone. PUZZLES & MYSTERY The bizarre and dreamlike world of Lost in Play is filled with mystery, unique puzzles, and mini-games. Challenge a pirate seagull to a game of clicking crabs, serve magical tea to a royal toad, and collect pieces to build a flying machine. Be a part of this modern point & click game that will reward your curiosity and leave you excited for the next piece of story. IMAGINATION COMES TO LIFE From what seems like a normal morning at home to a typical afternoon at the park, you'll soon find yourself on a whirlwind quest as you sneak into a goblin castle, explore ancient ruins, and soar atop a giant stork. Lost in Play takes you on a nostalgic roller-coaster! AN INTERACTIVE CARTOON With a hand-crafted style similar to animated shows from childhood, Lost in Play is a story meant for all. Whether you’re seeking wholesome delight or just a good time, the family can enjoy this story together. GAME FEATURES: A mysterious animated puzzle adventure. Filled with magical and magnificent creatures. Created with families in mind. Have your children watch you play! No dialogue. Everything is communicated visually in a universal way. Inspired by nostalgic TV shows such as Gravity Falls, Hilda, and Over the Garden Wall. Play cards with goblins, build a dragon, and teach a sheep how to fly. Includes 30+ unique puzzles and mini-games. Catch a derpy chicken. Maybe. ACCESSIBILITY For detailed accessibility report please visit the family gaming database Happy Juice Games previously worked on 'The Office Quest' and is a studio that focuses on pushing the boundaries of animated adventure games. We hope you love our game as much as we loved making it.

short_description: Solve puzzles, riddles, and embark on an exciting journey of discovery! Join Toto and Gal as they explore dreamscapes and befriend magical creatures. Lost in their imagination, the brother and sister must stick together and solve puzzles to find their way home.

_childDocuments_.review: . That's probably the easiest way to describe this endearing  inspired by all those spirited cartoons we watched as kids. But, behind the wholesomeness lies  The playful fancy permeates everything from the frisky visual style and charming animation to quite memorable music, equally quirky and mysterious, to whimsical sound design and funny nonsensical speech. Not to mention, the wacky childlike humour, crude but cute, made me laugh out loud quite a few times with its genuine, unabashed directness, free of any pretense. Simply disarming! I caught myself constantly grinning from ear to ear while playing this. Pure, unadulterated joy! It's a kitten with a yarn, a child with a... Oooohhh, shiny!!!  It's a nostalgia trip not out of some retro fad, but because it captures the essence of play. It's nostalgic simply because it made me remember what it felt like when I was a child. When the whole world  was my playground, and all the everyday, boring, mundane things would become portals into magical and extraordinary by the sheer boldness of limitless creative imagination. It's as natural as breathing to see a washing machine tab become the belly of a giant fish, a sister with a cardboard box transform into a monster, and your own grandpa as a helpful fairy guiding you along this wayward, capricious escapade, helping you come down from a trip. The title  may sound a bit generic at first, but it's never been more apt. The brother and sister duo are literally lost in their imagination that they need a bit of guidance to find their way back (the supper is probably getting cold). That's it, that's the story. Oh wait, what about that frog kingdom, green goblins and MacGuffin golden crown? Did we save the world or something? Who cares, it was so much fun. Hopping from chapter to chapter, from one fantastical world to another: running from an angry  monster, flying a pelican, sailing away, under the sea, venturing into a post-apocalyptic world, into the dragon's cave... disco? winding up in the  dungeon, and finally with the Sandfrog? where things get weirder as the dream and reality start to merge in something like the Alice's endless fall through the well - you finish how you started, at one helluva surrealist tea party!Did I mention you get to build your own dragon? And ride it over the seven seas and seven... um, thingamajigs. In-between chapters are these great, sprawling cinematic segments with beautiful scenery evoking awe-inspiring fairy-tale-like worlds filled with spectacular, majestic creatures. Catch the flight of  eels, ride a huge stag beetle, climb a mountain? with hundreds of eyes, help a barefoot giant get the  cactus out of his pinky, encounter a terrifying  sandworm, hop merrily over molten lava... These are automated sequences as colourful as kaleidoscopic retrospective, but by the time you finish the game, it feels like you've been through an adventure of many lifetimes, an amalgam of all the best bedtime stories. This is what I love about adventure games, this sense of, well, adventuring, which is at the essence of play. Investigating, improvising, clicking, testing, see where the curious spirit takes you. The game is intuitive like that and completely reliant on visual cues. There are no words, written or spoken (well, no intelligible words) that will tell you what to do, but instead everything is conveyed through pictures, from the hint system to all the puzzles and minigames tutorials. Lost in Play is a point'n'click at its core, but stylised and trimmed off most adventure games' pitfalls like pixel hunting, bloated inventory black hole and too busy screens. On the contrary, this part of the game just flows. There are only a couple of items to collect at most and you get to use them very quickly instead of dragging it with you endlessly. Even in those fetch-this-for-that sequences that require multiple steps, which is most chapters, things aren't convoluted. And if you get stuck, there are generous hints that either illustratively show you the next step or, when it comes to puzzles and minigames, reveal parts of the solution, just enough to nudge you in the right direction. With this picturesque hint system, you really don't need any guide because the game is designed for the whole family in mind, children and adults alike. This is the most impressive thing about the gameplay, this perfect balance in difficulty. Not too hard to be inaccessible to kids, but not too easy to be boring for adults. Now, when I say suited for children, it doesn't equal dumbed down and simplistic. Far from it, some minigames can be quite challenging. But overall, they have a nice range in difficulty and variety, not too frustrating and always entertaining, making sure you can't wait to see what's next in store. The game's bursting with various puzzles: board games (crab-checkers, oof), cards, physics based, time travel manipulation, 'blind' labyrinth driving (this one gave me trouble), redirect the lasers, jellyfish pattern recognition puzzle (loved this one), connect the story (mwah) and many more. All logical and intuitive in equal measure. My favourite must be the time manipulation puzzle inside a storybook where the goal is to get to 'Rapunzel' in a tower using three timelines, except it's actually a prince with a really looong beard. The gameplay is positively addictive, it's so easy to get lost in it, just like Gal and Toto. Hamuchikamamanina! - must be a bad hair day. Kopropichekterarapotoylem. Proktoko; shloiniki (sister?) Liza baka choina - lizard's tail? I just love this gibberish talk. It's so silly and nonsensical that I started writing it down and even translating. Well, at least tried to. The game is genuinely funny and effortlessly cute. There's gotta be a word for it. Adorkable? Cheeky? Fute? Even the snot bubbles are cute. Have you ever gotten cute-rage over a granny trying to get her purse back? Well, I have now. There are so many wacky details and amusing gags, a lot of them involving a hilarious goofy chicken, who's also a badass hero; a metalhead sheep; how about a flying sheep with pink fart propulsion;  elaborate cartoony plans; cat and dog running gag................................ Oh, there's also a huge derpy cat... just cause ;PLike I said, this crude whimsical humour is so blatantly direct and irresistible, such jovial, mischievous expression of childlike charm. Playing this frollicking romp made me so happy, plastered with perpetual gleeful smile; it's dopamine galore, literally feelgood. I felt like a delighted child again. And I don't think I can give this game a bigger compliment. I can recommend it to , it is meant for everyone: young children, old children, grumpy children, everyone who embraces the inner playful child (if not, they will), the childish and the childlike. I especially recommend it to jaded asses to put a smile on their faces. I dare you not to beam at this bubbliness. To paraphrase C.S. Lewis for the end:
_childDocuments_.name: Lost in Play

_childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play is a wholesome and whimsical adventure title that is truly a joy to play. Filled with cute cartoonish art and a vast array of puzzles, minigames and laughs, this is a game that the whole family can enjoy.Playing as a young brother and sister duo (Toto and Gal), players' first task as the sister is to capture your brother’s attention so that he will play with you. He is fixated on his hand-held gaming device and does not care for your mischief. However, once his imagination is spiked, the whimsical adventure commences. The two become completely lost in their vivid imaginations and the line between reality and fantasy is all but a blur. Their goal becomes to find a way home. Always working collaboratively, they find themselves in all sorts of bizarre situations, but they always have each other to rely on. Whether it be escaping from the goblin dungeon, freeing one another from the stomach of a fish, or sailing the seas, the two remain inseparable. There is no dialogue or even any text to read, but this feel-good story is extremely genuine, positive and authentically wholesome. The game is also designed to be family friendly and openly states on the store page "... have your children watch you play!", which I think is a fantastic concept. Despite the game itself being targeted for adults (due to the puzzles complexity), I think this would be a blast to play alongside young family members.Lost in Play is an excellent and diverse adventure game with some point and click elements. Featuring a plethora of differing puzzles and minigames, as well as constant new environments to explore and characters to meet. The game remains completely fresh from beginning to end. Gameplay consists of either Toto or Gal (or both), exploring a small area, picking up objects to use in other parts of the environment whilst completing puzzles/minigames along the way. I found the difficulty to be perfectly balanced, it was neither too difficult, nor too easy. The environments were small, which made it straightforward to know which items to use in specific places. Although inventory management based puzzles is something we have seen repeatedly, the constant influx of new stimuli and introductions to short minigames made me feel as if I was playing a new game every time the setting changed, or when a minigame popped up. This helped to maintain my engagement, never knowing just what I will run into next.The mixture of different mini games completely changes up the gameplay, making it feel fresh and exciting. The puzzles, although cute in aesthetic, are not braindead simple. I found them to be well-balanced, easy to understand, but definitely aimed at adults. Interestingly, most of the puzzles do not explain the goal, or if it does, it is in a very brief picture format (once again, no text). I could grasp almost every puzzle through this, and it was designed exceptionally well. There is also a hint system just in case you do not understand, or are just generally stuck. This gives a part of the solution, such as part of a combination, or the beginning solution to a pattern. I did find some complex puzzles which required a few resets and tries, such as the checkers puzzle, but it was not unreasonable or frustrating. The 30+ puzzles are completely different to each other, but some examples include card and board games, turn-based puzzles and even time-based puzzles, involving the manipulation of items in both the past and present to reach a specific goal.Lost in Play's colourful hand-drawn art is eye-catching and stunning. Inspired by cartoons, just  modernised to give its smooth and polished appearance. Each different area expertly portrays the vivid dreamscapes of a child's wildest imaginations. Ride beetles, talk to a pirate seagull, help three frogs and so much more. The characters overly theatrical facial expressions, dramatized colours, and wild environments all brilliantly portray the nonsensical universe both Toto and Gal have personally crafted.As mentioned previously, there is no dialogue, the characters speak, but only in random sounds, like the well-known “Sims language.” This cemented the separation from reality and the siblings' made-up world, further hyperbolised by the matching fairy-tale soundtrack. Approximately six hours. Yes None, it is linear with no collectable items.Lost in Play is a standout puzzle adventure game. Its feel-good story and eccentric environments, characters and mini games made it a complete blast to play. It is one of the rare titles without any major faults to comment on, and I recommend it to all fans of the genre, anyone looking for a family friendly game, or lovers of all things cute and wholesome. This is a brilliant game and a must play!

_childDocuments_.review: Gravity Falls season sure 3 looks interesting.This is basically CalArts: The Game.It’s as if Pajama Sam and Over the Garden Wall had a child together.As a 90’s kid who grew up with Saturday morning cartoons and adventure games from Sierra and Lucas Arts, this game feels like it combines the best of both worlds perfectly. The game plays very well and I especially loved the graphics and animations. Extra kudos for the tiny team behind this!It was really such an amazing experience. Imagination means so much to me and I feel like as we grow up we begin to replace our imaginations more and more with grown up things without realizing that we're all kids who have only gotten a little taller and wiser.     It took me back to my childhood, from when my siblings and I would get so much in trouble, to the time we took our bikes to the top of the hill and rode it all the way down crashing at moms backyard gate, to the time we got our first Nintendo and played for hours... good memories, and I hope to see more games like this in the future. I'm honestly generally not a fan of puzzles (because they make me look really stupid, really quick, let's be honest), but this was ADORABLE! It even motivated me to finally put some writing down for what I can only hope will turn into my own little game/visual novel one day. Just what I needed! This game is only a few hours long but every single moment is memorable. I loved the humor, the art style, the fantasy world, the characters, the music... just everything.Lost in Play manages to combine together two worlds that I always thought were kinda born to be put together into one package (animated series of today, and point & click adventure games), and does so while making a big effort in standing out on its own. The best part about the game is for sure the atmosphere, helped by the well-composed soundtrack and the absolutely great art that supports its presentation from start to finish, plus some stylistic choices (such as the entire game being dubbed via a gibberish language) that I qucikly began to associate to this game specifically as I played it. The premise of the story itself helps in this regard, a simple one about a pair of imaginative siblings busy exploring dreamscapes and made-up worlds. Gameplay-wise the game is very far from point & click adventure classics, since the puzzles often take the form of mini-games or small interactions with single objects, and the inventory rarelys gets filled to the limit. With a couple of exceptions, the game will feel like a clean and stress-free ride, which indeed is what the game aims for: don't expect enigmas that will make you pull at your hair while shouting obscenities at the screen, but rather some small puzzles that often are used as an excuse for some little humour moments here and there.Perhaps my only gripe is that the game can end quite soon, not because short games are a no-no, but rather because the 'I want more' feeling is very much present after seeing the final credits. More so when there are hints at what might have been possible within the story itself (I won't go in the specifics to avoid spoilers). It is so whimsical and wholesome.  I was so sad to have finished it.  Still, Lost in Play is definitely a game that ends before it gets repetitive and too long, and the experience itself is absolutely worth a buy, if only to go to a trip down memory lane and play a game that doesn't need complex gameplay or a bombastic presentation to tell its story and offer a few hours of fantastic fun.It's one of the best games I've played in the last few years, definitely recommend everyone giving it a try. Sure 20 bucks is expensive for 4 hours for a game today, but I believe this kind of game doesnt strive on longevity, but on the intensity and quality of the short playthrough. Today, many of us as busy adults now have at LEAST 10 games with relatively good quality, and more than 10 to 20 hours of content in them... and we dont have the time, the opportunity, the will or the whatever to play them. Then comes a game that delivers a fun, organic experience, with a great story and soundtrack next to it, and it comes in a short punch of +- 3 hours? That sounds great to me, honestly!10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Albert Einstein once said: “Logic will get you from A to Z; imagination will get you everywhere.”  is the perfect embodiment of this quote, as it blends together logical minigames with a story that appears to be born from the imagination of children, and which will transport you - the player - into a fantastic, dream-like realm of endless possibilities.In  you control two siblings - a brother and a sister - who during one sunny day start playing together in their living room and end up drifting into a fantastic world created by their own imagination, in which the things they perceive in reality are projected as surreal shapes and events. They embark on an illusory adventure of finding the way back home, aided by the whimsical characters that the two kids encounter on their path. Their story is contained into 15 short chapters, each of them having a distinctive theme, art style and scenery.The writing is absolutely stellar.  is a game of surprises waiting for you at each step. All the situations that the two children encounter are unexpected and outside our normal way of thinking; the amount of out-of-the box ideas put into the game is astonishing. The characters they encounter and their personalities are also quite unique. There are no horror or negative elements, the game is overloaded with friendliness, positivity and topped off with a very fine sense of humor.Essentially,  is a point & click adventure that’s best described as an interactive cartoon. Compared to other games in the genre, your actions will almost always be clear to you, and the characters you encounter will also make sure to tell you what items they expect you to fetch for them. There aren’t any obtuse situations like in older point & click games, in which you had to pixel-hunt for certain items or use them in very counter-intuitive ways:  flows easily and naturally, and how or in what order your inventory items have to be used is pretty straightforward.On the other hand, the minigames are a mix of easy and tough. Every few chapters you will encounter a minigame on which you might get stuck for 30m - 60m (a variation of checkers, a sokoban-inspired game of aligning crabs and a certain card game are among the most difficult). While  is a fairly short game whose core adventure can be completed in less than 2h, the rest of the time will be spent on these minigames, trying and retrying to beat a rather smart AI. The AI’s moves are randomly generated, so there’s no clear recipe on solving them. If I were to complain about something in , that would be the lack of a skip option - the game desperately needs one, especially for younger audiences. Currently there’s no way to progress further apart from retrying a minigame several times until the RNG is in your favor, and then combining it with a strategical and logical approach. There is a hint system, but it’s not very detailed - it only gives you a nudge in the right direction by showing you an image of your next goal in its completed state and not how exactly to reach it. captivates with its charming hand-drawn, cartoony art style. Transforming your gameplay into an immersive experience and making you feel like a little kid sitting in pajamas in front of the TV watching their favorite cartoon is what the game absolutely shines the brightest at. Also stellar is the soundtrack that perfectly complements the animations. The game is fully voiced, yet the language is unintelligible although the gibberish speech adds a nice nuance which emphasizes even more the idea that whatever happens in the game is surreal.The game supports three different input schemes: controller, mouse+keyboard or mouse alone. They all function pretty well, and each have advantages / disadvantages in usability. Personally, I preferred playing it with mouse-only since it felt more accessible than the others especially during minigames, while transitioning between scenes was easier with a controller.There are 19 achievements in the game, most of them being story-related. The missable achievements are easy to obtain even during a first playthrough without using a guide, but the game also has a chapter select in case you skipped any of them. None of them require any finicky skills, nor do they have any time restrictions.The concept of  is a sweet and heartwarming one, showcasing the innocence and the astonishing power of children’s imagination. The game feels very much like a labor of love, given the attention to detail that the developers put into it. Playing it is a wholesome experience, albeit one that is not fully suited for children due to the few difficult puzzles present in the game and the inability to skip them.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? It is a an adventure for kids, or for the young at heart. You play a cute red-haired girl (and her older brother) and solve funny little puzzles. Do they make sense? No, not really, at least not more than in an average point and click adventure. You have to solve one puzzle after the other, and as soon as you achieve one thing, something else becomes possible. Quite long - but simple - puzzle chains. And quite funny ones, always accompanied by little animations and funny sounds (or is this a real language?) There is an inventory as well, but not a large one and manipulating it is mostly automatic. Just select an item and the object where you want to use it. Every few puzzles lead to a (logic or action) minigame. The logic minigames require a bit of thinking, or trying out all possible combinations. Lucky for me, you can always use a hint function to cheat.The game is obviously made with much love and if  all the funny and cute little animations don't make you smile you have a heart of stone. There are 15 episodes to play through, a gamepad is recommended. I played with a 8BitDo Zero 2 pad and it worked fine.A cute, family-friendly adventure with easy puzzles, not so easy logic minigames and many charming animations.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play is probably the most charming point & click game I have ever played.Positives:+ A fully and beautifully animated adventure; the colourful art style, the whimsical plot, and the imaginative scenes are all reminiscent of Gravity Falls, my favourite animated TV show.+ An interactive cartoon worthy of its name: the game smoothly interweaves cutscene and gameplay, with an extraordinary well-balanced pacing.+ Manifold puzzles and mini-games blending naturally with the narrative, some are so brilliantly designed that I wish there were more levels in them:* standard point & click puzzles, nothing with moon logic (but some requires keen observation);* brain-teasing logical puzzles with gentle difficulty, the mechanics of which are similar to those in the usual puzzle games;* captivating board/card mini-games.+ Built-in hint system for every puzzle, subtly pointing to the right direction without spoiling everything.+ Language- (and possibly also culture-) agnostic: no words in the whole adventure; characters all talk gibberish (which is fully voiced-over!). Instead of real-world languages, players are well-guided by visual explanation of puzzle/mini-game rules and pictorial thought bubbles conveying what objects a character is looking for.+ Divided into 15 chapters to facilitate replaying and hunting for the few missable achievements.+ Wholesome, casual, and utterly family-friendly.Negatives: Negatives? What negatives? Okay, maybe a bit too short (around 4~5 hours with no replayability) to some players' liking. I would say this is a nonissue, considering how much delightful cartoony adventure and high-quality puzzles they have packed into it.Tl;dr: A bestest best.

_childDocuments_.review: I have picked up this game on sale for 10 dollars. Seeing that it is among the highest rated games on Steam I had high expectations going into it. Unfortunately, my expectations of a truly great game were not met. are top-notch. The playfulness and the attention to detail of the animations most certainly contribute to the high score of the game. And I can totally get behind that. Lost in Play is beautiful from start to finish. are pretty good, too, but it serves more as a background necessity than being something that shines on its own. I have just finished the game and not a single piece of music comes to mind that stuck in my head. It is purely ambient, which does not necessarily mean it's bad. It did its job.The gripes I have with this game are mostly .While the presentation is beautiful, the subject-matter that is presented stays mostly flat. The plot revolves around two siblings "Lost in Play" traversing imaginary lands on their quest to get back home through a Frog Portal which can only be activated with a Crown lit by moonlight and, to make things worse, the portal will be closed if they don't make it in time before the next New Moon. You would think it's a product of a child's imagination. Well, that's exactly it. It's the baseline of the game's story. A child's play. In some sense this is charming as it underlines the whole concept of the game. But it is an easy way out from a developer's perspective to not have to provide a coherent storyline, any in-depth explorations of the created world and most importantly, any logical grounding of many of the puzzles presented.It is clear that a lot of thought was put into this benign storyline regardless, with an ending that is connected to the beginning, and multiple references/"characters" making appearances throughout the journey. Ultimately, though, as a player, the plot is forgettable, incongruent and just outright boring. The protagonists, serving as anonymous player characters, do not have any depth to them whatsoever. The world that is presented is as random as it can get. There is the "But it's a child's imagination" argument - hinting at real world items that exist in their home -, but that experience is not what most people play games for. That said, one might argue that this game targets a younger audience. And I think there's certainly some merit to that. But this leads me to the next problem. The game as a whole is extremely easy and very short. I finished it in under 4 hours. Mostly, the gameplay is split up into1. collecting items for people2. puzzlesIn a traditional point-and-click adventure, collecting and using items in the right spot is what makes a puzzle. On top of that you might have some other dedicated puzzle screens like the puzzles in Lost in Play. However, in this game the item combination part is completely free, as in super simple, since you always know exactly which item to use where. I am not saying that you can't break with conventions to create something different yet intriguing. But the way it is handled here, it not only eliminates a landmark of Point & Click adventures but coupled with slow screen-transitioning makes it feel entirely like doing chores.The puzzles on the other hand, ramp up the difficulty immensely. Don't get me wrong, I enjoyed most of them, because this is where I actually had to think to progress. But most of the game happens in the "Everything is extremely simple" mode. This ramp-up in difficulty, I reckon, is not a good fit for younger or more distanced P&C audiences.:Did I enjoy playing Lost in Play? Not really, I mostly liked the art style.Would I buy a 20$ Lost in Play over a 10$ Monkey Island? Absolutely not.Should you buy Lost in Play? Only if you're a fan of excellent presentation and don't mind a shallow experience and when it's on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly sunny, disarmingly charming, the game seems to embody the spirit of adventure and boundless children's imagination. Brother, sister and their grandfather start their game on a boring day that quickly develops into treasure hunting, dragon flying, diving into the depths of the sea and whatever their fantasy allows them to draw. Adventures become more and more exciting, obstacles on the way to the goal become even stranger and fun, the game seems to be filled with bright colors and emotions. The plot here deserves to be embodied in a full-length cartoon, it is very funny, does without dirty vulgarity and modern trends, it is equally interesting to perceive it for both an adult and a child. It is impossible not to smile while playing this game, as if you yourself are returning to your childhood, when branches from a tree, a mother's scarf, a tire and a dirt road were enough to organize the largest space race in history with friends.The game is completely safe to play with children of all ages and is very friendly to its player. Most of the gameplay is a traditional point-and-click quest, but there are also puzzles. Here, the child himself may not be able to cope with most of them, there are tough nuts here, but the hint system can help with this. The system for using things here is quite simplified, it is very difficult to get stuck in one place for a long time, and dividing the game into episodes even more smooths out sharp corners. Episodes can be replayed separately at any time (which is especially important for achievement hunters). I really don't know what to criticize the game for. Unless, it may not seem the longest (it took me 5 hours), but in terms of eventfulness, these 5 hours calmly beat projects from huge studios. The visuals are fantastic, you literally play a cartoon. I previously called "Voodoo Detective" the most beautiful quest of 2022, but this game is very serious competition for it. The logic here is also in absolute order, only once in the whole game I had a serious question about the logic of the puzzle.Definitely, definitely, definitely try it. Gratitude for the pure and kind emotions that this world will give you will be priceless. This is the rare project that can be recommended to people who have been children at least once in their lives, just great.

_childDocuments_.review: In Lost in play we play as two siblings that play together during the day using their imagination and fantasy.The Characters speak gibberish while talking and apart from the game menu no words are used, so the game is multilingual by default.To progress through the game we play through different scenes with a mix of finding the right object, to use, and some logic puzzles.A integrated hint system can help you if you find yourself lost, but appart from some logic puzzles you will not find yourself struggling to much.The animations are super cute and the game made me laugh more then once.If you look for a classic point & click experience you will not be happy with this game.But for me… I totaly love this kind of super cute games and can totally recommend this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent Point n' Click.(Well, nearly pure a Pn'C: there are a couple of actions I didn't manage to achieve with a mouse, thus resorting to a keyboard. And, more importantly, an early mini-game calls for a modicum of reflexes.)The puzzles are great, intuitive, on the easy side. They are solved with intent and observation, as the clues are always nearby.In rare fashion, the mini-games are great as well, mixing puzzle and strategy (except for the arcade one mentioned above.)For a dose of  negativity, the game is still glitchy 5 months after release: I experienced a couple of crashes and as many freezes, all during loading screens, between chapters. And since it's 1 slot-only auto-save (a staple of amateur UI,) it can lead to replaying a chapter multiple times until it finally works as intended. At least it wasn't game-breaking.No flaws other than those two in my book.Pictures and sound are lovely, but what shines even more is the animation. It's fluid in both storytelling and gameplay. That aspect of the interface is particularly intuitive and smooth.Let's mention the humour as well: while I giggled quite a bit throughout,  the chicken escape episode made me laugh on every interaction. Buy it now before it's sold out.

_childDocuments_.review: Ah remember when you could just imagine a whole different world while playing with toys or when playing outside. Letting the time slip away as there was fun to be had. Lost in Play is about what you can guess based on the title: two siblings being lost in one of their play sessions.The game starts with a quick dream sequence, a look into the young girl’s dream which also gives us how whimsical the adventure will be, before it’s time to wake up for the day. She ends up waking up first, mainly due to the sun shining right in her face, and proceeds to wake up her brother (which is actually the first puzzle screen in the real world).These two siblings, while we don’t get their names in-game, are Toto and Gal. Today seems like it’ll be another boring day where they have nothing they really need to do. Toto is what you’d expect, a broody boy playing his video game and trying to not let his sister mess up his gaming streak. Well, after some puzzle solving to build a helmet to cosplay as a creature in one of their favorite comics, Gal gets her brother Toto to start playing with her outside. This turns into an adventure where innocently passing under a frog gate caused them to be transported to another world filled with weird, but familiar, creatures, magic, and goblins.Despite the game taking place in their imagination, making things more whimsical than they would normally be, the puzzles here are easy to figure out. They have a line of logic to it despite the imaginary and fantastical setting they take place in. And even though there is no dialogue, the characters will have a little speech bubble with a picture of the needed item. Each area will have a handful of puzzles for you to figure out, which completing one will help you progress in another puzzle in the area. As the game goes on, these areas do become slightly bigger, with more puzzles to do and slightly being trickier.There is a hint system in place so you can check if you’re a bit lost. While I didn’t have trouble most of the time, it does help if you just forgot where you needed to go with a certain item or the times where you are lost on what you have to do (which I only encountered twice).Honestly, the difficulty really comes with the minigames. There are two kinds: puzzle minigames and just traditional minigames. The puzzle minigames will give you the first two to get the hang of it before throwing you two hard levels to finish off on. These can be pretty tricky, sometimes the hint will help but sometimes not so much. Though it helps you can easily look them up if you’re just done with being stuck. With the regular minigames, the only difficult ones are where you go up against an AI. An early example is where you play a game with checkers, but you have to corner your opponent (and you can only go forwards with your pieces). These really straddle the line of being frustrating, with only one being not so bad. While you can pick up what the AI will do when faced with certain moves, it has enough of a random factor that can totally ruin your day.I did come to wish that there was an option to skip at least the minigames where you go against the AI if you’re stuck after a certain amount of tries. You have to hope that your moves and the AI’s will just click in place so you can finally continue.Though, I was disappointed at one sequence towards the end of the game. Right before you get to the frog gate, you get a cutscene that shows a handful of different scenes where the siblings are going through different areas. These looked like it would have been interesting to actually play, especially since one scene looked like it was a puzzle sequence, and it stinks that we couldn’t (whether it’s because they were originally planned to be levels but had to be cut out or there weren’t any ideas for them to be fleshed out and fun to play through).Aside from that, I loved the artwork here. It has a really nice and pleasing cartoon style and all the different areas are beautiful to look at. I did find the voices the characters had, so they’re just not moving their mouths without speaking anything, a tad annoying, but that was mainly when it was just the longer “talking” segments.Also, while this does have controller as a recommended way of playing, I do suggest mouse and keyboard instead. It might have just been me, but I had a good amount of moments in minigames where I clicked the button on the wrong direction, which ruined that try. Plus, I had a habit from other games where it will automatically use the item needed if you already have it in your pack and I always had to remind myself that I had to select the item while by the interact point (whereas with a mouse you just have to click and drag the item over, which felt more natural if that makes sense).Lost in Play made me so happy playing it. It really had me at the beginning with the brother being uninterested and broody, but I really loved how that they spent the whole day playing and imagining a whole world where they have to get back home. I especially love the credits where we get to see the real life counterparts of certain areas that seemed more out there. If you’re looking for a wholesome point and click adventure that takes place in two sibling’s imaginations where the majority of the puzzles are easy to figure out, Lost in Play won’t disappoint. Though, I do see a lot of people finding this game too short for the price (it was about 4-5 hours for me, and yes I used the hint system when I got stuck), and the minigames do lean towards being difficult (especially ones where you have an AI opponent).
_childDocuments_.name: Lost in Play

_childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play is a charming and feel-good Point and Click Puzzler that follows the adventures of a brother and sister as they find themselves in a dreamscape after entering it unknowingly when they were too engrossed during their playtime.Right from the bat, Lost in Play pulls you in with its high quality cartoon-ish artstyle and feel. The world in Lost in Play is so colourful and vibrant that it welcomes you in to meet and befriend all the magical creatures, be it whether they are friendly or not so friendly. The world and characters that you’ll see and meet are very well designed and unique. It truly resembles and reminds you of times when you’re lost in your imagination from days when you’re a kid.In terms or story, after getting carried away with playing, you’ll guide Toto and Gal (the Brother and sister) through their adventures to make their way back home before the “portal” they went through by accident closes before sun down. Fret not as along their journey they will meet and help magical creatures who will assist them one way or another. That’s not saying it’ll be a walk in the park for them as some creatures will be in their way as obstacles in their journey (except for the Big Cat, he’s just vibing at the “end”).Being a child-friendly game, Lost in Play exemplifies it well as being easy to understand regardless of what language you speak and such by doing away with any written text or spoken word throughout the game. This may seem tricky or risky but pays off by having a well thought out visual language and clues displayed that you’ll know what you have to do next or how to solve the puzzles.As a puzzle game, Lost in Play has a number of it and where its main strengths lay. Almost every puzzle you have to solve has a mini-game tied to it and every mini-game you’ll encounter is a fresh new one and not recycled. The sheer amount of work that goes into them should be praised as every mini-game brings in new ideas and lessons that after solving them, no matter how simple they may (which not all are simple) be, that after solving them you’ll feel a sense of accomplishment and never feel like it’s wasting your time. The mini-games also helps to keep things fresh and helps to break down the main puzzle in the area into enjoyable bite sizes.For the experience and joy Lost in Play gives the player, it is certainly a stand out for the Point & Click Puzzle game this year which has always been blessed. The quality, polish and heart that Happy Juice Games has embedded in Lost in Play should make them proud and for one should be applauded for establishing such standards and experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost in Play

_childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play does a lot of things right, but makes enough mistakes that I didn't finish it. It's a puzzle game based around two children who are (presumably) playing and imagining all the things in the game, rather than being whisked off to another dimension. This gives the game a lot freedom and variety in the set pieces and characters. The puzzles are generally fairly self contained, which is a breath of fresh air compared to some of the older ones where you carry objects around for hours. The art style and animations are beautiful, and the controls are great. Towards the end it starts to drop the ball as many of the puzzles I didn't think made any sense, even after looking up the answers.- The animations and art style are beautiful- Gameplay revolves around moving through self-contained puzzle areas that are usually 3-4 "rooms" each. All the items you need are used in those rooms, then lost when you move on - so there's no carrying something around for hours wondering what it's for- Wide variety of puzzles to solve- Nice sound effects- Really creative environments to explore- Puzzles are either too easy, or are very unclear in their goals. Usually the problem wasn't that I knew what to do but couldn't work out how - it was that I had no idea what I was supposed to do. On several puzzles, even with the hints giving you half the answer, I couldn't work out what the patterns were supposed to be- In the later part of the game, there's a lot of just walking back and forth between areas to take an item from one place to another- Several puzzles that take a long time to do have no skip option, and no hints- It's about 4-5 hours long, so don't buy it at full price

_childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play is a truly enjoyable point and click adventure game.  It has great art, charming and whimsical narrative without text/dialogue, and logical puzzles.  It's about 4 hours to complete.Some minor issues:- The audio level got a lot louder about 20% into the game- The AI based 2 player mini-games were more frustrating than fun, and a large difficulty spike vs the relatively straightforward point and click puzzles- SPOILER!!! _childDocuments_.review: Full Throttle, Grim Fandango, The Monkey Island series, Broken Sword and Day of the Tentacle. The 90's was such an amazing time for me as a gamer. All these adventure games that took your mind of school or whatever what was going on at home. They took you to a place full of wonder, full of amazing characters, puzzles and stories. Unfortunately the genre never got that popularity back and maybe a handful of games ever gave me that same feeling again.And here I was browsing Steam an coming across Lost in Play. With graphics that gave me that mid 90's feel and by the look of the trailer a true adventure type game. Point and click, but this time with some more puzzle heavy elements (which also is one of my favourite genres). Bought it, installed it and mannnn in a little over 5 hours you get such a gem of a game.Everything about this game is just perfect. The main characters (a brother and sister), the expressions, the people/creatures you meet along the way. How the first couple of puzzles requires logical thinking but the further you go there's some out of the box type puzzles as well. It manages to surprise, to spark that curiosity and wonder that's still somewhere in your adult brain, it gives you moments of laughter and feels profound all the way through.I can't recommend this game enough. Doesn't matter if it's not your 'type of game', get it, you won't regret it. It might be time to boot up all those old classics again after this. A-ma-zing game. Get it a whatever price, support the devs, they deserve every penny.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play is a point-and-click game, where you play as siblings Gal and Toto who created a surreal fantasy story while playing with each other. The game has no real language, everyone speaks gibberish, but speech bubbles showing what you should do appear. I particularly like the artstyle, it's cute and reminds me of cartoons from the 2010s. There's also a creative hint system that shows images that are clues on what we should do next in case you get stuck.Gameplay is mostly the same for its kind, finding and using items while interacting with characters. One unique thing is that there's lots of minigames, and quite varied, like how there's one where you piece events in a chronological order, reflect a beam of light, play checkers, etc. Most of them are quite easy, but some can be a bit too difficult for my liking. Still, it's pretty doable, and if you like cute point-and-click games, Lost in Play is worth a play.

Each chapter just kept surprising me!I also wrongly expected this to be an easy game, but no. Some puzzles required some serious brainstorming and trial and error to reach a solution. _childDocuments_.review: Lost in Play is a point-and-click adventure with great drawn visuals but where few things make sense and with restrictive controls and animations.+ Great drawn visuals+ Charming animations+ Great fantastical theme (excluding it not making much sense)* ~ 4 hour playthrough* Pseudo-language-voiced characters* No text dialogue, only animations and occasionally pictograms- Most things don't make sense; puzzles are non-obvious, intractability, controls, story, …- Character animations stretch their bodies- Slow animations- Repeated animation-lock-ins; made worse by actions not triggering as expected, and the need to manually select inventory items for interactions- No skipping of animationsIt started quite interesting, with an interesting, well-executed setting of kids playing with fantasy. But it quickly became irritating, and annoying, and lost all sense of direction, continuity, or making sense. All that was left felt like forced [animation] jokes where they do not make sense, confusion, and irritation.The fantastical world still had interesting aspects. Things that could be appreciated. The drawn world and characters. But it's an interactive game. And all interaction and progression felt irritating or annoying.Confusion: Some items worked as I expected them to, some worked where I did not expect them to, and some did not work where I expected them to. Characters stretch in animation. How far they can reach is entirely random between locations and interactions. The tip system is sometimes helpful, sometimes not. In one case I was able to skip a mini-game, in all others I checked, that was not an option. Most of what is based on physics makes no physical sense. The tip system was often not helpful.Irritation: Having to walk back and forth, slowly. Inconsistent interaction placement. Interactions leading to the character walking elsewhere then back to start the interaction. Animation lock-in even on repeated playback. Non-obvious intractability. Item and interaction combinations where they don't make sense. Everything confusing adds to the irritation.
