_childDocuments_.review: An immersive action-adventure game set in a mysterious, dystopian world devoid of humans. Here you will have the chance to do what a cat does best: meow, explore, scratch and annoy other characters.You play as a nameless orange cat that gets separated from his family and trapped in a strange, underground city full of humanoid robots. You will explore this world, meet some allies and try to both escape the sealed settlement and help your new friends with their ultimate mission.Since this is about a main character and protagonist, I’m referring to our furry friend as a , not an .Gameplay is fun and its short length prevents it from becoming boring or tedious. Still, I would have loved to play more in this wondrous world along with this smart feline. I clocked 9.8 hours at a leisurely pace, exploring the detailed environments and enjoying the experience. I managed to collect every object on my first run, and only missed a couple of memories. The puzzles are simple but effective, completely logical in its solving requirements, and make sense within the story needs. There is an adequate mix of platforming, puzzle-solving, NPC-interacting, exploring, sneaking and fighting to keep everyone entertained.This game nails the experience of being a cat. You can meow, purr, climb, fit through tight places, scratch various surfaces, push things off tables and shelves, walk on keyboards to produce satisfying gibberish, mess around with board games, sleep on surprising spots—even on top of people—and destroy stuff; and, most importantly, steal a smile from NPCs when you nuzzle up against them.The cat’s movements and animations are not perfect, yet still superbly done. He can realistically run, dash and trot; lick its paws, stretch, orient its ears and stare at stuff just like a real cat would. The animations are quite natural and a joy to look at. Only the sleeping position is not quite precise--a cat does not curl its back legs like a dog would, but this is a minor detail.Environments are detailed, varied and gorgeous. Each chapter has its very own ambience, distinguishable from the rest. The contrast between the organic and the machine is strong and meaningful, and the textures, colors, the lighting, even the platforming and exploration styles are defined per area. Most of them are relatively small and manageable, but still require attention if you are to discover all of ’s secrets. Collectibles abound, and while they are by no means numerous, they are missable and backtracking won’t be an option in several cases, unless you are willing to replay a chapter from the beginning.The story is good, bittersweet and sad; not very predictable. It is simple but it works, and leaves a lot for the player to reflect. Echoes of the global pandemic, ecological disaster and human hubris can be seen and heard everywhere, while still maintaining a fresh look on a post-apocalyptic Earth. There are lots of details, and the story is not directly handed to the player—you will have to make your own conclusions about the past, the present and the future. To me, this is not a bad thing. Rather, it is a sign of a sophisticated storyteller knowledgeable of current trends. Dramatically, the story delivers.The graphical settings are somewhat basic, and several advanced options are entirely missing.  Some people will miss stuff like ray tracing, vignette, depth of field and such. Personally, I play in a big monitor and would have loved the option to tweak the field of view—sometimes it feels too narrow, and motion-sickness might ensue. Nevertheless, the game looks beautiful.The music and sounds are great—some of them quite alien, as would be expected from a futuristic robot culture. It succeeds in setting the mood and tone for each situation and area, from the depressing and tranquil to the scary and suspenseful.Since the protagonist is completely background-less and anonymous,  could have benefited from fur and eye color customization. That element alone would have done wonders for the player to bond and care more about their cat.I paid full price with a 10% off for pre-order, and don’t regret it. It is in no way an outrageous amount for current standards, considering many games today are released costing three or four times that. Be not mistaken: experience-wise, the storytelling is carefully tailored here. Like a movie or a good short story, its quality is not defined by the overall length. It would be unfair to compare  to storyless, open-world games.Overall, I found  to be a great experience, with interesting gameplay and characters, and a fresh alternative to other dystopian, post-apocalyptic games. Playing as a cat is satisfying and novel.Mischievously recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: I was excited to play Stray, people were loving it. it seemed oddball enough that it might be enjoyable, and Annapurna as a publisher is a solid company.  They've published Outer Wilds which is one of my favorite game. And yet Stray just didn't connect to me.  In the game you certainly feel like a cat, and you're exploring a cybercity, but the controls felt stiffed.  Rather than a part of a large expansive city, Stray has one of the most restricted control scheme I've seen in a while.  There's places your can can "Jump to" and ways your can can walk in most areas, and if you want to try a different direction, too bad.  Every jump has to be towards a different platform, and every platform is limited. This might not have been as big a problem if the levels felt interesting.  The idea of a dead cybercity could work, and the trailers got me ready for exploration but as I played the game I realized how similar so much of the game felt, there was always something telling me where to go, whether it was other cats, or bright neon signs. The world seemed dead, which was intentional but also like a city that wasn't lived in, there's a vague enemy which the cat ran away from which clearly was designed based on the face huggers from Half Life 2, but other than that, the entire game revolved around exploration. But don't get me wrong, I'm a fan of games focused on exploration, when it's good.  The concept here had my interest, but after an hour, I started to ask myself if this was a title I wanted to keep.  At 30 bucks, it's not a full priced title, but that first hour made me question if it was worth the price and at the end of the day I decided I should refund the game.I truly love the elevator pitch, I love the idea of playing as a cat.  It might have been interesting, but Stray really didn't hook me in the first hour and at the end of my time an uber cutsy robot came to life but I just kind of sighed and gave up.I know a lot of people love this game and swear by it, but for me I just don't think it was worth the 30 dollars, and at the end of the day, I might wait for it to be on sale before I give this another go, or more likely just play something else from my backlog, because Stray was merely ok in my book.   Or perhaps I stopped just as the game was "Getting good" but the fact is the opening hour wasn't compelling and I felt like I was watching the clock to ensure I wouldn't lose my ability to refund it... that's not a strong opening for a game that will run people under 8 hours. If you enjoy this game, I'm glad you found something special here, and maybe I'm the odd man out, but the more I think about it, the more I'm shocked so many people took the risk here.   Perhaps this one just isn't for me.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, in 60 minutes of gameplay, the main word was "frustrating."I wish there was a better tutorial or guide accessible in the menu. I did find things easier when I turned on the reticule so I could visualize what I was pointing at. It's a bit frustrating when something works once (eg the "interact" circles on the cats in the initial scene) and then not afterward - I thought the interact circles were, essentially, the focus reticule, and thought I was doing something wrong because I couldn't get those circles to appear when I pointed at things... but actually it's just that the game didn't want me to interact with those things. If I'd had access to a guide that told me that the interact circle meant the game was guiding me, it would have been less frustrating. I was also frustrated when I could see items that looked interactive, but they were just for flavor. I had fun pushing cans and bottles around, but again that word - was frustrated when I dragged a lawn chair over toward the higher canopies so I could jump around and explore the inaccessible side of an alley, just to find that it wouldn't give me a jump option on that side of the alley.I got to the first Zurk run and I just can't manage with the buttons the way they are. First of all, I'm best at mouse navigation. On top of that, the "speed" and "remove zurks" buttons are only on the left side of the keyboard, and can't both be used at the same time. If I could have changed which keys were mapped to which actions, that would likely have helped. On the other hand, I suppose if I was playing this on the playstation, the navigation would have felt much better. So I guess that's on me for.... not owning the console? :POverall it's cute, but I expected more sandbox ability (they teach me how to scratch things but I can't scratch open trash bags?) and more cat-life-needs tasks (they have me drink water as long as I want, but don't tell me how much I need? I don't need to eat? I don't get to find things to use as a litter box? I hurt myself but it just goes away?) I get that those sandbox tasks don't magically appear in a game and they require development hours, and that sandbox freedom always has to be limited in some way. If the game is more about the plot than the roleplay, I can respect that's the devs' decision. Even so, I was disappointed. If I ever get past the zurk chase (or if my kid can do it for me), I'll probably come back and update this review, but for now, I'm just going to bed disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a game I have mixed feelings about. It does some things really well, and there is potential for a truly great game here.However, it’s also filled with some glaring flaws that make it just an average walking simulator, for lack of a better genre to insert it in.Stray has you play as a nameless cat hanging out with its feline friends, when suddenly it falls down into an underground city inhabited by nothing but sentient robots called “Companions”. Following the signs given to it, the cat finds an amnesiac drone companion called B12 that will accompany it through the rest of its journey in search of a way back to the Outside, recovering some of its memories along the way.While it’s not bad that the plot is that simple, it’s safe to say the game isn’t so much about the cat; but rather, about the underground, its story, citizens, and status as a cyberpunk dystopia.This is both the game’s biggest strength, and its biggest weakness. NPCs will often tell you very interesting information and give away small pieces of world building with most of it falling short due to almost none of the concepts being talked about being explored in depth. Even B12’s memories feel like short instances of exposition that end up generating more questions than answers.As a result, chances are by the end of the game you will end up wondering plenty of things about Stray’s world, with most of those questions being left unanswered.Visually speaking, Stray is beautiful. Not only are the graphics great, but the cats’ animations are some of the best I’ve seen in any animal in a videogame, or even animated movies for that matter. The effort BlueTwelve Studio put into making the cats’ movements as realistic as possible is commendable, and they created some of the most breathtaking cyberpunk environments I have seen in a videogame so far. The music is good and fits the game perfectly, but it’s not memorable. The gameplay isn’t great. It’s serviceable, but those who expect to be able to move around freely are probably going to be disappointed. Most actions can only be done when prompted, including jumping and interacting with most parts of the environment. It’s completely understandable that they took this approach in order to make movement and the cat’s actions more realistic.The gameplay loop can be divided into four different aspects: Puzzle solving, city exploration, action sequences and stealth sections. Puzzles tend to be very easy, with some solutions being very obvious depending on what your camera angle is when you come upon them. Cities are small but filled with small and subtle details, and one of the highlights of the game by far; finding B12’s memories is a fun task and worth the extra tidbits of world building most of the time, and the amazing landscapes make for a wonderful treat. Action sequences are pretty short, and mostly consist of escaping mutant omnivore creatures called “Zurks” and solving puzzles. Stealth sections are overall pretty well made, although they’re not difficult at all.The game does have some bugs that might be annoying, if only because you might have to restart from your latest checkpoint. I ran into three bugs in my entire gameplay, two of which were me clipping through objects or walls and being unable to progress until I restarted the game. As for the third one, the solution to a certain puzzle just wasn’t working, but restarting from the last checkpoint solved the issue. Considering checkpoints are abundant, they were small annoyances.In conclusion, I do recommend Stray, with reservations, but think it’s overall a solid game. It is a flawed and very short experience considering the price in some regions. It took me a bit over five hours to finish the game with an 87% completion rate. Despite all this, it is pretty unique and might be worth checking out when looking for a short, casual experience; or when trying to alternate with longer titles. More hardcore gamers might want to skip or wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I first heard about this game back in 2015, when it was just a concept with a gif animation, but it already seemed like a brilliant idea. Now it's finally a game, and it's much better than I expected.The star here is of course the cat, which gives the game a unique flavour. It's interesting to see the locations from his point of view, and it's fun to be a cat in general, sharpening nails, pushing things, etc. It's a real vibe.:) Our protagonist is very nicely crafted and believably animated, certainly the most realistic cat in the game industry so far.But that's only part of the experience, because the game world is also outstanding. We're in a dystopian, dark cyberpunk world, where there are no humans, only robots that mimic them. Among them, however, we meet a number of interesting characters, including our little flying companion, who helps us communicate with the locals and progress through the game. The story is simple, but it is interesting enough, with some surprising twists, and it’s quite touching in the end. The locations also tell a story through their great design, and they’re worth exploring carefully.The visuals are also amazing, with detailed, spectacular streets, rooms and spaces. It’s easy to get lost in, and each part of the world has its own atmosphere. Particularly outstanding is use of lighting and colors. The background music and the audio design are also excellent and complements the visual experience and the story very well.The game isn't long, it took me about 7 hours to finish, but it didn't feel short - the storytelling, gameplay and locations were tailored to the experience. I think this is a game that fully delivered what it set out to do, and I don't have any major criticism. A truly unique and fantastic experience, I recommend it!

_childDocuments_.review: If you have an affinity for  or are a fan of the , this game is a definitive must-have. Personally, the allure of its cyberpunk elements held a magnetic draw for me. While cats are delightful, they weren’t my primary reason for diving into the game.: The game's universe feels expansive initially, but by the end, you'll find it familiar and intimate. It's worth exploring every nook and cranny due to the intricate details crafted into each corner. From a visual standpoint, the graphics are a treat for the eyes, even without requiring much power or relying on technologies like ray tracing.: The narrative is compelling, offering the expected shades of dystopian character one hopes for in a cyberpunk setting. It might be a bit perplexing at the outset, but it unravels progressively, culminating in a conclusion that leaves certain aspects to player interpretation. This lends a mysterious allure, making me yearn for more background about the protagonists and the world's origin. My one critique would be the pacing of the story delivery – it took a while for the plot to truly ensnare my interest, urging me to continue playing.: Mechanically, the gameplay leans on the simpler side. Don’t expect a lot of challenging moments. There are a few deathruns to navigate and a handful of puzzles that range from easy to moderate. The game unmistakably prioritizes its narrative, which works to its advantage.: An honorable mention must go to the game's exceptional soundtrack. It accentuates the game's ambiance and truly elevates the entire experience.: An honorable mention must go to the game's exceptional soundtrack. It accentuates the game's ambiance and truly elevates the entire experience.In sum, for those seeking a fulfilling cyberpunk journey, this game is a goldmine. Its meticulously crafted world, thought-provoking story, and entrancing music make it a memorable experience. My only wish is for more content to further immerse myself in this riveting universe.

_childDocuments_.review: What an absolute creative masterpiece this game is. From the remarkably stunning visuals and sound design plus what I would consider an industry best soundtrack. The unique side quests that blend into the environment you freely are exploring. So many games recently are released with nothing stand out, no unique game-play or new spin on a game that makes anything different. This game; no, this experience is so fresh and competently opposite from everything else, I love it. It feels like so long since I have been this invested in the story of a game. Not only am I completely surrounded and captivated by a one of a kind landscape with so much to do, but the design language of this game and how the story flows is incredible. I never feel lost, but I always feel like I am discovering new things to interact with or areas to wander for what seems like hours. Bravo to everyone involved in Stray. This should be the new bar set for games coming out. It's a wonderful world that is optimized so well to keep from lag spikes or shader compiling to ruin the fluidity of this game. The story is 'Chefs Kiss' perfect. It is so separated from everything else in the industry now, and that alone makes it so much more memorable. When playing this game, you can tell that there was nothing but passion put into this project.

Gameplay wise its pretty boring, puzzles aren't that interesting and it feels clunky. I will say exploration is cool but rather restrictive due to the movement system. Storywise its also pretty generic. It tries to make you care about all the robots around you with their own plight but doesn't do enough with the characters you interact with and cycles through them too quick, outside the cat and robot companion (which is the bare minimum since that's who you literally play as for the whole game). Honestly this is a game to watch, not to buy and play. I can't recommend a game when your best way to enjoy it is to watch someone else play it.

_childDocuments_.review: After just completing the game I can wholeheartedly say this game was incredible in so many ways. NO SPOILERS HERE. This is just my honest review of this game and why you should give it a try.-Graphics: Visually the game is stunning the dynamic environments and locations all differentiated and unique in their own way, the graphics do not require you to have a NASA PC and even on medium i still got a beautiful experience overall. Graphically the game was stunning but the environment design really is what sold me here. -Gameplay: Stray is very simple from a gameplay perspective you have a few options Jump, Meow, Interact and Inspect (there are others ofc but overall its pretty much the same) the difference with Stray is that all its gameplay systems are incredibly polished and satisfying i never once felt like the game felt repetitive or boring, this was also thanks to the overall good pacing of progression in the story, which implemented gameplay elements to slowly build on your previous knowledge of the system while never fully deviating from the core gameplay. Jumping around as a cat through a cybercity is a cool premise but Stray executes it way better than i ever could have expected and the well-crafted gameplay emphasizes this. I only ever had 1 or 2 bugs when i played one where i got stuck on a rooftop where i had to reload from my last checkpoint (no big deal) and 2 the game has a few optimization issues when loading into new areas or interacting with the environment (typically it was just a small bit of ingame lag nothing more) these things will most likely be patched out soon but otherwise the game is super polished.-Story: OH MY GOD, the story this game had such an amazing narrative and even though you play as a cat the dialogue and characters really brought this game to life, every Robot you met felt unique and interesting and, each chapter of the story made it super easy to get off and load right back into the game which also helped to never drop the pacing, in terms of replayability it is a linear story game so not much is doable there but Stray offers a decent amount of sidequests and collectables all adding their own bit of spice to the story and worldbuilding such as B-12's Memories, Badges, Music sheets and more cool interactable world objects. All in all the story felt really good and I loved every moment of it.-In conclusion is Stray worth the 30$ pricetag? Yes, yes it was i went into the game kinda expecting to experience a small little story and cat gameplay, boy was i wrong Stray had way more in store than i could ever have expected and has left me wanting more cat adventures.I hope you find this review helpful whoever you are. Thank you for reading!CANT WAIT FOR STRAY 2 (it better happen)

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a cyberpunk platformer/adventure game with the selling point of playing as a stray cat. It doesn't do anything particularly groundbreaking with its setting, story, or gameplay, but it doesn't really need to; experiencing this sort of world from the perspective of a cat provides a new way to look at basic urban architecture and utilities, as geography to explore on foot. This is ultimately a game whose appeal is fairly surface level, but those who like cyberpunk dystopias and/or cats may find an enjoyable experience here.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray puts you in the paws of a small cat. Your goal is to get out of the Dead City, a cyberpunk place that is walled off from the outside world and only populated by robots. _childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I pre-ordered this game because i could play a cat and the graphics looked good. I wasn't expecting more than that, and I was okay with that possibility.Not only did the developers excel at all the details regarding a cat's movements and mindset, but they also showed a stunning world and fascinating plot between fun characters and amazing design. I did a small Discord stream as I played and, boy, were we all tugged around by the gradual world reveals and adorable kitty's journey.I'm still thinking about this game despite finishing it the day I got it haha.10/10, would cat again.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Game is beautiful! Story's amazing! Soundtrack has a pretty unique feel to it, really made the experience a lot more emotional for me. World itself is really compelling and guides you through its history bit by bit as you go on (If you liked 'Three Robots' from Love+Death+Robots, you'll love this. It's a lot less cynical and 'in your face'). Above all, it doesn't overstay its welcome. Perfect length. Worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Received the game from a friend for my birthday and I absolutely loved it, It was fun, adventurous and I liked the cat, exploring each area and interacting with all the robots!  The story is interesting, so yeh, I liked everything except for the weird, creepy eyes on the walls, which to me brings nothing to the game and there is no explanation for its existence in this world.  Producers, if you plan on making expansions or a Stray2, please exclude the eyes, it really doesn't do anything for an otherwise amazing game.  It doesn't fit into the story and seems out of place.  Hope everyone else enjoys this game as much as I did.  PS, a mini map hud would have been helpful.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: A must buy. Well worth the price of admission.Stray will keep you invested from the moment you begin playing, right up to the point you finish.It was a true pleasure to play and I hope everybody that plays it recommends it to friends and family.A most sincere thank you to BlueTwelve Studio and Annapurna Interactive for such a wonderful title.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is an outstanding game that offers a captivating story, engaging gameplay, and stunning graphics. The game's premise is unique, as players take on the role of a stray cat navigating through a futuristic city filled with robots and danger. The story is well-developed and offers a thought-provoking commentary on technology and humanity.The gameplay is simple but not too easy, with players having to use their cat-like abilities to explore the city and solve puzzles. The controls are intuitive, making it easy for players to get the hang of the game quickly.One of the game's standout features is its graphics. Stray's world is beautifully designed, with impressive attention to detail in every corner. The futuristic cityscape, complete with neon lights and advanced technology, is a sight to behold.Overall, Stray is a fantastic game that offers a compelling story, enjoyable gameplay, and stunning visuals. It's definitely worth playing for anyone who loves a good adventure game, and the unique perspective of playing as a stray cat adds a fresh twist to the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: 6/10  for me. here is whySo the game itself plays very well, I will say that the story is well written all the way up until the end where you get ABSOLUTELY NOTHING. No satisfaction from seeing your family again. all your new friends are either gone or dead. you dont even get to keep your robot companion. you get nothing. so playing it all the way through feels pointless
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: I normally am not interested in linear story-based games, instead preferring open world crafting or survival games, but I love cats and robots so I had to try this. I loved it. It's not really a platformer, instead opting for contextual jumping, which means the cat can't fall off edges or miss a jump. And it's not really a puzzle game either, with all the puzzles being easier than what you'd find even in a typical Zelda game. And the story is simple, but interesting. The game is not too long or too short. So it's a game that kids can enjoy as well as adults, although there are a few harder parts when you have to fight off zurks or evade sentinels. I'm having a difficult time pinpointing exactly why I loved this game so much. The lifelike cat animations make you feel like you're really a cat, and they're cute too. And the atmosphere and setting are really cool and interesting. And the robots are all pretty fun. I guess it sort of has the feel of a point-and-click adventure game, a genera I also like, only in 3D and without any vague frustrating puzzles. It's a fun game, you should try it.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely adored the game. I didn't have many expectations, the reason I bought it was simply because I wanted to play as a cat... But well, the post-apocalyptic cyberpunk setting was very aesthetically pleasing, versatile and so full of fascinating stuff! I just liked staring at all the tiny details and finding out as much as I could about the lore. Exploring was so much fun, the cat could go into all these secret passages, and moving around felt nimble and invigorating as this little creature. Plot-wise it was a very pleasant surprise too; the story really drew me in and the characters and interactions were so endearing. Each robot had their own personality and I loved the different expressions on their little screen faces... I also liked the references to some other franchises like Skyrim and Back to the Future haha.And while I'd call it a pretty wholesome game, it also got quite creepy and stressful at times. Thankfully wasn't a total horror game though! And not too difficult either, there's still some challenge and at least for me it was the perfect difficulty level, nothing felt super nerve-cracking and that's good lol. It's not a very long game, taking around 5-10 hours to finish on average depending on how much you like to explore, kill zurks, talk to robots or just chill for a bit while listening to the soundtrack or enjoy the scenery, but I don't think it really lacks much of anything. It'll be a nice replay experience too at some point!I don't really have any negatives. Sometimes the cat's movement was really strict like you had to be in a very specific spot to jump and I think that caused me a death once. And sure, character customization would've been nice to have but I wasn't too fazed by it. All in all, this game was a BLAST and I would love a sequel. <3
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: May be good with a controller but with keyboard and mouse forget the action sequences. You need a key combinations that may be easy on a controller but impossible on keyboard when trying to run and control direction at the same time so you will die for not hitting the keyboard commands or you will die because you cant control your direction and run.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: While this game ended up being something different from what I expected, I still enjoyed my time with Stray. I was thinking this was going to be a bit more stealth or action orientated but it ended up being more like an adventure game, filled with the classic item trading. While that isn't bad, the game sort of ends up not being about the cat and more about the companion, and then just sort of becomes like any other game rather than something unique. I do think there could have been far less dialogue and more atmospheric story telling, or even just flesh the game out with skills or further game-play elements, but what is here is just sort of fine. The game is very short too, being easily beaten in 5 or so hours, with not a lot demanding a revisit. I'd say maybe wait for a sale since the price might be too steep for what's here.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: After 2.5 hours I have to say I really, really fell in love with this game. Despite a few camera issues there is nothing I can or want to complain about. I love the setting and tho whole atmosphere as well as the worldbuilding. It's exciting to experience a game through the eyes of a cat - well almost since it's third person ;)So, thumbs up for the work and the art.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: This game is mostly an atmospheric visual novel. Expect a focus on great ambiance and music, but with a bit lackluster game playThey did add lots a detail in portraying typical cat behaviour, that's a plus.I enjoyed my play through, altho it felt a bit short/straightforward story wise (2,5 to 6 hours depending on casual roaming or progressing style play).With some more story/deeper world building and more freedom to jump wherever you like, this would be a great game non the less I'd still rate this a 7/10Buy this if you want a few relaxing hours and after the game listen to the soundtrack some more from time to time
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Seriously just so good. The game's atmosphere is by far what stands out most to me. Most of the scenes are a run down cyberpunk vibe, and exploring those environments as a little car is just a ton of fun.The story is also really entertaining, and the end brought some tears. Has great replay value as well, definitely the type of game you can hop on just to run around and explore a chill environment. Highly recommended, a no brainier for any cat lover.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Marvelous. Stray is an adventure platformer with a big heart. Lots of gorgeous world-building, combined with various mild puzzles, moderately open levels that you have to explore for various objectives, and the occasional chase sequence. Controls are very smooth on a gamepad, and the game is generally very intuitive. Most of Stray is pretty easy and stress free, but the Steam achievements add a significant challenge for veterans.I'll admit that the early chapters are a little slow and tough to get into, but as I stuck with it, the story and characters became more engrossing. The chapters have a lot of variety to them, and the game really does encourage you to explore for all kinds of bonus items. And if nothing else, it's a beautiful, soothing experience with the occasional heavy themes of loss and loneliness. The victorious ending, though tinged with a small tragedy, really does feel satisfying.This is not a game for those looking for serious platforming or puzzle complexity. Rather, it's for those who love good world-building and who enjoy the pure pleasure of exploration and adventure. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a game made by people who clearly love and understand cats.It's yet another indie game made with more heart than most AAA studios would dare to have in their games, and it certainly pulls it off well.The narrative is engaging and mysterious, and the gameplay is simple yet satisfying.It hits all the right notes with someone like myself who has a lot of experience with cats, and goes beyond the common tropes most media would gravitate to by showing a genuine appreciation for feline behavior through an attention to detail that's hard to overstate. The setting and supporting characters are fantastic and well thought out. The imagery is multilayered and complex but retains what is necessary to promote natural movement and traversal through an intelligent design. And the music is very well done and emotive, meshing well with gameplay and setting the right tone consistently throughout the story.As a pseudo-platformer adventure game with a dystopic future setting featuring a somber but hopeful plot experienced through the eyes of a small cat as well as a faithful companion, Stray executes a multitude of ideas in brilliant fashion and I hope to see more in the future.And it really makes you FEEL like you're a cat.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend too many games but I'd recommend this one. I enjoyed the story and the characters.The overall game play is pretty easy. The few quicker paced, action levels were pretty straight forward and there's many checkpoints throughout those levels that I took advantage of. Exploration is encouraged, and rewarded, but its not overwhelming. I'd recommend taking your time on your first play through, find all the little secrets and get to know the world.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a good game. I completed it in about 6-ish hours and I loved every moment of it. It honestly felt like playing as a cat. The rigging for the cat was perfection. Being able to scratch rugs, furniture and walls is amazing. Having to areas where you lay down and take a good cat nap, while hearing the cat purring in your headphones is the best ASMR. I honestly felt like the cat was the best thing and the effort they put into making it so realistic is amazing.The environments were super pretty. The characters in it were amazing even tho I wasn't able to have the cat rub on all their legs, I still felt like they were integral to the experience. You felt immersed in the environment completely. I honestly would recommend this to any cat or pet lover out there. This is one of those games I feel like everybody needs. Not going to lie, I teared up a few times with the emotional moments. And laughed at the part where a cat WOULD totally act that way (No spoilers! Sorry. If you've seen that part, you know what I mean!)

_childDocuments_.review: I opened the game expecting it to be a gimmicky experience, one that plays on the fact that you're a cat. However, Stray quickly proved me wrong and exceeded my expectations. The game's atmosphere is just lovely, seamlessly combining a cool cyberpunk feel that ties in with overgrown nature, creating a visually stunning environment, from the neon-drenched streets filled with life to the very top of the city.One of the things that stood out to me was the game's ability to convey so much emotion without relying heavily on dialogue. It's a rare treat to feel so connected to a game's story with such minimal words. The game's filled with heartfelt moments such as reuniting Doc with his son.The soundtrack is great and significantly enhances the overall experience. The tunes align perfectly with the mood, adding depth to the game and making each moment more memorable. I also enjoyed Morusque, the robot who serenades you whenever you bring her music notes, a charming addition. Listening to 'Cool Down' (music note 6) unexpectedly brought a smile to my face. Since we're still talking sound, the game earns extra points for letting players embrace their inner DJ, scratching vinyls in the club, a commendable feature!Regardless of your fondness for felines or your desire for a captivating platformer, Stray offers an excellent experience. I'd confidently give it a 9 out of 10.

All the good stuff you'd expect from a cat! Oh, and you're also on a mission to save the entire robot population. But that almost feels like a side quest when you're a cat.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a wonderful little game. It’s not a title that pushes the genre forward, nor is it a game that’s all about the microtransactions and making a quick buck. This is classic video-game territory; a title that just wants to tell an emotional story and allow players to explore a beautiful world.Split across 12 chapters, the story follows a stray cat that’s lost and separated from its family. As a result of its travels, the cat is thrust into an ancient mystery involving a long-forgotten walled city and its robot inhabitants. With a self-contained story and some memorable characters along the way, this is certainly not a game to be missed. And given the playing time is around 6-8 hours, it’s accessible even for those with a lot on their plates. With help from a small flying drone, you’re going to explore the city, solve puzzles and help residents along the way, all the while trying to return to your family above-ground.Each chapter has a pretty linear direction, combining platforming with puzzling to great effect. There’s a combination of safe code combinations, light physic-based puzzles and simple but effective fetch quests peppered throughout, breaking up any niggling feelings of monotony that may settle in. There’s nothing too strenuous here either, but there’s equally enough that requires you to think outside the box on more than one occasion.Graphically, Stray looks fantastic too. Whether it be neon lights reflected off puddles on the ground or something simple like your feline traversing on the rooftops, every part of this game looks fantastic. There’s a mixture of vibrant and dingy colours, whenever the script calls for it, and you’ll find yourself itching to explore the next area to see what else this game has in store for you.We’ve been graced with some wonderful Indie games over the years but Stray is certainly one of the most unique experiences out there. There’s a lot of love that’s gone into crafting this game and Stray deserves its plaudits. This is a fantastic game and easily one of the best I've played this year. 10/10 Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray doesn't know what it wants to be, and that's problematic.  The city segments were fun and piqued my curiosity about this collapsed technocracy, but the action segments were extremely tedious and kept me thinking 'when can I get back to the fun part?'.  It's like the game is trying to be two games to appeal to a wider audience: an animal simulator in some segments and a horror escape in others.  I also have some serious complaints about the plot, which I'll explain below.Obviously, talking about plot involves spoilers.  If you care about that sort of thing, you should stop reading here.Seriously, spoilers below.Spoilers.  You good with that?Okay, if you're still reading, I guess you don't care.First, the antagonist forces...The game already had an antagonist, established in the very opening.  That was gravity.  Gravity separated our protagonist (the feral cat) from his pack.  We didn't need any more hostile forces; reunion is a strong enough motivation to get us through the game.  The Zurks felt tacked on, tedious, and entirely unjustified.  They weren't even interesting or believable in the context of the setting... instead of being rats or cockroaches that would legitimately pose a threat to mechanical beings by damaging wires/casings/etc., they're bio-engineered garbage-eating bacteria?  Seriously?  Maybe the Zurks should have been trying to download data back into the network?  You know, to dovetail with B-12 being stuck in there?  Even a computer virus that was driving companions insane and pushing them to acquire organic bodies would have been better.  There was nothing in the setting to even remotely suggest biological science over computer science, so evil bacteria was a complete verisimilitude-smasher.  It made the Zurks feel like they were lifted from another story.  Not to mention the game sets up a premise of some larger chthonic hive mind for these things and then literally never revisits them.The Neco corp automated drones weren't much better.  While they were at least setting appropriate for the story being told, their rudimentary 'I see you and you die' patrolling was a snooze.  Since the game was leaning heavily on the 'cat simulator' button, it didn't need hostile forces at all.  Just let this random feral stray roam around a techno city and bewilder the robots as he tries to escape.Which brings me to the deuterprotagonist: there was no need for B-12 in the story at all.  Part of the animal simulator genre is the message barrier, which B-12 smashes through on your very first encounter with a companion.  At that point, the cat is rendered superfluous to the entire game, doing entirely un-cat things at the command of this robot he can somehow understand.  Seriously, the cat is reduced to a mount mechanic for B-12, which clashes completely with the intention the game projects.  If B-12 had downloaded himself into the cat's brain instead of that drone, I could justify it.  "Okay, we're sharing headspace with this robot, and he's giving us the agency to act with more intent."  Nope, that's not what the game did.  The mystery of the dead city should be an easter egg that we as human beings piece together incidentally through the cat's experiences.  Instead, B-12 spells it out for us every step of the way.So B-12 upstages the title character and forces you to focus on him as the protagonist.  Except he doesn't use any of the tools he obviously has at his disposal, up to and including the end of the game.  Why did he not download himself into the control mainframe just as he had downloaded into the drone earlier?  Was it simply to force a tedious heart-wrench for drama at the end of the game?  It certainly feels that way.  The game had already brow-beaten us with similar moments for Momo and Clementine, so why not again?  Ugh.As for the setting...While I liked the role that ultraviolet light played in the game, it feels like it was tip-toeing around something obvious for no reason.  Likewise, the 'lightless trees' was an overzealous sci-fi pull that could have easily been addressed instead with actual botanical science: that is, hydroponic grow lights.  That would have made the 'defluxor' more relevant as it could have been used to grow the plants, it would have increased the drama of the slums originally not having power (neon lights protest), and it might have softened the verisimilitude blow of the Zurks... especially if the plants had warded them off.  Lots of missed narrative opportunities, which is regrettable.If they'd taken the three city chapters of the game and interconnected them, minus the pointless action scenes and the pink tardigrade metal munchers, it wouldn't have left such a sour taste in my mouth.  When I was enjoying the game, I was enjoying it a lot.  When I wasn't, I couldn't wait for it to be over.  That is, what it does well it does very well, but what it doesn't it does abysmally.

_childDocuments_.review: Post cyberpunk is in!Of all the silent protagonists, a cat is definitely the best type. The world design stops being about creating spaces for humanoids but instead is able to intrinsically lean on things that make puzzle style levels so great - sanctioned and unsanctioned spaces. The feeling of being able to squeeze through bars, under some insignificant drainage or just scale a building totally sells everything about the cat's relationship to this world.The remaining helper robots - strays in their own right - are also brilliantly executed and while the lack of life is the point, the little, repeating actions as if caught in a loop really light up the areas they inhabit. Memories of who they used to serve, perhaps.Finally, the art and lighting is something out of a game with 10x the budget, the gamepad controls feel fantastic, with the use of vibration actually having nuance.

_childDocuments_.review: What I expected: well made but gimmicky game about cat in a cyberpunk city, since cats and cyberpunk are trendy topicsWhat I got: a fascinating look into the relationship between organic and synthetic beings, a downtrodden but hopeful tale about friendship, an intimate description of humanity through the perspective of a small innocence creature. A deeply touching experience that I respectfully object to every single claim that the game is somehow "wholesome" (it is not! It criticizes the fantasy of elevating humanity's physical form to something higher, more advanced, more less-human-as-if-our-flesh-and-bone-is-the-weakling-part-that-should-be-peeled-off, and cite the innocence of the orange cat as one of a few little good things scattered left in this world). It is not a "cat game" by any means, it doesn't make you feel like a cat, it doesn't give you total escapism from the human's perspective and the fulfillment to be a creature that is not us, but rather to showcase the trajectory of how that creature, much like us, smaller but not less emotional, would go and achieve such human objectives.If anything, the perception towards Stray fascinates me. The people who dislike it look negatively at the game because of how simple the gameplay is, how non challenging, how unsatisfying, how clunky it might feel, how it doesn't provide the utmost level of real . The press and game journalists leaving a thousand words praising Stray through buzzwords that sell the game to cat lovers, as if they think our plain brain demands pure  all the time. What do you people crave for, an utterly accurate cat simulator that satisfies your cowardy inner nihilism who's too afraid to walk out of the basement and shower a cat with love? Because if you do think Stray has the duty to jerk off what fantasy you want out of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ storydriven game starring a cat, then you are unsalvageable.But take my words: you don't need to be a cat lover to enjoy Stray. Empathy extends to any being with a single cell of organism. We don't owe anyone to be born good, to do good as if it's an invisible duty. We do it because humanity is inherently good, and we don't need a video game starring a little cat in a dismal future to fool ourselves that he  kind,  cute, and  pure, so he is the last bastion of beauty in this universe, while human is despicable and we deserved everything bad happened to us. Stray is a humane story. We might not be a fluffy cuteball, we might not understand them fully, but we are also kind and unwavering, our love is unconditional, just like how far the cat is willing to go to get back home. We are life, we are human, we are us. Never forget that.

_childDocuments_.review: I believe the reviews are only so positive because "haha cute cat game" because there is a severe lack of actual reviews on gameplay. The game is extremely short. 5-6 hours in length. Shorter if you don't go for collectibles. This wouldn't be a problem, except the game is 30$. Most games that cost 30 dollars have way more content or at least some replayability. I would argue this game has neither. There's no cutscene skip button, and one of the sections consists of sitting on a boat and moving through a sewer extremely slowly with nothing happening. It's already a pain to replay chapters in order to grab missed collectibles, I can't imagine playing the whole thing again. Other than that, the game pretty much plays itself most of the time. There's a few sections where you have to run away from cartoonish monsters but this isn't really very interactive either. Most of the actual gameplay consists of limited exploration and occasionally holding the jump button. Speaking of jumping, this is just automatic jumping from ledge to ledge. You don't actually get to control it.This isn't to say it's not somewhat enjoyable, because it is, and the stealth sections are probably the best part, but charging 30$ for a slightly interactive 5 hour story is pretty ridiculous.

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing experience, and a cheap one too, I have played AAA games that has half the length of gameplay but double the price. The fact that the developers didn't push the game for 40 dollars or even 30 makes it feels like a daylight robbery.The game look stunning with amazing graphics, it has really memorable characters with really fun gameplay despite its easy difficulty. Where the game does its best is with the exploration together with the music, exploring this beautiful cyberpunk/last of us- like world is what makes the game so memorable.Without spoilering anything, the story was a lot better than I expected before walking into this. Having the ability to do side quests, talk with civilians and seek secets around the map gives you a lot more freedom. Most of you can probably go into this and complete it in under 2 hours and then get a refund if you're focusing only on the main story, I however instead recommand to take your time, take it slow and enjoy this masterpiece instead of rushing though it.It's important to note, this experience may not be everyone's cup. You're a weak, defendless cat in a world where almost everything tries to kill you, don't walk into this and expect intense action gameplay. You will enjoy Stray if you enjoy similar titles like Limbo, Inside or Little Nightmares 1/2.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed my Lil Guy Simulator.  There is an obvious amount of love and joy that was put into seeing a little creature just walk along pipes and rails with such briskness and lack of concern, like he belongs up there and we're just lucky to see him go.My only complaint is how the game does toe the line of being a BIT orientalist.  I understand the city we navigate is based on The Walled City of Kowloon, which I absolutely LOVE as a setting and am appreciative that the inspiration is worn on its sleeve and straight up admitted to by the devs.It's just.  Did we really need THAT many dudes wearing rice hats?  Like, the weird thing is, it's not most npc's or even half.  But just enough of them wearing it to make me feel like someone on the devteam really thinks asians actually wear this hat that often around that casually?    And I get it's robots just wearing whatever the heck they find, but it just seemed more distracting and caricturistic than immersive or stylish.  I probably wouldn't have thought that much if it was literally just one guy but.  *Shrug.*All those words for what basically amounts to a microaggression aside:  The lil meowy guy was a joy to watch and seeing him navigate a setting I love was worth my time.I would say it was worth my money but I got this as a christmas gift from a friend, though I probably would have grabbed eventually at some point during a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a true gem in the indie game world. What makes it stand out is its extraordinary perspective: you play as a cat, exploring a rich and detailed world through the eyes of a furry little adventurer. The movements, behaviors, and interactions feel so realistic that you really feel like you’re roaming the streets of a futuristic city yourself.The graphics and sound design create a dense, atmospheric environment. Neon lights, narrow alleys, and intriguing inhabitants bring this world to life, making it both welcoming and mysterious. Every corner is filled with detail, inviting you to explore and uncover its secrets in a playful, charming way.The gameplay is another standout feature, blending exploration, puzzle-solving, and a touch of suspense. The controls are intuitive and smooth, which is essential in a game that emphasizes movement and agility. Stray strikes a balance between a relaxed pace and moments of excitement, making it perfect for players who love to take their time while exploring and discovering new things.For anyone looking for a fresh gaming experience and a unique story, Stray is a must-try. It manages to deliver a deep, atmospheric experience with minimal dialogue, creating a journey that will stay with you long after you’ve finished.Rating: 9/10 – A beautifully atmospheric adventure from a new perspective that captivates players from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: A really simple game with beautiful visuals, satisfying movement, cool characters and great soundtrack. Viewing the human world from the perspective of a cat, trying to figure out your way around familiar things, but as a tiny feline, was really fun. One problem I have with the game is a huge plot hole - if the creatures are able to consume metal, killing the robot habitants of this world, why can't they just demolish the city by eating everything in sight? I'm willing to forgive it, but that's pretty silly. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Stray

_childDocuments_.review: Stray was a fun game, I finished my first play-through in about 8 hours. The story is good, very heartwarming as you meet new characters and band together with a common goal. During my second play through I was able to appreciate some of the details I missed, as the memories explain a lot about the world and characters and answer questions I found myself wondering. I believe the storyline and ending left this game with a lot of potential for a sequel in the future (which I am really hoping for). I finally understand why everybody wants to be a cat. 10/10 would meow again. **ACHIEVEMENT HUNTERS**For those achievement hunters out there, I wanted to add that all 24 achievements ARE possible to get. I ended up with 3 play-throughs: 1st, just enjoying the game and story. 2nd, purposefully hunting achievements I missed in 1st go. 3rd, speed run in under 2 hours for achievement. The last achievement I needed was ‘Can’t Cat-ch ME’, and I would strongly recommend leaving this one for last as it near drove me insane, but I finally got it. Advice? Search YouTube/reddit for the achievement guide and find solace in the comment section knowing you are all full of rage and suffering together as a com-meow-nity. Best of luck and stay paw-sitive, fellow felines.

_childDocuments_.review: it was a lovely game - first game i played completely on the SteamDeck (works very very well)the one criticism i have is the frustrating placement of checkpoints around the stealth sections of the game - the stealth sequences are very long and a small controller misclick can have you restarting the entire sequence over and over.  i almost gave up on one particularly long sequence where movement had to be precise.however, my memory of the time i spent in this game will always be a very positive one and it was the best adventure/story game i played this year, likely to become a classic.

_childDocuments_.review: Performance: Very optimized game, uses a small amount of VRAM and performs really good. I had a few crashes that led to a memory leak. However, hasn't occurred since and the game works stable 165hz @1440p on an rtx3080ti. 4k @60fps you can superscale resolution safely to 150%.Graphics: Looks really good for such a tiny small game. Doesn't use a lot of texture memory but everything looks dynamic, lots of good lighting, reflection and shadows, which add to the atmosphere of the game. Awesome!Gameplay: I haven't got too far into the game but it seems fun, how you'd imagine a playing as a cat to feel like. There are elements of puzzle solving and collectibles too. It's refreshing being able to do "cat things".Artwork/Design: I love the art style, the story seems intriguing and I'm excited to see how it will play out. It reminds me of Spirited Away with the city design like CP2077. Music: It fits into the atmosphere of the game. Overall: so far, I would give it 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a really good game.It's short and to the point. It has an interesting story, set in a wonderfully-built world, and obviously you get to play as a cat. And cats are pretty cute. You can meow at everyone and everything, you can knock things off shelves and stuff, and you can jump up, down and around almost everything.And I feel the need to emphasise: this is not a game about cats, it's not a "cat simulator" like some people might think. It's a game where you simply happen to play as a cat in a somewhat strange but cool futuristic setting, in which you will learn very early on that all humans are dead and the only things left by them are the robots they created. The "how?" and "why?" I will leave to you to discover.Give it a try! You won't regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, with a nice cyberpunk vibe. The game-play is a bit odd, you play as a detective solving some minor puzzles and searching for locations and people. Aside to that there are action scenes with where you are chased or need to stealth your way through.So keep in mind if you want to play Stray (and I think you should definitely do) that it is a pretty relaxing game where you explore this strange world/city with a cat.It is not a difficult game and it is easy to pick up.Pros: - Wonderful art direction - Nice story - Good game-play loop - Overall just fun to playCons:  - Relatively short (less then 10 hours to see everything) - Mods really make the game shine (no Ray-tracing out of the box, missing some aliasing etc) - Pacing is a bit odd at times and ending feels a bit rushed. (although this is nitpicky.) - Auto-save is frequent but sometimes at odd places. Conclusion:Really original and fun game, definitely recommend this game. Nice to play for 15 minutes and pick it up later too. I can only hope for a Stray 2.Total score: 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Stray falls somewhere between decent and good, not reaching fantastic levels. Initially excited about it, the game left me somewhat disappointed. Controlling the stray cat feels clunky and the camera seems to hate you, exploration lacks rewarding moments, making it overwhelming.The game struggles to define itself; it's a mix of platformer, puzzle, and walking simulator, but doesn't excel in any. However, its strength lies in the ironically lively and warm dead city and its robots. Interacting with robots and engaging in side quests adds a fun element to the experience.Overall, Stray offers a unique world but falls short in gameplay. While its environment and the writing is engaging, the overall experience might not worth the full price. Consider purchasing it during a sale if you're still interested.

Playing as a Cat is literally a Dream Come True. Mostly you can do everything as a cat in this cybercity. Story was good and gameplay was satisfying. I roamed as much as I can. _childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this short and simple (ish) and without spoilers, this game ticks all the boxes for a spectacular game, which are in no particular order:1. _childDocuments_.review: Ending completely ruined it.Imagine a version of Final Fantasy X that plays out exactly the same as normal -- except, once you get to Zanarkand, Yuna just performs the Final Summoning and then the game abruptly ends. You haven't even finished crying over Yuna's fate, and the game is just over with no closure at all, leaving you to sit there and ask, "What was even the point if we couldn't save her?" And it's only once you stop crying, after the credits have stopped rolling, that you pause and realize that the ending that the writers chose completely contradicts what the rest of the game was trying to do thematically.That's Stray.The first 99% of the game is wonderful and beautiful. The art direction is incredible, the music is lovely. The atmosphere is more effective cyberpunk than Cyberpunk 2077's. The world feels real and lived in. The characters are all distinct and likeable in their own ways. The cat protagonist is animated and lively and feels like he has a personality despite being unable to talk. His relationship with B-12 is one of the most touching ones I've come across in gaming in quite some time.And then the last, like, five minutes happens and it all goes to ♥♥♥♥.Do yourself a favor. Play this game, and then once the cat protagonist and B-12 get on the subway, just stop playing. Pretend that's the ending and just stop. Let yourself believe that B-12 and the cat escaped together and went on to re-discover the beauty of the world together. Because, while that's still inconclusive as hell, that's a way better ending than what we got.*** SPOILERS AHEAD ***This game feels like it was made by a bunch of people who got too high on the smell of their own "What if humans are the real virus??" farts during the pandemic. For the vast majority of its runtime, Stray seems to be a game that's about perseverance and hope and the kindness of strangers -- a game about how we're all better off when we work together instead of going it alone -- only at the very last second to turn around and go: "Now that the last trace of humanity is gone, the planet can begin to heal."What????The characters you meet and form bonds with along the way? No follow-up, no closure at all. Their stories end exactly where you left them. How does anyone actually benefit from the achieved goal at the end? Impossible to say, because the game ended before it told us. The protagonist cat goes through so much growth throughout the story only to have it all wiped clean at the end when he just... goes home. There's not a moment of hesitation from him, not even a Frodo-esque "how do you pick up the threads of an old life?" moment. He's just home. It's fine. Shut up.What was the purpose of what B-12 did? What does opening up the city actually do for anyone? Why on earth would the writers choose to have the cat protagonist just run off into the sunset instead of going back to stay with the people who took him in and became like family? What was the point of any of those connections, in that case?Why is humanity the sudden enemy? B-12 tries to make this make sense with a line about how he has hope for the future because the robots turned out so great -- and this is said after it's established that humanity basically wiped itself out -- but how is that true when the robots behave exactly the same as humans? Humans are painted as bad because of the power-hungry police states that they formed in the wake of a plague -- but the robots are also oppressing each other! That's, like, the entire point of the Midtown sequence! How is that any better from what humans did?I wept openly over what happened to B-12, but I cried even harder during the credits when I realized that what happened to him happened for no reason at all. There was no reason for the writers to do that to him, neither from a narrative or a thematic perspective. It was like he never mattered at all -- that that bond between him and the protagonist cat never mattered -- because the protagonist cat just goes back to his old life anyway.If you write a story where you purposefully get the audience attached to a character just so that you can make that audience mourn them later and that's it, that's the whole point of the character because their death has no thematic purpose...... your writing is Bad, Actually.There's no justification for what happened to B-12. The ending is sad for the sake of being sad. Don't get fooled by "the story made me feel an emotion, therefore the story is good." No. No, it isn't. Stories can make you feel feelings and still be bad. Hell, David Cage made an entire career off of stories like that.The bonds you form with people don't matter. The trials that you overcome in life don't matter. The people you've met along the way don't matter. Sometimes people will just disappear from your life with no closure as though the connection never mattered at all, because it didn't, no matter how important it may have felt at the time. Humanity is a virus and we should just hand the world back over to nature. That's the message that Stray gives the player in the end.This game broke my heart, and not in a good way. I loved this game. I really, really, really was in love with it. I was ready to give it a 9.5 out of 10. But that ending seriously knocks it down to a 5 out of 10 for me. It's really that bad. So, I can't recommend this game to anyone. Not in good faith. Because what the game ultimately delivers in the end is not what was promised during the bulk of it.Just like my example with Yuna -- What the ♥♥♥♥ was the point of it all, when you can't save the person who came to matter most? Why bother telling the stories of Momo and Clementine if they never get resolved? Why bother developing the character of the cat protagonist, only to put him right back where he started at the end? Why go through the journey if the journey doesn't matter?Why waste your time and emotions with this game?

_childDocuments_.review: Environment is gorgeous, cat has some shader issues with blurring and the like, but that's common enough. As a linear experience, it's okay. I'm not a big fan of having a bunch of fake language scattered in with the real ones, and there's a chance for pure environmental storytelling, but then the robot speaks English at you, bypassing the cat and making it less an adventure in a strange world and more a point and click adventure with a cat as a cursor. The game also wanders back and forth between holding your hand and having no indicators where to find the single object that's currently gating progress. Then there's the chase sequences. Only had one, and I managed to get through it after a few tries, but in a walking simulator / linear narrative, it's basically a QTE blocking game progress. It's not an issue of skill or fun (it's not fun, though) it's an issue of accessibility. As far back as 1990, story-driven games with action segments have had the option of "I'm sick of this, skip it." When the story is the core draw, it's important to not prevent people from accessing it. Overall, I didn't see the appeal. Using a cat as an avatar added nothing, the environment, while beautiful, had little depth, and the gameplay loop was hampered by a general lack of agency combined with a messy environment with little to point the way forward but giant flashing signs and obvious UI elements. It was a linear storytelling experience with shoehorned chase sequences to seem like the player had more to do.

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is a distinctive adventure game that offers a refreshing perspective by casting players as a lost cat navigating a mysterious, dystopian city. The game beautifully merges exploration, light puzzle elements, and stealth mechanics, all seen through the eyes of our feline protagonist. The city itself is a character, rich in neon-lit ambiance and inhabited by robots with human-like dilemmas, which adds a poignant layer to the game's narrative.Graphically, Stray is a visual treat. The attention to detail in the environments is meticulous, from the flickering lights of a robot's shop to the somber, rain-soaked alleyways. The sound design deserves equal praise, with a soundtrack that perfectly complements the eerie, sometimes melancholic tone of the game. Where "Stray" slightly stumbles is in its gameplay mechanics, which, while initially engaging, can feel repetitive as the game progresses. The puzzle solutions are often straightforward, lacking the complexity that might keep more seasoned gamers on their toes.Despite these minor gripes, Stray is a heartfelt and innovative title that successfully delivers an experience unlike most in the genre. It's a compelling blend of storytelling and exploration that resonates emotionally, particularly for cat lovers. This game is about the journey of a stray cat, a commentary on loneliness, resilience, and the quest for belonging, making it a memorable addition to the gaming landscape.I would rate Stray an 85 out of 100.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, where do I start?Stray is one of a kind. A game like this is what I've been looking for. It's immersive, the graphics are beautiful and the story is heart wrenching. Stray is unique, there's certainly been a gap in the market for a game like this. As I've seen many reviews say, it's refreshing to see such a game on the market. It's addictive with an excellent story, with no additional cash grabs or traces of a 'pay to win' feel. The developers, and the whole team who worked on Stray, have gone above and beyond. Not only have they delivered a beautiful and unforgettable experience, but they've done so despite it being their first game. I've seen many people remark the price point, the price may be high, but that doesn't mean Stray isn't deserving of that cost. Yes, the game is short, with low replayability, but the quality of Stray makes it an adequate cost. Quality over quantity is definitely something the game delivers on. If you aren't willing to pay the price, wait for a sale. My personal thoughts on the game are just, wow. Everything about the game is beautiful, and does an excellent job on setting the atmosphere and tone. This is especially true with the lighting. The lighting in this game is beautiful, and one of, if not the best I've seen. Being able to experience a game like this from an adventurous cats perspective, is definitely something I didn't know I needed. It's super fun being able to explore through various means like climbing, and fitting into places you wouldn't be able to usually. I found the ending beautiful, but I would've loved that little bit more. Thank you for reading my (hopefully) balanced review! If you're considering purchasing Stray, I'd 100% urge you to do so. However, if you're a little bit iffy about the price point, I'd still recommend the game but when it's on sale. Alternatively, if you have played the game, you should write a review! _childDocuments_.review: From the early reviews I expected this game to be different from the typical FPS action game.  I thought it might encourage the player to view problems and challenges from the perspective of a cat, interact with other cats, and solve puzzles using the various capabilities a cat has... More or less.I'll admit that the protagonist is fairly catlike, cute, and has some typical cat behaviors.  But it doesn't take long before all of the trappings of a fairly typical FPS action game arrive.  The game play becomes very grindy - you have to perform an extended sequence of actions, hops, jumps, dodging, and eventually, even shooting to make progress in the game.  Even a single mistake several steps along the path gets your kitty dead, then you have to wait a while while the game reloads and start over from the beginning.I have played countless PC games back to early Atari games and platformers.  This is the first game I needed a non-mouse and keyboard control setup in many years, order to get anywhere at all.  I bought a gamepad for Stray and figured out how to use it.  Even with that, Stray is difficult and often too frustrating to continue.  I have to set it aside and go back to another recently played game for a while.Normally I would set the game at its easiest level of difficulty and practice it to get past the more difficult obstacles.  But there isn't any such option.  Stray is one difficulty level fits all.  So grinding through replay after replay is most of what I do in this game.My wife was hoping to try it after I got through.  She got the same impression I did from the advertising.  But after hearing me growl and hiss at this game for an hour or so on several evenings, she's decided it's not the right place for her to start gaming.To sum up, if your hands are gamepad-hardened and full of twitch, you'll likely have a lot of fun with Stray.  But if you've been tearing it up using your mouse and keyboard for several years like me, be ready to get hammered.  Over and over. A whole lot.

_childDocuments_.review: This is going to be one of the I finished the game and had a great time BUT reviews.  I recommend the game wholeheartedly, IF what is in the OFFICIAL tailors intrigues you, it's the hype train that surrounded this game that let me down.  The gaming community sold this game as some kind of next level never been seen before 100% original experience, and it's not.  Social media had me wrongly expecting a non-verbal adventure that used original methods to convey a story.  I imagined that to be something similar to how foreign language children's cartoons or films are at times so well acted in the physical sense, that you can enjoy them without understanding any of the dialog.  This was not the case in Stray.The Dev's advertised the game as a new spin on a somewhat low stakes adventure game with some platforming, puzzles, stealth, a lot of exploration, and great small characters, and that is exactly what it delivered.   This was a charming story told in an immersive world, with a neat story and truly unique platforming.  The platforming is something I've never seen before, you cant die!  Dont worry there are other things that can and will kill you in the game, but the typical one does not apply here.  Playing as a cat changes the stakes and the way you move across big open vertical spaces.  Typically, I am not a fan of platforming games, but Stay does it in such a unique and refreshing way I really enjoyed these sections.  I had so many great moments in this game, special characters, little beautiful secret spots, learning about the world and lore.  Most of the negative reviews focus on the game being cute, linear, low stakes, and having non-traditional platforming.  While these criticisms are all fair, the official tailors explain most of this before you make your purchase.  Plus, if a game is fun, well made, fun,  has a good story and the game play mechanics fit the experience the Dev's are building I'm all for them.  Here, every mechanic (linear or not) fit's the game and it's world.  Not every game has be (insert your favorite sub genera here) to be worth your time. My one legitimate criticism of Stray as a game were the bugs.   A few times I had to repeat sections or re-acquire items that did not save properly.  It only happened three or four times, but especially when moving between chapters, I lost items in my inventory.  As much as I like this game world, it was frustrating to have to do things more than once for them to count.I did not love this game in a way that I dreaded it ending, but I did enjoy my time in it's world and absolutely wanted to finish the story and see what happened.  I recommend it fully, even if I was misled by some of the hype surrounding it.  I paid full price for this game at release and after finishing it I totally feel it was worth the money.  I think that if you watched the official trailers, and are interested in what you saw in them you will very much love your time in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an ok game. From the initial hype around the game, I think the game is a tad over-hyped. Here's what I think could make the game better:The game is primarily a walking simulator, I say this with about an hour or so of gameplay. The fact that you have to just walk around, with very little exploration, is kind of dull after a few minutes. You are basically blocked off from entering certain areas, thus forcing you on a designated path. A little bit of exploration/adventure aspect would make the game a bit more fun. Instead of having an empty terrace on a building, and me just jumping through it, doing nothing much, how about ther is a short section in the terrace off at the side where I can go and do something, like pee or something? Or maybe a snake/rope lying around, and the cat can play with it? Maybe it plays with a laser dot moving around?Secondly, the guidance for showing the path is not subtle at all. Showing the Follow me sign, or the neon light arrow, are very on the nose. The blinking lights going in a particular direction to tell you that you're supposed to in a certain direction is annoying to watch after a point, especially considering you can't really go off the pre-determined path (which I mentioned earlier)Thirdly, add a few cat features like playing with rope, licking yourself, scratching behind the ear with the hind leg, playing with a laser dot, etc. The lack of yarns for the cat to play with, lying around throughout the game, is a big surprise.Gonna recommend after finishing the gameplay, but I still do think that the game missed some classic features to make the game more fun for cat lovers, some missed opportunities for sure. But the game's story is awesome which I really liked. I do agree with one of the negative reviews which says that the game is not really about the cat, but a scientist, which is kinda true, but I don't mind that, the story was still fun. If you don't go in with the expectations of the game's story just revolving around a cat, you will definitely enjoy the story.
