_childDocuments_.review: Two years ago, I stepped into the paws of a cat when I played through the phenomenal experience that was . To celebrate the game’s anniversary this year, I decided to step back into those same paws and re-experience the game all over again.Set in a science fiction dystopian world where humans no longer exist and robots are the main inhabitants,  sees a friendly orange stray cat leave the outside world and enter a walled-in, decaying cybercity. Here, we must find our way back out of the city, but with the help of robots and a drone friend named B-12. From the desolate streets of the Dead City and Zurk-infested sewers to the robot-populated slums and Midtown, this quest will take our cat protagonist and B-12 all over.When I originally played, I absolutely adored this game. After revisiting it two years later, my opinion on it hasn’t changed much.  is a visually charming video game with an intriguing and emotional story that kept me engaged throughout. The game, while mainly being a platforming adventure, also includes some puzzle-solving that isn’t too challenging, stealth-like sequences, a little action in the form of killing Zurks, and a big emphasis on exploration. Furthermore, the game isn’t too long, so it shouldn’t take players too much time to go from start to finish. It took me some time to get through it because I like to explore every nook and cranny in video games. In addition to all this, the game’s cyberpunk visuals feel perfect and just right, and the soundtrack is so soothing. On a side note, I do hope the movie adaptation of the game is still happening because it would be amazing to see.Overall, the game is a wonderfully beautiful experience that I can never forget. As a cat person, I adored seeing the world through the lens of a stray cat. I won’t spoil too much more about the game and its story, but to me, it is well worth the price tag. Plus, the ending always makes me emotional. Worth every minute!

_childDocuments_.review: A little disclaimer is necessary.  like this: This is an actual review, not just some ascii art, the word "cat" or similar. I mention this because 17 days after release, and unlike any popular AAA game, the reviews are constantly above 95%, at the same time that most of them only have ascii art or similar, and over 20% of 60K people who reviewed this game on Steam didn't get an achievement you're necessarily given after about 15 minutes into gameplay. I completed Stray yesterday. This disclaimer isn't a complaint about the game.Most people have very high standards when scoring games and a scoring of 50 out of 100, to them, means that the game was terrible. My scoring is to be understood as 50 being just what you would expect or see in any average game, not some unplayable experience or similar. 100 would be a masterpiece or cult game, and 0 would be effort has to be actually made to make it that badly (for most people, this is as high as 50 or 40). Please  to fully understand it.Stray's graphics are mostly just what you would expect. However, there are notable exceptions, such as excellent lighting in some locations. Our cat, even though it's not customizable at the moment, has very smooth and realistic movement. There are also some hardly noticeable negatives, like specific textures that feel like they were made in a hurry, and a location that you can go back to, where a fan will stay stopped until you step right in front of it. Then as soon as you step away, the fan will be re-stopped. These things can be fixed, but they're unlikely to be noticed by the vast majority of players, since you're not meant to go back to those places or not going to pay much attention to how good some specific texture is. I want to mention that you shouldn't be expecting PS5-like graphics on games like this one. Keeping that in mind, they did a good job. As a side note, a lower camera would have given a greater immersion as to the player feeling they're a cat, but I understand that this increased immersion would probably result in frustration from a more limited visibility around you. Adding an option to the menu doesn't sound like a bad idea.The game comes with a very good sound effect quality.  are also well done. , volume is consistent and nothing is too loud or quiet. One of the few big negatives in this game is its music. It's very scarce, forgetable, and feels repetitive. It barely adds anything and you'll soon stop expecting for any music to play.Both analog sticks are fine. However, developers had 16 buttons in any standard controller to assign actions to. Out of those 16 buttons, 3 don't do anything, 3 do something which you will never use, 3 are almost never used, 1 will only be used in a specific part of the plot, 2 are well assigned (one of them being ), and the remaining 4 are used to do absolutely everything there is to do within this game. There's big room for improvement here.About the jumping mechanic, being a pre-calculated jump rather than a free jump, I think this was the best choice, since free jump wouldn't have coexisted well with the complexity and positioning of the objects in the different maps of the game, and would have likely resulted in collision glitches. It would also make it near impossible for the cat to be able to walk a straight line on a very thin surface without falling, be it due to the player moving the analog stick a little bit, or due to errors in collision calculations. However, the cat will often jump to an area which was not the intended destination, this is specially frustrating when you are required to move fast . Again, room to improve.Difficulty tends to be low and consistent, with some very isolated sudden spikes. Difficulty is given to you "as-is", and there's next to nothing you can do to lower or increase it. No room for challenges and the like, due to the nature of the gameplay. Puzzles are more of the same, and they could certainly have tried harder to design clever puzzles. The game rewards you a little bit for exploring on your own, but rewards are insignificant or not worth it, it tells they didn't put much effort there either.Sorry for making it all into a single category, but I'm not here to narrate the plot. The plot is, for the lack of a better way to say it, good enough. It's not a Hollywood movie or a mindblower, but they were able to make a decent plot for a game in which the player is a cat, and that ability in itself is an achievement. Same goes for the gameplay. The game world is beautiful and it has enough size and interaction for it not to feel empty or artificial. The game doesn't constantly put you into new mechanics, but there's enough variety to keep you entertained. Optional content is not huge, but it is appreciated, and it's also appreciated that none of it is forced to make it to the credits screen, in other words, you won't be forced to do things irrelevant to the plot, but you can go away from the plot and do other things if you feel like it. As I said before, I completed Stray yesterday. The game didn't feel too short or long to me, but it's leaning more towards the short side. I don't have a problem with it, I think this game is a unique experience and it's worth playing, specially if you want something unique or if you like cats more than the average person. In case you're interested, my gamethrough was neither a speedrun nor a 100 %, I just played it as I wanted, and I made it to the credits screen in Why would I make a general score higher than each of the individual aspects? Well, this last one is more of my subjective opinion and biased because, needless to say, I love cats. Even though none of the individual aspects of the game shines by itself, the talent with which they were put together, the uniqueness of this game, and my personal experience with it, made me choose this score. Would I buy "Stray part 2", or another similar game? Yes, I would. Maybe even more than one, if they existed. This isn't your generic casual MMO, but Stray was able to touch my heart and keep me entertained, and for me that is enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Hugged my puppy and teared up after playing this amazing masterpiece.Stray is an adventure game developed by BlueTwelve Studio and published by Annapurna Interactive.Gameplay: 9/10The best cat game I've ever played. The controls feel very fluent. There have been a small amount of bugs I encountered on my first playthrough, but nothing game changing/breaking like most Triple A games. You traverse whole cities and towns with nothing but your paws, a friend you meet in the game, and the most important feature in my opinion: the Meow button. The parkour in the game is pretty accurate, reminds me a lot of how Assassins Creed handles parkour, that's a good thing. You sneak, push things off and scratch furniture, like a normal cat, but the game actually rewards you for doing it, like turning on a switch by standing on it, scratching a clothrag down to open a drawer to reach a roof or ceiling. The game rewards you for exploration in the most cat-like methods possible. I also love the cute mechanics of scratching carpets, sleeping in beds, doing cat things, etc, there's definitely some boop-on-the-nose mechanics, and it brings out humour and joy.Visuals: 8/10Great looking game, most of the animations look realistic, and the environments are breathtaking and detailed.Story: 8.5/10From Wikipedia: "The story follows a stray cat who falls into a walled city populated by robots, machines, and mutant bacteria, and sets out to return to the surface with the help of a drone companion, B-12. The player traverses the game world by leaping across platforms and climbing up obstacles, and can interact with the environment to open new paths. Using B-12, they can store items found throughout the world and hack into technology to solve puzzles. Throughout the game, the player must evade the antagonistic Zurks and Sentinels, which attempt to kill them." A simple, yet effective story.Overall: 9/10Stray is a cute, fun and heartfelt story with the best cat gameplay I've ever experienced. Absolutely worth getting.

_childDocuments_.review: Aahh, Stray... The cat game everyone was waiting for!... I am going to keep this review like the game: Nice (not amazing!) and short.To start off, I enjoyed my time with it. In my opinion when it was over, it had just started overstaying its welcome, so the game's length is just perfect. I finished at around 7 hours with some achievement hunting but definitely not a completionist run.On the positive side, the game's of very high quality. With stylish visuals, great graphics, an awesome cyberpunk setting, interesting soundtrack and very good sound effects. It really is a charming project.On the neutral side, its story although interesting, is very cliche and predictable. There are some interesting touches throughout the story telling, but you really need to look for them, since almost all characters encountered are forgettable. I think that some of these aspects were done on purpose, and that's why I do not absolutely criticize the game for them. I just wish there were one or two interesting characters, since the basis with the cyberpunk setting is there. Also on the neutral side, the game's environments although very beautiful, feel a bit same-y and the grim-dark atmosphere gets a bit old. That being said, the environment fits the story perfectly, so I guess the story is to blame again.On the negative side now, I was very disappointed when I realized that the game is ALMOST a walking simulator. It is not a walking simulator, but the gameplay really is nothing interesting. Apart from some stealth-based areas and some light puzzle elements there is nothing more to it. The exploration aspect is too narrow, and the control over the cat's movement is very limited with Assassin's Creed inspired movement where every jump or interaction is a guaranteed success with a simple press of a button. I would love some cat platforming. And some combat... After about 3/4 of the game, I was really sick of JUST running around without much more to do. Granted, there are some extra buttons you can press, but they are nothing special and also feel very limited. I think this lack of real gameplay mechanics is due to the developers' focus on the cat part of the game. Ok, yeah, controlling a cat is interesting, cute etc etc, but still, some gameplay elements are needed in order to make Stray really shine!I loved everything about the game, mainly except for its gameplay. Or rather lack of. If the gameplay was meatier and less movement-limiting with some combat mechanics, Stray would have been amazing. Now it's just decent.6/10A recommended game for its interesting world and main protagonist but still, I don't think that anyone would really lose anything but skipping on this one. I hope a sequel will address my issues and prove to be a real masterpiece. Until then, I kind of feel disappointed with Stray.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR; at the bottom.Don't waste your time. Sure you play a cat and do cat things, but that's the only saving grace of this game. Take that out and you have a very basic sci-fi story about environmentalism with the worlds most boring gameplay and quests that are basically just "goodluck finding it! here is a subtle hint now go figure it out while we give absolutely no direction"!Now put the cat back in, what do we have? A main character whose actions make absolutely no sense. They act like your average protagonist, helping those in need etc. But why? It's a cat. Not only do cats not really care about that kind of stuff- especially if they don't even know the person, but somehow the cat understands speech? This cat should not be able to understand speech, it didn't grow up around humans or anything else except other cats/wildlife.When you start the game you have your cute little cat group, then BAM you fall down and have to claw your way back up. Great, conflict is set in motion immediately and your main goal (to be assumed) is to get back to your home.Then suddenly you're helping the people of the underground and uncovering all this lore. But, you're a cat. A cat would not care. That is the fun of being a cat. Your actions, your motivations, MAKE NO SENSE FOR YOU TO BE A CAT. They should have made the main character a child if they wanted an underdog or unexpected hero, it would make more sense than a cat. If they really wanted to make a cat game, they should have just make something more like untitled goose game.By the way, in the end, you don't even get reunited with the cat family. That was the only thing keeping me going the whole time. The only thing I cared about and it didn't even have any pay off. They should just remove the entire first tutorial section of the game and it changes NOTHING.TL;DR; It's not worth the money or your time (even if it's only a 4/5 hour game). The gameplay is boring and the story isn't interesting, there are times when where you need to go is so blatantly obvious a toddler could get it, while other times you get so little direction you might as well just watch a walkthrough. It has good graphics and the reactions and interactions the cat has is cute, but that's all that carries this waste of a concept.

My son recently downloaded Stray and in less than a week, he had already played for over 80 hours. _childDocuments_.review: "Stray" is a captivating 3D platformer that blends elements of stealth and combat, where players control a cat navigating a world designed for everything but feline exploration. Divided into 12 chapters, the game alternates between linear platforming, action sequences, safe hub areas, light stealth, and combat segments. The simple yet serviceable plot revolves around an alley cat guided by a robot companion, B-12, through a city filled with decommissioned robots and menacing creatures. As players progress, they learn more about the world, its factions, and the quest to reunite with the protagonist's litter.The game's visual prowess, characterized by impressive graphics, textures, lighting, and atmospheric effects, is highlighted by the lifelike animation of the cat and expertly crafted environments. The city is moody and immersive, with hub areas offering vibrant visuals and a minimalistic HUD that adds to the overall appeal. Interactivity is a standout feature, with nearly every object in the environment being interactable, contributing to the believability of the game world.Despite visual excellence, the camera's proximity to the action and the intrusive interaction indicators slightly detract from the experience. The sound department falls short compared to the visuals, with unremarkable ambient music for most levels. However, the Slums area stands out with groovy tunes, showcasing the potential for music to enhance the gaming experience. Sound effects, particularly those associated with the cat and the environment, receive praise for their high fidelity.Stray's movement mechanics shine, offering fluid and natural controls that make exploration enjoyable. The game encourages finding routes through the world rather than relying on timing or precise jumps. The three hub areas—Slums, Antvillage, and Midtown—are rich in content, quests, characters, and exploration opportunities. Linear levels introduce new mechanics, but combat and stealth segments, while present, receive mixed reviews, with the latter feeling awkward due to limited tools and movement capabilities.The diegetic navigation system, relying on lighting and signs instead of traditional markers, enhances immersion. While the game's narrative is not its strongest suit, the overall experience is positive, reflected in its overwhelmingly positive rating on Steam. Stray's appeal lies in its next-gen graphics, the embodiment of a cat's perspective, engaging platforming, and well-crafted open areas. Despite occasional missteps in combat and stealth, the game's strengths, including great music in certain areas, make it a short yet replayable gem.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know what compelled me to write this review. Maybe I subconsciously feel that I haven't wasted enough time with this game just yet. Or maybe I saw that people on my friends list have it on their wish-list and I want to warn them. Whatever the case, here's the tldr: playing this game was the most bland and shallow experience I had in a long time. I am not saying it's the worst game ever made, it is technically mostly competent and quite playable. But it lacks anything that raises it above "playable" in my opinion.While the trailer might evoke some mystery, this game isn't about uncovering any of it. The biggest question "What happened to the world?" is answered in the first third of the game via a text diary with the blandest answer imaginable. How does a cat read a diary? We'll get to that, but its also one of the many questions left unanswered in a way that doesn't intrigue you, but makes you think the developers had no clue either.Another question I have is why our catagonist is doing any of this. The game seems to expect it to be an intelligent being with the capability of higher thought and levels empathy that are just not present in  a cat. I have to conclude that so much time has passed before the start of the game, that cats have evolved higher intelligence and are just held back from total world domination by their lack of opposable thumbs.But let's turn to gameplay for a while.You run around, have contextual jumping and interaction prompts and an inventory (how is never fully explained and leads to more issues down the line). The jumping prompt is sometimes quite finicky and makes the movement feel quite clunky. But the biggest enemy to deal with during the entire game is the camera, at least when playing with a gamepad. Some of the contextual interaction prompts are cat-esque things like scratching rugs, doors, etc, but feel like the developers' entire knowledge about cats stems from internet memes. None of it feels authentic and reasonable. And while yes, there is a dedicated meow-button (and let's ignore that cats don't tend walk through the world mewing all the time), it's always the same tone. While I still can't distinguish between the meows for "put more food in the bowl" and "clean the litter box", I can definitely tell you that there are a wide range of meows for different situations, which makes the meow button very disappointing.Early in the game you go from purely interacting with the environment to dealing with NPCs. They might all have individual names, but none have any personality. If they have more than one line to say, that's probably because they want to send you on a fetch-quest. Yes, really. They've been living there for hundreds of years, but really need you to pick them some flowers to complete their collection. Many tasks can be done even before you were told about them. The problem with this is best highlighted when the game offered me to steal one specific item from a store before giving me any reason for it.Sometimes these "side-quests" and especially the main story require you to solve puzzles. But calling them that is quite a disgrace to any real puzzle game. The game offers very few methods to interact with the world, and these methods can barely be combined, which you would need for good puzzles. The height of complexity literately is "open box, then interact with thing inside of box".While traversing the world you will find some optional hidden secrets, and I am surprised how many I've missed in the later parts of the game. Those were the most enjoyable part of the game because there was no hand-holding and no awkward puzzle-design. Just awkward climbing, which was tolerable.What wasn't tolerable is a certain companion who quickly after entering the story wants to take over as the main protagonist. He was quite unbearable every time he talked for himself and sits at the center of many frustrations I have with the game.Frustrations like: he can digitize and materialize items at will, but somehow garbage-disposal was an unsolved problem which required the creation of omnivoral bacteria that were supposed to deal with it, but instead evolved into hamster-sized creatures for some reason. Where to even begin with this? How did bacteria turn into living creatures in such a short time? What were the bacteria supposed to do with the garbage they ate? Where does it go? Where are new materials for new garbage even coming from? And if the Zerg are supposedly eating everything, "even metal" as one of the diaries claims, why do we never see any of it. There are plenty of garbage piles with robot arms and legs sticking out that have been incorporated into this generic alien growth, but none if it seems go get broken down.And I just can't not mention them: the eyes. What were they thinking? They are so comically bad, I couldn't believe it when I first saw them. What purpose do they serve? Both for the game and for the Zerg? How do they move without any visible sinews? How do they see without an optical nerve? Why do they not react to my op flashlight? Maybe they're not eyes after all.And speaking of op flashlight: I absolutely hated the part where after absolutely crushing every single zerg I encountered, the game took control away and made me effectively lose in the cut-scene. Huge Xenoblade Chronicles 2 vibes!

_childDocuments_.review: It was a summer afternoon I was at home with covid and a high fever and this game made that day something very nice.Stray is an adventure / platform indie game set in a cyberpunk future featuring a cat.The atmosphere is one of the best ever recreated in a video game and the graphics (despite some fps crashes) are extremely beautiful and accurate.I could spend hours talking about how immersive the game was for me and how many details I enjoyed despite never being a lover of platform games.The lack of a bit more advanced gameplay and the short time needed to finish the game still disappointed me but which I think will be solved with future updates and additional dlc.Stray is a game with a lot of potential and despite the flaws I mentioned it is a small masterpiece I very much hope that the developers will release a sequel sooner or later because I totally fell in love with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: dfijgpifrwoqwkfojwfdjckqdmfvoinqdvuqwopnmcdokmvopkfnvmojpkvmcodfvmpfmvfsklmvmosjkvdfsajdsnfndjlnfjsnnmcnnwuiouwtjiopjfadpoiafkaopi...So, come on, shoo from the keyboard! I'm terribly sorry... What am I talking about? And yes, Stray!The action of Stray takes place in the distant future. While walking with his moustached companions, a stray red cat falls into the sewer and finds himself in an underground cyberpunk city where there have been no people for a long time.Humanity destroyed the planet's ecosystem and tried to hide in bunkers supplied with oxygen with the help of a new kind of plants that do not require the sun. But in vain. People died out, and only robots remained in their settlements, who built their own kind of society, where many consider the blue sky on old photographs to be fake.However, to arrange a real revolution in this underground world and return the sun to its inhabitants, one very brave cat is enough. And he will definitely need courage here: after all, the sewer is teeming with mutant parasites, devouring both flesh and metal with great speed.I'm sure Stray will disappoint many. For someone, it will be too simple. Too short for someone. For some, it's too quest-based (in the first hub, you'll have to sweat a little with mini—missions). And you won't find a deep cyberpunk plot here - after all, the main character is not some smoky detective with implants, but a red—haired cat.But the most important thing about Stray is how it is made with love. It's very hard not to get into it. I have no doubt that this quiet summer the game will become a hit, and the Annapurna Interactive publishing house will once again record a bright and original project in its portfolio.1. Perhaps this is the most feline game in history. The fluffy main character is made with great love.2. Amazing art design and music.3. Well-tested gameplay: the puzzles are logical and do not cause stupor, the locations are well readable, none of the mechanics are annoying or boring by the end.4. _childDocuments_.review: I'm not a cat person, so I didn't know what they hype was all about with this game. I still got it, completed it and I must honestly say I still don't know what they hype was all about. This is fine game, quite enjoyable for the 5-6 hours it provides, but doesn't really go beyond that.The game is very simple and mostly very linear. It's also at the best when it is linear. The control scheme is very simple - you just move with analog, and if something is highlighted nearby you can jump on it with A button. All the jumps are pre-programmed and you cannot fail at them. The gameplay mostly has you figuring out how to proceed trough the current corridor.There are two open areas in this game. Those are very dense, with multiple levels you can jump on, including roofs. It's possible to run around there for a long time doing random stuff to NPCs or looking for hidden items. The bad thing about those ares is the save system - or the lack of thereof. The game only saves during control points. In the open area it usually also saves when you get an item. In the second open area I was playing for 45 minutes with no save in sight. Quitting a game doesn't save it, so you lose progress if you decide to quit. While usually it never goes above 2-3 minutes, in open area you can be screwed. Also, I found the chapters taking in those open areas to drag. There are few sections in the game when the gameplay changes a bit. There are chase sequences, very light stealth sequences, and you also unlock some temporary abilities. All those provide nice change of pace from the usual find-your-way gameplay.The story is alright. There are few not-very-memorable characters you meet on your journey. During most of the game you have an ally that translates stuff for you, and most of the story is about them, not the cat.Now, the cat. The cat is strange. Sometimes it's treated as animal and it's cute. You can walk on a computer keyboard and write random stuff, or toss books around and make a mess. Like a real cat! But then the story for the most part treats you as a human, and the further you go the more you'll think "why am I even playing as a cat?". I could suspend my disbelief for the most of the game, but last 3 chapters just went too far. I'm a cat, I don't know what you mean by "turn on computers". All I can do with computers is step on the keys and write random stuff, like in chapter 3. Ultimately it bothered me a lot during final stretch.The game looks really good. I made a ton of screenshot. There are a lot of nooks and crannies to explore, and you might want to do that for the collectibles. There are only 2 types of collectible - big and small memories. I think the big ones are mandatory for the story to progress, while small ones are hidden around the world. You can see postcards of the places where the memories are hidden for the current chapters, but those are all glitchy and corrupted to make it harder to find. You also can see how many are you lacking in chapter select. Some of them are very easy to find, while others require you to work for them. Each memory will have your ally say a sentence or two about his past. You won't learn too much from the small memories, but big memories tell you a lot.The city you explore feels like Midgar from Final Fantasy 7 in many regards. It's all dark and gloomy, with neon lights and strange languages on display. I dig it. There are also places where nature is taking over, so it's not very monotonous. There's also plenty of colour inside houses(and you can enter a lot of those). You encounter intriguing robot culture, which is explored a bit, especially if you talk to everyone. You can see if you walked to someone, as the prompt changes, so it's easy to keep track of who to talk with.All in all it's worth playing at the asking price, but it's not amazing. I suggest it for a nice distraction for a slow weekend.

_childDocuments_.review: I was skeptical about Stray, as I am a dog person, and am not easily impressed by fancy graphics.I assumed that this game would be little more than a tech-demo with a very lifelike cat-avatar, and that the novelty would end there.  I am very glad that I was wrong.Let me address my own skepticism first.  The gameplay is a little simple, the platforming is done at the push of a button, and the puzzles, while fun, are also simple.  This may be a turn-off for some people, however, it is done in such a way to service the experience of playing as an animal.  This cat is an exceedingly good boi, however, he isn't a genius, he's not got any special powers innately (other than being genuinely the best boi), and acknowledging that allows this game to pull off a bit of a gameplay miracle in my opinion.The games' simplicity allows the story to progress at a near perfect rate.  There are no sections where you will feel hopelessly stuck, there are few points where the story feels like it's being padded, and I was never bored.  There is a narrative here, and the game frames it through the innocent eyes of this stray cat.  He is an active participant in the narrative, sure, but he is ultimately servicing the goals of the other characters you meet along the way.  His innocence combined with his instrumentality, reminded me of another legendary video game character.  Ellie from the last of us.The Last of Us is funnily enough, the closest comparison I can draw to this game, albeit with their wholesome-to-scary ratios flipped.  Both games take you on journeys through brutalized cities infested with monsters to aid the suffering populace.  Stray is less threatening, but it makes navigating dangerous activities feel that much tenser.  There are points in this game where the visuals are so striking and disturbing, that when contrasted with my cute cat protagonist, I felt helpless, and above all else, intrigued and invested in the world.  The environmental storytelling on display here is top notch.  You slink and hop through the world with the natural ease of a cat, and the story matches your pace.Your companion character's overall plotline is a little predictable, but again, it never bogs the story down in melodrama or forced sentimentality. The emotional highs this story reaches make an impact because the game has successfully illustrated the scope and importance of the journey the two of you are on together, and never takes you away from it, or each other.  You become connected to all the characters in this game, even if they are only traveling with you for a brief period of time.Ultimately the hype around this game is well deserved, and you do owe it to yourself to play it, ideally in one or two sittings, if you've got about 5 hours on hand and want to be whisk(er)ed away on an awesome post-apocalyptic, visually striking, spooky, wholesome and emotional adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe people are still releasing games without difficulty settings to appeal to a wider audience. I actively avoid games that are punishingly hard for me because I don't find it fun or rewarding in any way. I suppose I don't know a lot about game design but I can see that  are introduced to the scene in visible, planned bursts that you trigger with proximity and I can't imagine it would be that hard to have a few modes that change the amount of triggerable events within the scene. There could also be an option to skip these parts and instead watch them like a cutscene, which I would happily have done and still found the pace of the game engaging. This would mean more people play, enjoy, and finish the game, and less people, like me, are inclined to just stop because we're not having fun anymore. To swing between a a gorgeous, engaging, story focused puzzle game with an incredible score and a timed puzzle game where essentially the floor is lava and if you make a single wrong move or can't get a button prompt to show up you have to start completely over was an unpleasant whiplash that made it hard to decide if I would recommend this game to others. I have seen other people play it with ease and I think the pacing of a puzzle game with interspersed with more urgent levels is interesting and fun, but to release it at only one difficulty setting seems to either be incredibly dense on the part of the developers or serve to make a statement about the illegitimacy of enjoying games that just aren't very hard in that specific way. Overall kinda disappointed after waiting so long for the cat game.

_childDocuments_.review: Visuals, music, sounds, atmospheres, the use of colors, the details... Simply beautiful. It's a short, contemplative game, which is best enjoyed at a slow pace with a will to explore. It features a small but touching story, wrapped in a balanced and varied level design alternating oppressing exploration, relaxed stroll, moderate platforming and chase.   It is also one of the most pessimistic visions of mankind's future I've seen in a game. Shed a tear at the beginning and the end, laughed many times in between.There are a few downsides, however:- auto-save is a bit too far spaced, and I found it to be quite frustrating at times when on the hunt for side interactions/achievements.- instant motion sickness when I started the game. I heavily lowered the camera sensitivity, then it was fine, but it inevitably made navigation a bit slow, and thus occasionally frustrating.- optimal exploration became frustrating (yeah, third use of the word) on the last town level, as several climbing opportunities seemed to lead nowhere and broke the immersion.- not a bug-free game, though I seem to have been way luckier than other players: couple of minor clipping-through-the-environment moments, a spinning enemy, physics a bit wonky when with numerous items, and one character slightly floating above ground are the only ones I met in my playthrough.Stray is a little gem, but slightly buggy and frustrating here and there. Don't go in expecting an ambitious game; it's more of a lovely visual/audio experience than anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: With under six hours of gameplay, it probably cannot demand its $30 list price. But, I think this is a game that you should get to experience eventually. Let's say that you fed an A.I. with every video game ever made, and asked the resulting model, "Make me a French game, from Annapurna, featuring a cat." "Stray" might be what you'd get: a sort of cyberpunk Paris, filled with a Daft Punk-ish soundtrack, and simple puzzles al la Gobliins or Twinsen. This isn't to say it's formulaic. It's just that, despite its novel wrapping, it's maybe a bit too simple. The controls are easy, but not precise. There's limited places where the cat can actually go, and there's really no skill or luck involved in getting the cat into high places. The characters you meet are designed for localization -- which is to say that none of them speak English, and instead all speak in short text-boxes. Most of those boxes are petri-dish-shallow, with a character being defined more by their clothing and activities in the world than any text. And that's where we get to the part that's special. Stray's world is LUSH. There's so much detail EVERYWHERE, and it is all carefully polished to be alien and yet familiar. The artwork is to the level one would expect from an Annapurna game.There are a few cute points and some genuinely laugh-out-loud moments. There is a dedicated 'meow' button. The story often drags you along before you're done exploring. I think I skipped most of the midtown section because I found myself through the one-way advance-the-plot door before I'd even explored half the town. I am quite bitter about this. This goes with the bipolar pacing that starts slow and gentle at the start, but does a mad-dash downhill race to the finish that leaves you feeling disappointed in the game's length.It appears I can go back and pick up whole chapters and assuage my completionist tendencies, so maybe I can get a second chance at the midtown section. But otherwise, I don't see an ounce of replayability in the game. With rare exceptions, the game is on rails, and the only deviations from that are a tiny number of hidden collectibles, and a slight re-ordering of when you collect certain items. There's certainly nothing that changes the experience or the ending.In the end, I'm a little disappointed in the game's short and linear story, but it has a beautiful world and an endearing player character.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is overrated. It s*cks. I didn't expect much, but holy f*ck! It's more like a tech demo than a game.If you're hoping for an immersive adventure, then leave your hopes at the door. You'll never leave railroads. You may feel like you can explore two "open areas", but they still feel like a corridor. All these so-called sideways are scarce and useless. You'll visit almost all of them while fetching some quest sh*t, so they're a part of a railroad anyway. And the others have either nothing or one of a few collectables. The gameplay is boring as f*ck. It's basically "press x to win" and "run, Forest, run" (in action and stealth scenes). And why does this game have stealth sequences if they're that bad? You can hide from a chasing droid by jumping into a box right in front of it. Or, you know, just run around a corner. Either way, it'll instantly lose you.  And the platforming part is not even a platformer. You just spin a camera and constantly ask, "where the f*ck is this flying A?" You think there are multiple parkour paths to the desired destination above, innit? Bad for you. There's only one path. The game even has "puzzles" that are simply "pull the lever down" or, at the very end of the game, "tear the wire" sh*t. Need to be said, each action scene presents some new "mechanics" to completely forget about them by the end of it. With such astonishing gameplay, the game can play itself for all I care.The story is empty and almost absent. I don't believe we fell all this way down and survived. And I don't believe we fell into that sealed city-scale bunker. There's an interesting idea about human extinction, but it's too vague, and it was never fully developed. Even collectables don't help it. And the main story is poorly written too. Where are we going? Why are we going? And why do all story-related NPCs have story-driving tricks up their sleeves? And no, "we're going up to the surface" doesn't answer these questions.  The story starts with nothing and ends with nothing, leaving no feelings and memories about it. The protagonist even might be whoever else but a cat, it wouldn't change jack sh*t in the story—and in the gameplay too, apart from a few unimportant cat-like features, to be honest. I really didn't like the story, and I genuinely hate the ending. The game is full of cheap tear-jerking scenes. "We will threaten to kill this character, and that character, and the other one too", said the devs in every chapter. "Feel pity for them, you, the player." I don't know them. I don't give a single f*ck about them. Even about our main companion throughout the game.  Their personalities and stories are too sketchy. They are like cardboard cutouts. No one cares about cardboards. You may sacrifice them all to Cthulhu, I shan't shed a tear. And why should I? The other NPCs here are utterly useless. They have like one line to say and one answer to a question. Sometimes even a bunch of them has one same answer to your question. And these robots don't differ from humans: they eat, they drink, they have children, they go to a barbershop, they speak English in a weird font. It would be no different if they'll actually be humans. If all the robots have consciousness and personality and think for themselves then why do we have police forces that act like some humans are giving them orders? Good soldiers follow orders. And they're really good soldiers, 'cause that's literally the only thing they do. And who gives orders to flying security droids? Empty-headed police robots?  As we're speaking about "life", I have to mention this.  It was a pain in the a*se to take screenshots. The game froze almost every damn time I pressed F12. The graphic is not that impressive, but it consumes resources like it's f*cking Forza Horizon 5, no less. The design was good, sometimes even atmospheric. The Slums are the only good example of level design in this game: they actually feel like a part of a small city and have more than one way up to the rooftops. This one level was created with care, while the others—in a higgledy-piggledy manner. Three different designs were used for locations: infested, city and "restricted areas". They work well on their own but not together as a whole. The robots look pretty nice and cartoonish. But the cat gives me uncanny valley vibes. And cheap-a*se headcrabs' rip-offs are the worst. Their quality is drastically worse than that of the other assets. They look like headcrabs, jump like headcrabs, sound like headcrabs. Duck test's passed. I cannot say anything about the music and sound design. It was really unnoticeable and forgettable (if it even was at all). Robots' babbling makes it seem like they speak their own odd but fairly typical "robotic" language. Stray isn't as long as you may assume, judging by my playtime. I would finish it twice as fast if I didn't take that many screenshots and didn't find chatting and reading a book more interesting while the game was running. The game doesn't know what it wants to be and what it wants to tell. And I definitely don't want to recommend it to anyone, even to the craziest cat-lovers. And remember, if the protagonist weren't a cat, this game wouldn't sell that well and wouldn't have a high rating.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm indeed a little late to this party. But today was my first time playing this game, I played through the whole thing and didn't use any external assistance, which will be important later. This game has a story I was never expecting and a slight horror element to it caught me off guard in a good way.First off, the graphics in this game really are top of the top. Considering it was made with Unreal Engine, you're going to be a bit of fuzzy spots especially when it comes to enhanced detail, but overall, it is amazing. Judging by the credits, you can see why they hired many 3D artists. The artwork plays into the main theme of the games dystopic cyber-driven environment. No humans, minimal amounts of life, and a society driven solely by robots. The colors are the only way one can communicate emotion and as you progress, it gets brighter and more vibrant.As for the progression itself, it was fine, but I do have some grumbles. You get a little companion that can help you as you progress through the game and complete the puzzles, but sometimes his direction can be vague and you have to use the environment around you to really figure out where you are. Often times, I got lost to where I needed to go or do which I guess does add more opportunity to explore and interact with things, but overall, when it isn't clear on what to do, it can be frustrating. The puzzle do require some good intuition to solve however. You have to look in all directions, figure out when you can jump to or what spaces you can crawl under, and what can you interact with.Lastly, the story element. It is by far the most integral part of the game. It. Is. Outstanding. This game plays with your emotions so erratically like a pre-schooler finding a new toy and tossing the old one aside. It's calm one moment, creeping dread the next, and then high-intensity chases and escapes after that, all while the game pulls your heart strings, especially at the end. I got so emotional where I thought there had to be a different ending, but no, right back to main screen. it was one last twist that made me want more. I want to know what happens after. WHERE ARE MY KITTY FRIENDS FROM THE BEGINNING, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥?!Humans love a good story. We love when we are told a story we participate in while being told through the perspective of something we wouldn't have known otherwise. It's what makes Stray such a good story. I'm hoping there will be more from them.

_childDocuments_.review: What a profoundly whimsical protagonist!  What a beautifully poignant and meaningful setting!  What a wonderfully and intentionally haphazard yet utterly intriguing story!  Literally what can possibly be to complain about in a game with all these things going for it?Oh right, it is an adventure game, so it still kind of sucks to play at times.  Kitty controls just fine, honestly, even with the keyboard (and I have heard the game is easier with a controller); that is not the issue.  The issue is how I want to claw my eyes out when wandering past the same set of NPCs and buildings for the tenth time trying to remember which random hallway held the single hard-to-find element I need to access to get to the next segment of the game.The other issue is that the developers for some reason thought this largely stunning and wonderful adventure game needed some segments that objectively ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sucked, so they decided to create the Zurks.  Actually, the Zurks being in the game, like basically everything else about the setting, is awesome, and I love them as story pieces.  I would love watching the movie adaptation of this game.  But I absolutely hated every second the game made me spend interacting with them.  At least 2 hours of my playtime has to be repeating the same three or four segments over and over again (or walking away from my computer to have a snack or something just to try to bring myself to be willing to face those segments again).  And the annoyance is not even linear; just when you think you have a handle on how to deal with the Zurks, the game throws a curveball and has the ones you previously got rid of respawn BEHIND YOU when you die and pop back up now in the middle of a room completely packed with enemies instead of totally cleared out.  Why did Annapurna Interactive hire a sadist to work on the cat game?  Was that just their way of giggling and knowing they were increasing the playtime of the game significantly through no actual storytelling effort?Whatever.  This game is still so great overall that I cannot possibly disingenuously give it a thumbs down, but just be aware that unless you get off on checkpoint-style games where you often have no defense against a horde of enemies that this game will not quite be the purely good-hearted exploration of whimsical themes that we all (or maybe just I???) expected.  But it is still extremely worth playing.  Just maybe consider watching a walkthrough if you are in danger of putting your keyboard through your monitor in rage.

_childDocuments_.review: This game suffers from the same shader cache related frame rate drops when entering new areas as many other poorly optimized Unreal Engine 4 games. I experienced drops down in the low 40s using an RTX3080 and i9 processor even when turning the graphic settings way down. Another issue I had with this game is that the camera following a jumping cat gave me quite a bit of nausea because the fov is too low and zoomed in and there is no fov setting. There is also no skill involved in jumping because you can only jump where the game allows and you never miss. However, the worst part about this game for me were the groups of little creatures that constantly jump on you and cause you to have to replay the same sections over and over again. There is also no manual save. Overall, I did not enjoy my time spent with this game and I cannot recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's definitely a game for all of the cat lovers out there. It could even be a great gift for a loved one or friend who you know likes cats and video games. I'm not fond of cats but I couldn't pass up this game with how unique it looked and it was a fun ten hours to get all of the achievements. I enjoyed jumping on tables and other places that I need not be and knocking everything off, meowing incessantly at any sleeping robots, etc. Graphically, the game is beautiful. Its setting is urban and many of the areas are rather linear but there's plenty to explore in the bigger parts of the game such as the cities, where the beloved feline is dexterous enough to explore verticality. There's a few 'collectibles' that you can hunt for, such as these cool little badges that can be pinned onto the cat's vest to accessorize it. Climbing and jumping onto platforms is simple enough, you just press one button while looking into its direction and the cat will do its jump animation. The game recommends the usage of a controller but my keyboard and mouse worked perfectly fine. I just had to rebind the 'meow' key, which was left-ALT by default, to another button as it became apparent how integral this command was when dealing with the hostile creatures (more on that next). To make the game less of a walking simulator, in the first phase of the game you'll often encounter these giant tick looking creatures (zurks) that will chase you. The second game features flying robots (sentinels) that you'll have to sneak around in order to complete your goals. In general, the game is not at all too challenging and is very much more of a casual experience. Most of the puzzles I had solved inadvertently before realizing it was even part of a puzzle.  Given that you can beat the game in less than 5 hours, or around 10 to 12 hours for getting all of the achievements, it can be argued that $30 USD is a bit too pricey for how short the video game is. But if this particular team developed this video game as a sort of experiment then there certainly should be a sequel or prequel that hopefully has more features to it.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Stray is a MASTERPIECE and I recommend it to absolutely anyone who wants to have a great time in a special little adventure game; as a cat? As a cat!Stray was an absolutely incredible experience! Before I get started with the review, I want to lay down a little bit of base information. It took me around 10-ish hours to complete the game at a leisurely/slower pace, I am one that really enjoys exploration in adventure games, but even then I did not complete all of the "side quests." With that being said, the story is the PURR-fect length! The game never felt boring, but lasted enough to satisfy purr-fectly. Now on to my review; there are plenty of others so I will try to condense most of what I have to say. Jumping right into Stray, I immediately noticed how smoooooooth the controls and animations were and the scenery was honestly more than what we typically see in AAA games these days. The interactivity between the other cats was also a very warm welcome into the adventure. Stray is also filled with many "mini-puzzles" that you have to play through in order to progress the story, 99% of the time they are the purr-fect balance between having to think vs. leisurely completing. Think of them as what you would see in Uncharted, except a bit easier. And if you ever got stuck, the majority of the game you could call out b12 to help give a small hint on what was to be accomplished. The game never pressured you into using b12 for this, but it is a nice touch for more casual players.Every SINGLE NPC in the world is interactive! You can run up and communicate with every one of them, some of them only stating a line or two, but the MAJORITY gave multiple lines, and even asked for items to give more information on. I never felt like all the NPCs were just there for the sake of being there.So what about game play and level progression? While traveling in Stray can be linear at times, it NEVER feels like it! The amount of detail in the few cities of the game is absolutely incredible with an outstanding amount of verticality. Every area feels different, every shop is different, every home you enter is different. All of which have different gimmicks in them, things to find, cat-like things to do (like scratching a carpet, playing with a ball, or accidentally getting a bag stuck on your head etc.!), and more places to explore. I was never bored with the amount of exploration you can do in Stray. The tasks you go on with different NPCs and characters is never boring and most importantly, never feel like they are just THERE TO BE THERE. Every single thing you do in Stray progresses the story in some way, shape, or form, disregarding side quests that progress relationships with characters, unlockables, and extra lore. There are two main ways of progressing through the story: Playing the levels and Unlocking memories. Playing through the levels is what gets you to the end goal of the game, but as you play along, you unlock memories that explain more about the world you are trapped in. Everything from the current circumstances all the way back to when the humans roamed the earth. What about the characters? There are a few side characters throughout the story that help you progress, but they are all very meaningful and memorable to the plot. The most important side character, however, is B12: a little robot companion. B12 was an absolute pleasure to have around and gave a meaning behind everything that happened in the story. I don't want to spoil anything so I'll stop here!In conclusion, Stray is all, and more than, we could have ever asked for. Tears shed, happiness arisen, it's incredible how many emotions can be provoked from a game about a cat and robots. The lore and story was absolutely fantastic. Level design was filled with variety and was never boring. The length of the game was perfect! The graphics and animations were some of the best I have ever seen. There is always something important to be doing, nothing felt tedious and boring. But most importantly, you got to adventure as a cat, do cat things, and have an absolute blast throughout your experience of the Cat·astrophic cyberpunk world that Stray put us in! I waited years for this game, and man was it worth it!10/10 Stars, would recommend Stray to anyone that owns a platform it is sold on! (Psssst, $30 is an absolute steal for this game)

It's pretty straightforward and gives you lots of opportunities to embody a cat, whether rubbing up against a robot's legs, clawing at furniture, or finding cosy places to snooze. Unfortunately, the narrative doesn't quite reach the emotional hit it's looking for, but it slowly shows its hand throughout, with plenty of interesting details to learn. Pairing a common pet with moody sci-fi has worked well, resulting in a unique, engaging game with strengths that outshine its flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is frustrating, and I'm sad that it's frustrating because I REALLY want to like it. Playing as a cat, knocking stuff off tables for no reason, befriending cute robots? It sounds like the perfect game. But the controls are so clunky that I can't enjoy it, and the hints are so vague that sometimes I have no idea what I'm supposed to be doing.I have to hit a button for every single jump, and considering this is partly a parkour-type game, that gets really tedious. Sometimes the game selects the wrong thing to jump on (something below instead of above, for instance), and I end up aimlessly jumping back and forth between the same objects trying to select the correct one. I constantly get lost -- I wish that the little robot buddy that helps me would give better hints than "go to the building with the orange sign." I'm there, but how exactly do I get in!? It took me waaaay too long to find the tiny window I was meant to jump through. I just played for an hour and most of that was helpless wandering around.I often have the option to show things I've collected to the robots. I usually don't know what to show them, or what I've already shown them. The mice enemies (Zurks) are too fast, and sometimes I'm struggling to shake them off while also trying to figure out where on earth I'm supposed to be going. It's hard to complete an escape scene when you're too busy shaking off enemies to know where to escape to!I love, love, love the concept for this game, but I'm getting so frustrated that I don't think I can finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic platform/puzzle game. I love cats -- I have three of them -- and this was an absolute pleasure to play through. There are lots of spots in the game that they let you just take your time and enjoy the surroundings, they have areas where you can have the cat lay down and you can have a nice screenshot scene without any UI (the UI is already minimal as it is, but the screenshot areas let you have no UI at all). There are a lot of humor scenes, mostly dealing with cat-related stuff. You get rewarded for exploring and just...being as much of a cat as you can. I both wish this game was longer, and am glad it's as short as it is. The game took approx 4 - 5 hours to beat. This is well worth the money I paid for it and I wish I could experience it again without the knowledge that I have now. If you would like to know if the cat survives:Yes, they do. However, that doesn't mean the ending isn't sad in its own right.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game is purrrrrfect! Plays really great on a XB controller on PC.Barely any bug/oddities were noticed - it felt VERY well finished and polished for an indie game.It's got Portal vibes with the physics problem solving, but clearly isn't portal. It's got Halo Jr vibes with storyline similarities, but clearly isn't halo.I just LOVE that the devs designed a world that is (gameplay) optimized for cats, but done so artfully that it still "looks like" it was designed for humans. Bravo.I still would have been (barely) satisfied if the game was half as long as it is, and I'll be thrilled if a sequel or expansion comes out. I did beat the game after just 8 hours, but this is in the ballpark of ideal game size/duration for what it is, and for me as a person. I think if it was a 40+ hour game, it'd lose a lot of players' interest before beating it. I'll probably come back to this in the winter and play through a second time with the hopes of unlocking every memory, I missed about 8-10 of them on first playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to get the game despite internet's increasing unhealthy obsession with cats and the "slightly" biased 'overwhelmingly positive' reviews for the game.As for the game-play I wished for more freedom controlling the cat. This could have been easily a movement focused game in the veins of . Especially since cats are so agile. But almost never the movement flows and a lot of times traversal just feels downright clunky. Then there are the Zorg/tick/facehugger hybrid enemies. Why? At one point you start to fight them since you get a weapon. So everything that was special about a cat character is gone. Unfortunately also the story is pretty bland and the npcs aren't very memorable.Visuals and atmosphere are spectacular most of the time. but then there's this meat-growth at some places in the game; and boy is it badly made. Yeah, I know graphics is not everything but these things are destroying the immersion so much. It really is the ugliest asset I've seen in any game. And i played .I could only recommend this game if you're one of these weird cat fanatics or if you are willing to pay ~28€ for a admittedly gorgeous graphic demo.If you want a game with an animal as the main character that got gameplay and worldbuilding right, check  or .

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a 'small child in a scary world' indie game, its a 'small cat in a scary world' indie game. It's strange this hasn't happened before, that there aren't more games where you play cats and dogs and things. Non humanoid characters are a bit of a rarity. I suppose because it limits your interaction, without hands or speech there's only so much a cat can do. This does give Stray a unique style of play though. More of that in a moment.After being separated from your friends, you find yourself in an underground city, infested with headcrabs and populated by robots. You team up with a little drone and set out on a journey to get back to the surface, helping people and doing lots of climbing and puzzles along the way. The city itself has a kind of Chinese cyberpunk thing going on and I must admit its style and overall visual design is impressive.But what does it feel like to play as a cat? That's what were here for, we've seen robots before. Well, you look at the world differently, you're no longer looking out for ladders and handles to turn, the world becomes more vertical, you can squeeze through the gaps in railings, knock things over and generally be a pain in the arse. The game has lots of these little interactive moments where you can take a nap or scratch the ♥♥♥♥ out of a couch. They don't provide anything for gameplay though, just a moment of role-play. There are puzzles to do but although much of the game is a linear series of encounters, the bulk of it is the semi open robot village areas and here's where I start to have problems.For the first half an hour the game is moving along quite nicely, but things grind to a halt when you start having to do quests in the slums. Go talk to this person and do the thing they want, usually collect some item, but to get that you need another item, to get that you need another item etc etc. The place is a pain to navigate and requires you to infer something really obtuse in order to progress. Real point and click adventure game logic. What is it with the French, eh?Without a protagonist that can emote properly you need to rely on the other characters and again I think Stray fails here. The characters are just boring, the way they talk is all the same. Despite the snippets of backstory you get and the clothes they wear they're simply one note. I couldn't describe any of them in terms of definable character traits. But, you might say, this isn't about the robots, its about being a cat, its about their story, about being a stray, but its not really. They clearly had a lot of fun making a game to be played as a cat, the level design is fun as far as that's concerned, but really its this world and the plight of these robots they want you to connect with and I didn't really. Even the companion doesn't have much going on outside of the backstory they slowly reveal. There's no humour, there's no drama, everyone's just nice to you, its a little bland which is an odd thing to say about a game with such a unique premise. The unique premise is the cat by the way, a world of robots and a neon totalitarian state are two things you've seen before despite being mashed together here. I don't want to be hard on Stray because I think the price point is about reasonable for a 5ish hour story (if you try for the collectibles and exhaust the interactions), its just I'm not sure i'd ever replay it. Playing as a cat is its one unique selling point and I've done it now. Every other idea has been recycled from somewhere else. The cat is cute though.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR at the bottom.Longer review:In Stray you play as a cat and the game does a masterful job of nailing the experience of verticality, from sitting atop buildings to running around the ground level between all these "giants" the game really sends home the experience from a cats eye-view. The sound design is also an excellent touch, lots of unique and quirky music throughout this game, with sudden upticks when the action hits and subtle creepy chords when things get a bit dark. Not to mention the exceptional sound design, I've heard games get animals right plenty of times, however when your game is based around a cat as your protagonist you generally want to nail the sound, and they've done just that!Moving onto the actual game play, this game isn't the most challenging and neither is it very long, without following optional objectives one could easily finish it in 3 to 4 hours. However, this is by no means a negative factor, this game is definitely meant to be played at a slower pace, in a more relaxed and layed back manner, and the puzzles are fairly entertaining! In my opinion Stray is more about the story and the connection between the world and the characters than anything else, and it should be experienced in this manner. (You can always achievement run the 2nd time ^^)Now for the movement and the interactions - How wonderfully the developers, artists and animators did in this department! The environment is so alive and interesting, and the various individuals you meet on your journey are often vibrant, varied and individual in their design. So much of the area that you explore looks totally unique and hand crafted, it's just an excellent environmental experience. As for the cute little fuzzball that you play as, the movement and look feels so natural and authentic, they really did a paw-some job.. (:The only nitpick that I have for this game, would be the fact that I would love to see more of this world, and I wish the game had one more act. Although I stated earlier that the game being short isn't a negative factor, I do believe a little more to the story could have gone a long way towards rounding it off as a truly epic adventure. HOWEVER, this game is still excellent and I would whole heartedly endorse giving this game a try, it's a game for just about anyone unless you hate cats and/or story games. Enjoy! Catch-mew-later~ ;3TL;DR - A lovingly crafted game with beautiful graphics, an engrossing sound track and an engaging and touching story. It's short and sweet, and they nailed the feeling of a cat so well. 9/10 would drop paint on robots again!

_childDocuments_.review: Stray is honestly one of the best games I have played,The visuals, even on a low spec gaming laptop like mine are absolutely beautiful, and the game went in a direction I completely didn't expect. In later sections, the drone enemies also pose a new challenge, although they are much easier to avoid.My only complaint really is that there is no punishment for error, jumping over obstacles can only be done when it is possible, and there is no way for the cat to fall off unless it is a scripted event.This does however help the game stay very linear, and overall the positives completely outweigh the negatives.I don't want to give away too much about the story itself, since the game isn't super long10/10 game

_childDocuments_.review: I have two cats of my own so the general idea of a cat game, a brand new one nun the less, certainly intrigued me. I figured it would be a nice chill game away from my normal taste and a way to relate with my furry friends. Stray delivered that and so much more... The game so well executed what being a cat entails from splashing around in puddles to chasing around butterflies to even knocking things off tables. But beyond that, Stray delivers a story that is fresh, entertaining, and even a little sad. It's the perfect cocktail of serotonin and sadness that draws you in and keeps you longing for what there is to come in each and every adventure you partake in. I highly recommend you give this game a try whether your a cat owner yourself, or someone just looking to find something new to play, Although it wasn't what I initially portrayed the game to be, it was a pleasant surprise, one I definitely recommend experiencing yourself. Who knows, maybe you'll find yourself acquiring a furry friend of your own come the conclusion of the game. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: Lost, alone and separated from family, a stray cat must untangle an ancient mystery to escape a long-forgotten cybercity and find the way home. Stray is a third-person cat adventure game set amidst the detailed neon-lit alleys of a decaying cybercity and the murky environments of its seedy underbelly.  See the world through the eyes of a stray and interact with the environment in playful ways. Stray is developed by BlueTwelve Studio, a small team from south of France mostly made of cats and a handful of humans.

name: Song of Nunu: A League of Legends Story
detailed_description: Two best friends, one wild adventure. Join best friends Nunu and Willump on an adventure across the frozen wilds of the Freljord. Discover the unbreakable bond between boy and yeti as you traverse a land both beautiful and treacherous, making new allies (and enemies) on a journey of family, friendship, and magic. Song of Nunu: A League of Legends Story is a single-player story adventure developed by Tequila Works. Dive headfirst into an immersive narrative set in the undiscovered reaches of the Freljord, where every snowy step brings you closer to the truth about Nunu and Willump’s past. FORGE AN UNBREAKABLE BOND Play as Nunu, a young boy searching for his mother with the help of his best friend, Willump. United by their endless imagination and shared love of snowball fights, the two will have to work together to navigate the Freljord, saving it—and each other—from the danger that lies within. UNLOCK AN EXTRAORDINARY WORLD Hike, climb, and sled your way across the Freljord, a frostbitten land full of harsh blizzards, ferocious wolves… and enchantment. Use your head to progress through the frozen landscape and uncover what secrets lie hidden beneath the ice. JOIN LEGENDARY CHAMPIONS Meet the powerful League of Legends champions of the Freljord, including Braum, Ornn, Volibear, and Lissandra—whose twisted magic threatens to bury the world in Dark Ice. Friendship finds a way in Song of Nunu: A League of Legends Story.

That said you will receive emotional damage for falling off the map as Nunu or Willump.

_childDocuments_.review: At its heart, Song of Nunu  is a joyous celebration of friendship between Willump (the Yeti) and the child Nunu (Notai clan).  Through thick and thin, the two unlikely companions have snowball competitions; play the flute and dance together; go on nail-biting sled rides and meet some amazing characters as they search for Nunu's mother in the icy realm of Freljord.  They support and encourage one another when the chips were down and bravely fought off ice wolves as a well-oiled team.  It was such a heartwarming and enjoyable romp to experience! Willump the yeti is such a goofball character who pulls funny faces, loves to eat berries and mushrooms and goes on strike when he's had enough.  You are able to hug him!   He becomes grumpy later in the game, but you soon find out why.  Willump is also a nifty dancer!  Who knew that yetis could dance?!Nunu is a young boy searching for his mother and the Heart of the Blue.  This is really a coming of age for him as he discovers what true courage is and how size really doesn't matter.  The downside of his character was that he talked too much and he had a really whiny voice which drove me nuts at times!The graphics in this game are really lovely and I often stopped and had a look around me.  I loved the blue ice theme throughout the game. The music was divine and was heavily flute based due to gameplay using the flute to open doors or activate slides.  Depending on the circumstances, the music emphasised the action taking place.Gameplay was platform heavy, but quite easy with some puzzle sequences.  There is combat involved and that can be frustrating for less dexterous people (more on that later).  There are cute little poros to find on each level and intricate murals to discover.  Most of the characters you meet are really well defined and believable and you have to battle a couple of them.  The most difficult part is remembering the flute notes you have to play and hitting the right keys in sequence.  This is a major part of Nunu's character as was throwing snowballs.Now, I am not the most dexterous of people, but I was delighted to see how accessible this game is for peeps like me.  In the accessibility section you can fiddle with things that make the battles easier whereby you don't lose life.  This god mode makes it easier on the sled sections too.  So for those who are hopeless at combat or have to play on keyboard like me,  this game is very forgiving in battles.I guess this is a game suitable for kids 8 and over.  The wolves and other characters are probably the scary part but there is no blood and gore.  Be aware that this is not a God of War game, but an enjoyable adventure of a boy and his friend.  Combat and gameplay are simple and can be repetitive at times....some reviewers found it boring. Most people completed this game in 5- 10 hours, but it is really not meant to be rushed through, but to savour every moment and explore every nook and cranny of this vast world.  Highly recommend..9/10  I'm heading back now to pick up my missing poros!

_childDocuments_.review: I have enjoyed almost everything released by Tequila Works and was not let down by Song of Nunu. It has similar themes to RIME and GYLT.. a child who has suffered a loss embarks on a journey into a spirit-filled world to find answers. This game is more 'cartoonish' than RIME, with more animated cut scenes. Nunu is a small boy who is searching for his mother's spirit and a "Heart of Blue" magical item. He is accompanied by Willump - a blue comical Yeti with four arms (who knew... I assumed that Yetis were two-armed creatures!).Song of Nunu is best played with a controller. You are armed with snowballs to throw and a flute to play. I found the musical sections too hard to coordinate with the keyboard/mouse. You control Nunu directly and, at times, Willump (when he carries Nunu). The two work together to solve problems and overcome obstacles.The path is fairly linear and there is no time spent wandering, wondering what to do next. There are different areas/chapters to explore with some sub-quests that lead you to the main quest. No fluffy errands to run and almost no inventory to manage.... just a complicated landscape to navigate with many obstacles. The puzzle elements focus on how to use the environment and your powers to move along. The art is beautiful and the soundtrack is fantastic. The voice-overs are professionally done and fit the characters quite well.Although there is a good bit of platforming, it does not require precision and I missed very few jumps (which is unusual for me). Some sequences involve figuring out the timing of your actions and then executing your plan, with perfection. These situations usually took me a few tries to get things right. The combat was tough for me. Although this is not the focus of the game, there were enough assaults by wolves and magic creature to keep me on my toes. There is a boss fight at the end that, for me, was brutal. Achievements are fair. Once you have finished the game, you can return to individual chapters to find missed collectibles or complete unfinished tasks. This makes up for the single auto-save slot that does not allow you to go backwards while playing the first time through.I highly recommend this to those who enjoy a heart-warming adventure and don't mind working out puzzle timing and engaging with enemies. It is a wonderful adventure but a bit tough if your reflexes aren't quick and you aren't comfortable with attacking/evading under pressure.

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been told that the heart is the strongest muscle, and by the gods does this game have a mighty heart! If you ever wondered what a “My Neighbor Totoro: Norse edition” would look like, this is pretty much spot on!Song of Nunu is a quirky puzzle platformer in the BanjoKazooie variety where you have 2 colorful main characters that work as a team to overcome the Freljordian wilderness in a quest to find the legendary heart of the blue. On their way they rescue poros, wrestle with wildlife and share a stew with a mustachioed gentleman of the highest order. This game is a pretty chill (hehu) and simple game and the story is lighthearted and genuinely cozy. Coming from a rerun of Dark Souls this game was like the antithesis of the soulslike formula that has become so popular and I actually loved it. The exploration was there, but minimal, the story melancholic and beautiful like an aurora and most importantly the characters are as they should be, larger than life! If you have lived under a rock for the past 15 years, and somehow missed the sensational show Arcane (Go watch it! Now!), you might realize that this game's story takes place on Runeterra, the world of League of Legends. However, having finished the game from start to finish I can gladly say that you need not bother with endless lore videos explaining the various factions and weird historical happenings, the game stands sturdy on its own legs and leads you into the Freljord and its inhabitants with a playfulness that is truly captivating. Also way to go to not turn Lissandra into a cardboard cutout saturday morning cartoon villain!Every now and then you come upon a game that really resonates with you and from now on I am really interested to see where this story goes! This game is easy, so do not expect a harsh and unfriendly freljordian dark souls to beat the life out of you. However what it lacks in bite it sure makes up for with heart, and if you have any love for a great and cozy story this is as good as it gets. Highly recommended, even if you can't stand the LOL from where it came!
