_childDocuments_.review: This is a weird one.This is mostly a solid Doom Eternal-ish indie shooter with varied and mostly great-to-look-at levels, mostly satisfying gunplay, and all that jazz.But it's just bogged down with design decisions that are just bizarre, man. And not the good kind of bizarre.What is this save system? Why are there survival horror save points in my fast-paced boomer-shooter? Why does the game autosave after an absolute non-issue like me pulling a lever, but not before the gоddamn boss fights and not at the start of the level? I HATE E2M5 with passion precisely because of this.Why is the main progression system almost entirely locked behind secrets? Why are some of those secrets platforming challenges?Why does a 6/6 on ammo counter means that I have 6 shells left? Why does the rocket launcher splash damage zone look way smaller than it actually is? Why do half the enemy attacks lack any visual feedback for damage taken? Why does the Gluon gun variant lack literally any impact whatsoever? Why can I just casually walk right past the pre-final boss gauntlet?All of this isn’t a big deal by itself, but man, this stuff adds up quick and makes this game feel mediocre as a result. If you're new to indie shooters, there are dozens of better ones out there. If you’ve already played them, you can still get some enjoyment out of this, I guess.6/10
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: It doesn't bring anything new to the table, but it's tightly made - and that's not a bad thing; a solidly made game doesn't need a gimmick to make itself stand out. All of the weapons (except the shotgun) feel good to use, the maps are mostly passable, and the game can look beautiful when it wants to. Particular props to the art direction of the enemies in the game, which are all distinct and give easy visual cues as to their purpose almost immediately.The only problem is that with the slight beefiness of some of the enemies, and the speed at which they move, the game starts to fall into Serious Sam Syndrome on occasion - falling into the "hold S and shoot type of gameplay, thanks to a lot of concentrated mobs that are hard to kill and which are chasing you at high speeds. This is only really a problem occasionally, in episode three specifically.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: The action is fast, the game is hard and the feeling is right, in fact it seems to be back for a few minutes to Duke Nukem 3D or Quake or similar games. I've tried other titles in the same genre (Hellbound, Project Warlock) and I didn't like them, at all. This one is actually fun, this one has actually a gameplay. It's more on the side of Ion Fury or Dusk. For this reason the vote is positive, despite some problems. Highly recommended if you like these old shooters.What are the problems? (as requested by the developers, the criticism is to improve the product)- Checkpoint saves. It's quite manageable, but it's there, and I don't think it can be fixed- Some opponents take too many hits to fall. Things like this should be limited to large spaces like arenas (Serious Sam style), but certainly not in narrow corridors or small rooms- In several moments I ran out of ammunition- Sometimes (like in E3M4 but not only) you are forced to throw yourself into a dangerous area where a lot of demons of different types (which would need different weapons) shoot and come at you, all together, with no possibility of shelterThere are of course some very positive things. For example the dual mode of some weapons (quickly changeable with a right click). It's a great thing, because it adds strategy: the powerful mode consumes more ammunition.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best of the boomer shooters to me. I own most of the ones that are out, like Dusk, Prodeus, Amid Evil, Project Warlock, HROT, and I forgot what else. I saw this and thought it had potential, but it is really the most enjoyable of the retro fps games I've played.I love that you have a katana that you can make into a spear and throw. It does a ton of damage and I regularly use it to 1 hit enemies. The bow is also fantastic, as well as the supershot gun. There is a dash ability, and it charges, and you can find items to make the recharge faster, or your shotgun stronger, hold more ammo, etc for all weapons.The music is pretty amazing too.Really surprised, I haven't heard of this and saw a couple of reviews, and just thought I would give it a try and I am glad I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Glad I got this game for only 1 USD on Fanatical because after 3 hours of playing it I was bored to death. This is probably the most cookie-cutter boomer shooter I've played. The best analogy I can come up with - Dread Templar is like "The Best of" compilation album of a mediocre tribute band. Nothing it does is particularly bad or wrong, but there is no original bone in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Felt like leaving a review since this game's flying under a lot of people's radar and unjustifiably so. The recent full release was a great opportunity to revisit it after having played through the first 3 chapters about a year ago.There isn't much story and these kinds of games really don't need one. The ending's Tchernobog-esque where the big bad wants to siphon off your accumulated "dread force" only to, predictably, get annihilated instead.Speaking of Tchernobog, this game knows its ancestors and is ripe with homages to them. In fact, you'll be hard-pressed to find a single classic FPS that isn't referenced in one easter egg or another. Pretty cool.As for the gameplay, it feels great. Really responsive with a good selection of weapons (and upgrades) and good flow of combat. There's really nothing in particular I was missing. If I had to name one shortcoming, it'd be the OST. While the individual tracks are good, there's like only 1 track per chapter and it gets repetitive after a while. I'll chalk it down to this being a one-man project.All in all, this game does not have any major flaws but, on the flipside, doesn't have anything outstanding or memorable going for it either. Just solid all-around.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely nails that nostalgic 1999 vibe.The movement and shooting is pleasing, which is good because that's the majority of the gameplay.A lot of weapons to choose from, to the point that you can forget what you have.The weapon / character upgrade mechanic is simple enough without disrupting the pacing.Levels design is a hit or miss, but the soundtrack slaps so hard it's easy to overlook some of the less fun areas.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to give this game a shot despite the middling reviews. Sadly, they're right.A boomer shooter lives and dies by its gunplay, because that's all it has to offer. A boomer shooter without visceral and tight gunplay is like a pizza place that can't make a good pizza. You can be a hamburger place and make a mediocre pizza, and that'd be fine. But you are a pizza place, Dread Templar. The hit feel is simply not there in this game. So much so that the developers clearly felt the need to add hit markers. I can see why, because if not for the hit markers, I wouldn't be able to tell when I'm hitting an enemy and not. It's *that* bad.This may be mostly because of the gunplay but; killing most of the enemies is a chore rather than being satisfying (especially that one tanky *and* fast melee enemy). I'd describe them as "annoying" instead of being "challenging". The visuals aren't very impressive. The music is well composed, but still quite generic. Level design is "passable", though way too linear. (Come on boomer shooter devs... DOOM laid out the blueprint only.... literally 31 YEARS ago) Everything about the game is "just enough" or "mediocre" or "not enough", it's not impressive whatsoever, doesn't break any new ground. So I don't see why you would play this over any other boomer shooter on the market right now, of which there are many. Nothing about it stands out.Hopefully the developers learned a lot making this game and will use all of it in their next game. Best of luck for the next one, but sadly this isn't it, chief.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: While Dread Templar is a pretty good retro-inspired shooter and gets a lot right; from the guns to the story to the action, I feel the overall experience for me was weakened by the mis-use of the power that is John S. Weekley’s work. Can it be fixed in future updates? I don’t think so. Should the developers seriously consider a more adaptive music approach to the sequel; please, yes, please; the game was good, but not worth the literal headache after 16 hours of game play.The final outcome here; for me at least, is a game that has so much engaging action and interesting game play mechanics, but over the long run time falls short on longevity and consistency, with the noise turning a normal exploration for tokens into a frustrating speed run without breath or air. I shouldn’t crave the sense of relief I get at the end of the map, just to have a moment to collect myself in a brief instance of pace change, as the tracks change, sometimes, between maps.Give Dread Templar a try, but take some breaks, unless headaches are your thing. But also, if you miss this one, you’ll only regret that awesome weapon customization mechanic.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: I was having a lot of fun with this game for the first 3/4, but stuff happened irl and I wasn't able to finish it. Finally I reinstalled the game and decided I'd just start a new playthrough, only to find that the gems you get for perks in game were completely absent from where they were supposed to be. What you're supposed to do before starting a new playthrough is click the setting the resets all blood gem locations, the only issue with doing that is that IT DOESN'T ACTUALLY RESET ANYTHING AT ALL. Furthermore, I've learned this has been a problem for multiple people dating back months ago and the dev still hasn't fixed it. It's a crying shame, because the game itself is fun and the music is amazing, but I can't recommend something that breaks new games.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: A solid old-school shooter, with retro graphics, a fascinating background, creepy enemies, classic weapons, and a dynamic and fun gameplay, pumped by a powerful soundtrack. There are some interesting mechanics, like , but overall the game is rather similar to the classics of this genre, especially to the first Quake. As in all old shooters, you can carry all the weapons you want, your walking speed and agility are very high, and you can pick up health and armor. After a while it becomes a bit repetitive, but after all, this is the bane of all shooters. I recommend it if you like bathing into the blood and guts of your enemies while running around at superhuman speed in a desolate and nightmarish landscape. Can you ask any better?Cheers guys!

_childDocuments_.review: What I really want to rate this game is a Neutral. It's a solid 5 or 6 out of 10 for me, reason being that whilst it ticks all the " Modern FPS with a Retro Nod" boxes, it doesn't excel in anything and feels lacking in some core aspects. Combat wise, Gun design is ok, but the differentials in its utilities are not very prominent. I've reached E2M2 on the "hard difficulty equivalent" only really using pistols and shotguns. The only time I used any other weapon was when I was fighting a boss and ran out of ammo for those guns. The katanas are cool, but again, I have no reason to use them aside from when I've run out of bullets.Enemies are quite varied, and yet not varied enough. I approach most of them the same way, using the same weapon,  Strafe, double shot gun, strafe double shot gun. Occasionally switching to pistols to conserve ammo or to deal with enemies that are further away.  Last of all there's bullet time, which I also did not use at all aside from the tutorial. There was simply no challenge that seemed to require it and I tend to forget about it being there until i see the resources scattered around the map and go "ahhhh.. i really should use that more often".The upgrade system is cool, but it is locked between 2 levels of locks. Firstly you need to find resources to enable the upgrade slot, then you need to also look for the upgrades. I think given that finding the upgrades themselves are already a challenge, I see no reason for having slot unlocks linked to such a progression system. It punishes players who dont look for secrets, limiting their "fun". My last critique on the upgrade system is that the guns don't feel cool to use until further skills are unlocked, so the difficulty associated with actually getting to use them locks out the fun of the game from other players.Level design is servicable, with secrets scattered throughout. Nothing that really differenciates each encounter from the next. They aren't Duke Nukem or ION Fury levels of "cool secrets", but some are quite enjoyable to find.All in all, I think if you are an FPS fan, you might find something to enjoy here. I would definitely continue to play the game despite my criticisms of it. But if you are looking for a game to showcase what modern boomer shooters are amazingly capable of, unfortunately, I don't think this is the game to do that.** Review after additional 7 hours: The game definitely gets better midway through episode 2 in terms of enemy design and lay out. Im enjoying it much more now. I still feel the same in terms of how the guns feel, and how the progression system is set up. And for the game to pick up so long after E1M1, ultimately it is still difficult to recommend this game. If you enjoy boomer shooters, and enjoy looking for secrets, this is a good game, or else I'd probably suggest picking this game up discounted.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a high quality old school ‘Boomershooter’ FPS that will likely split folks. It looks nice, it sounds nice, it plays nice and has a varied play style of play due to its upgrade system. It even has some imaginative environments and fun boss fights in the later half of the game! Unfortunately to get there you have to trawl through a couple of highly uninspired chapters that scream “generic” more than any other old school FPS that I’ve played in the past 5 years.I want to make one thing clear. Dread Templar is really good. If you are a hard-line boomshoot connoisseur, then you will absolutely devour ol’ Dreddy here to the same degree that e-girls create drama. If you were to break it down to its mechanical parts then it not only does everything right, but takes other concepts other modern boomshoots have used and refines them nicely. The act of pulling the trigger on a gun, with both the audio and visual feedback of firing is satisfying. Enemies die in spectacular ways and the gibs from their exploding bodies are some of the best I’ve seen. Exploration in the sprawling levels is rewarding. The movement is absolutely spot without snags that plague some other unity titles, and it straddles the balance between Quake’s simplicity and Doom Eternal’s chaotic meta. It is a title that not only nails mechanical reliability, but also expands on the basics that so many games have used until recently.Two elements about Dread Templar help it stand out (mechanically at least) come in it’s recharging meta and its upgrade system. While neither are strikingly original, they seem to be sublimely balanced.First is the way it treats its recharging resources. Aside from a slow charging dash (which I will add is quite well balanced: fast enough to charge as to not be forgotten as useless and slow enough to charge as to not be over spammed) there are the constantly recharging throwing spear, the arrows for the black bow and the charge-on-kill bullet time features. While I have noted some folks forget about these features, when used frequently they vary up the gameplay a lot. The dash and bullet time are useful for huge, difficult fights, while the throwing spear is a single shot, alt fire for your melee weapon that does high damage to multiple enemies. The bow finally is a 4 shot, long ranged sniping weapon with a tiny charge time. These two weapons help enormously not only with ammo efficiency but also act as great long distance tools. All these elements mean that even when the player may end up in situations where resources are limited there is always an option to use bar the basic melee weapon. Granted it is not 100% clear about this, and I can imagine a few folks not cottoning on to this and finding the game frustrating, once the player understands the meta it becomes a whole bunch of fun.Even with these rechargeable extras, as the game goes on the fights become increasingly difficult in the enemy attacks where the base weapons just won’t cut the mustard. Thankfully the upgrade system helps overcome this problem. Here player expression is fully realised, giving players the ability to enhance their abilities and weaponry to suit their playstyle. Do you like the black bow and you want to lean on it more? Enhance the number of arrows it has, enhance the damage and then make it so each successive arrow does more damage than the last. Like crowd control and weapon switching? Get the ice shotgun and then enhance the revolver so it does more damage to frozen enemies. Make dashing cool down faster, incoming damage less, increase bullet time, turn some guns into overpowered versions of themselves. It really does have a huge variation of styles that allows for any player to lean into whatever playstyle they prefer, and even if they don’t like their choices, they can be reset later. Unlike Forgive Me Father’s style of upgrades, which is peppered with useless junk that cannot be changed, here you can play around with enhanced shotgun damage or overpowered bullet time pistols and then, come the next upgrade station, you can switch things out to hellfire pistols or longer range shotgun blasts.After all that praise one would presume that Dread Templar would be amongst the pinnacles of the throwback shooter genre, rubbing shoulders with Ion Fury and Dusk, though here is the part of the review where the predictable “BUT” comes in.For all its mechanical fanciness Dread Templar falls short for the first two chapters. Here it is a matter of taste, but it is clear that there have been absolutely tons of boomshoots in the past few years and to stand out from the crowd you need to have some unique elements. As much as people can speak about “gameplay is the most important thing”, aesthetic is a major element in which people emotionally attach themselves with in media. 2022’s Fashion Police Squad for example was somewhat flimsy in places gameplay and level design wise, but won out with the over-the-top settings and charming settings.Dread Templar does not stand out. It is another game where you crawl through hell as a bad-ass dude out to kill all the zombie enemies hunting down Satan for vengeance, shooting double barrel shotguns while relatively cool heavy metal plays. For the average person who has not got the greatest attention span, you have played this before. You have played it many, many times before.This is worst in the first two chapters. Initially you will have not accumulated enough upgrades to make the weaponry interesting and, as such, everything seems to be so generic that it becomes predictable after a level or two. It is not bad, just bland. This is made considerably worse due to these chapters effectively remaining in the same setting and using the same music over and over. Differentiating E1M2 from E1M4? It is you fighting through crypts of zombies, just as E1M1 was, and E1M3 was, and most of E1M5 is all the while the same sounding Rob Zombiesque OST plays endlessly. I can see this easily putting folks off very quickly, playing for about 30 minutes and then just thinking “What is so special about this?” before casting it aside and then proclaiming the whole old school FPS genre has become stale.The most frustrating element is once you pass the second episode the settings really unfurl with their more wild concepts, such as deserts made from the sands of time collapsing in on themselves due to your actions, or fighting through a huge celestial library / castle place where it becomes clear that the worlds are stored in paintings. If the crypts were held back a world or two then the first impressions would have been much better, setting the player up with some cool upgrades to be able to carve through the predictable crypt levels to reduce the monotony, but as it is you need to play for at least an hour and a half before you start to get to the good stuff, and I cannot see too many folks to have that kind of patience.In summery, Dread Templar is a good game. A game I would advise to both the old school adherent and to people with the patience to cut through the opening levels. However if you are starting to have got your fill of these types of game and need a shakeup of the formula, Dread Templar is just too slow to get to the fun stuff and will no doubt bore you with its predictable opening chapters. A good buy then, but only for those who absolutely need more boomshoots in their life.

_childDocuments_.review: Embrace the Dread Force and Unleash HellDread Templar is a masterful blend of classic 90s shooter nostalgia and modern FPS elements, creating a heart-pounding and exhilarating experience that leaves players on the edge of their seats. From the moment you pick up the controller (mouse and keyboard), the game captivates you with its impeccable pacing, making it difficult to tear yourself away from the relentless action.One of the standout features of Dread Templar is its exceptional pacing. The game manages to strike a perfect balance between intense combat sequences and moments of respite, creating a dynamic flow that keeps players thoroughly engaged throughout the entire journey. You'll find yourself constantly on the move, strategising and adapting to the ever-changing challenges presented by the fiendish enemies. The difficulty level is expertly crafted, ensuring that as you progress, the challenges escalate proportionally. The game doesn't hold your hand, but it also doesn't feel unfair. Each encounter provides a learning opportunity, forcing you to refine your skills and tactics to survive the relentless onslaught. This finely-tuned difficulty curve keeps you motivated, as overcoming obstacles feels genuinely rewarding.Weapons play a pivotal role in any first-person shooter, and Dread Templar delivers in this aspect. The arsenal of weapons at your disposal feels incredibly responsive and satisfying to use. As you unlock and combine dozens of upgrades and skills, you'll find yourself mastering the art of destruction, turning your enemies into artistic displays of red-mist. Speaking of enemies, the monsters in Dread Templar are not to be taken lightly. They are cunning, ferocious, and relentless (especially those gun wielding zombie dudes), always ready to exploit any moment of weakness, where a momentary lapse in focus can lead to being swiftly overwhelmed, these typically manifest from situation where you are not paying attention to monsters further off in the distance(I am referring to those purple brain monsters who can mortar fire for days) or just bumb-rush you until die. The feeling of danger lurking around every corner keeps you constantly on your toes, adding an extra layer of excitement and challenge to the gameplay.Dread Templar doesn't just offer a high-octane experience; it takes it to a whole new level. The gameplay can escalate from 0 to 100 in a matter of seconds, immersing you in adrenaline-pumping battles and heart-stopping moments. It's an experience that will keep your heart racing, your hands sweaty, and your mind utterly absorbed in the chaos.Considering that Dread Templar was developed by a small indie company, it is nothing short of remarkable. The dedication and passion poured into this game are evident in every detail. From the polished mechanics to the captivating level design, it showcases the studio's talent and potential in the gaming industry.If you're a hardcore FPS enthusiast seeking an adrenaline-fuelled challenge, Dread Templar should undoubtedly be on your must-play list. Embrace the Dread Force, unleash your inner hellish fury, and embark on a journey of revenge that will leave you begging for more.PS: That side mission with the mining cart, that sucked.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is an old-school shooter elevated by an incredible soundtrack. The guns are largely staples of the genre, though the trap launcher and bow add some welcome wrinkles. From what I've played of the games 25 levels thus far, environments are interesting and varied and there are a plethora of enemy types. If you're a person who likes deep and involved stories, there isn't much of that here. There is narration between episodes, but I found this to be boring. The environmental storytelling is pretty solid though, and there are lots of secrets to find so it pays to search each level thoroughly. Overall, this is another boomer shooter with all of the trappings you'd expect. It's not going to revolutionize the genre, but it's a lot of fun and a welcome addition to any enthusiast's collection.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't write Dread Templar off, like I did at first.It may look like "just another Quake-like", but it really nails the kind of action and level design I expect from a Quake-type game. Not to mention, this game manages to make good use of an upgrade system, which I find some games don't quite do well enough. Mix and match passive buffs and perks, as well as weapon upgrades, to your heart's content, as you acquire more throughout your time playing. Don't like your chosen batch of upgrades? No problem, just switch out what "runes" you find, mid-mission. Not even weapon alts are permanent, if you don't want to keep one equipped. This ties really, really well into the secret hunting. The more secrets you find, the more powerful you end up becoming, and the secret hunting, as well as the puzzling Super Secrets, are really satisfying and cleverly placed. I don't mean to draw too many comparisons to Quake, but it really does remind me of the best of Quake community maps, particularly Arcane Dimensions. And, unlike certain other recently released Quake-likes, the level design is FAR from bloated. Levels are really tight and well-paced, with a lot of verticality, nooks and crannies, and impressive views.My only gripes may be that the art direction causes a lot of environments to look... overly samey, like a lot of similar, very detailed texture work and colors. It gets a little mushy. Also, I don't care for the neon fuchsia atmosphere of the "hell" levels. It looks like a Tiktok influencer puked all over it. IDK, maybe they were going for a "color out of space" type look, but it doesn't work for me. The only other thing is, so far, the "story" is unironically edgy. Like, maybe it's just such good satire that I cannot tell whether the writing is being genuine or not, but the narration and origin of the titular Templar is a bit... corny. Its nothing terrible tho.Overall, I'd say this is an easy recommend if you want a fairly well designed Quake-adjacent experience. I keep finding myself being pushed (just on the normal skill as of now) to actually switch up my weapon use and, for once, use the bullet time at vital moments. And those upgrades to your arsenal/buffs are vital to improving, or even changing the experience. Talk about a rewarding time. I often find some games either have arsenals that don't really feel purposeful in their implementation, or the "oh so popular" bullet time ability is needlessly tacked on for some cool factor. But that is not the case here. I am far from dreading spending more time with this game, its just the kind of thing I love. Color me impressed.

_childDocuments_.review: Silver upgrades are flat enhancements like Damage, Rate of Fire, and Spare Ammo capacity.Gold upgrades are interesting enhancements that change how the weapon works.Pistols and SMGs have reload mechanics, but no other weapons have this except for the double-barrel shotgun with a gold upgrade.There are 3 ability icons: Melee Throw, Regen Bow Ammo, and Dash. To make better use of these, there should be an instant attack button for "Melee Throw" and for the Bow. Additionally, the number of arrows should be shown on the Bow's icon. The Bow regenerates its own ammo and has its own icon.The maps seem a bit too big and there is no map. The fear of missing any upgrades kills the flow of the game.Pistol/SMG ammo and shotgun ammo are clear, but the other ammo types are hard to understand. You mostly use pistols, SMGs, and shotguns because there is plenty of ammo for these weapons laying around. Also, it is hard to find the right weapon if you don't start the fight with it higher than 4.All in all, I enjoy the game but not enough to finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is what you get when you mix Quake 1 and Painkiller. But sadly it wasn't as enjoyable to me.Good looking and fun for the first 2 episodes, then the game becomes a gamble : if you haven't unlocked enough perks this far, you die. That simple.I played on Normal difficulty, it was pretty nice the first episode with the discovery of the arsenal and overall level design, the door unlocking routine etc.The second episode is leaning toward Doom Eternal mechanisms : you need specific weapons for specific situations. Thus making it more of a challenge. A bit harder, but still manageable and satisfying.After those, the game is throwing a ton of sh!t at you for the sake of it regardless of your stuff.I love games like Duke Nukem 3D and Brutal Doom. And whenever an indie gem shows up I feel the urge to take a bite.But maybe I am just too old for these "hardcore" fps. I am definetly too lazy to go any further at that point. The game is too demanding. Perhaps if I chose the easiest difficulty I'd say otherwise, but it's meant to be played the default way right ?Difficulty aside, Dread Templar may be better if :- it wasn't so perks-dependant because the enemies grow stronger the more you progress, and you must upgrade your character and items. Perks shouldn't be mandatory in games imo, especially when they are hidden.- it had a weapon wheel system to ease gun selection during critical action.- the "you are hit" feedback was more obvious. You don't always realize how low HP you are, cuz there is no hint except the little scream covered but music and sounds.- better ragdolls. The weapons have a nice vibe to them, but it flattens right away when enemies just drop down or explode. They don't fly and bounce, it's a shame. Ragdoll is the easiest reward in gunfights.On the positive side of things, I really like the aesthetic of the game. And the soundtracks is gorgeous !Didn't come across any bug neither, pretty clean job.Despite my bitter experience on the game and the fact I gave up on it, I want to give devs a chance and recommend it to others, should they be aware of what they step in : not a walk in the park.

_childDocuments_.review: Had the privilege of getting to play Episodes 4 and 5 early, and had a really good time. _childDocuments_.review: Well worth playing, with good combat, variety of weapons and plenty of secrets to find.The game starts slow, but if you give it some time, it really shines. For me it opened up somewhere around the end of the first and the start of the second playthrough; invest some time into exploring secrets and as the game progresses the runes start coming together, synergy cranks you damage output to eleven, new ways to deal with enemies come up, and finally you start to feel like an unstoppable dread force plowing through packs of monsters. greatly vary in visuals and presentation; first is kinda meh I guess, full of dilapidated ruins and withered vegetation, somewhat brownish; second is tombs and castles painted in blue and violet tones. Then come the icy expanses and frozen villages of the third episode, strangely reminiscent of Alice Madness Returns' underwater world. Fourth is abandoned desert settlements, and while I generally detest desert levels in games, in this case they were pretty good, and music easily makes it my favorite episode. Fifth, by way of music and you traversing backwards through rehashed pieces of earlier maps, is very Dusk-ish, not in a bad way; good episode, except for a couple fleshy levels which I really don't care for. are rather short, and that works to game's advantage; you are never really lost or looking for a way out, combat encounters are spaced out well with an occasional squad of mobs here and there to keep you on your toes. Ammunition is abundant if you are willing to look for efficient weapon combos to take monsters out; more is hidden away in secrets, if you're really hurting for ammo. are fun, sound meaty enough and look amazing (okay, shotgun is kinda bland and its banshee variant looks weird).  Golden runes, if you're willing to look for them, can turn some of them into completely different versions of themselves, making you adjust your strategies or synergize with other weapons: dual SMGs become monster-melting hail of death burning through your whole ammo supply in a couple second (frankly, they are a panic button of sorts), shotgun chills enemies and makes them open for double damage from Lethal-slotted revolver, rockets burst into forward cones of ice needles and so on. The most underwhelming weapon is the rocket launcher actually, with way less damage output than you would expect - on higher difficulties only the first-tier enemies can be killed with a single rocket (with 3 level damage rune at that), and while ammo supply is plenty, it just takes too long to kill anything as opposed to, say, split second combo of banshee+revolver, which takes down most enemies in one go. is good. It can get a bit repetitive in the first episode, especially if you're hunting for secrets for the first time, but later episodes have some beautiful pieces. This is the kind of soundtrack worth listening to even outside the game. Fits episode themes  nicely and helps further set distinctive mood for each level. are okay. Placement is usually logical, so you can usually tell that something's there if you look around a bit, although there are some brutally miniscule wall indentations and hard to discern texture misalignments (aggravated by the game being somewhat sloppy with texture alignment generally), but they are pretty few, most of them I got by sheer luck and from erc's guides. Secrets have runes, ammo and much needed health and armor - especially in Nightmare difficulty, which only has health packs in secrets, so it's worth it looking for them.Most of the levels have super secrets, which have an element of puzzle to them, and it's always fun discovering a piece and wondering where it should go. are few and mostly related to level geometry, a missing piece here and there; in a couple levels state of objects is not saved properly, so after loading a side area count resets to zero, or keys spawn again even if you opened the doors already. Nothing gamebreaking. There was only one time when I had to load after getting stuck in some dark hole in a broken down ship.All in all, after working my way from Hard to Nightmare+ in four consecutive playthroughs, I consider Dread Templar one of the high-tier fast-paced shooters, worth playing and replaying.

_childDocuments_.review: Wait until it's fully released. Right now there's 2 episodes, 10 levels total. Roughly 2 hours of playtime right now. If you care about finding secrets, you'll probably get more time out of it. Overall, the levels are a lot of fun. This game isn't as polished as something like Dusk, and the level design and loadout aren't quite as good, either. The trap shooter weapon in particular feels a bit out of place and not super useful. I like the rest of the guns, though.There's a foundation for a good game here. The level design is good and the enemy design is really cool. Unfortunately, right now there just isn't enough to it to justify a $15 price tag. Even the $12.74 sale price I paid for it seems kind of steep, considering you can beat it in a day or two.Also, the boss of episode 2 (what is currently the final boss) is brutal. Like, so annoyingly difficult that it's not fun. I'm not a fan of bosses that can kill you in one hit, especially when they also have moves that slow you down, thus making it a lot easier for that one hit kill to land. To top it off, he's just a giant bullet sponge. The "shoot at it until it dies" philosophy of retro FPS games works best when bosses don't take ages to kill. Granted, the final boss of Doom can be beat in 5 seconds. That's no good either, but it's better than what this game is doing. I spent about 30 minutes on that final boss before finally giving up.Anyways, the reason I'm not recommending this game is primarily because there just isn't enough content for it to be worth the asking price right now. And I'm salty about that boss. I would imagine that when the game is fully released and all 5 episodes are there, I'll give this game a positive review.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good. Nay, ace. No doubt about it. If it wasn't up against the stiff competition that is the years upon years of high quality 'boomer' shooters, this would be a completely unqualified early access recommendation. Ultrakill, Ion Fury, Post Void, Project Warlock 1 + II, Amid Evil, DUSK, HROT, Maximum Action, GTTOD, Prodeus, Cultic, etc - be they full games, early access, or just demos, the retro, 'boomer' shooter genre really is booming. I also cannot wait for the likes of Into the Pit, Fortune's Run, and Forgive Me Father.  I started up a playthrough on the hardest difficulty and finally got a handle on  getting through levels whilst taking minimal to no damage. It was a blast. The one thing Dread truly nails is superb action committed to dodgeable projectiles and no-hit runs. Presentation is gorgeous and refreshingly colourful. Golden upgrades transform a weapon such that you can carve out a unique playstyle. It takes a significant investment in the weapons to unlock the privilege after all, yet it also doesn't force you to commit to anything you've invested. Great stuff. I like the quick switch between similar weapons. For an amateur like me who can't do the fast weapon switch method used by speedrunners in Doom Eternal, RE: Village, etc, this really delivers the illusion that I can. The bullet time is a great ability given how finger-click fast the action is. Level navigation is ace and well paced with save points, even if it's not the most inspired level design in the world. It's all very readable and I enjoyed seeking out secrets (including references!). Action is silky smooth and gives great gory feedback. Certainly no complaints there. Dashing makes platforming much more interesting. There's some flirtation with more 'out there' enemies, weapons, and level design, but as it is I need a lot more like the electric trap launcher and the power fist. The soundtrack fits it like a glove. Bosses are a highlight, particularly the (current) final one wherein you have to be cognizant of aerial damage. Panic inducing, that one. Despite its excellent name and action, it lacks something definite to call its own other compared to its genre compatriots. Bullet time, a dash, and its upgrade system, sure, but elements like its power glove tease something more. This is a derivative and nostalgic genre by nature, but perhaps there's some way it can become more distinctive going forward., I feel the dash and the katana throw both need to disrupt the player flow less with their cooldowns. Dashing like a maniac is liable to get you killed anyway (I'd assume) and I can't see any reason why I can't switch back to my normal katanas right after a javelin throw. Creating these clamps on player power and killing momentum feels antithetical to the fun of the genre for me. It's hard to have bullet time and not be immediately compelled to slide and dive. Med kits on the hardest difficulty being reserved for secret areas is perhaps too brutal.  That seems unnecessary. Everything else feels pretty reasonable. Even committing to med kits as secrets feels okay given the game's focus on avoiding all or most damage. It's doable.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a lot of thoughts I have on this game, and if you had to ask me what my thoughts are for episode 1 and 2 I'd say the game is excellent. Dread Templar knows what it is, and what it sets out to do, but whilst progressing throughout the game past episode 2 there are cracks which start to form. Some levels do a bit of work stitching these cracks back together, and almost make you feel as though you're back in the first two episodes, but their appearance is few and far between. Whilst I know this sounds bleak to start with, I actually do recommend this game, but not by that much, as the game is just *fine*, and as I got further into the game I felt as though I had more of an obligation to complete it rather than wanting to complete it, and upon completing it I felt as though a curse had been lifted from upon me. There are DEFINITELY worse games you could spend your money on, especially if you want something which has a LOT of playtime for such a small price which even goes on sale for around $5.: 6.5/10Moving onwards from episodes 1 and 2 however, the game starts to take a turn that most other games in the "boomshoot/retro FPS" space don't, in that it actually starts to slowly become.. Worse? It's weird. Every single FPS I've played within the same genre space have only gotten BETTER as they've progressed, with Dusk almost blossoming into a work of art in some specific levels, Incision only ramping up from the beginning, and Cultic improving throughout. Dread Templar doesn't do this, and if I had to present a graph signifying my enjoyment of the game it'd look erratic. Overall, Dread Templar could've cut out about 70% of the levels from Episode 3 and 4 and ONLY kept the good levels and then the endings and it'd be a more compelling and interesting game than it currently is, as many of the levels feel just like an after thought. Episode 3 itself is a point of contention for me, as whilst the first two episodes featured enemies which rushed at you, Episode 3 feels almost like they tried to take the games combat flow into an entirely new direction, as if someone new was designing this episode. Episode 3 adds an enemy which is faster than you, and spawns in large groups to the point they feel almost as if they're the primary enemy in this episode, taking it from something where you're meant to rush into a group and take them out one by one, to a backpedaling simulator. Episode 3 is also where some levels almost begin to feel.. Incomplete? There's weird level geometry in many places, almost as if the design of the levels feels as though it was rushed, and this only more apparent as you progress further into episode 4, with there being weird pits you can fall into which don't equate to instant death, which could effectively soft-lock the player into a reset.Weapons in Dread Templar are both powerful and superfluous, with many of the counterparts of certain weapons just feeling lackluster as you get further into the game. Dread Templar's Bazooka ends up succumbing to this within episode 4, with it requiring an exorbitant amount of ammunition to be able to down certain enemies. On top of this, there is an upgrade tree which can alter your weapons, but many of the weapons don't get meaningful upgrades which make them worth using outside of very specific cases, and even if you do acquire these upgrades they require increased ammunition to use them which cuts into the reserves of the alternate weapon for that key which makes it feel as though it's almost not worth picking them up.Bosses are... Wtf are the bosses in this game? Easily some of the absolute worst bosses I've ever seen in an FPS, in terms of both mechanics and difficulty. NONE of them are hard whatsoever, as I beat all of them except the first boss in a single try on Hell Difficulty. Realistically these add nothing in terms of difficulty or complexity to the game, and whilst I understand they were likely added because they were meant to be the capstone for each episode, they could've been removed and killed in cutscenes and I wouldn't have felt as if the game was any better or worse.

_childDocuments_.review: I covered Dread Templar in an article, as well as many other games from Realms Deep 2021, which you can read and see screenshots from my website -  -_____________________________Dread Templar just released into Early Access, and have seen some more recent gameplay of it, I broke down and decided that I would go against my will of Early Access games, and bought it. I'm sure I'll regret it later when I'm unable to finish the full game till launch, but that's a problem I'm willing to deal with to give Dread Templar a try, as there isn't an up-to-date demo on Steam.The demo levels I played are here, but altered to flow better, and not have just one BIG map that I could get lost in. The path of the levels were simple, but offered some exploration and alternative paths to go. Secrets are plenty and range from easy to find to multi step puzzles to get the best secrets. What really helps Dread Templar is the inclusion of a metal soundtrack, which I say even rivals Doom 2016s soundtrack! Combined with the gothic ruins, monstrous creatures to kill, and powerful weapons with fast movement speed is the perfect combo for addictive gameplay! Oh and mix in some slow-mo as well! One nit pick I do want to say, not so much about the game, but about some people commenting about the game, is saying the movement system is better than Quake. Those people clearly never played Quake. Dread Templar lacks any form of bunny hopping or a way to increase your movement speed like you can in Quake. I tend to jump around or bunny hop out of habit in every FPS game, so I would have noticed if there was a way to move around faster, but there isn't other than the short dodge mechanic, which doesn't really make you "faster" in any sense.The weapon selection is pretty good and covers all the basics. Starting with your duel katanas that can then be combined to be a spear which kills most basic enemies in one shot. You also start with Duel pistols, and eventually you pick up Duel Uzi which share the same weapon slot, but can switch between on the fly by pressing the same weapon slot key. The same works with the shotgun and double barrel shotgun. You also have access to a magical bow that regenerates shots after a short time, a trap launcher which acts like your stun gun or trap layer, and your rocket launcher type weapon, with more to come later. On top of that, there is also an upgrade system! Each weapon type can have two basic emblems which do simple things like give more ammo or faster fire rate or recharge time or damage. You can also equip one legendary emblem which can drastically change your weapons, such as giving your pistols and Uzi no reloads, electrifying your katanas, pistols having infinite ammo during slow-mo, turning your shotgun into a sniper rifle, and that was just the few I found in the first episode! However, you can't just go and equip these right off the bat, you have to unlock the emblem slots with Blood shards, which you will find as you progress through the game and in it's many secret or the harder "side areas". This really makes you want to look through the maps and try to find everything you can.Now I only completed the first Episode and stopped. Not that I was bored, but because I needed to finish up some other games. Plus this would give me some time for the game to get some updates with more content and closer to the full release, then I can binge the whole game at once. I know that kind of goes against my logic of playing something through to completion before I review, but again, this game is in Early Access and not the full game. Things can and will change.Either way Dread Templar is great fun and I can't wait for the full release in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of old-school first-person shooters with a modern twist, Dread Templar is a blast from the past that you shouldn't miss. The game masterfully captures the fast-paced, adrenaline-fueled action of classics like Doom and Quake, but adds enough unique elements to feel fresh and engaging.The gunplay is incredibly satisfying, with a wide array of weapons to experiment with—dual katanas and shotguns are personal favorites! The combat system is smooth and brutal, and the level design encourages exploration with secret areas, upgrades, and clever puzzles.The art style blends retro pixel aesthetics with modern lighting and effects, giving the game a gritty, old-school charm. Plus, the soundtrack absolutely slaps, though i'd definitely add a bit more variety of it.What really stands out, though, is the game's progression system. The Templar skill tree lets you customize your playstyle, unlocking abilities and perks that make combat even more fun. You get to approach battles the way you want, whether that's close-quarters carnage or long-range destruction.If you are a masochist, go ahead and play on the maximum difficulty since it's just painfully hard. If you’re a sucker for fast-paced, blood-soaked shooter action with a hint of nostalgia, Dread Templar hits all the right notes. It's a love letter to the '90s FPS era, with modern sensibilities that make it more than just a tribute.

_childDocuments_.review: Among modern FPS titles that are deliberately classic "boomer shooters", Dread Templar is the most mediocre and bland game I've ever played, and honestly I don't know how I feel about this one, on paper, I should have enjoyed it since I enjoy "boomer shooters", but in practice I was left dissatisfied and frustrated, and by hour 5 or so I just wanted it to end already.For me, the main downside is the AI behavior, AI spawn system, upgrade/rune system which falls flat and to a lesser extend, the lack of sound feedback and cues from enemies & the environment.Cons:- Enemy design is just mediocre and cheap, as soon as enemies spot you, they just charge at you or spam projectiles mindlessly, and that is it, that is the only behavior of enemies, even 20+ years old games have better enemy design and AI behavior.- Enemies are extremely fast and spammy, imagine 10s of them spawning right in front of you, spamming projectiles while the rest rush on you.- Most weapons feel underpowered and require you to use runes to make them perform okay, and even then most of the runes felt underperforming or not worth using at all. - Many runes are locked behind secret areas.- Rune descriptions are vague and don't mention all the details completely (have to look for guides to completely understand the details).- Player projectiles getting stuck in level geometry, walls, ground, etc.- Enemy projectiles sometimes going through walls.- Lack of sound feedback from enemies and some of the environment.,- Lack of ambient & environment sounds, they're extremely on short loop.- Music is extremely repetitive and plays in short loop, (had to mute it after 30 mins).Pros:+ Optimization and smoothness across the levels is the only positive thing I have to say about this game, it plays very smoothly.

_childDocuments_.review: I want to like this game, but everything about it is kind of boring. It checks all the boxes of a boomer shooter in the most rote, by the numbers way. All the boomer shooter weapons are there, but none of them feel particularly good to use or have any interesting gimmicks--from the hour or so I played I didn't see any gimmicks. The levels go for that classic boomer shooter design emulating the best stuff from Doom, Quake, and Levelord, but the exploration is unrewarding.The game has a good look, but other than that I don't have anything positive to say about it. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar does everything right and rarely falters in any of its facets. Gameplay is as tight as you should expect from a game of its kin. Move fast, dash, slow down time and combine your katanas into an unstoppable spear of death on your way to victory.Weapons pack a wallop just as a good arsenal would. You got your standard accoutrement of armament ranging from your dual pistols and SMGs, shotguns in both single and double barrel flavours to your long range Bow and Arrow (with an infinitely refilling quiver on a cooldown), angry Hell Rocket Launcher and Revolver and - Dread Templar's BFG - the Infernal Fist that erases everything in its path; disappointment is not a word in this game's dictionary.Graphics are instantly reminiscent of Quake with its crunchy 3D models and textures and brown colour palette in the first Episode, cosmic green skyboxes with a world drenched in purple haze and neon pink ooze in the second Episode - and its incredible closer - and a massive library occupied by phantom clerics wherein - upon interacting with a painting Mario 64-style - it leads to frozen scapes and shipwrecks with ghostly crew still on board in Episode 3.Clever level design with passages and pathways that lead you right where you need to go after you flick a switch or grab a key and side areas that are riddled with enemies and hazards but reward you with much-needed upgrades, though I got lost but those occurences were few and far between.Oh yeah, upgrades. The game has an upgrade system that thankfully does not adhere to the derivative tree scheme and instead opts to ask you to gather Emblems and Blood Gems in order to unlock upgrade slots for your weapons or your person (using Blood Gems) and equipping said Emblems. Be sure to find every secret you can because your benefit will go beyond the simple armour or ammo cache.Music is majestically metal and legitimately the best soundtrack I've heard in a good while courtesy of the much underappreciated PRIMEVAL - who should receive as much recognition as Hulshult does. If you don't know who he is, he has composed the soundtracks to many Doom mods including the immensely enjoyable Ashes 2063 and Ashes Afterglow. I was very impressed with how good performance was, considering how often my laptop gets brought to its knees by even the least graphically potent games. However, bullet time did consistently tank my performance so that remains to be addressed.At the time of writing, there are two complete Episodes with three boss fights, with a third currently in the works. The game is planned to ship with five Episodes. The first level of the third Episode has been released and it's stunning. I was able to finish my first playthrough on Normal difficulty in a little over three and a half hours with some light secret searching. I spent another hour replaying levels to unlock achievements I had left and obtain some upgrades. I saw nearly everything in about five hours.Overall, Dread Templar scratched ever itch I have in a boomer shooter and it's one that you should not skip if you fancy yourself a good Retro FPS. It's a very polished and competent shooter that has barely any bugs even in Early Access and will seldom leave you bemused. The future is looking bright for 1C and T19 and I'm very excited to play every subsequent content update.

_childDocuments_.review: Boring, don't bother.Nothing about this game is interesting or original. Almost all of the levels are visually uninteresting, expect for a couple exceptions.Most engagements start by going into a room or around a bend and getting jumped, then kiting them back around to kill them, just playing round corners; because the AI is super basic. Every enemy aggros instantly, and either runs directly at you, or shoots you as soon as you show your face. If you try to play more aggressive, you just get swarmed with enemies and projectiles, then die, because the dash is on a three second cooldown and there are no other movement options.All of the weapons seemed designed around what this type of game SHOULD have, without any thought for why that's the case. Most weapons have one or two others that do what they do but just better. And when you upgrade them, you can turn most weapons into generalists, so you only have to switch when you run out of ammo.Speaking of upgrades, they currency to get them is only in special secret rooms, but are required to have any fun in the latter third of the game, as every enemy becomes a bullet sponge, or just straight up immune to certain weapons. (Why is the horde enemy immune to rockets? This is not fun.) So you better hope you were getting those early onAlso the bullet-time mechanic. Your meter lasts for about 5 seconds, and refills are sparse. What is the point of this mechanic if you don't want the player to use it?What is the actual core of this game? This is a patchwork of borrowed ideas and sloppy execution that seems to have to underlying spark of creativity or drive.A few more things real quick:- The story segments are just cringe, and the voice acting is bad.- The movement and jumping feel loose and unrefined.- Bad sound design across the board (I've never heard a more flaccid shotgun in my life)- Every retro filter looks like it's bad on purpose. Why even include them?- I've played this for 11 hoursSome good things about the game, the first area is pretty good and the save system is a good idea.Bleh
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a beautiful looking game, I love how the weapons look, how the enemies are designed, the levels look great and there are cool visual effects used everywhere such as waterfalls of sand and strong winds and burning buildings and dense fog and so on. Weapons feel meaty and powerful to use. Soundtrack is solid. Some optional side arenas bring a nice change of pace to the combat based levels. I loved the one where you had to run uphill and dodge giant boulders rolling down. But...   Art alone is not enough to carry a game. The movement feels terrible. There is no acceleration/deceleration curve, you just stop instantly midair when letting go of the arrow keys. Crouching just snaps your camera up/down with zero smoothing. Then there is a slow motion mode that I forgot even exists after the tutorial. Your dash move is always on cooldown when you need it. There is a reason all the platformer games reset your dash cooldown once you land on solid ground instead of putting it on a timer. You can upgrade it but it barely helps.   Speaking of the upgrade system, it's terrible. First you have to find a type of currency on the levels to purchase upgrade slots and then you have to find the upgrade items. The upgrade items are everywhere but the currency is insanely hidden and limited that I only had half the slots unlocked by the end of the game. You end up with tons of upgrades but nowhere to use them. This should be the other way around, everyone should get the slots but only the serious explorers get to choose between the items to put in the slots.   Combat is pretty awful too, you spend half of it reloading because that's fun in a boomer shooter. Enemies have infinite range so they attack you from the other end of the map. The particle effects from enemy attacks stick around for far too long making you wait before you can pass through and engage in combat. A bunch of enemies just jump/charge inside you from behind corners making you get stuck inside their collision, hard to tell if it's by design or a bug? Either way it feels horrible. After combat arenas you'd expect to find healing items and ammo to restock but half the time they just aren't there so you have to be super conservative with your approaches to everything. Good way to kill the pace. Not much fun though. This would be fine if you could quick save/load but that is not the case here, all you have are rare checkpoints and manual save points scattered on the map.    Level design? Invisible walls everywhere. Instakill death pits everywhere. See that ledge over there that looks like leads to a secret area? You jump to it, only to be stopped by an invisible wall and fall to your death. Oh look, a cave entrance? Looks promising. Nah, it's just a fake blocked by an invisible wall. Reward exploration? Nope.   Then we have these annoying cutscenes that you get after pressing buttons that open doors. Very janky and take you out of the game for no reason. I'm not even going to talk about the mediocre story/voice acted cutscenes between the levels...   One final thing, the music goes on full blast 24/7 no matter what is happening on the screen. Are you exploring or fighting? Safe zone or combat zone? Boss fight or trash mobs? Does not matter. Music just does not care or react to anything.

_childDocuments_.review: I am in genuine awe as to what lays before me.Who in their right mind thought it would be a good idea to hide the game’s most interesting and useful upgrades (the one half decent innovation this game has) behind the monotony of scouring its insipid levels for obtuse “super secrets”? Imagine, in a genre all about fast, frenetic action, putting such emphasis on one its most riveting aspects, secret hunting! Yes! The mechanic that is often there to reward observant players with EXTRA (i.e ADDITIONAL) pick ups or easter eggs, is now mandatory! That is of course, unless you’re fine with just playing a mediocre boomer shooter without engaging with its central upgrade mechanic.In addition, these “super secrets” range from obtuse, to stupidly simple. This begs the question, what the hell is even the point? It wouldn’t be such a problem if the game didn’t constantly make it feel as though you’re missing out by not slogging through its levels mashing the use key on every pixel or deciphering poorly worded text box hints.This is only exacerbated by the fact that by embarking on your search for these “super secrets” you are also unwittingly signing up to participate in what I can only assume is part of a new wave MK Ultra experiment. While you slog through these levels searching for these precious upgrades, you will be tortured by what is one of the most appalling soundtracks I’ve had the misfortune of listening to. Generic, flaccid approximations of “metal” infused with, for some ungodly reason, sea shanties and what I swear are samples of “Flight of The Sugar Plum Fairy.” This infernal mix will lay siege to your eardrums with a ceaseless one minute loop on replay from the moment you enter a level until the moment you leave.The kicker here is that the few moments of mercy this game allows you when it finally shuts up after a boss fight and allows it’s ambient sounds to kick in, are actually somewhat atmospheric and pleasant.The upgrade system the game totes and some of its reviewers laud, is one of the only things that it does decently. Even then, it is given far too much credit. I’ve seen mentions of “builds” and i cannot think of a more hilarious way to describe what is an incredibly  bare bones system. You are quite literally slotting in ammo and fire rate upgrades of varying levels. These upgrades seem to stack, which does sort of allow you to equip two fire rate upgrades, for example, which allows you some variety. Thing is, I’m not even entirely certain this works. I’m only hoping it does, because it’s the only semblance of a “build” I can manage. It’s not like the game provides any observable numbers or stats to help fine tune a “build.” As a matter of fact, the game sometimes doesn’t even explain what the hell some upgrades do. What on earth do you mean I’m “luckier” ? Are critical hits a thing? Are critical misses a thing? Is that why some of my shots seem to disappear into the void? Is there a chance the game will uninstall itself and load a good game? This luck upgrade is a GOLD rune by the way, implying it’s one of the big, game changing, must have upgrades.Some of the gold runes do alter your weapons enough to where it’s a bit cool. Pistols turn into infernal pistols with slower ROF and higher damage (wahoo) and your katana become electrified and can stun surrounding enemies for the nano second it takes you to swap to a weapon that doesn’t blow.The only compliment I have for Dread Templar is that the gameplay itself isn’t terrible. It’s decent. It’s a stock standard boomer shooter with an alright bullet time mechanic. It has mediocre enemies, the grand majority of which bum rush you and perform Old School Runescape-esque animations. Other enemies include the average summoner enemy and the “pepper you  from afar” variety. There are some palette swaps introduced as you progress.I can sum up Dread Templar with my very own #dreadtemplarmoment which was solving one of its super secrets and arriving at an amazingly accurate recreation of the Quake difficulty selection room. I was then immediately reminded that I could be playing a much better game.Dreadful indeed.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: It's pretty rough around the edges, but there's a lot of fun to be had for retro-shooter fans! The most important thing I can tell you is that Dread Templar starts off rather weak, and then builds up substantially as you get further. Except for that last episode, that one is a bit of a rush to the end, but it's alright. That penultimate episode is an absolute gauntlet though and I think that's where Dread Templar peaked for me.Once you get enough runes to upgrade your arsenal in various ways, the game becomes a lot of fun. There's a lot of cool upgrades and you can really hone your weapons to how you want to use them. There are some overpowered ones that carried me through the entire game once I've got them though.The game is a tad janky, the animations are very stiff, voice acting isn't good, story.. what story? (no idea what's going on lol), sound effects are fine in general I guess. Music is good, there's definitely some great tracks, it's a bit of a shame that some are repeated for multiple levels, it's one of the quirks I always enjoyed about retro fps's - each level having its own destinct music and theme, but I suppose there simply wasn't the time or budget.Where it lacks in music variety it definitely makes up for in the environment. The level design is all around great and varied, you'll travel through dungeons, cathedrals, hellscapes, mountains or even an egyptian desert. Arsenal is also all-around great, I especially enjoy the Black Bow and some of the hellish variants you can upgrade your basic weapons into. The only weapons I didn't really use is the Katanas and the Trap Launcher. The RPG also kinda fell off for me towards the end, but I can assure you the game is perfectly beatable even when you don't use everything. I didn't even touch the bullet-time mechanic the entire game, as I personally don't find those very fun, but from what I could tell, it seemed to be executed fine in this game.This game will also definitely click for secret and easter eggs hunters - there's a *lot* of those in Dread Templar.------Overall, game's fun, it has its jank, but the core aspects that are fundamental for a retro fps are there, and they're done well. If the animations will ever get improved, then this game would really be elevated to an 8-9/10. For now I'd say it's just about above average. It's not anything we haven't seen before, but it's mostly well made and fun as you get further and further.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar's not , but it isn't good either. There's just too much thrown together in regards to the player's arsenal and skills that combat becomes messy, and it falls apart when combined with the poor enemy and encounter design.There are twelve total weapons, with ten of them available by the start of Chapter 3 (of 5). Add the rune system on top of that, which allows you to modify each weapon or pair of weapons, and you've got a lot of customization. Except it doesn't do much for you. With such a large weapon pool, weapons are bound to overlap in their effectiveness; the Black Bow, Inferno Rocket, and Inferno Revolver all serve the same purpose— hit things from afar. The SMGs, Shotgun, and Super Shotgun are equally useful in close combat, which makes the rune system partially obsolete, as you really have more than enough at your disposal for most encounters. Having too many options isn't an entirely bad thing even if it may make some of the runes obsolete, as long as the encounters are fun. However, on the higher difficulties, you're stuck to either corner peaking far distance enemies or back-peddling close-ranged enemies. This isn't an issue in the first two acts of the game, but it becomes very prevalent in the last three. The health and hitboxes of enemies feel a little off as well, with every flying enemy requiring two shots from the Black Bow, Inferno Rocket, or Inferno Revolver, no matter which runes I use. Head shots, which you can perform with the Black Bow and the Inferno Revolver, don't exist for most enemies, and for large enemies, are either very easy to hit, or very difficult to hit which makes enemies feel like bullet sponges. Secrets are a huge part of Dread Templar and the normal secrets are obtuse at times, too often hidden behind walls with misaligned textures, but the super secrets, hidden in most levels, are way too hidden for the average player. I think I found two or three in my first playthrough while actively searching for them, and with the super secrets rewarding golden runes, it feels like a shame to miss out on the gameplay altering runes. Blood gems, which are used to unlock the slots for runes, are tied to these secrets, so if you aren't an avid secret hunter, you'll end up having a worse experience.The rune system, which is initially interesting, is too dull the majority of the time. There are two types of runes: silver runes, which might increase ammo or damage, and golden runes, which alter how the gun actually feels. Silver runes are useless progression. Wasting blood gems to get to the golden rune slots feels bad because getting 60 more SMG ammo doesn't change the way the game is played. This is only exacerbated with the Inferno Weapons that require more blood gems than normal weapons, and it practically requires you to find the secrets to use the golden runes.Bosses are more of a footnote than anything else, as they're all very easy to beat with circle-strafing. Bullet time feels tacked on as you're not really encouraged to stay in the heat of combat. Music never ends and can feel grating after a while, especially if you're just looking for secrets after clearing a level of enemies.Dread Templar has a lot of minor issues that drag it down, which is a shame, because it's first two chapters, while reminiscent of older shooters, feel really good to play and have solid weapon progression.

_childDocuments_.review: I initially did not recommend this game.  I've left my original review down below.  I opted to give this game another chance and the gameplay was good enough to change my mind, but consider this a thumbs up with a massive asterisks.   However, my initial sentiments were spot on.  This game locks power progression behind secrets, which are often obtuse.  I do not enjoy secret hunting, and ultimately used a guide to find the ones in episode 1-3, giving up around episode 4.  I do believe the time spent was worth it as I had additional upgrade points I would not have had otherwise.  The problem was this was work, not fun.  Really big miss from the developer.  If you are willing to put up with some BS, as well as an incredibly generic episode 1, this game is fun enough.  I played it through on hard.  I did have fun.  Fun that was unnecessarily hampered though.  If the developers make a sequel I would simply suggest remove the secretgating and make more of the same, and you'll have innovated enough. _childDocuments_.review: Generally when you start up a game, it's like planting a seed. You start with something simple(or at least simpler) and then branch out into something more complex. From the start, the mechanics hint at what's going to come, what interesting tools you'll have and what interesting enemies you'll face, what cool potential areas you can run into, the first steps of the plot suggest that some very cool stuff is going to happen later.After half an hour of Dread Templar, what I mostly feel is that I've already seen all the game has to offer, nothing about it seems to suggest that it's ever going to get more complex in any real sense. I run down corridors, enemies go "blargh!" I back off, shoot them while they go blargh and fail to kill me, run forwards again. The art design makes the original Quake's brown tech corridors look exciting. The weapons are generic FPS fare bland enough to make me miss Doom's loadout. As far as I can tell there isn't even locational damage or anything of the sort to spice up combat even slightly.Other Retro shooters, like DUSK and Cultic, have engaged in some of the same heavy metal horror aesthetics, but they brought a lot more of their own to the playing table, their weapons were more satisfying, enemies more interesting and levels more fun. The few times I felt some excitement when playing Dread Templar was when there were actual open areas where the Doomguy levels of fast movement were actually part of the gameplay. Every interior area is just completely wasted.There's some sort of vestigial RPG/upgrade system, but as far as I experienced it, it just gave me extremely vague damage bonuses. The level design also suffers a lot from relapsing into unreality. I understand that this is probably an intentional retro move, but it robs the game of a lot of interest. Most other shooters have areas that feel like real places in some sense, they have a believable size, shape, structure, rooms have purposes other than being brown and filled with gross water. It helps the gameplay because you can predict something about the shapes and sizes, you can perhaps intuit that between room 1 and 2 there ought to be another, secret room or that you can drop down from room 4 to reach room 3 that you had to bypass earlier.That sort of stuff makes secret-hunting fun. It makes you use your brain to find secrets, Dread Templar's secrets are just "here's a brown hole on a brown wall reached by jumping on a brown ledge." There is no satisfaction to finding them, especially since they seem to generally just contain supremely generic pickups.The soundtrack is pretty good, though. I enjoyed listening to it even if nothing else about the experience was particularly motivating.

_childDocuments_.review: A shockingly good boomer shooter considering, i bought this in early access on a whim and didn't expect much more than basic arena action. Dread Templar is fantastic in exploration and level design, finding runes that drastically change the look and feel of your weapons, solving puzzles to super secrets that are both satisfying and rewarding, and the levels themselves are just fun to roam around in. Combat is basic, shoot enemies until they explode into gibs or ragdoll to the ground, nothing extraordinary but the guns feel good, sound ok, and enemies are the right amount of annoying to not push you over board. A criminally underrated gem in the genre, and 100% worth the $20.

_childDocuments_.review: I'M ONLY RECOMMENDING THIS GAME BECAUSE I BELIEVE IT IS A PRODUCT WORTH INVESTING IN.Otherwise i don't think i could recommend this game in its current state. It's fun, fast paced and stylish but has many many flaws. From what I've seen of the game going from open beta to early access the team behind it are working hard and trying to make the best product they can, that's why i think its worth buying the game to support the devs.The things i enjoyed:-Gunplay is nice and responsive-Wide array of weapons to choose from and have fun with-Really good art-style-Interesting and varied levelsI think the thing this game has going for it the most is the really fun gunplay, its super satisfying to pop an enemy with a shotgun blast or lay into a big enemy with loads of uzi shots.The downsides of this game:-2 hours of gameplay for $20aud. (going to be fixed when out of EA)-No option for newgame+, i found this really odd considering that half the stuff i was unlocking for my weapons wouldn't be able to be equipped unless i replayed the campaign twice.-Really annoying final boss. (i understand that a final boss should be difficult but some of the ♥♥♥♥ it throws at you is just cheesy)-Personally i found it hard to manage all the weapons i had, they're all fun and varied but swapping to the right one in the middle of combat i found tough.-The bullet time may as well not be in the game, for how long it takes to charge to full and how little you get to use it when you pop it... there's no point even having it in the game. Needs a big buff.-Easy to get lost if you don't remember the map very well, a map screen would be a nice addition.-It's so hard to tell when you've been hit by an enemy, especially in the final boss fight. Without glancing at my health-bar i wouldn't be able to tell how low or high on HP i am.There's probably more but my short term memory is so bad i can't think of any.The cons far outweigh the pros, but from what i can tell it's definitely a game thats going to get much better with time and love from both the devs and the community playing it. Honestly in it's state rn i'd play it over and over if they added newgame+... thats all i really want, everything else is meh but still a downside.TL;DRno newgame+, game short rn, worth buying to support devs otherwise not worth $20.
