_childDocuments_.review: Yet another boomer shooter in the year of our Lord 2023. I usually enjoy these types of games, but Dread Templar is so bland, so unremarkable, that it may have single-handedly killed my enthusiasm for the genre. There are so many details in the design that scream amateur; enemies spawning behind you and out of your field of vision, weirdly placed pick-ups and checkpoints, and a grating metal soundtrack that never ends. That may be the biggest tip-off that this game is mediocre; the music itself is actually okay, the problem is that there is no semblance of pacing. There is never a moment of reprieve, the drums and guitar are constantly shredding, so you're urged to keep moving at the expense of exploring the various areas. This also makes it harder to tell when the player is in danger, as there is no combat loop to indicate when a fight is about to happen. The bosses are lame and easy compared to the hordes, and the difficulty mostly comes from projectiles that have misleading hit boxes. Explosives don't have proper visual feedback, so I was constantly walking into the blast radius of shots without knowing it. The story is there, and that's all there is to say about. The biggest problem with this game is that it is uninspired. It doesn't take any risks, and that is crucial to a genre such as this. You need to do something that gamers haven't seen before, otherwise I can think of five other, older games that do what Dread Templar does, but better

_childDocuments_.review: What the hell is wrong with these reviews man? "Secret hunting bad", "Enemies react too fast", "This game is just boring". Wtf? Is there some kind of hate campaign for this game? I don't get it.It is a good "boomer shooter" with everything that you would expect from such a game. No it's not some revolutionary masterpiece but does that deserve the mixed reviews? Fk no.Anyway my ranting about people's stupidity aside... The 3 standout things about this game imo is the soundtrack (self-explanatory), the secret hunting and weapons changing appearance based on upgrades.This game has some of the best secret hunting I have seen in a while, with some of them requiring to solve puzzles that are scattered throughout the levels. It was immersive and something that is absent form any other game in the genre I played.Some upgrades for your weapons will drastically change how it functions and will also change how it looks. For example the Frost Banshee shotgun will change it to an icy cannon that will slow enemies or Hellscreams will change your default generic pistols to the hellish ones seen in the cover art which fire enemy piercing projectiles.Some weapons need to be reloaded here. Which would in theory be a dealbreaker for me (I HATED reloading in Prodeus) but.. it's actually not a problem at all. Your main workhorse weapons do not need reloading, only ones that do are pistols, smgs and revolver. Then you can get upgrades for your pistols and smgs to remove that reloading. So the only gun that remains is the revolver which is done for balancing reasons as it by itself is VERY strong.Level design is.. alright. First episode is indeed quite boring but when you get to the end of second one that's when the fun begins. First 2 levels of Episode 3 are my favorites and the music there is the best. It won't compete with Dusk or Amid Evil on level design but it's still acceptable. Especially considering all the lore you will encounter while secret hunting. It's very vague and open but can let you do some speculation on what could happen in a potential sequel.Enemies do offer enough variety. They are generally tankier than enemies found in DUSK and so that means they can corner and overwhelm you if you fight too many of them at once. But if that happens, use your stun gun, you have it for a reason.People saying you cannot beat the game without upgrades are just bad. Yes it will be harder, maybe even a lot harder in some areas but then... turn down the difficulty if you don't want to bother looking for secrets.You see if a game has secret hunting but can easily be beaten without them then.. what's the point of the secrets? You gonna go secret hunting, get way more guns and health than you should and then proceed to beat the game with your eyes closed? Is that what people want?Anyway TLDR. Good game, don't listen to the negative reviews here. They are absolutely moronic.

_childDocuments_.review: There's a bit of an influx of boomer shooters these days. In the last year or so they've flooded steam, to the point where it's closing in on looking like the same trend that brought us millions of side scrolling puzzle platformer pixel art roguelike metroidvanias, where they did less and less innovation and more and more just trying to be the next Hollow Knight, Rogue Legacy, Spelunky, Super Meat Boy etc etc.And Dread Templar seems like it could fall into that trap. Another underworld themed old school fast paced FPS with more modern weapons, fighting hordes of demons and zombies in that classic labyrinthine vertical level design with key hunting and secrets abound.However, not only does Dread Templar do all of these things really well (level design that's fun to navigate and hunt for secrets, visceral gory combat with good feedback, decent soundtrack, great weapons), but it has enough modern fun twists that elevates it from all the, well, Doom Clones.There's actually good melee, there's bullettime, there's dashing, there's upgrades, and weapons have twists to them that are pretty unique and complement the arsenal in fun ways.The upgrade system has some boring stat boosts, but what adds another dimension to it is the last upgrade spot, where if you find golden emblems, they can change how that weapon works and even looks like.The art, visuals, is on point, not too retro, but looks authentic while still crisp and timeless with no clashing elements. The combat feedback consists of a lot of blood flying around, bodies exploding, enemies twitching, the weapons fire in bombastic fashions - And Dread Templar makes the melee feel like actual melee, instead of that annoying usual default in AFPS games where it's basically a pinpoint accurate shortrange infinite ammo pistol, that's frustrating to use when it has a swing animation but only hits things dead center right against your face. Dread Templar feels like you're actually swinging your dual katanas, they hit enemies in a generous area, also at a decent distance, and causes enemies to twitch and falter for a second.The altfire spear throw is just such a fun and unique ability. It pierces multiple enemies, does high damage, it's pretty generous in its hitbox, fodder usually explodes, and the balance seems good in the cooldown and lack of swords for that duration.You have right from the start dual pistols with a high firerate and loud gunshots that send dust and blood flying, you pick up dual SMGs, same deal, a workhorse mid-range shotgun, a great double-barrelled supershotgun, a bow with limited ammo but slowly regenerating arrows, a electric trap launcher that you can still use to launch straight into a crowd for AoE stuns and minor damage, a great rocketlauncher, and some other silly weapons (a Powerful BFG fist that I've seen).It all controls well, feels great to move around dashing and jumping and shooting in bullettime or otherwise.Performance is really, really good for a Unity Engine game. Playing on a 6 year old laptop (i7-4710HQ 2.5GHz, nvidia 840M 2GB VRAM, 12GB RAM, win10x64bit) I played it on my usual lower resolution (960x540, standard for all Unity & UE4 3D games these days for me), but I had 60fps constant in all my time and levels, never once did it dip, absolutely rare for Unity, and I've played a lot of much worse looking unity games with simpler geometry, less effects and worse combat feedback that have struggled to run.So this gets a solid A+ from me even on that department.But I'll probably leave it here for now, maybe return to it later in early access, or wait for release for all episodes to binge through. I'm pretty confident that Dread Templar will turn out great.

_childDocuments_.review: As far as Boomer Shooters go, there are so many better options out there. In my opinion; titles like DUSK, Amid Evil and Ion Fury are so much better than Dread Templar and that has to do with some key issues. First off is the graphics. Now I know this game is supposed to look old, but there is a nice way of doing it and a ugly way to do it and unfortunately, I think Dread Templar looks.. dreadful. This also has to do with the choppy animations that do not line up with attacks. There seems to be no real consistency between artstyle and graphics themselves, something that is very present in the beforementioned boomer shooters.One other big issue is the sound design, or rather a lack thereoff. Enemies have alert sounds, but most of them do not make any noise when they attack or charge you. This is crucial in games where there are big arena's, I would love to know when a enemy is directly behind me. Also, most of the sound effects sound really cheap like they were taken from some free website. The impact of the weapons is therefore reduced, you want to feel like actually fire a killing machine when popping off the Super Shotgun, but it just sounds.. meh. Oh and the soundtrack is very much a Mick Gordon wannabe, just put in 86 guitars, play it very fast and loud and these boomer shooter fanatics will surely eat it up. There is no real sense of atmosphere within the soundtrack and with moments that are sometimes more quiet, it would have been good to have several layers of music move in and out to accomodate the current situation.Then there's the level design, which is clunky at best. I'm at Episode 4 at the moment of writing and gotta say there were some levels I actively disliked playing. I guess the arsenal of weapons also don't really hold up. I find the upgrade system to be pretty convoluded for no reason. Hiding potential crucial upgrades behind secrets is very bad, especially because some of these secrets are very weird in the way you need to find them. As you can tell. Not a big fan of the game and it's a shame, beacuse I do think there are some talented devs behind this. It's just not there in almost all aspects.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has been binging retro shooters recently I picked this game up on a whim, and I just can't get into it. This game feels fairly generic, like it has no vision of itself, as if someone fed all the 90s shooters available into an algorithm and this is what it spat out. If you like Doom/Quake/Blood/Shadow Warrior - play those instead, this game does not add up to the sum of its parts. I would go so far to say that if I didn't know any better I would think this is a  of retro shooters.The gun play is fine, not great but passable, the sword play is great, I like the swords, I like being able to throw the swords and feels rewarding to be able to kill even hard enemies in one throw - everything about the swords is top notch. I don't mind having upgrade systems but it feels quite tacked on. The upgrade system subscribes to the "vertical" upgrade system - do 5% more damage to an enemy, reduce cooldown by 8% etc.  "Oh hell yeah, now I can save 1 shot on each enemy" it all seems rather pointless, allowing the player to do something new would be fantastic, but I suppose that none of the games fed into the machine did that so we can't do that here.Then there's the music,  it is so repetitive and generic that it killed any enjoyment of a level after a single listen. What is worse about it is that Levels 1 & 2  - I said to myself that if Level 3 used it again I would drop the game at that point right then and there, fortunately it was different for that level, still bland and repetitive. Music really is a subjective thing, I get that some people will like this sound, but I personally don't dig it, it takes away from the experience to such an extent that were I to play through it again, I would turn off the music and listen to anything else. I think this is a shame, because buried under some absolutely tone deaf music there is the potential to have some great tension-building ambience and environmental sounds.The visuals are also fairly bland and generic. "Hey kids, did you like Doom, Quake or Blood? Well come check out our game, we have done exactly that again!" - Well maybe not so much Doom. The point is, I feel I've seen them before, but unlike other titles on the market that use familiar aesthetics like Dusk or Graven (another game in early access), this game doesn't try and do anything interesting with its setting, just more uninteresting retroism in lieu of any actual substance.I know it's still in early access and I am hopeful that it will improve at some point during development, but for now I cannot recommend this game.TL;DR: I feel like I've played this game before in almost every other retro shooter available on the market and would not recommend it over almost any other game in the genre without significant improvements. There is a good game buried somewhere in here, but I just can't enjoy it for what it  be.

_childDocuments_.review: This game's textures and animations are very poorly made, which could be overlooked as part of a 'retro' style were they done with care, or if the gameplay were good enough to compensate. The latter is unfortunately not true. The enemy AI is janky and  the difficulty level is ramped up by volume of enemies, rather than their uniqueness. For example, take the 3rd boss fight, which I found to be completely unbeatable playing on nightmare mode (the animations are particularly bad for this boss fight). The boss itself does not move, and allows you to more or less take it down to 2/3 hp without returning damage. It then summons a wave of 5 creeps that can each oneshot you unless you dodge all their shots. This then repeats after killing the first wave. I have played Hotline Miami, and Path of Exile. Occasionally, dying to a boss in a ridiculous way makes the game a better experience, but in this game it is just infuriating. This game is still under development, so perhaps they make some changes, but as of now I would recommend not to buy. Get Dusk instead.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game but I think my biggest gripe is lack of cohesiveness if that's the word. - I mean the UI definitely leaves something to be desired, functionally as well. The UI almost does not exist for me whenever I'm playing the game. It's hectic action and the appearance of it all definitely does not catch your attention on important information. The flash and sound of a skill being up is nice but is not pronounced enough imo and could be portrayed better with the distance between it and the other two skill icons so you can just tell from position, or possibly even design of the flash and sound cue. I don't think the health goes red when you're low and the armor value is always there in the same color with no quick way to see what it's around on the corner of your eye.- There's also stupid superfluous information which is the maximum number a value could be. This is denoted with health and ammo and possibly other elements. The hierarchy of information is just not presented well enough for a game that is meant to be as fast as this game.- I think we can all agree the upgrades menu is really bad but that's not hugeBut other than the UI- The separation of different icons connected to a switch is nonexistent. All that needed to happen is the change up the color but there are separate doors with the same icon in the same area that don't respond to the same switch for no reason. - The AI seems really basic with the only command of "run directly towards the man shooting you"- The information that is presented to the player of the monsters intention is lacking in my opinion- BUT WHY IS THERE NO ANIMATION CANCEL FOR RELOADS? Every single good FPS puts animation cancelling in its game. A game that is fast paced should definitely include it in the game since you'll be running around switching weapons. If there is no animation cancelling on reloads, it could be way simpler to just make the end of the reload have more flair. The double barrel shotgun I say is the worst offender. Partly due to animation cancelling the reload is second nature and also the end of the animation is a slow pull of the barrel upwards instead of a huge snap, like slamming the shells in. Minor things- Quite annoying that you are unable to melee with the katana in throwing mode when you have it, but you can when you threw the katana. This makes breaking boxes and other destructible items an absolute chore to hit if you have katanas in javelin mode. - Why is the second version of the pistols silenced mac-10s. That's the weirdest choice ever. I had fun with the game. The katana javelin feels great, having weapon secondary action being swapping to the weapon that consumes the same ammo is great. The music fits the game. The environments feel an appropriate amount of dreadful. It's just such a shame for me that not being able to reload animation cancel the super shotty and UI shortcomings  is going to lead me to not play this game any further.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is competent, and can be fun. However, it has plenty of issues that are weird for a Boom Shoot, and jsut the overall mechanics are not good enough. For example, bullets come out of the gun, not out of the middle of the screen, which means you can be aiming at something and not hit it. The movement and weapon selection is also weird and clunky. When 95% of the enemies just run at you in a straight line to make you slower when they hit you, and fumbling around your keys to get the revolver and not the rocket launcher that does damage to you too, is far from enjoyable. Lastly, the bigger issue is that the gameplay can be hugely enhanced with runes, however, rune slots and new runes can best be found by finding secrets. If you're not looking for secrets, or cba to find them, the basic runes and limited rune slots are not sufficient to make any changes to the gameplay - thus they dont give you a feeling of power progression. _childDocuments_.review: I don't really play FPS a lot, but I am interested in this genre. Dread Templar picked my interest, so I decided to give it a go. Movement feels good and responsive, guns shoot, music rocks, enemies slay and are being slayed too, retro-style graphics are stylish but detailed enough to contain more... details; power-ups are plenty but the currency you pay for installing those upgrades is not, which is a good thing - it makes you choose between preferred guns and therefore between playstyle. But that's pretty much it. Dread Templar has seeds of a good game scattered here and there, but they did not grow in some memorable and engaging mechanics.The music is just there... it's not a bad music, it's just metal. Metal everywhere. Even when you're just walking with no one in sight. Feels goofy. Save system is weird. I mean, where is autosave? I'm not against having an option to save in different slots but after two hours of playing I started question myself why would I need different slots anyway? It's not like if I find more secrets the ending would change, is it? And why do I need to press several buttons to save in the only slot I use? Too much work for something trivial. Also, sometimes (at least in the first chapters) these checkpoints at which you can save are close to each other which doesn't really makes sense. You can save here or 50 metres away, it won't really matter.The enemies lack some sort of interactivity. Yes, they are different in their attacks, but all you can really do is shoot them. The only reall difference in that sense is target's size and (sometimes) speed. But it honestly looks uninspiring and feels boring to just walk and shoot. Would be cool if some enemies reacted to your arsenal differently depending on what guns you are choosing to use. Because for now it seems like you just need to use weapons that deal more damage. That is until you run out of bullets.Also, explosions. I want to see their impact. But really you don't see the explosion itself, there is no immediate visual responce. Yes, enemies die around some radius, but it's not as satisfying when you actually see fire and smokes. Just a side note.Normally I don't ask for a refund of games I find nice, but for now I'm not in a position when I can buy whatever I want. Right now it cames down to a question whether I should keep Dread Templar or not, and I decide against it simply because I didn't find my limited playtime promising. The only thing I hold against Dread Templar is lack of more nuanced directional and artistic approach. It's just a game. Not bad, not good.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is G.R.E.A.T GREAT.Ive heard some people compare it to shooters such as quake, which it shares only a similar aesthetic in the first chapter, chasm and even duskThe game however, shares only aesthetic similarities and a similar weapon loadout to those gamesThe game is more similar to modern shooters such as doom eternal, as unlike dusk or quake, the movement is alot more deliberate. there is no bhopping or momentum in the movement, However, the game makes up for this with its bullet time mechanic and dash move, both of which force the player to time their movements in response to the current situation or the environment. this means that you dont bhop around insanely fast like a cracked up ♥♥♥♥ but your forced to make deliberate movements in order to succeed.The weapons too are similarly great, weapon switching is heavily encouraged through reload mechanics and a fast swap time, while this may seem ♥♥♥♥♥♥, it encourages the player to make the most out of their loadout and utilize every weapon appropriately. The level design is great, however the first act is quite boring and borrows heavily from quake. The best levels are the latter half of episode 2, and the one episode 3 level playable now is the best, with an awesome aesthetic and great verticality, the level reminded me alot of that one underwater stage from mario 64 with the ships its great.Ultimately, the game is still in early access, however, the mechanics which make it good already exist and the dev is still actively creating the game and its definitely something worth playing for any shooter fan, if you can get past the initial slog of the first 2 levels

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure the developer enjoyed their first time working, and I'm sure they enjoyed the best lunches that welfare can buy. For the studio's first game, this is an ambitious but ultimately annoying entry into the new wave of generic boomer shooters. I'm tired of pretending that the industrial djent-step that Doom 2016 pioneered was ever good, and it's not much better in this game. Hiding so many upgrades and powerups behind secrets is the mark of an amateur, not to mention a telltale sign of a micro penis or some other mental illness charade. The game's cutscenes, which seem to be under the false impression that they're telling some kind of story, are a clear indication as to why it is a bad idea to hire voice actors from fiverr. Main character sounds like the protagonist from Party Hard. Weapons don't tell you what they do when you first pick some up so get ready to fire one as an experiment and load the most recent save. Also no quicksaves, because then you might be in danger of going at your own pace and not starting a six minute segment over and over again until you run out of life and your flesh withers into dust. When are these english-challenged cultured heroes of society going to learn that the pinnacle of video game save formats was perfected with quicksaves and quickloads? Movement speed feels too slow, the dash needs to be removed from all video games, and almost every single enemy type (while unique in design in places) just runs at you with no variation of attack unless you stand perfectly still and let them hit you. Oh yeah, and this game is the reason that Jesus is dead.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a retro, low poly first person action shooter/brawler and spiritually a ripoff of 1990's games like DooM and Daikatana.  However, it's not the 1990's anymore.  Oops.  While the game is well optimised, it's incomplete and unfinished.  There's a slew of issues here that gamers should be warned about. The game has been in Early Access since 2021 and while it's still getting updates, it's deep in Development Hell.  There's no reasonable expectation that this will ever be completed, as the game is now nearing the developers promised deadline to complete the game, but is far from finished.  Whether the developer lacks the time, funds, or skill/talent required to complete a video game isn't really something gamers should be expected to accept as an excuse.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets and low resolution textures, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the 1990s.  It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Unethically, the developer sold keys to this abandoned Early Access game into cheap, nasty game bundles, where they knew it would be advertised and sold as a complete game.  This seems to have been done in an attempt to mislead gamers into buying a knowingly faulty, defective and incomplete product.  When a developer does this for a game they have zero practical intention of completing, this is essentially a scam, an intention to get paid for a broken/unfinished product.  Often this is done as an exit strategy, as the developer takes the money and runs.  No refunds have been given, the developer kept all the money they took from gamers.The developer has used a number of Unity assets for the game, which in itself is certainly no crime, but they fail to acknowledge the use of the work of others in this game.  Claiming the work of others as your own, failing to properly advise gamers and credit those who did the actual work for this game is highly unethical.Dread Templar has a laughable, eye watering price of $15 USD (for an incomplete game!), for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games, let alone the sheer number of free games available on Steam.  Given the defects and shortcomings, it's impossible to recommend this.  If you want a good, frenetic action shooter, try the Doom reboots (available cheaper than this unfinished game).

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a game of mixed quality. The levels in episodes 1 and 2 are great, while in 3, 4 and 5 they vary from good to borderland terrible.  The devs could easily have cut 70 - 80% of the maps in episodes 3-5 and combined the remaining maps into a longer great final episode.The weapons are similarly mixed, there's lots of them and they're quite varied but in order to make most of these guns even remotely viable in the later episodes you need to upgrade them.  This is a fine system on paper, the problem is that most of the really good upgrades are hidden behind incredibly obscure secrets, as in borderline impossible to locate without a guide obscure.  I did my 1st playthrough on hell difficulty with a guide open to find all these secrets and with the loot and upgrades from these the game generally felt very well balanced.  If I didn't have the guide open I guarantee my guns would have hitting like wet noodles and I'd constantly be on the verge of dying from the lack of heals and ammo.  It's a strange choice balancing your highest difficulties around locating secrets.Another choice I don't understand is the lack of quick saves, quick save/quick load spam is a key part of any good boomer-shooter, Cultic, Doom, Dusk, Ion Fury all great games and each allows you to save anywhere to your hearts content.It's not all bad, some of the levels are very good, the ability to freely change your weapon and character upgrades at any upgrade alter is great, the boss fights are surprisingly good for an fps.  Though I did end up using only 3 main weapons for most of the later episodes every weapon except maybe the trap launcher along with the alternative RPG and Infernal Gauntlets all fill a niche use.  I was having to swap weapons frequently to deal with different enemies which helped keep the game engaging.7/10, Dread Templar is absolutely not a bad game but it does suffer from the overall quality declining the further through the campaign you go and a couple of questionable design choices hindering player enjoyment.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, here we go again...First, the negative:Many gameplay basics are off. Hitboxes don't work well, you miss enemies clearly in your crosshair, or get hit though the enemy clearly missed. Enemies attack you through walls.Often enemies spawn in your back or on top of you, leading to dumb, unfair situations.Lots of backtracking through the whole level, trying to figure out where to go next.Many of the weapons feel useless, I usesd almost exclusively the Pumpgun, which is OP.No real ranges of attacks, leading to pixel sized sniper fights vs enemies across the map. Oh, there is no sniper weapon - Pumpgun will do though.Weapon switching feels fiddly and unresponsive.And the game is ugly as sin. I am tired of excusing bad graphics with "D'uh - retro". Its not 97 anymore and while I get the Quake 1 inspiration, this just doesn't cut it anymore.So, seems to be quite terrible? Yes and no.I had a lot of fun in the first few levels, then it started to get tedious. And beggars can't be choosers, in a huge flood of god awful boomer shooters, this one isn't that bad. It never reaches the greatness of games like Quake 2, especially in the modernized version, but there are many far worse games out there.It has some neat ideas, the upgrade system is ok. The whole gameplay is fast and furious, stafe - boom, strafe - boom. In the moments it works, it works very well.And the soundtrack kicks a lot of ass.Solid 6,5/10, play if you really loved Quake 1 and need something similar.

_childDocuments_.review: Boomer shooter with katana, bow and guns and many secrets. This game is decent personified. It does more or less everything okay at the very least. The graphics are what you expect from a modern boomer shooter. You have nice variety of weapons, but since you can upgrade them you might just end up using a few anyways. Multiple different enemy type, some more annoying than others. The story is a bit confusing, but in these type of games it is not that important anyway. You shoot stuff and move through places. The levels are varied, but at the same time not really that different. Every level has many secrets that give loot, armor or new upgrades for your weapons. This is a difficult game to recommend. It is just an average game. Some games have to be average too. You can't have just great games and bad games. It is impossible to not compare it to DUSK, but Dread Templar lacks the soul and feel of movement that made DUSK great. Though I don't regret playing this game, I wouldn' recommend it to everybody. If you are on a boomer shooter binge and have played everything else, then this might be good enough for you.TL;DR: Average boomer shooter with some good ideas and decent metal music. I recommend that you buy this on sale and that you have to enjoy boomer shooters more than the average person. This is not a bad game, it is just not great.

_childDocuments_.review: Quick Summary: Dread Templar is a game that starts out strong but gets relatively stale around the halfway point. I'd give it a 6/10, it's far from a terrible game but leaves a lot to be desired. I would only recommend this game if you've already played the amazing "boomer shooters" on this platform and are looking for something new and want to pick it up on sale. Full Summary: Dread Templar's first two episodes are pretty well-done, the levels are enjoyable and the enemy placement is good. There are also enough supplies to comfortably get through them on the higher difficulties. Unfortunately, the level design for episodes 3-5 is varied, but I mostly didn't like them. A mixture of boring areas, increasingly confusing secrets, and seemingly unfinished levels really hindered my enjoyment of the levels in the latter half of the game. This is a game that basically requires secret hunting, so I'd spend 30-50 minutes in each level to find skill points and upgrades for your character and arsenal. I would recommend using one of the guides on here if you plan on playing at all, you'll need them. In the third episode onward, there were tons of invisible walls in levels that hindered exploration for secrets and even some unfinished environments. It feels like they forgot to do certain things, like notify the player when they're about to leave the level or switches no longer playing cutscenes showing when a door or area is opened (the first two episodes featured this prominently). Also, the levels seem to have either too much or too little ammo and health, no in-between.The upgrade system seems kinda forced. You find silver and gold medals to upgrade your character and weapons, allowing two silver medals and one gold medal. For whatever reason, the descriptions for the upgrades aren't clear; if I get a medal that increases damage, it doesn't say how much damage is increased by.The weapons are interesting and pretty varied which makes it all the more disappointing realizing how spongy the enemies are from episode 3 onward. By the end of the game, I found myself using the revolver that can sometimes one-shot with a gold medal upgrade just to clear the hordes of bulky enemies as fast as I could. It's disappointing since there are some pretty cool weapons that are made obsolete by how annoying it is to kill enemies.The enemy design is mostly interesting, but most of the combat in this game consists of walking backwards while melee enemies try to hit you and ranged enemies walk around until they can shoot you. There are a lot of enemies in this game and the levels usually put them to good use, but the enemies introduced in episode 3 and 4 are very bulky and annoying to deal with, especially the flaming dog things that shoot you on sight.There's also a tower defense mode, but I didn't play it all that much. More of the same, but your upgrades and weapons from the campaign are basically required. The music is alright with some good tracks, but it'll loop a lot if you're looking for all the secrets, with most tracks being about 2-4 minutes. Tracks are also used in multiple levels, usually back-to-back.Overall, the game took me 17 hours to get 100% achievements on, but cheats can be used to speed things up a bit. I hope my review is helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: Old school vibes with some new flavor.  You will recognize some of what I will assume are the games that gave the devs their inspiration.  You can tell they took the love of the old school games and added cool weapon ideas and a sort of balancing act in the skill tree.  Want to focus heavy on shotguns?  Go for it and when that doesn't suit the level re-balance your character traits and try again.  Weapons you think might be kind of pointless at first have a strength that you have to experiment to find.  Combos of tech, abilities and weapons may take the creature down faster.  It is fun to get faster at switching weapons in the heat of the moment.  I think my favorite part is the secret areas.  It takes me back to the old Spear of Destiny days and the game even takes time to make fun of its self for having so many secrets.  Even if you missed the games back in the day or maybe you weren't even alive when they came out I think there is enough here to keep most shooter fans happy.  Just when you think you are figuring out the enemies they know when to stick a grenade in your shorts.  Happy hunting oh and by the way the cool pistols on the game banner are in the game a little later.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, but with caveats. I'm being generous here after having seen the ending credits and seeing that pretty much everything was done by one guy; with that in mind, it deserves a bit more appreciation. Still, there are issues:-Chapters 1 and 2 are pretty decent. Chapter 3 falls off towards the second half. Chapter 4 was really really rough. Chapter 5 was fine. Overall, the levels would come to like a 7/10 overall-Secrets are neat, and the upgrade system allows a bit of building, but the game is balanced around secret hunting which was rough, especially when levels can be 10 minutes long sometimes, but secret hunting drags them out to 30-40 minutes of backtracking and looking around.-The game doesn't really innovate on the genre; it's kind of just more of the usual retro shooter fare. In 2018/2019 I would've been fine with this, but having played games like Cultic and Turbo Overkill, I'm now looking for a bit more from games in this genre.Overall, a 7-ish seems fair, and on that mark I did enjoy a good chunk of the gameplay. Pick this one up on sale if you don't mind the caveats above, since it's a net positive time overall.

_childDocuments_.review: This was bought for me as a Christmas present and recently finished it, so I can thank my friend for gifting this to me; I genuinely did enjoy my time playing it until the final episode.Dread Templar is a good game and satisfies that itch for a quick bloodbath, but it does suffer a few issues. The music is good, composed by a guy called John S. Weekley, and fits the game rather well; if you plan to just blaze through the campaign. The music can get a bit much when you stop to secret hunt like I did, though. The sound is good enough, but one or two weapons sound a little lacklustre, like the rocket launcher.The gameplay and gunplay are quite fun and has some variety to it as well as a bullet time mechanic. You get upgrades you can make to each weapon which you can swap around to find what suits you. These upgrades are fairly heavily locked behind secrets, however, which does give you some incentive you explore but are very well hidden and are many. There are a lot of different enemies allowing for some varied encounters and quick target prioritisation. The game also has things it calls "side-areas" which are a nice little addition and meant to be a little harder, early ones introduce tougher enemies sooner, while later ones are more gimmicks and/or platforming.Now for my complaints. While the enemy has variety it lacks in intelligence, most will just beeline for you and if the ranged enemies start attacking when behind cover, their shots may go through that cover. The bosses are too easy in all honesty; my deaths to them being my own stupidity. The last complaint I have is with episode five of the campaign, E5M1 is fine, but the last two maps before the final boss just weren't up to the standard of the rest of the game.I wish the best of luck to the developer for future endeavours and hope they do make more.

_childDocuments_.review: A cool game with a ♥♥♥♥-ton of issues.I found myself enjoying the game during my second attempt at finishing it (the first one lasted about 30 minutes due to the first levels being rather uninspiring). Generally its shooting is nice, the weapons feel appropriately punchy and the feedback (animations and gibs) are satisfying. The movement is a bit boring, but since the levels are typically small it does not hinder the experience all that much. The idea behind the throwing sword and the bow is cool as well as they can be easily incorporated in-between combos.The upgrade system is an interesting idea that is, in my opinion, botched by the way said upgrades are acquired, that being my finding secrets. Although some upgrades can be found on a few levels, many of the golden tokens which change weapons in a more substantive way seem to be exclusive and can be easily missed without a guide. This destroys the idea of player expression as a fun gun type can be accidentally omitted and many can be found in the later levels making them obsolete by the time they are acquired. A more fitting system, I think, would be to use the tokens to buy a given upgrade which would actually allow players to choose the options they see as the most fitting.That being said there are some baffling design choices that do, actually, hinder said experience. The save system is just unpleasant to use (why can't I simply interact with the crystal to create a quick save?) and feels like a more convoluted and less balanced checkpoint system. The aforementioned save crystals can be very close to each other and because of their placement they encourage save scumming which leads to another issue - the music. The music is fine. Great, even. Too bad almost every track is used twice in a row, making them overstay their welcome. Because there is no dynamic music in the game, the player's ears are being bombarded with blast beats during 15 minutes-long secret huntings which gets irritating fast. Not only that, but when the game loads the song starts from the beginning which furthermore adds to the auditory tedium. Also, weapons reset as well which results in the need to readjust each weapons after every respawn (especially the sword as it is not ready to be thrown without a semi-lengthy (in combat, at least) animation, cool).The levels? Usually fine, sometimes bland, other times fun and creative. Their creativity shines the most when they diverge from the generic FPS levels (frozen caves with ghost pirate ships are my favourites from the bunch). The secrets, however, are rather cheap. Many of them rely on wall-humping (yes, the wall textures differ slightly, but it is often hard if not impossible to notice) and the way the player interacts with them can be rage-inducing - especially when there is no feedback after using a wall or a button or if the interaction area is very small and a wall I used just did not open and lead me to believe that there was no secret there (thank god for the guides). I also got stuck twice and had to reload the save. Many enemies are also annoying. I especially hate the flaming rabbit-looking ass which is unnecessarily tanky and its projectile is barely visible while hitting like a truck (it is a common issue with projectiles in this game - they tend to blend with the environment). I often felt like I was playing Doom 3 again - after being hit by a corner-peeking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for the 10th time (ranged enemies tend to attack too early after going around corners which also sucks and creates unfun combat scenarios) I had to adapt and abuse the AI in order to scrape by (the health pickups on the Hell difficulty are way too scarce IMO).And you know what? Despite all of these issues I completed the game, had fun, and I am willing to finish it again on the Nightmare difficulty (because the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ achievements for finishing the game on Hell and Nightmare cannot be unlocked by doing the latter, thanks). Do I recommend the game? Yes, but only if one is ready to endure some amateurish design and, dare I say, jank.Oh, and the Defender Mode is fine, too. It's way too cramped and easy, but it's a fun treat nonetheless.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary:A fun, fast paced FPS that combines elements of Quake, Blood and FEAR to good results. Dread Templar has a well-judged difficulty curve despite being a challenging game, meaning you're unlikely to give up even in the hardest areas. There's a decent plot and some interesting puzzles, all handled in a way that doesn't slow the pace of the combat or disconnect you from the game.Cons:- Some weapons are too weak to use effectively even after extensive upgrading- Upgrading and time-slowing systems feel a bit superfluous- Doom 3 style enemy spawns can make the game very trial and error at timesNeutral:- Most secrets are embedded in complex puzzles that are easy to miss and sometimes very hard to figure out- Game doesn't seem to pause when saving, which can lead to cheap deaths if you're rushing to save e.g at one point I thought I'd cleared an area, saved, and on exiting save I got blown up by a straggling kamikaze that had flown right up to me while I was saving.- Frequent use of invisible walls and imaginary boundaries can make exploration confusing at times. Again can also result in sudden death via you falling through spaces you thought you could walk over because they look the same as others.Pros:- Brilliant synth metal soundtrack and gothic/eldritch horror atmosphere.- Combat is smooth, fun and incredibly satisfying when you start to nail it.- Encourages you to approach battles strategically and pick the right weapon for each job, leading to extra satisfaction when you figure a strategy out, and an overall feel that the game is never a slugfest- Very well judged difficulty curve with no real spikes or walls to come up against, that gradually ups the challenge firmly but fairly throughout the game.- Literally tons of contentConclusion:Dread Templar is a rapid fire eldritch horror FPS that provides a stiff but fair challenge across a very large game. It makes you approach combat thoughtfully and gives you lots of different strategic options. Although the time-slow and RPG aspects feel tagged-on at times, the game gives you control of how you play and which parts of your arsenal you focus on, and as such each player can mould their own playstyle. With 5 very large episodes and multiple side areas and secrets, there is absolutely tons to do, and plenty of reason to return to the game after completing it. Add to this the fact that the game performs smoothly like butter, and Dread Templar is worth everyone giving a try, you're sure to find something you like regardless of your gaming preferences.

_childDocuments_.review: For the most part, I had fun. The upgrade system was interesting, and most of the levels looked cool and the overall aesthetic was good. That said, some of the gameplay leaned towards being a bit frustrating (lots of bullet sponges that move faster than you do, lots of enemies that fire the instant they see you, some giant lads popping out of boulders in the 3rd episode). I felt that the earlier levels were stronger than the later ones, as interesting layouts gave way to wide open spaces full of large groups of enemies. But, weapons were fun to use (I liked the bow) and some of the upgrades made the spongier enemies late-game easier to deal with.Some of the secrets were interesting and fun to track down, though they seemed to become more sparse late-game (or perhaps, way better hidden). And there were a few interesting levels I really enjoyed, though again, most of my favourites were early-game. Another comment I have is, the player movement felt a bit too slow. Though, it's possible it felt slow because many of the late-game enemies move faster than you do.All that said, it was made by a _very_ small team (end credits all fit on one screen!). For what it is, and as someone who likes the genre even when it's a bit janky, I enjoyed it. It's no DUSK, but it doesn't have to be. If you like the genre and can forgive a few rough edges, I'd say it's worth picking up.

_childDocuments_.review: Can't be arsed to complete. Beautiful environments and weapons. Well designed overall. There are two big problems with the gameplay. _childDocuments_.review: I knew this was going to be a faster paced boomer shooter, as movement abilities looked to be emphasized here, but I had no idea how different from the norm this would end up being. If I had to find a comparison point to put it against, it really reminded me of Quake, but faster. Enemies don't die quickly and they feel like they are placed in such a hateful way. It's a struggle of a game, but at the same time, a true joy. The underlying gameplay is fantastic, it just so happens that it is a really difficult game. I really enjoyed that aspect of it actually once I got used to what was to await. The game does a lot different so it's worth breaking down each aspect that really shined for me. While initially I didn't find the upgrade system to be very interesting, it really grew on me as time went on. The gold tier unlocks actually can drastically change how you are playing the game and layering on silver upgrades to help boost that ends up being a fun discovery process. The secrets are actually pretty challenging to find, so you are not always able to find every upgrade the first time you go through a level, so there is a replay value there to try to figure that out. The other aspect I want to call out is the levels. Each episode has a dramatically different theme and a different feel to how they are traversed. There are layers to some of the levels that help boost the overall immersion of playing the game. Some feel like the typical slog (that isn't necessarily a bad thing) while others feel more like a build engine influence. It's a fun balance to keep things fresh for what ended up being a longer game than I was expecting.

But its when your complaints are small and clearly identifiable, that you know they've nailed the important stuff.TLDR: It scratches that doom itch, if you've recently contracted it!

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar: the perfect case of ''I wish there was a 'mixed' button in steam's reviews.Basically, the game is.... fine. Yup that 's it. It's enjoyable in a discreet way, but... I don't know. This is my first time reviewing a game that, in paper, ''should' be good, astonishing even, but in reality... is mediocre (but still, perfectly enjoyable.I gave it a little thought and I believe is this : the game tries to 'put' a lot of mechanics (not just fighting ones) together and, for that, doesn't achieve greatness in any of them.Case in point? gun play: weapon feel... weak, but you can upgrade them... only that doesn't seem to improve that much (maybe the third upgrade, but even that feels like a reskin in some cases). Or what about level design: maps are big but convoluted, with a lot of secret hunting (my favorite thing to do in a boomer shooter). Problems? welp, maps are big but empty, convoluted but they look all the same: add that to the almost boring gunplay, junky enemies, 'woobly' performance, a story that has no bite (and a little bit too edgy without being fun), Doom 2016 wannabe soundtracks that are repeated for most levels and not that great (srly, people. Boomer shooter doesn't mean rock blasted into you ear, it must follow the pace... speaking of...), an unsteady pace, graphics that could be good but wasted in uninspired scenarios...welp, I'm not that eager to search for any secrets (and some of them are really well designed).... or to finished the game....Ok, after all my ranting, why the thumbs up?Because the game has been done with some ''love'' for the genre, it's almost undeniable, but it tries to hard to unite things without really knowing how. Anyhow, I believe in supporting such developers and hoping their next game will be.... better. (And, again, the game is enjoyable, and if discounted, it is recommended).

_childDocuments_.review: Now that Dread Templar is fully out of early access I can wholeheartedly recommend this title. It's a boomer shooter so expect the usual, fast movement speed, dash move, fixed health and armour, a full roster of weapons to choose between and a slow-mo bullet time mode. There are plenty of secrets hidden in each level, the finding of which is immensely fun and rewarding. There are more often than not, side rooms containing extra challenges in either combat or platforming, but mostly combat. There is a robust upgrade system that doesn't unlock static skills or abilities, but allows you to unlock slots under specific weapons and you find runes that have enhancements to those weapons. You can swap these runes around at certain points in levels and allows you to mix and match for your playstyle. The level design is great in most levels, a few are a little lacking or sometimes lack a little direction but these are rare cases, most levels flow nicely together and are often expertly laid out so you revisit areas previously locked off helping you gain a stronger understanding of the level. The weapons are good, have decent feedback and all pretty fun to use. As the difficulty climbed I found even the weakest of the guns useful in certain situations I was often stuck in. Specifically referring to the trap launcher that helps you stun enemies for a few scant seconds to help give you some breathing room. While most enemies are programmed to bum rush the player, having added effects like some enemies slow you on hit or others that are immune to rocket damage help to make the lineup of creatures varied and fun. I often found myself reaching a new room full of enemies and taking a quick second to analyse the best one to focus on first instead of just mindlessly circle strafing until everything died. Boss fights are a little underwhelming but this is a boomer shooter so that is to be expected. The story feels like it was ripped straight out of an edgy 14 year old boy's notebook, this is a good thing. It's light on details, doesn't bog things down and is just plain stupid fun. If you're a fan of boomer shooters or curious to see what they're like, this is hardly a bad place to start. Fans of these shooters can expect to find a ton of fun and cheeky references to past titles like Blood and Quake.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar, a game that seems to receive a rather mixed feeling from those who have played it.It's a little difficult to describe, on the one hand, those stating the game is mediocre aren't exactly wrong, but to consider it bad because of mediocrity would be unfairly judging it.Everything Dread Templar does, it does right, from the pulsepounding metal soundtrack, the sound effects, the guns, the enemy variety, the visuals, level designs, it's all exactly what you could want from a retro-fps.  There's nothing particular that stands out about it, but that's ok, because if the worst thing that could be said about it is that it feels like every other retro-fps, then that means it's a very fun and enjoyable experience that you'll slip in to like a comfy pair of pants and have a blast with.Since buying it in early access, and playing it in to full release, I've been having a lot of fun with it, dashing around blasting bad guys, finding secrets and playing around with the upgrade system.  It feels a lot like Dusk, but with a hellscape level design instead of a boondock village, with blade wielding demons in place of chainsaw hillbillys.  If you like Dusk, this is more of the same in a different skin, and given how immensely successful Dusk is, that's pretty high praise.  Bonus praise has to be given to the soundtrack, which really amps up the frantic shooting and dodging with it's heavy guitar riffs and thumping drumbeats.  It's a great example of a retro-fps being what a retro-fps should be, and well worth the low price it's being sold at.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: A retro-inspired FPS that struggles to set itself apart from other games in the genre, but still manages to deliver good quality gameplay through a solid upgrade system, weapon switching combat akin to Doom Eternal and a great metal soundtrack. The base movement speed feels like speedrunning Quake without any of the cool tricks, but it's ok once you get used to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best modern boomer shooters I've played.There's enough variety and good balance in weapons and enemies. Level design is good and there's not much need for wandering around unless you're trying to find all hidden content. Bullet time feels strong enough but isn't too OP. Overall there really isn't anything to complain about.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Many enemies in Dread Templar are as fast or faster than the player, which seems designed around a slow-mo meter mechanic that simply builds up too slowly and drains too quickly. Each episode swaps out its enemies for a new set of equally bad ones -- some choice enemies include ones that are both faster than you  slow you down if they get too close, enemies that immediately create a fart cloud as soon as they see you and snipe you from inside it to make themselves impossible to hit, and enemies that are straight up immune to explosive damage and come at you in swarms when you would most want to use explosives on them.Since the vast majority of combat encounters in Dread Templar are fast swarming enemies coming at you from the other end of a long corridor (along with some snipers in the back), the first guns to come out are generally the single shot accurate high-damage weapons like the bow, inferno revolver, and explosives (which is funny when the game introduces the enemies that are immune to explosive damage, meaning you have one less tool to deal with them). Once enemies get close enough, the next weapon to come out is the trap launcher, to avoid getting swarmed, and maybe some slow-mo (if you even have any). When every combat encounter plays out the same way, every combat encounter feels like the same combat encounter.Dread Templar has maybe 1-2 music tracks per episode and loops them throughout entire levels, back-to-back, without breaks. These tracks are 100% energy all the time. This means you're listening to the same high-energy metal for up to 2 hours at a time. Worse still, some level ambiance is tonal and not in the same key as the background music. At one point, I simply turned the music off and played in silence.Later in the game, I got an upgrade that turned my SMGs into hand-held miniguns that chew through ammo but absolutely obliterate enemies. This is cool, but I realized I was running into the Doom 2016 problem: a self-perpetuating upgrade system in lieu of good encounter design built around a well rounded roster of weapons. Every combat encounter in Dread Templar is a chaotic mess designed to be dealt with by an upgrade system that didn't need to exist. At the very least, the upgrade system in Dread Templar makes secret hunting feel very rewarding.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:-Tight, fast, exciting gunplay!-Environments are varied and really weird, very fun to explore-Great variety of guns to find and upgrade-This game's version of "BFG" feels awesome to use-Wide variety of enemies to fightCons:-Secrets are both a pro and con. They are fun to find, but you won't ever find them all by yourself. You will need to alt+tab every few minutes to see where the next one is. It's honestly kind of annoying, but also a central part of the game.-Normal difficulty is too easy-Soundtrack is appropriate and fits the theme well, but can get a bit repetitive after about 20 minutes into a level. I also don't particularly enjoy metal type of music-Story is pretty surface level. Not much to it.I haven't had this much fun since Amid Evil! This game gave me a much needed break from Apex legends.  Overall great retro shooter with exotic, interesting environments. Strong recommend to anyone who enjoys shooters. Give it a shot!

_childDocuments_.review: It’s a surprisingly good throwback shooter! I acquired it back when the game was still in EA and decided that I won’t touch it until its full release. And boy, the wait was worth it, because playing it from start to finish in a matter of few days was a great experience. In terms of the oldschool gameplay, the basic but satisfying shooting is there along with the mid-90s era graphics and all provide a very good reminiscence of the good old days, plus it being coupled with a plethora of weapons to choose from and additional unlockable skills only adds to the already rewarding experience.However, the biggest downfall for me is the lack of better weapon switching mechanics for mouse + keyboard, as in the brink of the moment with lots of enemies on screen you want to utilise the weaponry as best as possible, but doing that while there’s a lot of stuff going on screen and with constant movement it’s hard to swiftly select the best weapon for the current situation – a perfect solution would be adapting the weapon wheel for all control devices or providing a better graphical indication of what’s currently chosen. Maybe in future patches?Nevertheless, what matters the most is already there and it’s a must for anyone wanting some old-fashioned shooting with an additional skills progression.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Pro:+ The movement is fantastic, commands are responsive and tight+ Very good weapon roster that gets even better with upgrades+ Very well designed roster of enemies, each of them stays relevant for the entire game and along with your weapons it allows for different approach for each fight+ Very good level design, the game does nto shy away from variety in its levels, from confined prisons to large eldricht vistas+ Fantastic soundtrack, each one its a bangerCons:- While the art direction is fine, even great in some point, of all the recent boomer shooter this is the first one that feels 'ugly' too look at, might be personal preference but it feel more rough than something like Dusk with which it shares the minimalistic visual style- Some jank like very prominent invisible walls in some of the later chapters maps and enemies clipping into the walls while strafing or jumping- Overdose of secrets, while secrets are an amazing addition to any fps, Dread Templar sort of overindulges in it and when most of your level have 10+ secrets you simply stop caring searching for them, especially some are quite obtuseDread Templar is a very competently made boomer shooter with fantastic moment to moment gameplay that will keep you entertained for 10 to 15 hours depending on your difficulty of choice (i played at Hard) and if you want to find every single upgrade in the game. That being said if you are player new to the boomer shooter genre there are more polished and suitable title to try before this (Prodeus\Amid Evil\Dusk\Ion Fury) but if you are a lover of the genre it is surely a game worthy to stay in your collection.Recommended with 7/10

_childDocuments_.review: All in all the game is pretty good. The gunplay is rewarding and incentivises you to switch around and try out different strategies. I like the weapon switching with the Serious Sam style choosing of weapons. one thing I'd like to see is that you always switch to the same weapon. I.e when pressing 3 i always switch to the double barreled one instead of the last one I used. Also the final Boss feels somewhat underwhelming. After collecting most gold runes I was pretty decked out and the final boss felt more like a push-over. And the story and the "cutscenes" are a bit to phoned in, like the mic quality seems low. Graphicaly speaking the game tries to go for a late 90's early 00's look, which honestly has been done to death. Some of the environments could look gorgeos with a bit more interesting lighting and more varying texture work. So all in all a good shooter with a really cool upgrade system and good mechanics but like most of these quake and doom like shooters lack in the graphical department and the presentation (although the music is truly good). One thing missing are more ambient tracks for when the player is looking for secrets.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Templar is a very enjoyable boomer shooter that doesn't quite reach the heights of the modern genre greats from past few years due to some design decisions and other minor flaws that hold it back, but it is definitely worth playing especially if you are a fan of the genre.Weapons feel satisfying, there is a good amount of weapon variety and every weapon (or weapon type in some cases) comes with some amount of customization that lets you tailor your arsenal to suit your playstyle. While I loved the idea of the customization its progression was perhaps too closely tied to finding secrets in the levels as instead of making you feel like you are rewarded for the optional exploration or discovery, it instead turns exploration in to a sort of mandatory part of the game which hurts the overall flow and pacing.This is in part due to the level design which is probably the weakest aspect of the game, not due to the structure of the levels themselves but because of the lack of visual clarity which is in part due to the visual fidelity of the textures and in part because the game doesn't really do a good job of utilizing typical level design tricks that subconsciously point the players attention where it needs to be. There were quite a few occasions where some of this result in breaking the flow of the game and especially when combined with seeking out secrets it sometimes really brought the pace to a halt.Soundtrack is excellent and generally goes pretty hard, which is something I enjoyed a lot and felt like it works really well as long as you maintain that steady flow of advancing ahead mixed together with a steady intake of fights. However the moment that the gameplay flow gets interrupted be it due to looking for secrets, not figuring out how to advance in the map or even using the manual save points (more auto-saves or a quick-save function would do so much for maintaining the pace) - it can become repetitive, as your attention gets more directed to the music while the gameplay is not keeping you fully engaged.That being said, despite its flaws I had a blast with Dread Templar and found this one to be an easy recommendation especially for the fans of the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: The game's opening levels and music are *fine* but likely won't impress you much - then the game gets better and better as you move away from Episode 1.Great music, great level design (although a bit too many invisible walls to my liking) and engaging gameplay.This is one of the better titles that the retroFPS revival has spawned. Awesome stuff!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome boomer shooter, with some nitpicks.The great:* Awesome weapon variety. Most weapons have 2 variants (think pump shotgun/double barrelled, or dual pistols/dual uzis). * Great upgrade tree/tier system. Incremental upgrades for each weapon category(pair) for things like damage/ammo, then gold(ultimate) upgrades that can change the weapon playstyle completely (pump shotgun to freezing shotgun for setting up combos)* Solid headbanging music* Level design and overall aesthetic is great. You start slow with swamps and catacombs, then you are steppign through paintings into a frozen cave helping a ghost pirate captain, then in a hellish floating cathedral/castle* A ton of secrets, and super secrets that reward puzzle solving and sometimes knowledge of retro shooters.The good:* Enemy variety is very solid, and their patterns a fairly predictable, so very little that's unfair. Only complaint is sometimes they spawn behind you (rare), and that the relies on recolors, which do admittedly do different things... but a sprinkling of 4-5 more across E2-E4 would solve it* Difficulty seems well balanced too. You have your standard easy-normal-hard-hell(very hard), then a secret Nightmare difficulty if you really want it. The lower levels scale damage down, but the higher levels make health packs spawn less, finally limiting them to only secret areas. This is fine... but I'm playing on Hell, and while I play a ton of these, I am generally flooded with ammo. Scaling ammo drop rates down a touch on Hell E3-E5 would be good, and would force me to swap to new weapons more, and change up my strategy, rather than relying on the same combos.The neutral:* Secrets, progression and upgrades. Seemingly 90% of your upgrades are found inside secret areas. Harder to find secrets can have gold upgrades(special weapon variants/abilities) and Super secrets that have puzzles attached which always have gold upgrades and sometimes new weapons, earlier than you would otherwise get them. This is fine for me because I like to secret hunt, but if you don't enjoy that, it will hurt your playthrough a lot.The not so good:* The music tracks (which is great) reset to the beginning when you load or die. If you are struggling on a section, you will hear that opening section over and over again. This is just straight up annoying, and can make you dislike the otherwise great music, by pure repetition.* The sounds effects that exist are great, but there need to be far more. General atmospheric sound like fire etc is limited, and the in between parts of levels can feel a bit static without them. More importantly, enemy attack sounds and spawning need to be much more audible and distinct (or exist).* General level creation jank. I get that this is probably a single developer, but level jank like walls floating slightly above the floor, misaligned textures or being able to exist level boundaries is simply painful when you **hide secrets behind these kind of things**. I have left levels more times than I can count, wandered around and never been 100% sure if I was meant to be there, or there was as secret I was missing. Is that patch of wierd wall a secret, or a mistake? Better spam E to make sure... which is fine for me, but I can see if driving many players up the wall.Overall, a great game with some serious love and dedication put into it. Just needs a tiny bit more polish to be truly excellent, but I would still recommend it regardless, if you know what you to expect.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like old school shooter and if you like Doom, then you will probably like this game as well. It is a fast paced boomer shooter, that is all about hell, demons, secrets and secret areas and unique upgrades, that allow you to experiment and tailor the game to your liking. For those people, that have tried similar games and had issues with getting lost, this game is pretty linear in most ways.I can definitely recommend the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing the first chapter during early access had me concerned, but things pick up considerably starting in the second. Dread Templar gets a lot of things right - for example, no hitscan enemies - and the weapons start to feel pretty great after you've discovered a few gold runes throughout the game's numerous secrets. I wouldn't say anything about Dread Templar necessarily *excels* compared to the elite of the new wave of retro shooters (DUSK being the most obvious comparison), but it marks a quality "B" entry in the genre for anyone looking for more. Normal mode can be a bit easy, the 5th chapter tails off somewhat in quality as the game stops introducing new enemy variants or map designs, and I never really came around on the trap launcher. But overall I had a pretty good time with Dread Templar and I'll definitely be keeping my eye on T19 going forward.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: The level design of the first episode did not wow me but the gameplay was so fun it left me deeply intrigued.By episode 2 I realized I was playing a game with potential to be great.By episode 3 I was convinced - this is the best boomer shooter I've played in... possibly ever?DREAD TEMPLAR takes the best elements of all my favorite shooters - Doom, Quake, Serious Sam, Blood, Duke Nuke Em, and somehow ups the ante. It succeeds in the areas where these other games fell short. The level design is sufficiently complex without ever feeling tedious. The secrets are rewarding and encourage the player to explore the levels in-depth without a penalty for time spent exploring.The handling is smooth and the action is intense, keeping you on the edge of your seat as you slaughter your way through hoards of enemies. There is a wide enough variety of enemies that the combat does not feel repetitive or forced.Sure, the story is lack-luster, but if I wanted story I wouldn't be playing a boomer shooter. This game is phenomenal, fans of the genre will be thoroughly pleased.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Templar

_childDocuments_.review: Another of these old school FPS games that gets a lot right, movement is slick, enemies are challenging and pretty much all the weapons have a use even in later levels thanks to how customisable they are.Some of the levels about halfway through the campaign start to get a bit too cramped (with movement as good as this you really want to actually have some room to jump about)the music is extremely good and you'll be headbanging during combat downtime, just wish it didn't restart the track every time you die.Also I didn't make these rules but it is an unwritten rule of FPS games that if you have an enemy that summons clones of itself, the clones have to die when you kill the original, that's just how it is..The game could also benefit from a bit of a redraft as a lot of the tool tips and I suppose dialogue are clearly written by someone for whom English is not their first language, it's by no means illegible there's just some bits that could do with tightening up

_childDocuments_.review: If you love indie darlings and boomer-inspired shooters, then Dread Templar is for you. If you love hard-rock inspired themes to rock out to as you send every blasted demon to hell, then Dread Templar is for you (the composer, John S. Weekley, has done a phenomenally good job here). If you love having the ability to use slo-mo, then Dread Templar is for you. If you love games that throw their narrative to the wayside, and instead let you turn off your brain and just have fun, then Dread Templar is for you.Now, the weapons themselves may not sound as punchy as they ought to, but they certainly kick ass. The variety of firearms is equally grand, and the ability to upgrade them, and even change how they appear and act (similar to Forgive me Father) is equally stunning. Note: Upgrading the Gauntlets with the 'Boss Killer' tag, is basically a cheat.Now, weapons are only ever as good as the enemies they go up against, and Dread Templar has a good selection of monsters, none of whom are hit-scanners, thank Christ. The enemies in the first two episodes probably evoke a closer feeling to Quake, as do the environments, though as you continue into episode 3, you will see some truly unique creations, along with some Dusk inspired levels in the final episode. That said, I feel the levels in episodes 3 and 4 are not as strong as they were in the opening two. I especially am not a fan of the invisible walls that are implemented to stop you going places you shouldn't.Moreover, as you progress, you will see upgraded reskins of  prior monsters, which basically become bullet sponges - probably the games way of keeping up with the player as you upgrade your health and weapons.On a further note, finding the secrets is incredibly rewarding and fun. The occasional puzzle solving needed uncover the 'super secrets', adds another layer of immersion and creativity.On a technical note, the game ran buttery smooth. I encountered one glitch (I needed to pick up a map, but I initially could not), though loading a previous save fixed this. I also noticed, enemies could occasionally shoot through walls - that was a tad annoying. That said, no known problems.Dread Templar is an easy sell. Think Quake married with Dusk, and you have the right idea. What's not to love?
